events.title: Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that took down Outlook and other 365 services
events.summary: A Microsoft outage on Thursday and Friday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365. The company apologized for the lengthy delay and said it did not suspect malicious activity. Microsoft said Saturday service had been restored across products. Microsoft issued an apology Friday for a wide-ranging outage that shut down Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products, as the company worked to restore service nearly 24 hours after connectivity problems began. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously," a Microsoft spokesperson said Friday. O n Saturday , Microsoft said it had addressed the underlying issue and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions. The connectivity disruption stemmed from "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade," Microsoft said in a Friday statement. The software giant added that the underlying cause of the outage had been addressed and that they were still working to restore services to some customers. Engineers scrambled to solve connectivity problems that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday. Email and calendar service Outlook, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, were largely down during the morning hours in the U.S. on Friday and throughout the Asian and European business days. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products were also hit. Users began to regain access to email and other services Friday morning. Nvidia live updates: CEO Jensen Huang resigns, Colette Kress named interim chief CoreWeave CEO Intrator tells CNBC he has canceled his planned share sale program Meta head of infrastructure will leave and be succeeded by former AWS cloud exec Amazon’s Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses In an update around 10:30 a.m. ET on Friday, Microsoft noted "encouraging recovery progress" and said that "service availability and email delivery performance [was] improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure" as Outlook and other Microsoft 365 tools began to come back online. In an earlier update Friday morning, Microsoft said that email queues were "approaching normal levels," but that intermittent issues were expected as recovery efforts continue. It had previously given updates by region, with Asia Pacific services among the first to start normalizing. Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online gradually stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages. Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said it would issue a full report once its assessment of the outage was complete. The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said. Microsoft shares traded largely flat Friday. Governments and businesses review impact Governments and businesses across the U.S., Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption. The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X. Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage. U.S. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told CNBC's "The Exchange" that he asked for a briefing on the outage. Gottheimer worked at Microsoft prior to serving in Congress. "Is there something that went on that's nefarious here, or is this just something else? These outages occur in a lot of the companies, but the size of it and the length of it and the timing of it," Gottheimer said. Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected.

events.title: Pacers hold off Knicks in NBA Cup thriller, Spurs rout Warriors
events.summary: The New York Knicks look unlikely to advance to the NBA Cup knockout rounds after falling to the Indiana Pacers. The shorthanded Indiana Pacers held off New York 106-104 on Friday to leave the Knicks’ bid for an NBA Cup repeat in tatters. The Knicks won last year’s in-season tournament in what proved a curtain-raiser to their run to a first NBA championship since 1973 . list 1 of 3 Salah breaks Egypt scoring record, Tunisia lose to Libya in AFCON qualifier list 2 of 3 Goalkeeper Owono handed 12-match ban after De Miguel death list 3 of 3 Mauricio Pochettino announced as new Manchester United manager But after coming up short in their bid to erase a 14-point third-quarter deficit, the Knicks fell to 0-2 in Cup play. They are not mathematically eliminated, but in three prior editions of the Cup, no team with two group-stage defeats has reached the knockout rounds. Pascal Siakam scored 19 points to lead a balanced Pacers attack. Aaron Nesmith scored 18 points, Kelly Oubre Jr added 16, and Ivica Zubac and Andrew Nembhard chipped in 12 apiece to lead Indiana, who were again without injured star Tyrese Haliburton. Jalen Brunson scored 33 points and handed out 11 assists for the Knicks, who tied it at 87-87 early in the fourth quarter, only for the Pacers to pull away again with a 15-2 scoring run. The Knicks made one last push, cutting the deficit to two, but Karl-Anthony Towns – who scored 23 points and pulled down 15 rebounds – missed a potential game-tying basket with nine-tenths of a second remaining. “Very proud of our team. We were pretty big underdogs coming into this game,” said Pacers coach Rick Carlisle, whose team outscored the Knicks 50-30 in the paint. “Second half, it got difficult. New York is a championship team. They know how to make comebacks,” Carlisle said. “Our guys stuck together and kept fighting together.” The Knicks are last in East Group B and will host the Cleveland Cavaliers and Miami Heat in their last two Cup group games. In Miami, Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo scored 37 points each to lead the Heat to a 133-121 victory over the Cavaliers. Adebayo added 14 rebounds, and Davion Mitchell chipped in 22 points and 17 assists to help the Heat improve to 2-0 in Cup play – top of the group – and 6-6 on the season. The San Antonio Spurs, who fell to the Knicks in last year’s NBA Cup final before losing to them in the NBA Finals, crushed the Golden State Warriors 123-85, their 11th straight victory pushing them to 2-0 in Cup play. Stephon Castle scored 32 points and Victor Wembanyama added 12 points and 12 rebounds for the Spurs, who opened the game on an 18-0 run and led by as many as 43 against a Warriors team playing without injured superstar Stephen Curry. LJ Cryer scored 20 points to lead the Warriors as none of the Golden State starters scored in double figures. Veteran Draymond Green finished with four points and was assessed a flagrant foul for a shove from behind that sent Wembanyama crashing out of bounds midway through the second quarter. In the last game of the night, the Los Angeles Clippers improved to 1-1 in Cup play – just 3-8 overall – with a battling 113-112 victory over the Oklahoma City Thunder. Darius Garland sealed the victory with a three-point play with less than a minute remaining, driving for a layup that tied it at 112-112, drawing a foul and converting the free throw. LA’s Brook Lopez scored 11 of his 26 points in the fourth quarter, and the Clippers withstood a 40-point performance from Oklahoma City’s two-time reigning MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander – who came up empty on two attempts in the waning seconds.

events.title: Singapore-based billionaire Leo KoGuan vows to halt Nvidia buys after Jensen Huang exit
events.summary: Leo KoGuan, who has a US$13.2 billion fortune, began investing in Nvidia in March. Leo KoGuan said he will not buy more Nvidia shares after Jensen Huang’s exit, calling Huang “the supreme creator” and saying, “No further investment without Jensen.” KoGuan said he has invested about US$1.3 billion in Nvidia, but his stake could not be independently verified. He began buying in March and has also backed Tesla, SpaceX and Alphabet. Huang was abruptly removed after reports of three affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China. KoGuan said investors should buy and hold super-intelligence companies for the long term. Billionaire investor and Nvidia shareholder Leo KoGuan expressed support for Jensen Huang on Nov 13 and said he will not increase his stake in the tech company with someone else at the helm. “No further investment without Jensen,” KoGuan said in a text message, saying he has invested around US$1.3 billion (S$1.7 billion) in Nvidia. In a series of posts on X, KoGuan called Huang “the supreme creator” and acknowledged that while the executive had made errors, “we must prioritise rewards” rather “than punishments”. The posts followed Huang’s abrupt ouster from Nvidia after reports of three affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China. That ended his decades-long reign over a company at the centre of the artificial intelligence buildout and, by extension, the global economy. Singapore-based KoGuan, who has a US$13.2 billion fortune, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, began investing in Nvidia in March. It was a notable move for an investor whose net worth for years had been tied up largely in one stock: Tesla. The size of KoGuan’s Nvidia stake could not be independently verified. Earlier this week, KoGuan said on X that he is also an investor in Space Exploration Technologies and Google, whose parent is Alphabet. He told Bloomberg that he plans on increasing his positions in those companies. Investors must buy and hold super-intelligence companies for the long term, he wrote on X. “I hope and plan to invest in Jensen Huang if he creates or buys” another super-intelligence company, he wrote on Nov 13. “I hope he will offer me the opportunity to invest in his future company.” Bloomberg

events.title: UN says 25 seafarers killed in, around Hormuz since US-Israel war on Iran
events.summary: ‘Situation cannot become new normal’, says UN’s Khaled Khiari, as Iran reports three more vessels hitting mines. At least 25 seafarers have been killed in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the US-Israeli war on Iran broke out in February, according to the United Nations. Khaled Khiari, assistant secretary-general for the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific, gave the figures , which cover the period up to November 11, during a UN Security Council briefing on Friday. list 1 of 3 Why is Trump saying ‘no deal necessary’ with Iran as he sidelines JD Vance? list 2 of 3 Iran threatens unlimited response over Strait of Hormuz after US attack list 3 of 3 The Gulf must build security that can outlast this war “This situation cannot be allowed to become the new normal,” said Khiari, urging the “full restoration of maritime navigation in the region”. He pointed out that security incidents in and around Hormuz have been rising, with October recording the highest tally since the start of the conflict. The UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO) tracked 136 security incidents involving vessels in Hormuz and the wider Middle East between March 1 and November 11. It said 35 of those incidents came in October and 10 in November. “Every day brings new reports of maritime incidents,” said Khiari. “These incidents are unacceptable,” he added. “Civilian vessels and commercial shipping must not become targets.” His remarks come as Iranian authorities on Saturday reported that three oil tankers had hit mines while travelling through “unauthorised” or “restricted” areas of Hormuz, catching fire. Tehran has warned vessels that they must receive Iranian approval to cross the waterway during the conflict, and has repeatedly attacked ships accused of violating its protocol. “Any offending tanker that travels in the restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz will be set on fire by hitting naval mines,” Iran’s navy warned in a statement carried by the country’s IRIB broadcaster. Iranian officials have insisted the strait will not be open until the US meets its demands , which include an end to the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, the lifting of economic sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts, and an explicit announcement of an end to the war. The US military claims it has cleared the strait’s main routes of mines and that the waterway is open for commercial shipping. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is approximately 65 percent below pre-war levels, according to the latest report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). Khiari, in his remarks to the UN Security Council, said “the present maritime arrangements in the Middle East remain costly, unpredictable, and unsafe”. “Disruptions to maritime navigation continue to have significant global economic consequences, driving up energy, transport and insurance costs, fuelling inflation and threatening food security amid severely constrained fertiliser shipments.”

events.title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop, but chaos will continue after 10,000 flights were delayed and 6,600 canceled
events.summary: Passengers at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport saw flight-information boards full of cancellations and delays during the FAA's ground stop on Friday. Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu via Getty Images The FAA lifted its national ground stop Friday around 8:30 p.m. Eastern time. It cited "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety" when it closed airspace in the afternoon. Now, airlines will have to get their operations back in order, which will take days. The Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop, which halted flights nationwide, was lifted Friday night after stranding travelers in airports and canceling more than 6,600 flights. Even with airspace reopened, the hourslong closure on Friday promises to snarl air travel for days as airlines scramble to get airplanes and crew back in place — and thousands of delayed or canceled passengers back on their way. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said late Friday that the "public was never in danger" during the airspace closure. He said "all your loved ones are safe," and that the federal government was working to resolve the issue. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a press conference that the FAA system experienced "inconsistency" in its data systems that communicate with airplanes. Because of that, a ground stop was called around 3 p.m. He said there had been 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the stop, all of which landed safely using alternative systems. Duffy and Mullin said the nation's air-traffic control system was outdated and blamed Friday's issue on its age. They called for Congress to cough up $50 billion for its modernization — up from the $30 billion previously pitched in September. Read more Business Insider coverage of the nationwide ground stop : Nearly 5,000 flights were canceled across the US after an FAA ground stop. Here's what to do if your trip was affected . Trump's transportation chief demands $50 billion to prevent another huge FAA fiasco FAA SMART AI system vendor, Microsoft say ground stop wasn't their fault Photos show trouble at airports nationwide as FAA grounds all flights 'I called my mom and cried': Passengers describe chaos at JFK during nationwide ground stop Two Canadian airports are bracing for travel chaos to ripple north College football games could be derailed by the FAA ground stop "I have already replaced some of those switches with President Trump, and our new IP switches did not go down," Duffy said. "It's the old hardware that went down." The IP switches are new voice communication systems designed to replace the decades-old analog voice switches that much of the national airspace system still relies on. Duffy and Mullin also said the fault wasn't related to AI or cybersecurity. Mullin said he'd seen "zero evidence" that the issue was a cyberattack or a problem with artificial intelligence, which he dubbed "SI," for the Trump Administration's preferred term, "superintelligence ." Duffy said they were still "working on the details" of exactly what happened — what caused it and how it could be prevented in the future. He said he couldn't guarantee it wouldn't happen again when asked if the traveling public should feel safe when flying in US airspace. That flying public was stranded in airports around the country — checking airport monitors only to see their flights delayed or canceled. Because the events of the day weren't the airlines' fault, passengers would have little recourse for meals or hotels . A timeline of events during the FAA's ground stop After the ground stop was issued around 3 pm Eastern time, Duffy said just after 4:15 pm that the nationwide flight traffic halt came "following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." People were quick to question whether SMART, a new FAA AI tool to help air traffic control that started deploying this week, was involved. ASI, the company that makes the SMART system for the FAA, said that Friday's issues weren't "based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC." Duffy also said SMART was not at fault. Mullin said earlier Friday, when asked if the AI system might be related to the outage : "That's what we're looking at." He also said that it had "no indication" the ground stop was related to Microsoft, which had faced massive issues across its services this week. Meanwhile, the FAA had said the ground stop was due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." More than 6,600 flights had been canceled within the US, or in or out of the country, as of 9:45 p.m. Eastern time, according to data from FlightAware. Chicago O'Hare topped the list with 395 cancellations, while Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson — the world's busiest airport — also saw over 350 flights canceled, as of that time. More than 200 flights were canceled at major airports in New York, Boston, Texas, and Denver. Homeland Security said FAA ground stop wasn't a safety issue Mullin said the ground stop wasn't a safety issue. He called it a communications-related issue. He said he didn't want people to assume this is a safety threat to the American people or "another 9/11." Still, many planes had to divert or turn around. Among the flights affected was Delta Air Lines Flight 958, which was traveling from Los Angeles to New York's JFK. Almost four hours into its journey, at 4:11 p.m., the Boeing 767 turned around and diverted to Cincinnati. Another Delta flight, from Atlanta to JFK, changed course over the Eastern Seaboard and diverted to Baltimore. And an LA-bound flight from Puebla, Mexico, operated by the Mexican budget airline Volaris, diverted to Tijuana — barely south of the US border. Delta and Volaris did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Passengers wait at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Friday after the FAA's massive nationwide ground stop. Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP via Getty Images Pilots in the air have a system for these issues Mark Stephens, a retired Delta Air Lines pilot, told Business Insider that pilots have a system for these situations to maintain safe distances from other aircraft and land within their limits. Planes en route during a ground stop can still land; they "continue via the flight plan, and then start using backup methods." He said there are digital tools that can connect them with air-traffic control and their airline's dispatch to obtain routing or other information. Stephens said that unless someone tells the pilot to divert, the plan is "stay the course and do what you're trained: aviation, navigate, communicate." The last time a nationwide ground stop occurred was in January 2023, and it lasted only about 90 minutes. Before that, it was in 2001 on 9/11. Stephens said this could create a snowball effect into the weekend: "Long delays will turn into a crew rest nightmare," he said. events.title: The nationwide ground stop disrupted my flight to a Vegas conference, but I hitched a ride and got there in 6 hours
events.summary: Vanessa Santos in the back of the car, driving from Phoenix to Las Vegas. Courtesy of Vanessa Santos Vanessa Santos was set to fly from Phoenix to Las Vegas for a business conference. She got caught up in the nationwide ground stop and thought she'd miss the event. Santos got off the plane and was lucky enough to hop a ride, driving six hours to her destination. This story is based on an interview with Vanessa Santos , 43, a business consultant for female founders from Phoenix . It has been edited for length and clarity. I got a message on the app that my 1:45 p.m. Southwest Airlines flight from Phoenix was slightly delayed, giving me a chance to dash to Starbucks. The delay was longer than expected. Then, as we finally boarded the plane, I overheard the gate agent telling another employee something about a ground stop . We were told to deplane A man sitting across from me looked alarmed. "This hasn't happened since 9/11," he said. We sat at the gate for 45 minutes, then were told to deplane. The announcer said the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had grounded all US flights. Santos speaking at a previous conference. Courtesy of Vanessa Santos Nobody was complaining, and the general attitude was that there was nothing we could do about it. However, over time, people began to panic, asking whether they should rebook. They were trying to open the app, but it wasn't working. Next, someone said it was the result of a cyberattack . The energy changed, and I decided I didn't want to stay there anymore. I was due to speak at my friend Alexis's business conference the next morning, and I couldn't think of anything worse than letting her down. It had been months in the making, and she was relying on me. No rental cars were available Then I remembered another friend, Marisol, in the city who'd told me she was driving to Vegas. I texted her on the off-chance she hadn't set off. If she had, I would have rented a car. Fortunately, she was still at home. She said she had room in her Kia SUV for one more person: me. I was so relieved, especially after I discovered that no rental cars were available. And so began my impromptu road trip . Marisol's husband, Francisco, drove with her up front. Marisol's friend, Jess, and I sat in the back. On their way to Vegas: Francisco and Marisol Isuala (front) and Santos and Jessica Hernandez. Courtesy of Vanessa Santos I called myself a passenger princess because I felt so spoiled. We stopped at Buc-ee's to pick up snacks and In-N-Out for meat patties. We sang along to a '90s hip-hop playlist — millennial throwbacks —and had great chats. I would never have experienced that on the plane. It took six hours The journey was a cool adventure from start to finish. It rained hard, so we had to pull over several times. It didn't matter. I was getting to Las Vegas against the odds. All in all, it took seven hours, including breaks, to drive 300 miles to our destination. I was excited to be moderating my panel after all. It was Friday the 13th , and unlucky for other travelers stranded at the airport. I felt bad for them. For me, however, it was a pretty awesome day. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.summary: Netherlands’ 7-0 annihilation of Greece means the Germans will likely need to win on Monday to reach the quarterfinals. Tijjani Reijnders netted a first-half hat-trick as the ⁠Netherlands thrashed Greece 7-0 in the ⁠Nations League on Friday, while Germany earned a 3-1 victory away to Serbia in the other Group A2 game. The Dutch were 5-0 up at the break, with Crysencio Summerville putting the hosts ahead in the sixth minute before Reijnders ran ⁠riot and Jurrien Timber notched their fifth before half-time. Timber scored again just before the hour mark, with Donyell Malen netting the final goal. list 1 of 3 Mauricio Pochettino announced as new Manchester United manager list 2 of 3 Inside the circle: Senegal’s wrestlers turn tradition to Youth Olympic gold list 3 of 3 Goalkeeper Owono handed 12-match ban after De Miguel death Germany took a third-minute lead through an own goal, and Florian Wirtz added a second 11 minutes later. Brajan Gruda scored on his debut five minutes after the ⁠break before Srdan Babic pulled one back for Serbia, who finished the game with nine men. The Netherlands are top of the standings on 11 points, and Germany moved level on eight points with Greece to leave the three sides battling it out for two quarterfinal places on Monday. Germany will host the Netherlands in Berlin while Greece host a Serbian side that has lost all five fixtures. Greece and the Netherlands both came into the game unbeaten, but ‌the Dutch destroyed the visitors in a devastating display of attacking prowess. The opening goal came after Greece lost possession close to their own area, before a poorly controlled ball by defender Konstantinos Mavropanos fell to Summerville and he slipped his shot past the keeper. Joey Veerman threaded a pass through to Reijnders, whose strike found the roof of the net from the edge of the six-yard area in the 12th minute, and six minutes later he finished off Malen’s pass across goal. Reijnders completed his hat-trick with a simple tap-in after Denzel Dumfries nodded the ball down in the six-yard box, and Timber netted from close range with Malen providing another assist. Timber’s second came after Dumfries’ cross was pushed ⁠away by the keeper, and Malen got his well-deserved goal following some neat skill and a lay-off from ⁠Dumfries. Jurgen Klopp had a difficult start to life as Germany’s manager , winning just one of his opening four games, also against Serbia. Klopp had used his first international window to experiment with a 44-man roster split into two separate squads, but his chosen 11 put in a dominant display under heavy rain in Belgrade, especially in the ⁠opening half. Germany went in front after a Kai Havertz header went in off Babic, and when Havertz had a shot parried away by keeper Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, Wirtz was there to convert the rebound. Klopp’s side missed chances to ⁠finish off the game in the first half but looked well in control after Gruda’s ⁠solo goal. Gruda collected Joshua Kimmich’s pass inside his own half, drove forward largely unopposed and drilled a low shot into the far corner from outside the area. Babic’s goal gave Serbia hope, while Germany continued to attack. Kimmich had a goal ruled out for offside, and Derry Scherhant hit the post before Vanja Dragojevic’s red card in the 74th minute. Serbia had ‌another substitute, Andrija Zivkovic, sent off late on. In Group B1, Switzerland earned promotion to League A thanks to a 0-0 draw in Slovenia, while Scotland earned a 2-1 win over North Macedonia thanks to a John McGinn double. Scotland captain Andy Robertson made a record-equalling 102nd ‌appearance, ‌drawing level with Kenny Dalglish. Slovakia were held to a 2-2 draw at home by the Faroe Islands in Group C3, but the point was enough for the hosts to clinch promotion. Iceland romped to a 5-0 win in Bulgaria to remain top of Group C4, with Andri Gudjohnsen providing a hat-trick.

events.title: What do Christmas market traders say about rising prices?
events.summary: Nils Borstel said his business was making less money despite more than doubling the price of a sausage Mention Christmas markets these days and the conversation often turns to rising prices – from £8 bratwursts, £11 Yorkshire pudding wraps and even £5 for a few marshmallow sticks. But what do the people behind the stalls think? Are they benefiting from the hikes or are their own profits being squeezed? Traders at Manchester's Christmas markets told the BBC they were feeling the pressure of increasing bills for staff, ingredients and energy, with some saying they were making less money despite charging more. One trader said it costs at least £4,000 a day to run each her four stalls, while another has cut prices to keep customers coming back. Nils Borstel, 25, helps run Bratwurst King, a family business which has operated at the markets since 1999. He said a sausage that previously cost £3.50 now sold for £8, with much of the increase taking place over the past five or six years. "But we don't earn more money," he said. Manchester Christmas market traders explain prices Borstel, whose family operates four stalls across the city centre, said rising costs for meat, electricity, staffing and accommodation had forced the business to increase prices. About 15 workers travel from Germany to help run the stalls, alongside staff recruited in the UK. He said that despite busy crowds and dry weather during the opening weekend, people appeared more cautious about spending than in previous years. For example, some customers were now buying one portion of food to share, rather than purchasing one each, he said. Borstel said he had seen a change in spending habits since 2019, when customers were more willing to buy food and drinks without worrying about the cost. He acknowledged that prices were high and did not want to increase them, but said the they were necessary to cover expenses. Poppy (left) and Neve questioned whether the portions they bought justified the prices Among those questioning the costs were Neve and Poppy, both 18. Neve, a student, said she had spent about £15 on one dish, while Poppy, who is taking a gap year, paid £11 for a Yorkshire pudding wrap. "I think it was pricey for what it was," Neve said. Poppy also felt she had not received much food for the money, although said it was tasty. Both said they enjoyed going into the city and looking around the markets, while Neve sympathised with traders, saying she thought the cost of renting space could force businesses to raise prices. Charlotte Whittle, director of CT Catering, has been trading at the markets for 10 years and now operates four stalls. She said each stall cost at least £1,000 a day to run, bringing her total daily operating costs to at least £4,000. Whittle, who employs a range of staff, said customers often underestimated the work and expense involved. Before the markets opened, her business spent two weeks preparing its stalls, with another two weeks needed to dismantle them after Christmas. CT Catering director Charlotte Whittle says her business employs 57 people across four Manchester market sites She said the costs included staff wages, accommodation, deliveries, storage, packaging and card payment fees. Parking three vans in Manchester city centre could cost £100 a day alone, she said, with the vehicles needed to replenish stock throughout busy trading periods. "They think that you're just selling cookies," she said. Whittle, who began her business selling homemade cakes at street food markets, said the cost of stock and packaging had increased significantly over the years. Although she had increased some prices, she said she had chosen to absorb part of those costs rather than risk putting customers off. "We've had to take a massive cut on profits," she said. She also argued that the standard of street food had improved and customers were receiving food comparable in quality to that served in restaurants. But not every trader has responded to rising costs by putting up prices. Clark Murphy, whose family has traded at the markets for 22 years, runs Mr Crimble Crumble, which sells fruit crumbles from two stalls. He said the business had kept most prices unchanged for three years and had reduced the cost of its largest portion by £2. Clark Murphy (left), pictured with his nephew Davis, said his business had reduced the price of its largest crumble Murphy said cooking oil and biodegradable packaging had become more expensive, but the business wanted to retain customers who returned each Christmas. "We haven't increased our prices for three years now," he said. A notice at one food stall offered customers £1 off each drink or dish if they paid in cash He said the business remained profitable, although margins were under pressure and card payments added to operating costs. At another food stall, a notice offered customers £1 off each drink or dish when paying cash. "Card fees are crazy – help us keep it simple," it said.

events.title: Analysis: Companies love a ‘rockstar’ CEO. Until they depend on one
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s resignation has put Nvidia’s succession planning and its dependence on its founder under scrutiny. Analysts and industry experts say Huang’s value extended beyond technology to supplier relationships, customers and his influence across the AI industry. Nvidia’s transition raises a broader governance question for boards: Can a company remain resilient when one leader becomes central to its strategy and identity? When Jensen Huang quit, it struck me how quickly the conversation shifted from his departure to whether Nvidia could manage without him. It wasn't about whether the company had the technology, customers or talent to keep growing, but whether anyone else could do what Huang had been doing for the business. That made me wonder: did investors believe in Nvidia, or just Huang? The company is hardly short of capable people. Interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been with Nvidia since 2013. Nvidia has experienced engineers, established customer relationships and a leading position in the artificial intelligence chip market. But, listening to guests on CNBC this week, I noticed how much of their concern was about the influence Huang had built outside Nvidia. On Friday, just a day after Huang quit, Dylan Patel of SemiAnalysis told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" how Huang would persuade executives at smaller companies that make critical components to commit capacity to Nvidia. This helped it secure "the majority of supply chain capacity," he said. Without Huang, competitors could try to persuade those suppliers to allocate more capacity to them, Patel argued. And so the big question is, how much of Nvidia's advantage comes from its technology and how much comes from the relationships Huang built? There are obvious benefits to elevating CEOs to be rockstars . They can attract investors, open doors and give a company a new identity. A charismatic leader attracts attention, reassures investors and makes a company's strategy easier to sell. Huang was particularly good at this. He helped shape the conversation about where AI was heading and made Nvidia central to it. Donning his trademark leather jacket, Huang took to stages around the world , courting world leaders to lay out his vision and explain why Nvidia would be at its center. Before Huang resigned, Eric Ross told "Squawk Box Asia" that Huang "is the company." That may sound like an endorsement, but it also helps explain why his departure has raised so many questions. Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon made an interesting distinction on the same program, also before Huang's departure. Nvidia had capable executives who could keep the business running, he said. What was harder to replace was Huang's vision. "They need a visionary like that," he said. But for a company whose valuation reflects not just what it sells but expectations of what AI could become, replacing that vision may prove harder than replacing the CEO. Duncan Clark pointed to another part of Huang's job. He had become a bridge between Silicon Valley, Asia and Washington, and one of the most prominent voices for the wider AI industry. "I don't think you can replace him with one individual," Clark said on "Access Middle East" on Friday. Replacing him with multiple people is "going to take time, and it won't be the same," he added. That distinction may be important. Nvidia's board has begun a search for a permanent CEO and said it will consider both internal and external candidates. But whoever takes the job may not personally assume every role Huang had come to play around the company. Some of his responsibilities and relationships could end up being spread across Nvidia's broader leadership team. For now, the board is emphasizing continuity. New chair Harvey Jones said Kress is backed by an experienced leadership team and that Nvidia expected its operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption. Kress, meanwhile, pointed to Nvidia's people and leadership team as strengths as the company moves forward. Other boards will be watching, particularly those that have allowed their CEOs to become the face of everything their companies do. When a charismatic leader is the only person outsiders hear from, it becomes harder to convince them that anyone else can take over. There is also the question of accountability. Clark described Nvidia's situation as a governance failure. And my colleague, "Squawk Box Europe" anchor Steve Sedgwick , raised a similar point on Friday about how corporate America has approached ESG. Much of the political debate has focused on its environmental component, Steve said. President Donald Trump has repeatedly attacked environmental and climate policies using phrases such as "green scam." But Steve questioned whether the governance element has been overlooked, particularly at some of America's biggest technology companies.

events.title: UK-EU breakthrough will allow airport-style checks at Eurotunnel to avoid border ‘chaos’
events.summary: Eurotunnel owner Getlink wants to replicate ‘airport experience’ at Folkestone and Calais, without making people get out of cars Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be introduced at Eurotunnel in an attempt to prevent “short-term and long-term chaos” in Folkestone and Calais . In a breakthrough for travellers, the European Commission has agreed to a new system in which an “eagle eye” camera system, already used in Rome and Paris airports to supervise fingerprinting and facial imaging, will be used at the border between the UK and France. Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the Eurotunnel owner, said it had tried to replicate the “airport experience” but wanted to go much further. Instead of getting out of the car and getting biometrics taken at a terminal building, holidaymakers and business travellers will now be greeted with special drive-through terminals in Folkestone and Calais. Both sides are now equipped with 120 kiosks under the case of an eagle-eye camera that will be monitored by police, similar to e-gates at airports where police are not physically present at each gate. In the coming weeks, Leriche will meet UK and French authorities presenting a 40-page proposal to allow Eurotunnel to become a “laboratory” for an “intelligent border” using emerging tech and lessons learned from the US and Singapore. The entry and exit system (EES) requires all third-country citizens including British passport holders to submit fingerprints and facial images as they enter and exit the Schengen area, but has been delayed for years. EES was supposed to be active across the EU by 9 September, but nine of the 27 EU member states, including France , have yet to be deploy it fully because of continued technical issues. It has always been a logistical nightmare for Eurotunnel and a potential cause of miles-long tailbacks at the approach to the terminal. Originally, Getlink had planned to use a tablet to hand to the passengers in their cars to allow them to self-fingerprint and capture a facial image. It also looked at a system involving passengers parking up and going into the terminal to get fingerprinting. But both models would have required the physical presence of police officers for first-time fingerprinting. Leriche said: “We told the authorities: it is going to be a mess. Many people are going to the wrong place and you can’t have police jumping from one place to the next to solve the issues. It would also means customers would have a bad experience, particularly at peak time. “This is not something people in airports experience, but nobody approached this before, thinking we could have an airport experience at the border here. But we said: why not?” He said that after “many, many discussions” with the European Commission and the French authorities, finally they were “authorised” to trial “eagle-eye cameras” at each kiosk. “The French authorities are also on board because for them it is more efficient, too, so we are all aligned on the trial,” he said. The trial will last two years, but Eurotunnel hopes the experiment will become permanent. Each car will be able to pull up to an individual kiosk, with two stands per vehicle to read passports and take fingerprints and facial images. “It will prevent the chaos in the long term and the short term and if the experiment works, as hopefully it will, then it will become permanent,” said Leriche. He said the company had been inspired by visits to the US/Mexico border controls, where drivers and passengers remain in their cars. The requirement of having a police officer present each time a first-time passenger, or “primo” as they are known, submits their fingerprints was designed as a safeguard against subterfuge. Criminals, for example, could use a fellow passenger for example with a “clean skin” fingerprint. Leriche said he had no idea when the system will be introduced by France. “It has been delayed and delayed and delayed, but our kiosks are there, they are can function but the connection with the French system is still not working. It is a question was are asking all the time.” This week it emerged that the EU had filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in the implementation of EES.

events.title: The ANC’s implosion was decades in the making
events.summary: Zuma squandered Mbeki’s gains, while Ramaphosa’s dithering turned the ANC’s promised renewal into a fight for survival. South African statesman, former Premier of the Western Cape, ANC National Executive Committee member and two-term Ambassador to the United States. When the expected implosion of the African National Congress (ANC) came in South Africa’s 2026 local government elections, it was still surprisingly dramatic. The ANC remained the largest political party, but its share of the popular vote declined to 32.5 percent, essentially leaving it a rural party where its governance power is not entirely dependent on coalition partners. It is now a Black African party without minority voters. Significant elements of the Black middle class and sections of the Black African rural and working classes showed disaffection through defection and abstention. This leaves an ANC dependent on other parties for coalitions in the urban metros and cities, while facing a confident and emboldened white community, quite surprised at how easily Black power could be diluted so soon after apartheid. But the seeds of this implosion were sown over three nine-year leadership phases. The first transition in this evolution was after the nine developing years under President Thabo Mbeki, which had their weaknesses – like the HIV/AIDS epidemic – but bequeathed to his successors significant advantages: gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 5.4 percent, unemployment at 25 percent and significant savings for infrastructure expansion. Significantly, the ANC secured an electoral share of 65.7 percent in the 2006 local elections, with the greatest ever proportion of minority votes. These nine years sowed the seeds of a so-called left-wing impatience with the rate of redistribution of the growth advantages. These advantages were squandered during President Jacob Zuma’s nine devastating years in both economic and electoral terms. The devastation, disguised as “radical economic transformation”, was in fact state capture. The Madlanga Commission demonstrates the perversion of South Africa’s criminal justice system. The Nugent Commission exposed larceny in the revenue services. The Zondo Commission dramatised how public enterprises were cash cows for the corrupt at the expense of services like water, energy and roads, while only the most loyally incompetent were embedded in the bureaucracy. The economic cost of state capture has been estimated at up to 500 billion rand ($30bn). The state capture scandal brought President Cyril Ramaphosa centre stage on a wave of “Ramaphoria”, with many willing him to be the midwife of renewal. His mandate was unprecedented, and his popularity even endured the setbacks of the COVID-19 lockdown. However, the nine devastating years inexorably gaveway to the nine dithering years, while the moniker of midwife yielded to the uncomfortable idea that Ramaphosa’s generation may well be the undertakers of the ANC. Nine dithering years (2018–present) “Dithering” is shorthand for hesitation, indecision and uncertainty. Even amid moral clarity, there is no moral courage to decide or act. Confusing priorities create a trade-off between tenuously maintaining the ANC base with a modicum of unity and seeking the approval and support of the nation. If Zuma operated by crimes of commission, Ramaphosa operated by omission – what he could not do. For one, Zuma should have been in prison, but Ramaphosa’s transfer (rather than dismissal) of Zuma’s intelligence boss to the position of commissioner of Correctional Services resulted in Zuma being freed on medical grounds. Even when Zuma was recommitted to prison by the courts, Ramaphosa’s general remission order meant he spent only a further two hours of his 15-month sentence incarcerated. Such dithering allowed Zuma’s uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) to grab nearly 15 percent of the national vote in 2024 and almost 10 percent in 2026. Secondly, the ANC carried into the elections the skeletons of malfeasance – with those complicit either tolerated or elevated – involving the corruption of state enterprises, COVID fraud, misappropriating state tenders and mismanaging shadowy intelligence funds. In the cliches of the day, “innocent until proven guilty” always outweighed “step aside” in the institutionalisation of impunity! Thirdly, before the elections of 2026, the ANC understood the parlous state of its local governance and popular sentiment about basic services. Yet it did not act with the necessary urgency. Rather than rescue ANC governance and salvage people’s trust, it chose to pass a death sentence on the ANC’s election campaign: the president applauded Democratic Alliance (DA) governance, while the chairperson proclaimed that ANC councillors could sing but not govern. On Ramaphosa’s watch, these acts of omission were accompanied by devastating economic data, with youth unemployment at 63 percent.

events.title: Southeast Asian leaders to meet as Trump visit highlights trade disruption
events.summary: ASEAN summit comes as US president embarks on Asia trip that will see him meet China’s Xi. Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Southeast Asian leaders are preparing to hold their flagship annual summit as US President Donald Trump embarks on an Asia Pacific trip that will focus attention on his upending of trade and traditional alliances. Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) are gathering in Manila, the Philippines, for a series of multilateral and bilateral meetings running from Sunday until Tuesday. list 1 of 4 Trump moots toppling Cuba authorities before leaving office list 2 of 4 Finland detects strike on Russian warship as Zelenskyy meets US envoys list 3 of 4 Chris Van Hollen launches bid to lead Democrats in US Senate list 4 of 4 Spanish court suspends far-right group over alleged hate crimes Trump is scheduled to meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr during a brief stop in Manila on Tuesday, before heading to the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, where he will have his fourth face-to-face meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in just over a year. It will also be the first time that Trump, Xi and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin will meet for trilateral talks, the White House has confirmed . Trump’s visit to Southeast Asia – his second since his return to the White House after his attendance at the 2025 ASEAN summit in Malaysia – comes after his administration announced new tariffs on dozens of trade partners, including most of the region’s economies, in July. Trump’s administration announced the duties of between 10 and 12.5 percent after the US Supreme Court struck down his steeper “reciprocal” tariffs in February. The Office of the US Trade Representative said it was imposing the tariffs on 60 trade partners over their alleged failure to clamp down on forced labour. The Trump administration is also conducting trade probes over alleged national security and “excess” manufacturing concerns that could result in yet more tariffs for Southeast Asian trade partners. Southeast Asia has weathered Trump’s trade salvoes relatively unscathed until now, in part as a result of the diversion of billions of dollars of Chinese trade through the region. US imports from ASEAN rose more than 29 percent to $453.6bn in 2025, expanding the trade deficit between the sides to $327.4bn, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative. Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, said, however, that Southeast Asian countries cannot guarantee that their luck will continue. “ASEAN has had mixed success in navigating US tariffs. Overall exports are up. But this is primarily driven by shipments of electronics which are largely exempt from tariffs,” Elms told Al Jazeera. “These shipments are also strongly tied to the AI buildout. If that falters, ASEAN will feel it,” she said. While ASEAN leaders have provided few details about the summit agenda, trade is likely to be among the main topics of discussion. For a bloc that often faces accusations of being a talking shop, one of the most anticipated tangible outcomes is the signing of the Digital Economy Framework Agreement, a pact aimed at easing cross-border data transfers and electronic payments. Initiated in 2023, the framework has been billed as a step towards building an ASEAN digital economy worth $2 trillion by 2030. Jayant Menon, a senior fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, said Southeast Asian leaders will be concerned about “what comes next” from Trump on trade. “So far, the recent tariffs appear to have had a limited impact on competitiveness of ASEAN exports. But this may change in the future, with more sectoral tariffs, in particular, or other measures such as export controls,” Menon told Al Jazeera. “Trump still retains significant autonomous authority over trade policy despite losing control of both houses, and could double down rather than back off,” Menon said, referring to the Republicans’ crushing defeat in the US midterm elections on November 3. Phar Kim Beng, a professor of ASEAN studies at the International Islamic University of Malaysia, said Southeast Asian leaders are likely to reiterate calls for increased trade within the region, a goal that has lagged aspirations despite decades of trade liberalisation in the bloc. “Whether measured from 1970 or 2025, intraregional trade remains paltry at 23 percent. In contrast, the European Union can cross intraregional trade of 67 percent easily,” Phar told Al Jazeera. Phar said he does not expect ASEAN to announce any significant measures to spur trade within the bloc, but its leaders will continue to “mouth the mantra of better and bigger” trade volumes. “Regardless of the tariffs intended by President Donald Trump, ASEAN will continue to muddle through by speaking of the importance of trade and more trade,” he said.

events.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after day-long global outage
events.summary: Products such as Microsoft Teams and Outlook have been out of service for much of Friday Microsoft has said its services have been fully restored after a worldwide outage affected several of its tools, causing disruption. The tech firm said early on Saturday morning that efforts to address the underlying problem had been completed and customers using Outlook, Teams and Copilot should no longer be affected. The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide. Microsoft apologised for the technical issue, which it said was introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and was not caused by a cyber-attack or an artificial intelligence agent. Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers. Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday. By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America. Services were beginning to recover by Friday afternoon UK time, nearly 24 hours after the issues first began to emerge. Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost? Published 13 hours ago Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world Published 14 hours ago In the UK, some parts of the NHS were affected , as were some schools and police forces. UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls and that there had been no disruption to the transport network. In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails. In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook. Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday. In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook. The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals. Pete says his business has been brought to a standstill Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business had been effectively brought to a "standstill". His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" had been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations". Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she had been due to complete her first house purchase after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that. "The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies," she said. "We're not the only one completing today - there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible." Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally. It launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, but by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world. By 13:32, the tech giant said there had been "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region. Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously." A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review. Experts said that while workers may have been happy to not have email access for a working day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services. "The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure. Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.

events.title: Ukraine is running out of options, and Russia knows it
events.summary: As Russian strikes push Kyiv towards compromise, Western governments are beginning to reconsider the security demands Moscow has made for years. Leonid Ragozin is a freelance journalist based in Riga. The trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States that took place in Abu Dhabi this week may not lead to a rapid breakthrough, but they clearly outline the trajectory of a conflict that might, after all, be nearing its end. If anything illustrates the political and emotional rift the two sides are yet to bridge, it is President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s remarks in Copenhagen this week , in which he lamented that Russian leader Vladimir Putin was still alive. Ukraine’s harsh reality, however, is pushing him towards an unsavoury compromise with his arch-enemy. Kyiv was compelled to enter the talks at the most disadvantageous moment, when it has few means to counter devastating Russian air strikes that damage its key industries and cripple essential infrastructure in major cities. One of Ukraine’s top negotiators, David Arakhamia, who leads Zelenskyy’s parliamentary faction, described the negotiations as among the most difficult he had participated in since 2022. He said the Russians had arrived with very strict instructions and that it had been difficult to soften the tone of the discussions. His assessment confirms that Russia sees itself as well equipped to negotiate from a position of force. Moscow, meanwhile, expressed optimism about the outcome. Putin’s aide, Vladimir Medinsky, said the talks had brought the two countries closer to peace. Even Arakhamia said there was momentum towards reaching a solution before the end of the year. That optimism, it needs to be noted, comes without any signs of Russia changing its position on the contours of the agreement. Just as it has for years, the Kremlin insists on a genuinely neutral, demilitarised Ukraine which honours the rights of its Russian-speaking population. If all this comes as a nasty surprise to many in the West, that’s because for most of this year, Western politicians and the mainstream media kept insisting that the tide of war was turning and that Ukraine was getting the upper hand. Their optimism was fuelled by Ukrainian long-range strikes targeting Russian oil refineries as well as by the snail’s pace of Russian advances on the battlefield. As late as September, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said that “in all but name, Russia has already lost the war”. Around the same time, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Russia was not doing well in Ukraine. When NATO leaders convened for the Ankara summit in July, it seemed that even US President Donald Trump had bought into the idea that Ukraine had the battlefield advantage. But Russia responded to Ukraine’s surge, backed up by European funds and US intelligence-sharing, with round-the-clock air strikes that are bringing Ukraine close to its pain barrier. Moscow’s message was cruel: any damage Ukraine and the West might inflict on Russia would be met with epic devastation in Ukraine, from which it would take decades to recover. The coming winter spells nationwide humanitarian disaster. Russian strikes on energy infrastructure have disrupted electricity and central heating supplies. Millions of Ukrainians, particularly in major cities, live in apartment blocks dependent on central heating, without which their homes can become virtually unliveable. Generators can provide temporary power, but their use is making the cost of war enormous for Ukraine and Western taxpayers who fund its war effort. It is these dire circumstances, rather than pressure from Trump’s administration, that have forced Ukraine to enter the talks. Zelenskyy would have waited at least until the spring had he not felt so pressed. Ukraine’s surge has failed to shift Moscow’s peace conditions one inch. Meanwhile, the Western perception of this war’s realities has undergone a considerable transformation. There are two major signs of the shifting landscape which directly affect the agenda of the Abu Dhabi negotiations. For the first time since the start of the war, a larger part of the Western establishment appears to be ready to discuss Europe’s post-war security architecture. The subject was first broached by US negotiator Jared Kushner, causing outrage in the warmongering camp. But Medinsky said after the Abu Dhabi talks that it was the central issue on the agenda. This topic harks back to the agenda which Moscow brought to the table in December 2021, a few months before the all-out invasion. It did so after the US and Ukraine signed a charter on strategic partnership which may have served as the decisive trigger for Putin’s decision to invade. The very idea of discussing Europe’s security architecture with Moscow became a strict taboo in the West for over four years, but clearly it is not any more.

events.title: Salah breaks Egypt scoring record, Tunisia lose to Libya in AFCON qualifier
events.summary: Salah scored twice late on Friday to take his international tally to 70 ​and surpass former captain Hossam Hassan’s record. Mohamed Salah scored twice in Egypt’s 5-0 thrashing of Malawi in the Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers on Friday, becoming the country’s leading all-time scorer with 70 goals. The 34-year-old former Liverpool star left it late in Cairo to overtake Hossam Hassan, scoring with a far-post header in the 84th minute and from a penalty five minutes into added time. list 1 of 3 US air travel in chaos after rare nationwide ground stop halts flights list 2 of 3 Mauricio Pochettino announced as new Manchester United manager list 3 of 3 Goalkeeper Owono handed 12-match ban after De Miguel death Hassan was fired as Egypt coach last week, and replacement Ali Maher made a perfect start with goals from Nasser Maher, Omar Marmoush and Mohamed Hany building a 3-0 lead by half-time. Egypt have seven points in Group B after three matches, three more than Angola, who host South Sudan on Saturday. Achraf Hakimi, favourite to win a second successive African Footballer of the Year award next month, also bagged a brace as Group A pacesetters Morocco crushed Niger 5-1 in Casablanca. Substitute Tolu Arokodaro scored twice within eight minutes as Nigeria beat Tanzania 3-1 in Uyo to get their campaign back on track. Tunisia suffered a shock home 2-0 loss to Libya, and Kenya scored in the final minute to snatch a surprise 2-2 draw away to South Africa. Alhassan Yusuf put Nigeria ahead after just 103 seconds and Alphonce Msanga equalised on 32 minutes following a rare Tanzanian attack. Arokodaro, scorer of six goals in his last five matches for Ajax Amsterdam, came off the bench for the second half and quickly made an impact. His near-post back heel off a low cross put Nigeria ahead for the second time after 52 minutes, and as the match reached the hour mark, he struck again from close range. An ultimately comfortable victory lifted the Super Eagles to six points after three rounds in Group L, one point behind Guinea-Bissau, who drew 1-1 with Madagascar on Thursday. Nigeria back on track, Tunisia in trouble Although bottom of the table with just one point, Tanzania are guaranteed a place at the 2027 AFCON as cohosts with Kenya and Uganda. That means Guinea-Bissau, Nigeria and Madagascar must fight for one place at the 24-nation tournament, the first to be staged in East Africa since Ethiopia were the 1976 hosts. Nigeria were in trouble after a 3-0 hammering in Guinea-Bissau two months ago, but now have a clear path to a tournament they have won three times. Away wins over Tanzania on Tuesday and Madagascar in March, and a home win over Guinea-Bissau, also in March, will assure qualification. Tunisia are in Group H, which includes cohosts and automatic qualifiers Uganda, and their record of reaching every AFCON tournament since 1994 is in peril. A 2-0 defeat at home to neighbours Libya leaves them bottom of the table with just two points, and a venue switch two months ago means their remaining three fixtures are all away. Ali Youssef converted a 44th-minute penalty for Libya, and Hamdou Elhouni, who once played for leading Tunisian club Esperance, doubled the lead in the 62nd minute. Victory lifted Libya from last place to a share of the lead on four points with Uganda. Botswana and Tunisia have two each. Uganda host Botswana in Kampala on Saturday. The Group D clash between South Africa and Kenya pitted two South African coaches against each other. Pitso Mosimane handles Bafana Bafana and Benni McCarthy guides the Harambee Stars. Former Manchester United coaching staffer McCarthy was the happier at full-time after Ryan Ogam equalised in the final minute of regular time. From a South African perspective, this was two points lost, although they remain on top with seven. Guinea have six, automatic qualifiers; Kenya, two; and Eritrea, one.

events.title: Food bank sees donations drop by 10% each year
events.summary: The year ending in 2024 saw a 9% drop, then another 13% in 2025, and finally a 6% drop in 2026 A food bank that has seen a drop in donations of about 10% each year since 2023 is hoping government stockpiling advice will not affect the public's generosity. Someone eats a meal provided by Cambridge City Foodbank "every two minutes" and it claims to have provided more than 260,000 in the past year. In October, the government launched its "Be Ready" campaign and encouraged households to stock up with enough non-perishable food and water to survive for three days in case of an emergency. Chief executive Steve Clay says he does not know if this will affect the Christmas appeal - their busiest period - but confesses: "It is a concern." A government spokesperson said it had "no serious evidence of stockpiling or indeed a supply shortage" with the campaign and it had worked with voluntary organisations and charities to address any concerns. Steve Clay, chief executive of Cambridge City Foodbank, said they had discussed the possibility that stockpiling would affect donations The food bank team estimates it will provide more than 45,000 meals to people in the city between 13 November and 15 January. Clay says that with cold weather and pressure on spending, Christmas is "more difficult" than the rest of the year. "Budgets are tighter, more has to be spent on fuel and energy," he said. "So people are contacting us all the time for emergency support and we need to make sure that the support is always there and is continuing to be there." Donations are used to purchase emergency hampers, treats or provide advice and assistance. While the food bank's doors close on Christmas Day, meals they have provided mean more people can enjoy the festivities. Every pound donated, up to the first £15,000, would be doubled as part of a match-funding commitment. Dr Liam Loftus, development director of the food bank, said: "As we head into winter and the cold draws in, thousands of individuals and families will be forced to make the heart-breaking choice between heating or eating. "This winter, can you take two minutes of your time to support our Winter Appeal? "You'll be helping restore hope and dignity to people facing hardship and providing one of your neighbours with their next meal at what should be one of the happiest times of year." The government spokesperson said of the Be Ready campaign: "We've worked hand-in-hand with voluntary organisations and charities, including food banks, to address any concerns and ensure the guidance is as accessible as possible. "Where households can act, that frees up emergency services to prioritise those most in-need during any emergency." Do you have a story suggestion for Cambridgeshire? Contact us below. events.title: Philippine court orders arrest of jailed, US-wanted celebrity preacher
events.summary: Palace denies timing of warrant is linked to Trump’s visit to Manila next week. A Philippine court has ordered the arrest of jailed celebrity preacher Apollo Quiboloy , who is wanted in the US on child sex trafficking charges, in a step towards his possible extradition, according to the country’s Justice Department. The department’s spokesman Polo Martinez told the AFP news agency on Saturday that the Makati Regional Trial Court issued the warrant of arrest and a hold-departure on Thursday after finding probable cause that he committed the offences charged. list 1 of 3 War, tariffs and China: What the US midterms mean for the Asia-Pacific list 2 of 3 Which countries and industries emit the most greenhouse gases? list 3 of 3 Microsoft hit by global outages: What happened and why? The Philippine government filed its petition with a lower court on Monday, three months after Washington formally requested his extradition in August. Under Philippine law, the court must now hold hearings before deciding whether or not to hand him over. The court issued the same orders against two co-accused, Teresita Dandan and Helen Panilag, both officers of Quiboloy’s Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) sect. The two women are still at large, according to local media reports. Palace Press Officer Claire Castro, speaking on behalf of the Office of the President, denied that the warrant was timed to coincide with US President Donald Trump’s visit to Manila on November 17 for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. “No, it was probably just a coincidence,” she said, according to the Philippines News Agency. Quiboloy, who calls himself the “appointed son of God”, is being held without bail while on trial for human trafficking in Pasig, which carries life in prison if convicted, AFP reported. He also faces a child abuse trial in Quezon City, according to local media. He has denied the allegations and pleaded not guilty to the Philippine charges. A US grand jury indicted Quiboloy in 2021 for conspiracy to engage in sex trafficking by force, fraud and coercion, sex trafficking of children and bulk cash smuggling, AFP reported. The FBI identified Dandan as the “international administrator” of a fake charity operation, and Panilag as a former top church administrator in the US, according to local media reports. Police said after his 2024 arrest that alleged victims were told they were having sex with the “spirit of God” and were threatened that “angels of death” would hunt them down if they told anyone, AFP reported. The church said at the time that members had “freedom of choice”. Quiboloy’s sect claims to have millions of followers and owns a television network. He is a close ally of former President Rodrigo Duterte. He ran for Senate last year from prison and received 5.6 million votes, but lost, AFP reported.

events.title: Siege fuels disease fears in Yemen’s Taiz
events.summary: Health officials warn that falling numbers of recorded infections may conceal a worsening disease crisis in Yemen’s besieged Taiz. Taiz, Yemen – The woman held the body of a young baby girl wrapped in a white shroud. “Our children are dying because of the siege . We have no open road, no medics and no medicines,” the woman said. list 1 of 3 Australia’s friendly against Jordan moved to Qatar over security concerns list 2 of 3 Yemen’s Houthis renew strikes on Saudi Arabia as UNSC extends sanctions list 3 of 3 Fighting intensifies in Yemen as Houthis deny targeting Mecca Wearing the traditional clothing of women from Jabal Sabir, the mountain that overlooks the city of Taiz and is one of its most famous symbols, she appeared in a short video widely circulated on social media on November 10. In her arms was the body of an infant from her family, identified as Gaza Ali Abdulmughni al-Shaqab, who had fallen ill and died after her family was unable to get her emergency medical care. The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms said the vehicle carrying the baby to the hospital was attacked by Houthi forces as it travelled through mountain roads. “She died, and we couldn’t get her emergency treatment because of the siege,” the woman said, referring to the ongoing Houthi siege of al-Shaqab, which lies on a front line between the rebel group and Yemeni government forces. The siege of Taiz and the surrounding areas such as al-Shaqab intensified in early October, when the Houthis advanced around the city and cut off the last major supply route into government-held areas. Fighting between the Iran-backed group and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government intensified over the summer, before the Houthis captured substantial territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast in September and then made further advances in Taiz governorate. Government counteroffensives have only had limited success so far, and the siege of the city of Taiz continues. The Yemeni government has accused the Houthis of tightening their siege on nearly two million people living in Taiz for more than a month, preventing the entry of food, safe drinking water, medicines and fuel. Human Rights Watch (HRW) said in a statement on October 29 that the siege imposed by the Houthis on civilians in Taiz “may amount to the war crime of using starvation as a method of warfare”. The Houthis have denied responsibility for the road closures, instead blaming Yemeni government forces. But HRW said that residents, aid workers and United Nations officials had all reported that the Houthis were to blame. International bodies have repeatedly warned of the crisis now facing Taiz. On October 14, the World Food Programme (WFP) said that it had been unable to reach more than 600,000 people in Taiz dependent on humanitarian assistance. The WFP described the situation as “especially alarming”, noting that most districts in Taiz were classified as facing emergency levels of hunger. For its part, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that health services in Taiz were failing because of a shortage of supplies. Nearly 250,000 people had lost access to essential healthcare, including more than 186,000 children younger than five years old, the agency said. It added that more than 1,400 cases of acute diarrhoea and suspected cholera were reported in just one week. “Twelve hospitals are at risk of closing or have had to reduce services due to a lack of fuel and critical supplies,” OCHA added. According to figures obtained by Al Jazeera from the Epidemiological Surveillance Department at Taiz’s Public Health and Population Office, 5,642 cases across three disease categories were recorded during the latest four-week reporting period. The vast majority – 5,228 cases – were of acute watery diarrhoea. There were also 232 suspected dengue fever cases and 182 suspected cholera cases. The number of watery diarrhoea cases decreased compared with the previous reporting period, but Dr Yasin Abdulmalik, the director of the department, said that was likely the result of residents finding it increasingly difficult to reach health facilities because of road closures between the city and surrounding rural areas. “The siege has led to a shortage of petroleum products, including fuel, whose prices have risen on the black market,” Abdulmalik said. “This has created an additional difficulty in travelling to hospitals and health centres for treatment because of higher transport fares.” “In reality, more than twice this number of cases were unable to reach [health facilities] because of the siege and its various consequences,” he said. Taysir al-Samiei, a health communications official at Taiz’s Public Health and Population Office, told Al Jazeera that patients’ ability to reach hospitals had fallen by between 60 and 70 percent by the end of the second week of the siege.
