events.title: Could one daily pill narrow the diabetes treatment gap in the Global South?
events.summary: Globally, one in nine people lives with diabetes, as blockbuster injectable drugs begin making way for tablets instead. Medication that has been a lifeline for patients with uncontrollable diabetes is now slowly shifting from injections to pills, a move that could fundamentally alter treatment for the disease – and who can access it. This shift could also affect the treatment of obesity, a long misunderstood condition once associated with overeating and laziness, rather than the metabolic disorder it is now recognised as. list 1 of 4 Can GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic cause vision loss? What we know about the risk list 2 of 4 Sweet scoop: Ice-cream study points to potential sugar substitute list 3 of 4 Food or medicine? The impossible choices facing Sudan’s chronically ill list 4 of 4 With every rainfall, Gaza risks losing access to power and healthcare GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) receptor agonists therapy isn’t new. The first FDA-approved drug, Exenatide, hit the market in 2005 and was followed by Liraglutide in 2009, which was seen as a revolutionary alternative to insulin. But the market has until recently been dominated by weekly injections like Ozempic and Wegovy (semaglutide), and Mounjaro (tirzepatide). These drugs have also proved successful for weight loss. Now, once-daily oral GLP pills are emerging as an alternative, especially for the diabetes-stricken Global South. Oral once-daily pills of the same wonder drug could make access more affordable, and less reliant on the cold chain that GLP-1 injections and insulin depend on – and that are harder to secure in emerging economies. One in nine people in the world between the ages of 20-79 lives with diabetes, and one in eight people globally is obese. The GLP injections come with a high price tag and are often not covered by insurance companies, which treat them as an elective drug. In the United States, Eli Lily’s Mounjaro costs about $500 for a month’s worth of doses; in the UK, about 199 pounds ($264); and in Saudi Arabia, 1,261 riyals ($336). In India, the brand is locally manufactured and available at 14,766 rupees ($157). In Pakistan, the imported Mounjaro is a whopping 220,000 rupees ($723), while the locally manufactured Tirzepatide from Getz Pharma costs 17,000 rupees ($61). While pills are usually taken once a day, injections are once per week. Pakistan has the highest diabetes prevalence in the world – 31.4 percent of its population suffer from the disease – followed by the Marshall Islands (25.7 percent) and Kuwait (25.6 percent). Many other Middle Eastern countries rank among nations with the highest diabetes prevalence. For many countries in the Global South, the relative affordability of oral GLP drugs, where the locally manufactured oral semaglutide is about $18 for a 30-day supply, could make them more accessible for diabetes and obesity patients, remove the need for refrigeration and make rural distribution easier. Dr Zakir Alavi is an endocrinologist in Karachi, Pakistan and has been treating patients with diabetes and obesity for nearly 30 years. “Pakistan is a country of contrast. We have, on one hand, childhood malnutrition, underweight, and stunted growth. On the other hand, we have childhood and adult obesity,” said Alavi. “And surprisingly, there is at least some element in the adult and childhood obesity which can be linked to a malnourished mother, and an underweight, premature baby.” Malnutrition during pregnancy can lead to low birth weight, and babies born small who gain weight rapidly in infancy face a higher risk of childhood obesity, according to doctors. Alavi said GLP drugs – whether the injectables or pills – have revolutionised the management of type 2 diabetes and obesity. They not only help type 2 diabetes patients manage their weight, but can also help non-diabetics tackle obesity, improving cardiac and renal outcomes, liver disease, obstructive sleep apnea and osteoarthritis. “They can be used for management of all these things when weight reduction is important, or sugar control is important, or both,” he said. Rayaz Malik is a professor of medicine at Weill Cornell Medica College Qatar, and a senior consultant at Hamad Medical Corporation in Doha. Malik has been at the front line of helping patients with diabetes and obesity, and he echoed Alavi’s views. “We looked at how much weight you need to lose to cure diabetes, the magic number seemed to come in at around 15kg, at least,” he said, speaking of research on the subject. With the wider availability of GLP medication in oral pill form, a cure for diabetes is closer than ever for many more people. Jens Juul Holst is one of the central scientists behind the GLP revolution that has given millions around the world a way to live with diabetes and, for those struggling with obesity, a chance to reclaim their bodies. A professor, physician and physiologist, Holst lives in Copenhagen and began his journey with gut hormones in the 1970s.

events.title: Ecuador wants to monetize its biodiversity — while still drilling for oil
events.summary: Ecuador is pursuing green bonds, debt-for-nature swaps and biodiversity credits to channel more money into conservation. But the government also plans to expand oil exploration and develop critical-mineral resources, drawing opposition from Indigenous and environmental groups. Ecuador will host the U.N. biodiversity COP18 in 2028 and officials say they hope to issue the country’s first sovereign green bond in 2027. Ecuador, known for its " megadiverse " Galapagos Islands, Amazon rainforest, Andes and Pacific coast, wants to protect its natural landscapes for years to come — but it faces a tricky balancing act. As well as preserving its nature, the South American country also plans to capitalize on its critical minerals and continue to extract oil from parts of the Amazon — both of which have led to protests from Indigenous and environmental groups. One way Ecuador is planning to channel funds into its nature is via new financial tools, such as "debt-for-nature" swaps and its first sovereign green bond. It is also aiming to raise its environmental profile on the global stage by hosting the U.N.'s biodiversity summit , known as COP18, in 2028. Ecuador, which uses the U.S. dollar, is no stranger to green finance. In March, IDB Invest, the private-sector arm of the Inter-American Development Bank, and Ecuadorian lender Banco Bolivariano issued a $120 million biodiversity bond to back conservation projects. The government also completed two swaps in 2023 and 2024 — deals in which a country's debt is refinanced on better terms in exchange for commitments to spend the savings on conservation. Together, they freed up about $1.1 billion for conservation in the Amazon and Galapagos Islands . Juan Carlos Blum, Ecuador's minister of environment and energy, said the country hopes to issue sovereign green bonds for the first time in 2027, to raise finance to protect its coastal and mountainous regions and the people whose livelihoods depend on them. The government is looking to the European Union for advice on such instruments, he said. The bloc set green bond standards in 2024. For Blum, one of the challenges is public awareness. "A lot of us are not aware of how we depend on nature, how we depend on the biodiversity, how vulnerable we all are towards climate," he told CNBC by video call. Another challenge for Ecuador, as it looks to protect its biodiversity, is its reliance on oil. The country is a significant oil producer in Central and South America and in October, the government announced plans to open up new tenders for oil exploration in parts of the Amazon , according to local media reports. The news was reportedly met with criticism from Indigenous leaders , who strongly oppose the plans. "We are being careful on that balance between biodiversity and natural resources use, renewables or not renewables, and it's a delicate matter," Blum said. "That's my day-to-day reality, dealing with balancing this." About 80% of Ecuador's energy was generated from oil and oil products in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency, while about two-thirds of its electricity was produced using hydroelectric power. Cracking down on illegal mining is a focus for Blum, who told CNBC he was aware of the environmental impact of legal mining, but that illegal mining was a far bigger problem. At Ecuador's first Bio Summit held Nov. 4 to Nov. 6 in Quito — an event aimed at helping the country's natural assets "enter the global financial system" — a new way of monetizing nature was introduced. Marcelo Salame, the event's president, told CNBC he is working on a project to bring so-called biodiversity credits to the country for the first time, to "preserve and monetize" a 260-hectare, or 640-acre, area of the Prosperina forest owned by ESPOL University in the port city of Guayaquil. Salame said biodiversity is "multidimensional," with credits reflecting a whole ecosystem rather than carbon emissions alone. Biodiversity credits work in a similar way to the carbon credits that large companies buy to meet sustainability goals, but track a range of measures such as the number of species in a given area or tree canopy cover, with the money raised funneled back into nature protection. But whereas carbon credits can be used to offset emissions, biodiversity credits cannot. "It's all about funding verified nature outcomes and not, to date at least, compensating for damage," Martin Vaquié, co-founder of Berlin-based Bloomlabs, a company that tracks the biodiversity market, told CNBC. Jerry Toth, a conservationist and co-founder of Ecuador-based Third Millennium Alliance, a nonprofit that aims to protect the "last remnants" of Ecuador's Pacific Forest, told CNBC that carbon markets can reduce the ecological value of a forest to a single metric: how many tons of carbon it stores. "That can be potentially dangerous because then you have people that are optimizing for this one metric at the expense of all the other things," he said.

events.title: Paranoid or practical? Britain’s ‘Be Ready’ citizen campaign
events.summary: People in England and Wales are rushing to buy tinned goods and wind-up radios – but what’s it all for? The British government’s “Be Ready” campaign has caused a rush on tinned goods, bringing back memories of the COVID-19 pandemic when supermarkets ran dangerously low on toilet paper and online vendors were price-gouging on the internet. In the 10 days since the campaign urging citizens in England and Wales to be ready for a national emergency was launched on October 22, sales of bottled water have risen by 67 percent; tinned and jarred food by 37 percent; and hand sanitiser by 83 percent, according to retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator. Wind-up radios, torches and power banks have also sold out at several retailers. British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, the campaign’s most prominent public face, says the government wants people to be “alert but not alarmed”. So what is Be Ready, why now, and is it really necessary? Be Ready is a three-year public information campaign being run by the Cabinet Office. Its launch on October 22 marked its first stage. The government is asking households in England and Wales to make sure they would be able to cope on their own for 72 hours if electricity, water, phone and internet services all fail in the event of a national emergency. The idea is that emergency services can then focus on people who require more urgent assistance. The campaign’s website features a checklist, starting with bottled water and long-life food that does not need to be kept in a fridge, such as tinned food, dried fruit and nuts. It also recommends having a torch, spare batteries, a charged power bank and a wind-up or battery-powered radio, along with cash in case card payments go down, a first aid kit, medication, warm clothing and blankets to hand. The new website covers England and Wales. Scotland and Northern Ireland receive their own advice through Ready Scotland and NI Direct. More than 500 organisations, including charities, businesses and faith and community groups, have signed up to spread the message. Official household preparedness guidance has existed since May 2024. What is new is the push to get people to act on it. Officially, the focus of the campaign is to ensure households can get through “everyday emergencies” such as storms, floods, wildfires and burst water pipes. The campaign follows months of heatwaves, drought and fires across the United Kingdom this summer. The government also highlights how unprepared Britons say they are. In a Cabinet Office survey this year, only 13 percent said their household was largely or totally prepared for an emergency, while 84 percent wanted more advice from the government. Independent research points the same way. A 2025 survey of 931 people by Bournemouth University’s Disaster Management Centre, part of its EM-PREPARE project, found that only 52 percent felt they understood the hazards they faced, and 21 percent said they were not aware of the risks at all. The same study found that 81 percent were willing to do more to prepare. In September, the National Audit Office, the UK’s spending watchdog, warned of threats facing Britain’s food supply chain. The security backdrop features, too. Ministers have linked the campaign to the risk of cyberattacks and hostile state activity against critical infrastructure. On Remembrance Day, Defence Minister Lord Coaker said the 13 percent figure was exactly why the campaign had been launched. The UK is also catching up with its neighbours. The European Commission’s Preparedness Union Strategy, adopted in March 2025, recommends that people be able to cope alone for at least 72 hours. Sweden posted 5.2 million copies of its crisis-preparedness brochure to households in November 2024, and Finland, Poland and the Czech Republic run similar campaigns. Shoppers in England and Wales have acted fast and enthusiastically. Supermarket chain Iceland said sales of tinned products rose 40 percent over the first weekend. Tinned-food producer Princes reported particularly high demand for tuna, meat and vegetables. Worldpanel found the equivalent of 400,000 extra people a day bought tinned meat immediately after the launch. Meanwhile, Canned Food UK, part of the Metal Packaging Manufacturers Association, has launched a consumer campaign featuring TV chef and author Theo Michaels, who demonstrates how to use canned food in tasty recipes. The rush has extended beyond the food aisles. Electronics retailer Maplin said torch sales jumped 284 percent; radios, 92 percent; and power banks, 106 percent, within days. Hardware store group Robert Dyas reported a 160 percent rise in radio sales, and at least seven wind-up radio models sold out across several outlets. Criticism has focused on tone more than substance. On BBC’s Question Time, an audience member accused Streeting of “scaremongering”, warning that the advice would trigger panic buying.

events.title: US air travel thrown into chaos after nationwide ground stop halts flights
events.summary: More than 1.5 million passengers face travel disruption as domestic and international airlines warn of knock-on delays. More than 1.5 million air passengers have faced travel disruption after the United States halted departing flights nationwide for more than four hours, with airlines warning they would take days to recover. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted the ground stop at 8:15pm Eastern time on Friday (01:15 GMT on Saturday), after a telecommunications outage affected the country’s 22 regional air traffic control centres. FlightRadar24 counted more than 4,700 cancellations and 10,000 delays on Friday, with 700 flights already cancelled for Saturday. list 1 of 3 Microsoft hit by global outages: What happened and why? list 2 of 3 FAA ground stop lifted: Why were US flights grounded, and what’s next? list 3 of 3 US agencies unite to combat rogue drone threats nationwide At Los Angeles airport, passenger Nicholas Erdodi, who had travelled from New Zealand to attend a conference in Chicago, told Al Jazeera he had spent six hours at the airport after being forced off his plane. “The challenge is you cannot ask anyone here what to do,” he said. “The lack of information is what bothers me.” He had been rebooked, but was unsure whether his next flight would go. Others affected included sport teams in the NBA, NHL and college football. Todd Curtis, an aviation safety expert and chief executive of AirSafe.com, told Al Jazeera that the failures appeared to be concentrated in the country’s air route traffic control centres. “There are 21 across the United States, one in Alaska and the other 20 in the lower 48,” he said. “These are the folks who handle the aircraft that are transiting from one part of the country to the other, and they rely on multiple handoffs between controllers.” US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said it would “take us some time” to restore capacity and that “we’re going to have some makeup to do.” He acknowledged that tens of thousands of travellers had been stranded , saying he expected operations to be back to normal for the Thanksgiving rush, which begins in less than two weeks. Cirium, an aviation analytics firm, said about 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to depart US airports after 4pm Eastern time (21:00 GMT), and that at least 827 flights had been diverted by 7:05pm on Friday (00:05 am on Saturday). The Associated Press news agency reported that the shutdown left NBA, NHL and college teams stranded, with NFL teams wondering whether they could travel in time for their games. The Nets were among five NBA teams scheduled to fly on Friday for Saturday games. There are 14 NHL games set to play Saturday. The San Jose Sharks were left waiting to fly to Utah, while the Florida Panthers reached St Louis before the stoppage. The Texas Longhorns had boarded their plane before it was grounded. “We are grounded and waiting to see when we can leave,” a team spokesman said. If they have to take a bus to Baton Rouge, the trip for Saturday’s 6:30pm kickoff would take about seven hours. Delta Air Lines said it was “safely resuming operations”, offering flexible rebooking, and warned that repositioning aircraft and crews would take time. United Airlines said it was resuming a number of Friday night flights. JetBlue plans to resume on Saturday morning. Air Canada said operations would return gradually, with disruption likely on Saturday, and Aeromexico was working to resume operations. In Mexico City, the Benito Juarez international airport said about 70 flights scheduled for Friday could be affected. In Canada, Toronto Pearson said flights that did not need to cross US airspace were operating as normal and that it had increased staffing to support affected passengers.

events.title: FAA lifts ground stop after more than four hours, but flight cancellations will stretch into the weekend
events.summary: The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon that lasted for more than four hours and disrupted thousands of departing of flights. The agency reported communication problems affected "multiple" air traffic control centers. Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare, and the last was in January 2023 after a failure of a pilot communication system. The U.S. halted flight departures across the country for hours on Friday for the second time since 9/11, blaming aging technology that was overloaded, affecting key information for multiple air traffic control centers. More than 10,000 flights were disrupted during the nationwide ground stop, and delays and cancellations were set to stretch into the weekend, if not longer. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a press conference late Friday that that telecommunications routers were overloaded with data. "They went down," he said. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday at the White House that there was no indication that the issues were a threat to the United States. He later said at a press conference that it doesn't appear to be a cyber attack, and that it "appears this was mechanically driven." The Federal Aviation Administration canceled the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday after it lasted formore than four hours and disrupted the travel plans of hundreds of thousands of travelers, including some sports teams. The agency earlier said in post on X that there was a "temporary telecommunications outage" and that it halted flights out of an "abundance of caution." When it issued the ground stop at about 4 p.m., the FAA said the communications issues were "impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers." These facilities guide airplanes at high altitudes along their routes. While the FAA lifted the ground stop, travel chaos continued at airports, which were forced to find places for parked planes. Delays were set to continue even as flights start taking off again. Carriers canceled more flights as the disruption wore on. JetBlue Airways told staff it would cancel the remainder of the day's flights, aside from European routes, as well as others scheduled for Saturday so that crews and planes are in place to resume operations, according to a memo seen by CNBC. Hundreds of flights into Newark, New York, Philadelphia disrupted after Verizon fiber line cut The government shutdown is over. The air traffic controller shortage is not Aviation industry pushes Congress for air traffic improvements, more hiring Why the U.S. has a shortage of air traffic controllers FAA system outage disrupts thousands of flights across U.S. A ground stop halts flights at their departure point. Disruptions tend to snowball if ground stops drag on as flight crews reach their maximum number of duty hours for a day. There were 11,000 flights scheduled to depart U.S. airports after 4 p.m. ET on Friday, according to flight-data firm Cirium, with 1.5 million passengers. There were about 600 diverted flights on Friday, 104 of them sent to other airports, Cirium said. International flights had started taking off from coastal hubs before 6 p.m. ET. The FAA said earlier in the night that flights will be allowed to depart as en route traffic facilities recover, "through coordination with the air traffic control system." The FAA's technicians are investigating, the agency said. Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare. In January 2023, the FAA halted flights because of issues with a pilot alert system. Before that, traffic was halted nationwide after the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. Technical issues have repeatedly snarled air traffic in the U.S. in recent years. Aging infrastructure and staffing shortages have angered airline executives for years. In September, hundreds of flights into Newark, New Jersey, and Philadelphia were canceled, delayed or diverted after a Verizon fiber cable was accidentally cut. Officials said it occurred during construction in New Jersey, severing a backup feed of key data for air traffic controllers. In 2025, air traffic controllers lost contact with aircraft heading to and from Newark Liberty International Airport , an equipment failure that led to massive flight delays and raised more concerns about aging U.S. aviation infrastructure and staffing shortages. "It's going to continue to fail," Duffy said Friday of U.S. air traffic control infrastructure. The U.S. is in the middle of an overhaul of the technology, and Duffy urged lawmakers for more funding. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis, the FAA said. The major U.S. airlines issued statements saying they would work with customers who were affected by the ground stop and encouraged travelers to check for updates. — CNBC's Kevin Breuninger and Phil LeBeau contributed to this article.

Trump has said the meeting is a chance for all three countries to reach a deal on nuclear stockpiles. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) lapsed in February. Trump then rejected Russia’s proposal to extend it for another year and demanded a “new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China. Expectations are low. “We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told the Reuters news agency, describing the meeting as the start of a conversation. Russia holds the most nuclear warheads, followed by the US, then China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. Trump plans on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but will steer away from discussing Russia’s war in Ukraine, according to a senior US official who briefed reporters on condition of anonymity. Elon Musk will also travel with Trump to China but will not attend the meeting, the official added. Trump is also not expected to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during the Asia trip. The planned summit has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain and the Soviet Union shaped the post-war order. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, however, dismissed the parallel, saying any agreements reached in Shenzhen cannot be imposed on others, but he still called the meeting “extremely significant”. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has voiced concern that the meeting could become a platform to discuss a Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back . Trump has pursued closer ties with both leaders despite a short-lived trade war with China last year and Russia’s continuing war in Ukraine, where Washington is seeking to mediate a solution.

events.title: Lagos Art Week confronts history, identity and belonging
events.summary: ART X Lagos celebrates Africa’s heritage and contemporary creativity. Lagos, Nigeria – A woman in an elegant red dress walks down a hallway, turning to take in her surroundings. A large painting catches her eye, and she steps into the booth for a closer look. Around her, visitors move between 15 partitioned exhibition spaces, pausing to study the artworks. Thousands have gathered to admire, connect with and collect works from across the world. It is the third day of ART X Lagos, West Africa’s premier and largest art fair, held from November 5–8 as the centrepiece of Nigeria’s annual art week. This year’s programme features exhibitions, installations, music, discussions and film screenings at the Federal Palace Hotel on Victoria Island. Galleries and museums across Lagos are also hosting exhibitions. Together, the exhibitions explore cultural erosion, migration and belonging, examining how art can preserve collective memory and reconnect people with their heritage. They also reveal a cultural side of Lagos that extends beyond its reputation for commerce, traffic and relentless hustle. Ndidi Dike, a contemporary sculptor and multidisciplinary artist, is among those exhibiting. Her installation, Residues of Past Encounters II, features a wooden canoe suspended above a glass surface, with sand arranged around its edges. Above it hangs fabric in the Adire style, associated with Yoruba women of southwest Nigeria, bearing silhouettes of tightly packed people. The sound of waves crashing against the shore plays softly in the background, evoking the Atlantic coastline at Badagry, a historic Nigerian town that was once a notorious transit point for enslaved West Africans. The sand and sound were sourced from the town. Dike’s installation explores the intertwined histories of the transatlantic slave trade, colonialism, memory and migration. The reflective surface beneath the canoe evokes absence, remembrance and the passage of time. “The sound of the waves makes you contemplate, makes you think deeper, and then you begin to imagine, perhaps, how those who have left our shores under various circumstances must have been feeling mentally, the prospect of leaving home and never, perhaps, seeing it again,” Dike told Al Jazeera. The work draws a connection between historical displacement and contemporary migration. Centuries after the transatlantic slave trade, many young Africans still undertake dangerous journeys to Europe, crossing the Sahara Desert and the Mediterranean Sea. Some die along the way, while others face exploitation and trafficking. “I find that there is a correlation between slavery and what is happening now. It’s always the best of our demographic that are taken or who decide to go abroad. For me, I think it’s good to look at that correlation between the historical and contemporary circumstances,” she said. Now in its 11th edition, this year’s fair takes the theme ‘A New Chapter, A New Decade’, drawing inspiration from the pioneering generation of Nigerian artists, architects, educators and thinkers who helped shape modernism in the country. ART X founder Tokini Peterside said the older generation demonstrated that innovation need not mean abandoning cultural inheritance. Instead, it can emerge from a deeper understanding of identity and the confidence to interpret it in new ways. “For me, the thread connecting these presentations is the idea that our histories are not simply things to preserve or look back upon. They are living sources of knowledge that can inform what we create next,” Peterside told Al Jazeera. “While the exhibitions are distinct, collectively they reveal a creative landscape that is increasingly self-assured, intellectually ambitious and deeply engaged with the world around it.” One artist whose legacy is being celebrated is Ladi Kwali, a Nigerian potter and ceramicist. Her work features in an exhibition titled Beyond the Vessel. Beside a large photograph of Kwali at work, her handcrafted pots and ceramics display motifs of scorpions, lizards and butterflies, alongside intricate patterns. Kwali came from a long line of Gbari women potters in the village of Kwali, near Abuja. Pottery was part of everyday life in the community, but her talent took her from local recognition to international acclaim. Her work has been exhibited and collected by museums and galleries around the world. Her portrait has also appeared on Nigerian currency. Jareh Das, curator of the exhibition, said preserving Kwali’s legacy would remind future generations of her achievements and inspire young artists, particularly in a country where documenting and maintaining cultural heritage can be challenging. “Culture is not always outside, but looking at what exists within and how you can draw from that, how you can rise above immediate challenges … through something as familiar as pottery,” Das said. Barbara Barungi, dressed in Adire, moves between booths in search of new works.

events.title: German spies granted sweeping new powers
events.summary: The controversial bill comes just months after a thwarted attack at Leipzig-Halle airport which Berlin linked to Russia. Germany’s parliament has approved sweeping new powers for the country’s intelligence agencies, allowing them to hack and disrupt adversaries under specified conditions as the government seeks to counter espionage and cyberattacks. The Bundestag passed the legislation on Friday by 308 votes to 190, with 71 abstentions. The governing Christian Democrats and Social Democrats backed the reform, while the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and Die Linke, or the Left Party, opposed it. list 1 of 3 Regional security dominates European talks in Dublin amid hybrid attacks list 2 of 3 Germany accuses Russia of failed drone attack on Leipzig airport in August list 3 of 3 What to know about Germany’s drone attack accusations against Russia The changes expand the role of Germany’s foreign intelligence agency, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and its domestic intelligence service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), beyond gathering and analysing information to actively disrupting certain threats. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described the legislation as a “reform of the century”, arguing that Germany needed stronger intelligence services to confront terrorism and hostile foreign operations. The government says the reform addresses a gap in Germany’s security system, as intelligence agencies to date could sometimes identify a threat but lacked the authority to intervene, including when no other agency was responsible or able to act. Under the new framework, the BfV would be able to take technical measures against serious threats, such as deleting stolen information from an attacker’s server. For the BND, the expanded operational powers would allow interventions against threats abroad, including disrupting the servers used by state-backed hackers. Russia accused of attempting drone attack The approval comes just months after German authorities found an explosive-laden drone near a cargo plane belonging to the Ukrainian firm Antonov Airlines at Leipzig-Halle airport in August, linking the incident to Moscow. Berlin formally accused Russia of attempting an attack at the state-owned facility, with Dobrindt saying Germany’s intelligence community had determined that a drone discovered at the airport was consistent with Russian technology. Russia denied involvement, but the accusation led to the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House, a cultural centre, in Berlin. Moscow responded by ordering the closure of a German consulate in St Petersburg and the Goethe-Institut. “The reform is a direct result of the Zeitenwende [epochal change] and closely tied to Germany’s foreign policy challenges since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022,” Florian Bigge, programme director at think tank Korber-Stiftung, told Al Jazeera. Bigge said the BND had publicly sought expanded powers since 2024 and that the approval came amid an “increasingly uncertain international order”. “The security reality has changed fundamentally in recent years,” Bigge said, adding that “Russia is the main trigger: sabotage, cyberattacks and drones. Plus fear of US unpredictability and reduced US intelligence sharing.” Dobrindt said Friday’s approved changes put German agencies on an equal footing with their European partners. During previous parliamentary debates, ministers argued that the BND should not have to stand by when other authorities cannot avert a particularly serious threat, while experts speaking to the Bundestag said Berlin’s capabilities “lack modern intervention powers” compared with their Western counterparts. Still, the reform has drawn objections from opposition lawmakers, particularly Die Linke, who expressed concern about privacy and the historic separation between intelligence gathering and police work. In a parliamentary motion opposing the bill, Die Linke argued that key provisions failed to meet constitutional standards for intrusive surveillance. The party has warned that the sweeping powers would effectively create a German secret police force, a prospect with particular historical resonance for citizens who lived under the Stasi, East Germany’s secret police between 1950 and 1990. In September, Die Linke won the Berlin city-state parliament election with 25.7 percent of the vote, allowing the party to appoint a mayor after forming a coalition government. Thus far, criticism has come from lawmakers and civil liberties groups, Bigge said, adding that “a broader public debate may still come” as the state expands what it can do abroad. “Germans want more engagement,” Bigge said, but caveated that “they mean diplomacy”. The main provisions are scheduled to take effect on December 31, pending completion of the legislative process.

events.title: ICC stops probe into alleged crimes by US troops in Afghanistan
events.summary: Although unrelated, the decision follows Trump’s refusal to have the court prosecute American citizens. Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) have issued a decision to halt the prosecutor’s investigations into alleged crimes by American troops in Afghanistan and instead to focus on the Taliban’s actions since 2021, according to court documents released on Friday. The ICC’s ruling, which was issued Thursday but only made public on Friday, cites “significant limitations to the Prosecution’s ability to conduct its investigations and secure evidence”. list 1 of 3 Israel’s ties with Europe are fraying. Can its election change that? list 2 of 3 US-sanctioned ICC wins Sakharov Prize, EU’s top human rights award list 3 of 3 Israeli soldier visiting UK faces war crimes complaint The decision follows feuds between the United States and the Hague-based ICC, notably after Washington sanctioned 13 current and former ICC staff members over the investigation into alleged crimes by US personnel and arrest warrants issued against Israeli officials. It closes not only the line of inquiry into alleged crimes by US troops, which had lain dormant since 2021, but also the probe into the ISIL affiliate in Khorasan Province (ISKP). The prosecutor’s office told The Associated Press and Reuters news agencies that it has already appealed the decision. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio previously said, “President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans.” In the October statement, Rubio also warned that “the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer.” It is not clear if the court’s decision to stop the investigation will affect Washington’s stance on the ICC. Regardless, the US is not a member of the court and does not recognise its jurisdiction. The court’s founding statute says that it can prosecute anyone accused of atrocity crimes committed on the territory of ICC member states. The ICC issued four arrest warrants for Taliban leaders last year. The investigation in Afghanistan began in 2020, covering offences allegedly committed by Afghan government forces, the Taliban, American troops and US foreign intelligence operatives dating back to 2002. In 2021, Karim Khan, the probe’s prosecutor, announced he would “deprioritise” the investigation into American forces, citing challenges in obtaining evidence. Khan was ousted from the court over sexual misconduct allegations earlier this year.

events.title: UAE Property: 'Should I waive the penalty if my tenant can no longer afford the rent?'
events.summary: Question: I own a one-bedroom apartment that I rent out. My tenant renewed only three months ago but has now lost his job and says he needs to leave the UAE . The tenancy contract says early termination requires two months' rent as a penalty. He has asked me to waive it because he has a family and says he genuinely cannot afford it. I'm sympathetic, but I'm also paying a mortgage and I'm worried the apartment could sit empty while I find another tenant. What would you do? Am I being foolish if I let him leave without enforcing the penalty? DH, Dubai Answer: There's the legal answer and then there's the answer I would give you after many years of dealing with landlords and tenants, and they aren't always exactly the same. Let's start with the contract. If you have an agreed early termination clause requiring two months' rent, that is the basis from which the two of you negotiate. A tenant losing their job doesn't automatically erase their contractual obligations. But of course, I wouldn't immediately turn this into a dispute . Ask the tenant when they realistically need to leave and whether they'll co-operate with viewings (presumably you will want to find an immediate replacement). Then, speak to a good local brokerage firm to establish how quickly the apartment could be re-let and at what level of rent. Suppose your existing tenant helps you secure a replacement who moves in immediately after he leaves. If you suffer little or no financial loss, insisting on the full two-month penalty may achieve very little other than making an already difficult situation for him worse. On the other hand, if the property is likely to sit vacant for six weeks and you'll incur cleaning, maintenance/preparation costs, or perhaps agency fees, it's therefore perfectly reasonable to negotiate compensation. If I had to be practical and you pressed me for my view, I would release him early provided he allows viewings , returns the apartment properly, settles utilities and rent up to the agreed handover date and perhaps pays a reduced termination amount if there's a genuine vacancy period. One piece of advice though: whatever you both decide ensure you put everything in writing. I've always believed the best landlord-and-tenant outcomes aren't necessarily the ones where somebody squeezes every last dirham out of the contract. They're the ones where both sides walk away feeling the agreement was fair. You have a mortgage to pay, so this isn't charity. But if you can replace the tenant quickly and help somebody through a genuinely difficult period without leaving yourself out of pocket, I'd call that sensible property management rather than weakness. Q: I own an apartment in Dubai that I bought as a long-term investment. My service charges have increased over the years, but the condition of the building seems to be going in the opposite direction. The gym has had broken equipment for months, there are regular problems with the lifts, the swimming pool has been closed several times and the common areas look tired. I don't mind paying reasonable service charges if the money is being spent properly, but as an individual owner I feel I have absolutely no influence. Can I refuse to pay until these issues are fixed, and how can I actually find out what I'm paying for? LM, Dubai A: Straight off the bat, I wouldn't refuse to pay. This puts you in a weak position and ultimately you will be falling foul of the law. Service charges in Dubai's jointly owned properties are regulated and the budgets are subject to Rera's approval. The charges can include security, cleaning, maintenance, utilities for common areas, insurance, management costs, master-community charges and contributions to any reserve funds. Your first step should therefore be to establish what the approved charge actually is. You can check this through the DLD Service Charge Index, Mollak or Dubai REST. DLD specifically states that management entities should not demand service charges before they have been approved by Rera. After you have thoroughly checked this out you can go ahead and separate the two issues of how much you're being charged and what standard of service you're receiving. A high service charge isn't automatically unreasonable if you're in a building with extensive facilities, cooling of common areas, several lifts, pools, landscaping and 24-hour security. But owners are entitled to question why facilities they are funding are not being fully maintained. Document the problems. Dates, photographs, emails and previous complaints are far more useful than simply saying the building is badly managed. Raise them formally with the management company first. If the standard of common-area maintenance remains unacceptable, DLD says owners can submit a complaint through Dubai REST using the Real Estate Violations System. From an investment perspective, I'd take this seriously. Poor building management doesn't just irritate residents, over time it can affect rents, tenant retention and of course resale values. Two identical apartments in neighbouring buildings can perform very differently simply because one building is well run and the other isn't. The opinions expressed do not constitute legal advice and are provided for information only. Please send any questions to mario@evadxb.com

events.title: 'I called my mom and cried': Passengers describe chaos at JFK during nationwide ground stop
events.summary: Riley Alexis Holmes is among the thousands of passengers stranded at JFK by the ground stop. Martina Nacach Thousands of passengers are stranded after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop. At JFK International in New York City, travelers crowded gates and waited for news. The FAA said the now-lifted ground stop was due to a telecommunications outage. Riley Alexis Holmes arrived at New York's Kennedy Airport on Friday evening with a ticket to Oregon, where she has plans to see her brother's closing night in the musical "Trolls Junior." First, she got word that her 6 p.m. flight was delayed almost two hours. Then came the news that it was canceled. "I called my mom and cried, and I'm just like sitting here waiting for information," Holmes, 24, told Business Insider Friday afternoon shortly after a nationwide ground stop started delaying or canceling thousands of flights and stranded thousands of passengers across the country. That also included Juliana Melo, 30, from São Paulo, who was heading home to her 1-year-old daughter after a week's vacation in New York City. "She's waiting for us in Brazil with my mother and the babysitter. So we are very nervous," Melo said at JFK, where fellow passengers crowded gates and sat on the floor with anxious faces. She said the airline had not yet contacted them to reschedule, so Melo and her husband were waiting at Terminal 4 for any updates. Officials said the FAA grounded flights out of an "abundance of caution" after a telecommunications issue . Stranded Delta passengers await information at the check-in counter at JFK International Airport on Friday. Martina Nacach Lennard Meijer, 49, traveled from Amsterdam to New York for a one-week business trip and was supposed to return to Amsterdam on Thursday night. Due to weather conditions, his flight was delayed and then canceled. He was rebooked and then canceled again, losing access to his checked bag in the process. After waiting an hour and a half in line, he got his bag back and finally secured a seat on a Delta flight scheduled to depart later on Friday. He's afraid to check his bag again. "I'm half waiting for news, half deciding to take some basic stuff out of here. So if I have another cancellation tonight, when I go back to the city and find another hotel last minute, I'll at least have some clothes," he said. Meijer said he's clinging to hope his flight might take off. "It's just a little exhausting being at JFK, and I can't wait to go home," he said. Stranded passengers waited for news as the ground stop dragged on into the night at Kennedy Airport. Brendan McDermid/Reuters Kieran Cullen, 27, had been traveling for over 24 hours after his overseas deployment ended. He was headed home to Jacksonville, Florida, stopping at JFK for a layover. "We were only expecting to be here for about five hours," he said. Then he said he started receiving text messages. The flight was delayed for 15 minutes. Then again for another 15 minutes. Hours later, he said, he finally got word his flight was canceled. "So far, not a ton of information, other than just live speaker announcements discussing the centers having rotating blackouts on frequencies, but nothing specific," he said. "It's over 24 hours of travel, so it's definitely a bummer." Cullen and his group plan to stay in New Jersey for the night and hope to get a flight home for Sunday. Holmes said Delta told her that if she does not reschedule her flight to Oregon in the next 24 hours, she can get a full refund. If she decides to reschedule the flight, she will not get her money back. She was waiting to see if she could get on a flight to see her brother's final performance. "My first initial reaction was I was very sad, but then I was really grateful that I'm OK and that everyone hopefully is OK," she said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Nearly 5,000 flights were canceled across the US after an FAA ground stop. Here's what to do if your trip was affected.
events.summary: People stranded at Miami airport amid the ATC outage on Friday. Giorgio VIERA / AFP via Getty Images Nearly 7,500 flights were canceled after a nationwide air traffic control outage on Friday. This is considered an uncontrollable disruption, so airlines aren't required to provide freebies. Here's what you can do if your flight is delayed or canceled. US airlines are canceling thousands of flights after a rare air traffic control outage affected the US . As of 10:45 p.m. Eastern time on Friday, FlightAware data showed that nearly 7,500 flights to, within, and from the US had been canceled since the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop — meaning no flights could depart — around 3:45 p.m. The stop was lifted around 8:30 p.m., but after so many cancellations, flight chaos is nearly guaranteed to stretch into the weekend. If you're wondering what your options are as the terminals pile up with people frantically trying to get a hotel or food voucher — don't rely on your airline to help out. According to the Department of Transportation, certain delays and cancellations caused by, for example, an ATC outage, are considered "uncontrollable" disruptions. That means airlines are not required to provide freebies such as hotel stays or food vouchers. Don't confuse the rules with the DoT customer service dashboard , which shows passenger compensation for flights disrupted by controllable factors, such as maintenance or crew scheduling. Pilots or flight attendants timing out due to the outage would not fall under crew scheduling. Airlines may offer goodwill vouchers to help out affected customers, but don't bank on it. Customers who book their own hotel or other transportation, such as a rental car or train, may be able to get eligible expenses reimbursed by their credit card. Here's what to do if your flight is disrupted. 1. Know your rights as an airline passenger in the US Airline passengers have some customer rights in the US. Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images According to the Department of Transportation, there is no law requiring US airlines to compensate passengers for disruptions caused by uncontrollable events, such as weather. That also includes air traffic control delays. The only rule carriers must follow is to refund customers for cancellations, even in cases of uncontrollable events. And that does not mean travel credits or vouchers — it must be to the original form of payment, and includes any add-ons, such as bags or seats. If you choose to travel but your flight is delayed or canceled, ask the airline for the reason — ideally in writing — so you know what you're entitled to. Airlines have different policies for disruptions they can control. The DoT's Airline Customer Service Dashboard — launched in 2022 — shows what the 10 largest US airlines promise in those cases, including rebookings, meal vouchers, and hotel accommodations. 2. Monitor your airline's app for rebooking options Most airlines allow customers to adjust their flights online. Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images When a flight delay or cancellation is announced, expect people to flock to the nearest customer service line for assistance, and for the phone lines to clog. Wait times can be painfully long, and the best alternatives will likely go quickly. However, some airlines offer the option to rebook on their website or mobile app and waive any fees, making it sometimes easier to make changes online than in person. If all available options are exhausted, have a plan B, such as waiting to speak with a live agent, contacting the airline through social media, or booking a hotel for the night. Direct messaging on Facebook or Twitter can actually serve as a virtual placeholder, and you may hear back via chat before speaking to a live agent. Here are the phone numbers for each airline: Alaska: 1-800-252-7522 or text 82008 Allegiant: 1-702-505-8888 American: 1-800-433-7300 Avelo: 1-346-616-9500 Breeze: No phone number to call, but you can text the airline at 501-273-3931. If you call this number, it'll tell you different ways to contact Breeze, like via email or Facebook Messenger. Delta: 1-800-221-1212 Frontier: No phone number. The best way to contact Frontier is via online chat or email. JetBlue: 1-800-538-2583 Southwest: 1-800-435-9792 United: 1-800-864-8331 3. Ask for a hotel or meal voucher The Hyatt hotel inside Orlando airport. : Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images For controllable delays or cancellations that result in a customer waiting at least three hours for a new flight or requiring an overnight stay, several airlines will offer meal or hotel vouchers .  Carriers offering both are Alaska Airlines, Allegiant Air, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Hawaiian Airlines, JetBlue Airways, Southwest Airlines, and United Airlines, per the DoT dashboard. Frontier Airlines is the only carrier that does not offer accommodations in the event of an overnight delay or cancellation, but it will provide a meal voucher. For US airlines not listed on the dashboard, or in cases where the disruption is uncontrollable (like because of a winter storm), or if the compensation is unclear, simply ask. It never hurts to request a meal or hotel during flight disruptions, and you might get lucky with a goodwill gesture from the carrier. 4. Check if your credit card company offers travel insurance American Express and Chase have travel credit cards. Illustration by Mario Tama/Getty Images Several major banks offer credit cards with travel insurance , such as  Chase's Sapphire Reserve  and American Express' Platinum Card . Both offer trip protection, meaning customers who purchased their flights with those cards can benefit. For example, during a major storm system, many passengers are likely to end up stranded in random cities across the US. However, banks with travel insurance included can reimburse cardholders for unexpected expenses outside their control, including hotel, meal, and transportation costs.  Travel insurance does not apply in all circumstances, like short delays, so be sure to check your policy before making a claim — but it also doesn't hurt to make the claim anyway, even if the answer is no. 5. Know when to walk away Consider renting a car or taking the train. Wang Ying/Xinhua via Getty Images Delays and cancellations are inevitable. Don't spend all day sitting around waiting — set a cutoff time. Once that moment passes, consider alternative ways to reach your destination, such as driving or taking a bus or train (which may also be covered by travel insurance). If you are stuck in another city and have no other option but to stay in a hotel or wait at the airport, decide how you want to spend your time and make a plan. events.summary: Emergency personnel and crews are on the scene after a tanker crashed into a river cruise ship in New Orleans on Friday. Matthew Hinton/AP A cruise ship and tanker collided in New Orleans on Friday, sparking a major rescue effort. American Cruise Lines said its riverboat, American Heritage, was docked when the collision occurred. Photos and video showed the cruise ship sinking and people being pulled from the water. A tanker collided with a cruise ship on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday, triggering a search and rescue operation, officials said. events.title: 'The line-up is huge': Australians caught up in US flight chaos
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australians stranded as US flight chaos grounds thousands of planes Adelaide woman Trish Crabb is stranded at JFK Airport in New York after thousands of flights were cancelled and delayed. ( Supplied: Trish Crabb ) A major air traffic control outage in the US has disrupted thousands of flights, leaving Australians stranded and warnings about global flow-on impacts, including international delays. Airlines are working to clear the backlog as US authorities investigate what caused the outage. Australians have been caught up in widespread flight disruptions across the United States after a communications outage forced aviation authorities to ground flights nationwide. More than 11,000 flights were delayed or cancelled, with passengers left stranded at airports across the country after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an unprecedented ground stop. The grounding has since been lifted, but airlines are warning it could take time to clear the backlog, with disruptions also affecting flights departing Australia for the US. Look back on our live blog for the latest on the issues affecting flights in the US and Australia. Sydney Airport said flights to the US would now resume from Mascot after being temporarily grounded on Saturday morning, and urged passengers to contact their airlines. The disruption has affected travellers at major airports including New York's JFK, Los Angeles International Airport and San Diego. Adelaide traveller Trish Crabb snapped this photograph while in line at JFK airport in New York. She was among thousands of travellers caught up in US flight cancellations. ( Supplied: Trish Crabb ) Trish Crabb, from Adelaide, was among those caught up in the chaos after her flight from New York to Miami was grounded. She and her husband were due to fly out of JFK Airport when they discovered their Delta flight had been cancelled. The couple are holidaying in the US and had planned to drive from Miami to Fort Lauderdale to board a cruise. "My husband is going to try and find us a hotel room somewhere close by, and hopefully we will be able to get a flight out at some stage," she said. Despite the disruption, Ms Crabb said passengers appeared to be keeping their composure. "Everyone was very calm," she said, adding most people were taking the situation in their stride. Rivkah Brown, from Myrtleford in Victoria, was stranded at San Diego Airport after her Delta flight was cancelled. Rivkah Brown from Victoria was stranded at San Diego Airport following a cruise in the US. She's now boarding a bus to get to Las Vegas. ( Supplied: Rivkah Brown ) Ms Brown had just disembarked from a cruise and was stopping over in San Diego before travelling to Las Vegas, where she was due to meet her fiancé. She said she would now take a bus to Las Vegas instead, a journey of almost 10 hours. "It's disappointing but it is what it is," Ms Brown said. The FAA ordered the nationwide ground stop on Friday, local time, after communications problems affecting air traffic control centres across the United States. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the issue was affected all Air Route Traffic Control Centres, with technicians investigating the cause. What we know about the US flight groundstop Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for the outage. The FAA said the decision was made because of "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety". US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said preliminary investigations pointed to a telecommunications outage, with no immediate indication of a deliberate attack. "There's no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It's just a telecommunications outage as of right now," he said. The outage affected the 22 regional air traffic control centres responsible for directing aircraft between airports across the country. At least 600 flights had been diverted, including aircraft sent back to their departure airports or redirected elsewhere. The order to ground all departing US flights was finally lifted after more than five hours. ( AP Photo: Tony Gutierrez ) About 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to depart US airports after 4pm Eastern time on Friday. Planes already in the air were able to continue to their destinations, with authorities prioritising their safe landing. The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a computer system failure at the FAA caused thousands of delays.

events.title: Canadian airports have taken on extra planes and passengers as the outage chaos rippled north
events.summary: A ground stop caused chaos across the US on Friday. Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images Canadian airports took on an influx of planes and passengers amid the now-lifted FAA outage. Toronto Pearson International Airport said it brought in more staff and made a plane parking plan. Cirium, an aviation analytics company, said nearly 1,000 flights were diverted on Friday. While Friday's nationwide ground stop has been lifted , airports in Canada are dealing with the influx of traffic and passengers from canceled and diverted flights. Toronto Pearson International Airport provided status updates on X throughout the day regarding its domestic and international operations. At 9:20 p.m., the airport said the ground stop was over — the FAA had lifted it around 8:30 p.m. — but flights to and from the US would still be disrupted. Still, that doesn't mean the chaos is over — with planes and crews displaced, it could be well into the weekend before things get back on track. Toronto Pearson said it brought in additional staff to manage the crowds and help travelers. "We are increasing staffing across the airport to assist affected passengers," the airport said. "Our support teams are being deployed throughout the terminals, with additional resources available in the U.S. departures area. We are also working closely with airlines and have implemented a parking plan for aircraft." Other airports, including Montreal, Calgary, and Vancouver, also implemented traffic management systems, NAV CANADA, a privately run nonprofit corporation that owns and operates Canada's civil air traffic system, said Friday evening on X . It said during the outage that its systems were "operating normally" and that it issued the programs to "safely manage traffic volumes." events.title: 'Plastic farmers' in Indonesia unaware of the dangers of burning waste
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Researchers investigate health impacts of burning plastic waste in Indonesia Topic: Recycling and Waste Management Plastic waste was regularly burned in limestone kilns in Sumberejo, a village in East Java. ( Supplied: Brawijaya University ) Ahmad Yani spent hours each day sifting through piles of rubbish, searching for recyclable materials to sell to help make ends meet. For decades, his family and other people in his village in East Java in Indonesia would buy truckloads of waste residue from factories recycling imported paper and cardboard. They would spread the waste on the ground, and separate plastics from paper and cardboard. The paper would be sold back to the recycling factories and most of the plastics to industries that needed fuel for furnaces. "It had become a source of livelihood for many low-income residents," Mr Yani said, adding he would make about 300,000 rupiah ($24) a month. Any plastics still left over would be used in his village to fire limestone kilns, to produce building materials to sell or use. Ahmad Yani says plastic waste from overseas has been coming to his village for decades. ( Supplied: Brawijaya University ) Mr Yani said among the rubbish he noticed food sachets and cat and dog food packaging with Australian labels as well as labels of countries in Europe. While burning plastic has helped support the family's livelihood, the smoke from their home and neighbouring households may be having devastating health impacts. He said some people he knew who had operated the limestone kilns had died from respiratory diseases and causes were never determined. Mr Yani said the burning of plastics in his village was no longer happening. It stopped about a year ago. Several local media reported companies had stopped distributing waste to his community to sort, which had sparked anger among locals who lost their source of income. The ABC couldn't independently verify the reasons for the change. But health concerns for people who have been exposed to air pollution from burning plastics remain. Women sort through waste in East Java. ( Supplied: Brawijaya University ) Researchers from the Climate and Health Centre at Brawijaya University were investigating the health impacts of air pollution in East Java when they found locals were burning plastic waste. One of the researchers, Sekar Aqila Salsabilla, said pre-screening tests earlier this year on those in their study produced some worrying findings. She said at least 20 per cent of the more than 4,000 participants across six East Java villages were at high risk of cardiovascular disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Sekar Aqila Salsabilla has been researching the health impacts of air pollution in villages in East Java. ( Supplied: Sekar Aqila Salsabilla ) "When we first entered these communities, one of the most distressing findings was that many people were unaware of the dangers associated with burning plastic waste," said Ms Salsabilla, who worked with more than 30 researchers as part of a broader study, the majority of whom had medical backgrounds. People earning money from sorting waste, known as "plastic farmers", knew their health was "slowly declining" but did not understand the source of the problems, she said. "Despite the income they generate, many do not realise that the long-term health burden they may face is likely to be far greater than the money they earn from handling and burning this waste," Ms Salsabilla said. Environmental activists say Australian plastic waste was in this rubbish heap in East Java, Indonesia, in 2024. ( Supplied: Ecoton ) Most plastic waste was no longer burned in people's homes but rather converted into refuse-derived fuel (RDF) and burned in a designated facility, she said. "But I think this only relocates the problem rather than actually solving it," Ms Salsabilla said, adding the facility still required humans to sort the waste. Emissions from open waste burning, such as burning plastics, include a variety of air pollutants, some of which have particularly harmful effects on both the climate and health, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). "Exposure to these pollutants, whether short or long-term, can lead to adverse health effects such as coughing, skin irritation, respiratory diseases, and other negative outcomes," the WHO says on its website. Environmentalists say plastic waste from Australia is often found in East Java. ( Supplied: Ecoton ) Ms Salsabilla said the waste imported to East Java was coming from places including Australia, the US and Europe.

events.title: India seeks to triple clean energy capacity to 900 gigawatts by 2035, but major hurdles remain
events.summary: India has set an ambitious goal to install enough clean energy to power over 1 billion homes by 2035 BENGALURU, India -- With the United Nations climate talks underway, India has set an ambitious goal of installing enough clean power to supply more than 1 billion homes by 2035, and has approved nearly $20 billion in power grid upgrades to ease bottlenecks that prevent some solar and wind energy from reaching consumers. The world's most populous country and one of the biggest carbon polluters is also among the fastest to expand clean power. Accelerating the shift away from fossil fuels is a key goal of this year’s climate talks, known as COP31, in Turkey. India announced the 900-gigawatt goal in late September. It covers nonfossil power sources, including solar, wind, hydropower and nuclear energy. It is nearly twice India’s existing target of 500 gigawatts of clean power by 2030. India's current clean power capacity of just over 300 gigawatts ranks it third behind China and the United States. Experts say meeting the target could lower electricity costs, curb coal construction and accelerate the transition to clean energy. The push comes as India struggles to use all the renewable electricity it can generate because of inadequate transmission infrastructure . The new goal refers to installed generating capacity, rather than the amount of electricity actually produced. “If the grid doesn’t catch up, then there is no way India can meet this target,” Nikit Abhyankar from the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley, said. “A robust and innovative transmission grid is an absolute must.” The government also approved nearly $20 billion in funding for transmission infrastructure and battery storage under its Green Energy Corridor plan. Economist Ajay Shah of the Mumbai-based XKDR Forum described the transition as the emergence of an Indian “electrostate,” in which electricity increasingly replaces coal and petroleum products. “So now in India you have two assets — not only do you have cheap labor, you also have cheap energy,” Shah said. The shift mirrors a global trend toward cleaner power, even as fossil fuel energy remains a key energy source amid rising electricity demand. Brazil, which ranks close behind India in clean energy capacity, projects renewables will supply nearly 90% of its electricity in the next decade, even as it expands oil and gas production. In the United States, where President Donald Trump supports fossil fuels, electricity demand is expected to grow by 40%, with natural gas remaining a major source. India’s clean energy expansion could help industries replace costly imported fossil fuels with domestically produced electricity. Abhyankar said solar and wind power, even when combined with battery storage, are increasingly cost-competitive with power from coal, oil and natural gas. Lower generation costs could eventually translate into cheaper electricity for households, though utilities also factor in transmission costs and other expenses. However, India’s continued dependence on coal presents a major challenge to its clean energy transition. Coal generated about 71% of the country’s electricity in 2025, according to energy think tank Ember. India’s power planners remain concerned about meeting growing demand and maintaining reliable electricity when solar and wind output fluctuates. Ghanshyam Prasad, chair of the Central Electricity Authority, said earlier this month that India could need as much as 150 gigawatts of additional coal-fired generating capacity by 2035. Ember energy analyst Neshwin Rodrigues said coal will remain important for years, particularly until large-scale batteries can store solar energy to reliably meet demand when the sun isn't shining. Existing coal plants also pose operational challenges. Many cannot quickly reduce output when renewable electricity becomes available, making it difficult for the grid to accommodate growing solar and wind power. Microsoft apologizes for email disruption, says AI agents not responsible Baby buried alive for 24 hours released from the hospital; father charged Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Researchers at Berkeley estimate that beyond approximately 35 gigawatts of coal capacity already under construction, additional coal plants would not be economically necessary under the country's new clean energy goals. Berkeley's Abhyankar warned that newly built coal plants could become stranded assets if the government meets its renewable energy targets. Meeting the 2035 target requires more than building more renewable power plants. Their electricity must be able to reach consumers. India’s rapid clean energy expansion is already testing the grid's limits. Although clean power accounted for 55% of installed power capacity by September, it generated about a third of the country’s electricity in the preceding three months, according to government data.

events.title: Trump's transportation chief demands $50 billion to prevent another huge FAA fiasco
events.summary: US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said that Congress needs to Homeland Security $50 billion to fix the matter at the root. Alex Wong/Getty Images Trump's transportation chief wants $50 billion to replace aging tech blamed for Friday ground stop. Markwayne Mullin and Sean Duffy cited old routers overloading for the repeated failures. Nationwide FAA halt delayed about 10,000 flights, and led to over 6,000 cancellations. The Department of Transportation says it wants $50 billion to replace aging technology that led to Friday's ground stop . In a press conference on Friday evening, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the US has "old switches, old routers" that became overloaded with data and failed, disrupting communications at multiple air-route traffic-control centers. "We should talk to our senators and our members of Congress to say 'we don't deserve this, America,'" Duffy said. "This is the greatest country — by the way, with the greatest president — let's give the money to fix this very real problem." "How many times does this have to happen before Congress gives the money to fix it?" Duffy added. During the press conference, Duffy repeatedly said the administration needs $50 billion to replace the hardware and software that has been around since the 1980s. He added that the system can no longer handle the volume of data moving through it. "We need one complete system. We need someone to come in and build the whole system. Doing it — nickel-and-diming it together — does not work. This is what happens when that takes place, " Mullin said. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures across the US as a safety precaution, while aircraft already in the air continued toward their destinations or were diverted as needed. The ground stop was lifted around 8:15 pm ET on Friday, but the disruption left airlines scrambling to reposition planes and crews. Roughly 10,000 flights were delayed and nearly 5,000 canceled, according to Business Insider's count. The officials said they have seen no evidence that the failure was caused by a cyberattack or system failures linked to artificial intelligence, but added that they are still investigating the precise cause of the outage. events.title: FAA SMART AI system vendor and Microsoft both say ground stop isn't their fault
events.summary: Passengers wait inside Dulles International Airport in Virginia after the FAA grounded flights nationwide. Daniel Heuer/Reuters Authorities are investigating the cause of the major FAA outage. Air Space Intelligence, the company behind the FAA's new SMART system, said it wasn't their fault Microsoft wrote that its products weren't involved either, which the Trump administration confirmed. What caused the nationwide plane chaos? Microsoft and the company behind the FAA's new AI-powered SMART system have something to say: It wasn't us. On Friday afternoon, thousands of flights were delayed after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered all planes grounded nationwide because of communications issues. At a press conference at the White House Friday night, Department of Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or attack caused by "SI" — the administration's preferred term for artificial intelligence. Some online had speculated that the problem was related to the SMART system, a tool from Air Space Intelligence that uses AI to monitor air traffic and prevent delays. In September, POLITICO reported that airline industry veterans were initially nervous about the new system because of the FAA's vague description. The SMART system began rolling out to wider use this week. But on Friday, ASI wrote in an X post that their system wasn't connected to the massive FAA outage. "The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.," the company said . Microsoft had its own problems this week, as a worldwide outage knocked out services like email for hours, snarling the workweek at major companies and inspiring memes from office workers. Some wondered online if Microsoft was connected. It quickly shot those suspicions down. "We have no indication that the FAA's nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services," the company wrote on X . At the press conference Friday night, Mullin confirmed Microsoft was not to blame. Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed antiquated equipment that was "overwhelmed" for the outage. Duffy, at the same press conference, demanded $50 billion from Congress to update FAA equipment. The FAA outage is nearly unprecedented, with only one other nationwide ground stop since federal aviation officials famously froze US airspace during the 9/11 terrorist attacks. The ground stop was lifted on Friday night, but not before more than 5,000 flights were canceled,  according to FlightAware.com . Photos from airports across the country showed crowds forming as passengers were taken off flights and planes lining up on the tarmac. Read the original article on Business Insider
