events.title: Flights slowly resume after US aviation agency lifts nationwide ground stop
events.summary: Transportation secretary Sean Duffy says the airspace is now open and the problem has been identified Chaos at US airports as stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt What to know about the rare nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA Flights in the US have slowly started resuming after being grounded for several hours on Friday due to a major communications outage, but authorities have warned that a return to normal operations will take time. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop about four hours after it was declared on Friday afternoon, delaying or canceling more than 11,000 US flights, according to aviation tracker FlightAware , and throwing airports into sudden chaos. The FAA confirmed the airspace was open in an advisory on its website . “So at 8.15 tonight, Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said. “But it’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon .” Duffy said the federal government had “identified the problem” that brought down the US air traffic control system on Friday and the system “is operational right now”. At a White House briefing on Friday evening, Duffy said the trouble began at 3.36pm, when air traffic control centres experienced ​instability in radar and communications systems. “What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” he said. “Our routers actually got overloaded with data, and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.” But the briefing on Friday evening with Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, quickly turned into a plea for funding from Congress to “fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system”. A notice from the FAA had earlier said the ground stop was imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”. Duffy said more than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the ground stop was issued. Mullin said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage did not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”. “There’s no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against it. It’s just a telecommunications outage as of right now,” he told reporters. The flight grounding caused widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo. Footage from airports around the country showed gates full, with planes waiting on taxiways. Passengers thronged concourses, desperate for information about an outage that had thrown their plans into chaos. As news of the airspace reopening trickled down to airline passengers on Friday evening, not all greeted the news with joy. A woman at John F Kennedy airport in New York who gave her name as simply Lola said she was frustrated. She had already rebooked her flight to Atlanta for another day and was going home. “I don’t like it,” she said. Amid the earlier confusion at US airports, the California governor, Gavin Newsom, called the Trump administration to offer more clarity to passengers who are trying to get to their destinations. “Americans are stuck at airports across the country. They deserve answers, clear updates, and a plan to get home safely. Instead, the Trump Administration is correcting reporters on AI’s “preferred name”. These are not serious people,” Newsom wrote in a post on X, in reference to Mullin correcting a reporter’s use of the term AI earlier in the day. In an interview on CNN, US congressman Ro Khanna said that he is waiting to be briefed on what exactly led to the technical issues and sparked the ground stoppage and for more public-facing communications from the transportation secretary. “There’s a lot of nervousness,” Khanna said of the feeling among passengers. “We’re waiting to be briefed in Congress about what, exactly, has happened. We just need communication from them. If they were there every hour briefing the American public, it would help and give us a sense of a timeline.” According to CNN, the FAA told airlines that the outages are the result of router malfunctions that are believed to have originated at Chicago Midway international airport and rippled across the rest of the US. The FAA said in a statement that they “thoroughly tested” their systems to confirm they were stable and reliable before clearing flights to resume. San Francisco international airport announced in a social media post that flights bound for Hawaii and Asia were cleared to depart. John F Kennedy airport posted on its social media that travelers should confirm flight status with the airline before heading to the airport. US airlines including United, Delta, Southwest and American Airlines announced they were resuming flights on Friday night after the ground stop was lifted.

events.title: FAA lifts ground stop as homeland security chief blames tech upgrades for ‘overwhelming’ antiquated systems and rules out cyberattack for now
events.summary: Millions of U.S. travelers were suddenly thrown into limbo Friday afternoon after the FAA announced a nationwide ground stop at all U.S. airports. Hours later, it was lifted, and federal officials used the incident to highlight the need for more funding to update aging systems. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy initially blamed a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. In a White House press briefing later on Friday night, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed the disruptions to technology upgrades, for “overwhelming” the antiquated equipment. “It’s going to continue to fail,” he warned. Despite recent hacking incidents of freezers in Europe and U.S. military bases, he said it “doesn’t appear” that a cyberattack was involved though he admitted that “there’s nothing certain right now.” Earlier, he ruled out a terrorist attack and said “This isn’t another 9/11.” Just days before the ground stop, the FAA announced it would deploy an AI tool to help air-traffic controllers During the briefing, Duffy also suggested that the problem was related to old equipment being overloaded. “Our fix gives us a pretty good indication that it was a legacy network problem that went down,” he said. Duffy also called on Congress to provide emergency funding to fix the FAA’s aging systems, saying the Trump administration needs another $30 billion, then putting the price tag at $50 billion. Still, the massive disruption comes as airlines in Europe suffered a wave of phony bomb threats this week. While they all appeared to hoaxes, at least one flight was diverted to a military base in France. Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said Friday that Europe appeared to be facing “hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare.” Meanwhile, consumers are still grappling with the aftermath of a Microsoft outage that shut down email, collaboration and AI functions. The company said Friday it had no indication that the ground stop is related to its global outage. The National Weather Service also said there has been no disruption to its radar systems Friday, denying talk online that it had caused the FAA communications issue. The FAA last issued a nationwide ground stop in 2023, when files related to an alert system for pilots was unintentionally deleted. It delayed thousands of flights, but they resumed soon after the disruption. Earlier this year, flights at New York airports were halted when a contractor accidentally cut a fiber communications line in New Jersey. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: FAA ends hours-long nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop Friday night after hours of chaos and thousands of delays and cancellations. Why it matters: The effects of the rare and extreme move will likely ripple through the weekend, with travelers stranded and airlines' planes and crews out of position. Driving the news: In a Friday evening press conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was issued after outdated air traffic control communications equipment suffered from "overloaded data, and they went down." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin added that officials are looking into incompatibilities between that older equipment and newer technology currently being installed. Mullin added that there's no evidence that the problems were tied to a cyberattack. Yes, but: Duffy and Mullin didn't specify the exact initial cause of the problems. "We're still working on the details of what went wrong today," Duffy said. Duffy spent much of the press conference pushing Congress for more funding for air traffic control upgrades. "I can't build things if I don't have money," he told reporters at the White House briefing room. He later added that similar problems could occur again without more funding. Catch up quick: The FAA initially issued the stop due to "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety." "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," the agency said in an earlier statement after the ground stop was issued. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates." Air Route Traffic Control Centers, often simply called "centers," mostly handle high-altitude en route airspace between airports. Between the lines: The FAA has been rolling out a new AI tool designed to help manage airspace congestion, but it's unclear if that system has any connection to Friday's communication issues. The developer of that tool denied any connection. By the numbers: As of 9 p.m. ET, FlightAware reported more than 6,000 cancellations over the course of the day Friday. Many travelers are stuck at the airport or on their planes on the tarmac Friday evening. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: FAA lifts rare nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The FAA on Friday lifted a rare nationwide ground stop that impacted more than 14,500 flights after a major outage affecting the US’ air communications system. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed “an incredibly old air traffic control system,” and said the government didn’t suspect any nefarious causes, such as a terrorist or cyber attack. He said the issues were connected to old equipment that was overloaded, and that flights should start taking off again over the next day. “Hopefully tomorrow, we are going to start to see far better movement,” he said, while trying to reassure travelers that the US remains “the safest system in the world.” The stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, caused widespread disruption and prompted shares in airlines to drop. American Airlines shares dropped more than 2% in after-hours trading, while United shares fell 1.6%. Those airlines are now navigating thousands of rebookings and frustrated passengers. This is only the third time the agency has ever issued such an order. The most recent was in January 2023; before that, air traffic was halted nationwide on Sept. 11, 2001. Duffy used a large portion of a press conference on Friday evening to blame the Republican-controlled Congress for withholding funds for air-traffic control repairs. He urged lawmakers to approve $50 billion to upgrade infrastructure through an emergency funding bill. “I’ve asked, the president’s asked for $30 billion. I want $50 billion,” Duffy said. — Jake Angelo

events.title: College football games could be derailed by the FAA ground stop
events.summary: The Texas Longhorns were among the teams grounded on Friday. David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images A nationwide FAA ground stop is disrupting college football travel ahead of key weekend games. Flights for the Texas Longhorns and Kansas State were grounded, leaving games in jeopardy. Other sports leagues will also likely be impacted. Your plans to watch college football this weekend could be derailed after a nationwide ground stop left some teams in limbo. College football teams across the country that were planning to travel Friday for their weekend games were halted after the Federal Aviation Administration issued the ground stop late in the afternoon. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said there had been a "communication issue" impacting air traffic control centers. The ground stop was lifted at around 8:30 p.m. Eastern time. At a press conference after the ground stop ended , Duffy was asked about the impact to traveling college football. He said "larger movements" would be prioritized, which could include college football teams that often travel on large charter planes. "I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA to schedule their flight times and make sure they can move to make sure we have games going off tomorrow," he said. Prior to the ground stop being lifted, several teams confirmed to Business Insider that they were grounded and still unsure of their travel plans, including the University of Texas and the University of Utah. The Southeastern Conference said it was monitoring the situation and coordinating with teams to determine whether schedule changes are needed. "The Southeastern Conference is aware of the FAA's nationwide ground stop and the potential impact on team travel for this weekend's competitions," the league said in a statement. "We are in close communication with our member institutions to assess potential disruptions and coordinate appropriate responses." The Big 12 conference said in a statement that it was also considering changes to Saturday's game schedule. "The Conference will continue to monitor the travel disruptions alongside its member institutions and provide updates for Saturday's games," the league said. The Texas Longhorns, who were set to travel from Austin to Baton Rouge for their Saturday game against Louisiana State, deplaned after the ground stop and headed back to campus. A spokesperson for the team confirmed to Business Insider that the plane was grounded and that the team was waiting to see when it could leave. The Utah Utes, which were supposed to play Arizona on Saturday, were grounded in Salt Lake City and returned to their football facility, a spokesperson said. Kansas State was grounded and unable to take off Friday evening, a spokesperson said. The team is scheduled to play Texas Christian University on Saturday morning. Baylor, which is set to play Brigham Young on Saturday, was also grounded, a team representative said. Some teams have already made other plans. A spokesperson for Purdue University confirmed the team was traveling to Iowa City via bus Friday evening after its plane had been grounded earlier. The team is scheduled to play the Hawkeyes Saturday evening. College football teams weren't the only athletes left in limbo. College basketball, as well as NHL, NBA, and NFL games, could also be impacted. The University of Southern California said its women's basketball team was grounded in Los Angeles after the ground stop. The team is scheduled to play the University of South Carolina on Sunday morning. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: One Microsoft glitch stalled courts, government offices and police—exposing how fragile America’s systems really are
events.summary: On Thursday, Nov. 12, a widespread Microsoft outage left millions around the world unable to send emails, open Outlook, or use workplace tools like Teams. At first it sounded like a corporate problem: unanswered emails, derailed meetings, employees unable to get work done. Some even welcomed the break. “Thank you Microsoft. Can you do this every Friday?” one X user joked . But the damage reached far beyond the office. Police departments struggled to receive online crime reports, hospitals fell back on other ways to communicate, and some government services were suspended. The disruption exposed how deeply governments and essential public services now depend on a single private company’s technology, and how something as ordinary as an email outage can interfere with the systems people rely on for public safety, health care, and justice. Police, courts, and governments lost a key line of communication In California, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department reported disruptions to its email and other essential communication platforms. The Los Angeles Police Department and the county district attorney’s office also had email problems. Law enforcement elsewhere was hit too. In Florida, St. Lucie County confirmed that its sheriff’s office and fire district were affected. Colorado’s Weld County Sheriff’s Office reported email problems and asked residents to call or text instead. Across the Atlantic, British police forces including Dorset, Cumbria, South Wales, Wiltshire, and Dyfed-Powys had trouble receiving online crime reports, according to The Sun . Some forces said officers and staff could not access Outlook. Emergency phone lines kept working. Courts were not spared either. In Maine, the state’s judicial branch warned that requests for protection orders submitted by email after 12:30 p.m. Thursday might never have reached the courts. In New York City, evictions scheduled for Friday, Nov. 13, were suspended; the city’s Department of Investigation said the decision followed consultation with the Civil Court. In Britain, The Guardian reported that a criminal trial in Manchester was suspended for the day, with jurors sent home and court staff searching for a fax machine. Some civil court judgments were pushed to Monday. In Colorado, the Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office said its jail could not process online bond payments because staff weren’t receiving confirmation emails. Anyone seeking an inmate’s immediate release had to pay in person. The outage also stalled legislative work and city governments. On Capitol Hill, congressional staffers struggled to reach their email and calendars. “There goes a day of legislative work,” one House staffer told Politico . The cities of Austin, Texas , Jacksonville, Florida , Richmond, Virginia , and Laurel, Maryland , also reported email or other Microsoft-related disruptions and pointed residents to other channels. Governments across the Asia-Pacific region were hit as well. Australia’s spy agency, the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, and the Australian Federal Police confirmed they had been affected, according to CNA . Singapore’s Government Technology Agency reported disruptions to government systems, though emergency services and Singpass stayed up. Japan’s Foreign Ministry said it could not send or receive emails, and the Philippines’ Supreme Court warned of delays in email responses and other transactions. Hospitals, airlines, and trains felt it too In Canada, Unity Health Toronto , which runs several hospitals, declared a Code Grey, an alert used for infrastructure failures, after staff had trouble sending and receiving emails. The network stressed that patient and resident care was not affected and its facilities stayed open. Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children, known as SickKids, also warned that some calls and emails to staff might not go through. In Britain, the National Health Service was affected. According to The Guardian , health care workers had trouble accessing emails, appointment information, and patient data, and some services turned to backup systems or paper records. The National Pharmacy Association warned of prescription delays as pharmacies struggled to reach doctors and patients through NHS email. Transportation companies faced a different problem: reaching passengers. Canada’s VIA Rail warned that travelers might not receive trip emails and pointed them to its train tracker and text alerts. Britain’s National Rail advised passengers who couldn’t open emailed tickets to retrieve them through their ticket retailer’s website or app. Airlines including India’s IndiGo and Hong Kong’s Cathay Pacific also reported email problems, although flights generally ran as normal. The hidden costs for everyone else Microsoft said in January that it had more than 450 million paid Microsoft 365 commercial seats, according to the Associated Press , though how many users were affected Thursday is hard to pin down. For people who get verification codes or password-reset links by email, losing Outlook could mean getting locked out of other accounts too. That could hold up online banking, payments, document signing, and other everyday transactions, even when those services were working normally. For small businesses that run much of their day on Microsoft 365, routine tasks like answering customers, scheduling meetings, or sending invoices could grind to a halt. The outage also gave scammers an opening. The University of Sussex warned students and staff about people posing as Microsoft engineers and asking for passwords or other login details under the pretense of fixing email. The full economic cost, including lost productivity and missed business, remains unclear. Why governments keep relying on one provider In 2022, Google, which sells a competing productivity suite, commissioned a survey warning about the risks of an IT “monoculture,” in which governments rely heavily on one company’s technology. Four years later, this outage showed how far that dependence has spread. The survey, conducted by Public Opinion Strategies, found that 84% of D.C.-area government employees primarily used Microsoft products. A 2021 report by Omdia , co-commissioned by Google and the Computer & Communications Industry Association, cited an earlier estimate that Microsoft held 85% of the U.S. government’s office productivity software market. Microsoft even offers Office 365 Government , a version of its suite built specifically for government agencies. Jeanette Manfra, then Google Cloud’s head of risk and compliance, wrote that more than half of respondents believed the government’s dependence on Microsoft made it more vulnerable to hacking or cyberattacks. events.title: Albanese, Bowen caught talking phones and 'dicks' in hot-mic gaffe
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts PM Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen caught on hot mic at COP31 climate summit A private exchange between Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen was inadvertently recorded at the COP31 summit in Türkiye. The Prime Minister's office said the pair were joking between meetings. Mr Albanese has travelled to the Philippines for the ASEAN summit, while Mr Bowen remains in Türkiye. A conversation between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen about phone radiation and "dicks" has been caught on camera on the sidelines of a UN conference. Mr Albanese's office said the pair was sharing a "joke" between meetings when the exchange was recorded by Australian media at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye. The comments were captured shortly before a business roundtable spruiking renewable energy transition investment opportunities in Australia began overnight on Friday. Anthony Albanese left Türkiye shortly after a business roundtable. ( AAP ) Cameras were rolling ahead of the event during which time Mr Albanese and Mr Bowen were privately chatting to each other. Mr Albanese put his phone in his jacket pocket and — as he did so — told Mr Bowen he had heard it was better to store the device away from the heart because "it can interfere with your rhythm". Mr Bowen responded in a joking tone if it was because the phone was "a little bit radioactive". The prime minister laughed, saying the idea "makes absolute sense". Mr Bowen then responded he was more conscious about putting his phone in his pants pocket. Mr Albanese asked, "Because of your dick?" The pair laughed and Mr Bowen agreed, adding it was "arguably more important than the heart". Hot-mic gaffe came ahead of roundtable The exchange, which did not appear to be overheard by anyone in the room but was captured by a news camera microphone preparing to record the opening remarks at the event, was later broadcast by Channel 7 after it was noticed in production. A spokesperson for Mr Albanese's office said, "They were having a joke in between meetings." Labor frontbencher Murray Watt agreed that the comments were made in jest. "This is really just about people having a joke," he said. While Mr Watt laughed off a question about where he keeps his own phone, and defended Australia's presence and performance at COP31. "I know there's been a lot of criticism from some quarters about every aspect of this COP, but the reality is participating in and in fact leading the discussions at COP is in Australia's national interest," he said. During the official proceedings of the business roundtable, the prime minister made a pitch to international investors to back Australia's clean energy transition. "If you're an investor, there's nowhere you'd rather be than Australia," he said. Mr Albanese said having abundant renewable resources, critical minerals and a stable investment environment meant Australia was well placed to capitalise on the multi-trillion-dollar industry. The prime minister left Türkiye shortly after the roundtable to travel to the Philippines for the ASEAN summit in Manila. Mr Bowen has remained in Antalya, where he is playing a critical role as the co-president of negotiations for COP31. The White House said that Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday. Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19. The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling "The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified. "In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there." events.title: Air traffic control, phone systems and emails are all down following China’s AI espionage scandal — is there a common answer?
events.summary: An old English proverb anchored in superstition from ancient Greek and Roman beliefs is that bad luck always comes in threes, but that does not mean bad luck was always random. The United States has now experienced two debilitating, unprecedented blackouts across critical infrastructure in two days. The timing is almost too coincidental to be a coincidence – coming on the heels of the removal of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO amidst an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, widespread recriminations about chip exports to China, and demands for tighter export controls and more hawkish policies against China. Could China and other hostile foreign actors be targeting U.S. infrastructure? It’s too early to know for sure, but the country deserves far more transparent answers than we have received so far. An extraordinary timeline, too coincidental to be a coincidence? At 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday , November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded every departing flight in America, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the third nationwide ground stop ever ordered. The first came on Sept. 11, 2001; the second more than 20 years later, on Jan. 11, 2023. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy would say only that “a communication issue” had struck every one of the 22 centers that guide planes across the country, and that technicians were investigating. A subsequent press conference by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did little to reassure anyone, with no answers about what happened and little reassurance that it would be fixable anytime soon, with airports sending travelers home and communicating that flight cancellations would persist for many hours at a minimum, if not days. It was the second time in two days that critical infrastructure the country cannot function without simply stopped, potentially for very nefarious reasons. The day before, Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and Copilot went dark in 74 countries and stayed down for hours. Both blackouts struck within a day-and-a-half of the most damaging China espionage story in years. Two blackouts, measured in billions in lost economic activity and inconvenience The last nationwide ground stop, in 2023, lasted about 90 minutes and still delayed more than 10,000 flights and canceled 1,300 . Friday’s lasted hours with no resolution imminent on the horizon. At the four-hour point of this latest ground stop, 10,243 flights were already delayed and 3,234 cancelled, with flights grounded not only at single regional airports but across the entire nation, suggesting systemic breakdowns rather than localized issues. Microsoft’s failure began at 11:17 a.m. ET on Thursday and spread across 19 Microsoft 365 services . Within an hour, complaints about Outlook were running at more than 2,000 times their normal level . Microsoft counts more than 450 million paid commercial seats , with many millions of those users locked out entirely from their inboxes and other critical services. The casualty list reads like a roll call of essential services: the U.S. House of Representatives was substantively incapacitated; a federal appeals court that could not send or receive email; Britain’s Parliament and its National Health Service, where the failure threatened patients’ prescriptions; Australia’s spy agency and federal police were sent offline as well. When a botched CrowdStrike update crashed 8.5 million machines in 2024, the Fortune 500 alone lost an estimated $5.4 billion . One risk adviser already puts Microsoft’s bill in the billions for Australia alone , not to mention the lost economic value in the U.S. or the rest of the world. This was the first time in history so many users were locked out for so long – with shifting and unsatisfactory explanations. Similarly, this is the first time in global aviation history where there has been a nationwide ground stop with no satisfactory, clear explanation and immediate fix. Reassurance first, explanation later does not work as a crisis playbook in these extraordinary circumstances Microsoft wrote the playbook for false comfort. For a full day it insisted there was “no indication” of malicious activity while its own bulletins showed it did not know what had broken. If it did not know for sure, then how could they know for sure there was no indication of anything malicious amidst shifting explanations? First it blamed elevated load, then servers that had unexpectedly dropped out . It found no recent change that lined up with the failure. Hours later, it was rolling back a network change that did . Early Friday, engineers were still trying to “pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx.” Only on Friday afternoon did Microsoft name a culprit : a flaw introduced during a network capacity upgrade, “not related to cyber.” That sequence is as nonsensical as it is falsely reassuring. No patient would trust a doctor who swears it is not an infection before he can diagnose the fever. You cannot rule out what you cannot yet explain, and nobody can feel particularly reassured from this disturbing sequence of events and shifting explanations. Suspicious timing and a 15-year track record On Thursday morning, Nvidia, whose board failures we dissected in Fortune this week , announced the resignation of Jensen Huang , the chip industry’s loudest advocate for selling to China, after he admitted an affair with a businesswoman U.S. officials suspect of spying for Beijing . Beijing has been vocal in calling it a smear amidst a rapid escalation of U.S.-China tensions. Lawmakers in both parties are demanding testimony and tighter export controls . Within three hours, inboxes went dark from Capitol Hill to Canberra. A day later, planes stopped and were grounded. Could that really be a coincidence? Perhaps we are being too conspiratorial, but there is a certain uncanny resemblance to Beijing’s favorite playbook, which is to divert from negative news stories by shutting down internet services and diverting public attention. For example, in 2011, a petition to free Ai Weiwei got Change.org knocked offline . In 2012, exposés of the family fortunes of Xi Jinping and Wen Jiabao got Bloomberg and The New York Times blocked in China and targeted by hackers . In 2014, as Hong Kong marched for democracy, a newspaper and a voting site were buried under one of the largest attacks the internet had ever seen . In 2015, China’s “Great Cannon” hammered GitHub for days for hosting banned news. In 2019, Telegram and the LIHKG forum were swamped as Hong Kong marched again. In 2022, news of the zero-COVID protests on Twitter drowned in a deluge of spam . Maybe this pattern of untimely hacks was merely a coincidence – or could it have been more than coincidence? Microsoft knows this adversary better than anyone. events.title: SpaceX launches Starship in key test flight of massive rocket
events.summary: SpaceX launched its 15th Starship test flight on Friday. In the test flight, Elon Musk's company tried but failed to recover both stages of the massive Starship rocket, with the booster splashing down in the Gulf of Mexico and exploding. Starship is key to SpaceX's plans to grow its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center. In a key test flight on Friday, SpaceX tried but failed to recover both stages of its massive Starship rocket. The rocket lifted off from the company's South Texas launch facility at 4:47 p.m. local time, or 5:47 p.m. ET. SpaceX had to abort its plans to catch and reuse the booster, instead diverting it to splash into the Gulf of Mexico, where it burst into flames. Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship mission to date, was the first time Elon Musk's company attempted to catch both the booster and upper stage, or spacecraft portion, of the massive rocket. Earlier on Friday, SpaceX obtained authorization from the Federal Aviation Administration. Hours later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after reporting communication problems affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers. The SpaceX license wasn't effected by the flight stoppage, a spokesperson for the FAA told CNBC. The upper stage of the Starship continued its trajectory into orbit after the company failed to catch and salvage the booster. The rocket is expected to fly around the Earth fourteen times in total. If successful, SpaceX will land the upper stage back at its Starbase facility on Saturday. Starship's success is critical to SpaceX and its ambitions to eventually lift cargo and people to the surface of the Moon and Mars. In the near-term, SpaceX needs to send more satellites into orbit to expands its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center. The company's constellation already includes over 11,000 active satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket has the capacity to carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, the company has said, representing about 20 times the capacity of earlier Falcon 9 rockets. In the previous Starship test flight, the company released 26 v3 satellites, and released another 26 in the Friday test flight, with the goal of "Starlink becoming 51% of the internet," SpaceX said in a post on X. When it comes to launches, "SpaceX is likely a full decade ahead of peers on this front," William Blair analysts wrote in a note out on Friday. "Even if tonight's catch is unsuccessful, a delay by a few months is not that consequential." Meanwhile, SpaceX is facing fresh criticism over restrictions imposed on its Starshield satellite internet service in Ukraine. Starshield is built on Starlink technology and is the military-tier of SpaceX's satellite internet service. Earlier this week, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country's military forces had experienced limits on Starshield without warning again, harming their ability to defend against Russia's ongoing aerial attacks. Similar limits on Starshield in Ukraine were temporarily imposed last month . Some U.S. senators have condemned the restrictions, and urged Congress to investigate SpaceX .

events.title: Mississippi River cruise crash has no fatalities, critical injuries
events.summary: Thirty-two people are in local hospitals and all passengers and crew are accounted for after a tanker collided with a Mississippi River cruise ship near the Port of New Orleans , officials said Friday. The big picture: With approximately 180 people on the ship, the rescue of all aboard is "truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a press conference. What they're saying: While the investigation remains ongoing, officials said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker appeared to have lost control, causing it to collide with the cruise ship. As passengers were disembarking after the collision, the cruise ship began to sink and eventually toppled over and flipped — leaving people in the cold water. The first 87 passengers got off while the ship was still afloat, Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said. She added it "was normal conditions" on the river and that there wasn't a high current. "I've never been prouder of a group of people than those people that came off of that boat," Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said. Catch up quick: The American Heritage, a vessel operated by American Cruise Lines, had docked for passengers to disembark at the port Friday afternoon about two hours before it was hit, according to a press release from the Port of New Orleans. A city spokesman confirmed to Axios that the riverboat had rolled onto its side in the water, which social media videos appear to corroborate. Zoom out: The Atlantic Asphalt tanker is registered in the Marshall Islands, and had arrived at the Port of New Orleans on Nov. 11. Per data from myshiptracking.com, the tanker began its current journey in Paulsboro, New Jersey, in late October. Zoom in: The tanker was immobilized on the river Friday at about 2pm CT, with two tugs positioned on either side. Another dozen vessels were in the water nearby as a helicopter roamed overhead and sirens rang out over the water. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: Photos show trouble at airports nationwide as FAA grounds all flights
events.summary: A passenger walks past a board displaying delayed flights at JFK International in New York City after the FAA issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" on Friday. Angelina Katsanis/Reuters Passengers are being taken off planes nationwide. The FAA ordered all planes grounded. The Transportation Secretary cited a "communications" issue at all air-traffic control centers. It's a bad night to be traveling. Passengers are being deplaned, and flights are delayed after the FAA grounded every flight nationwide because of what it called "extraordinary circumstances." Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was ordered because of a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." Officials have not yet said what caused the communication issue. As the ground stop became a multi-hour ordeal, passengers have begun to crowd boarding areas, have been asked to leave flights, and are scrambling to find their luggage. 'All flights have been halted' Passengers wait at McGhee Tyson Airport after the FAA issued a ground stop for all flights across the U.S. on Nov. 13. Adam Sparks/News Sentinel/Reuters Boarding areas began to fill up at airports across the country. On Friday afternoon, the FAA said in a post on X that there has been a temporary telecommunications outage. "Out of an abundance of caution, all flights have been halted," said the FAA. "Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis." The exact cause remains unclear A person stands in front of a departures board at Logan international airport after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety." Brian Snyder/Reuters Flight boards are flashing red and orange across all major airports. Transportation officials have not yet said why they issued the ground stop. The FAA is prepared to make a system update Passengers wait inside the main terminal after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" following the agency's earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues at Dulles International Airport, in Dulles, Virginia, US, November 13, 2026. REUTERS/Daniel Heuer Daniel Heuer/Reuters In some airports, stranded passengers are congregating in terminals as security check lines grow longer. The outage occurred the same day the FAA rolled out SMART , a new AI-powered tool designed to help manage air traffic. Air Space Intelligence, the company behind SMART, said Friday's disruption was not "based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC." Lines are growing in many airports Queues are forming at the Salt Lake City airport after passengers were told to disembark a flight to Chicago. Jon Lett Jon Lett, a passenger who was traveling from the Salt Lake City Airport to Kansas City, told Business Insider that everyone on his flight has been told to disembark and wait. Lett said that, though the mood among passengers remains "chill," there is no telling whether his flight will be able to depart anytime soon. Planes are parked on the tarmac Planes wait on the tarmac at Chicago O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, on November 13, 2026. KAMIL KRZACZYNSKI / AFP via Getty Images Photos show planes parked back-to-back at Chicago O'Hare International Airport. National ground stops are historically rare for the FAA. In January 2023, the FAA halted flights because of an outage involving its pilot alert system. Before that, nationwide air traffic was halted following the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Traffic outside the airports also began to pile up Traffic piles up outside a terminal at Dulles International in Virginia after the FAA issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" on Friday. Daniel Heuer/Reuters Passengers are stranded Air travelers wait inside the Frederick W. Smith International Airport in Memphis after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, 2026. Chris Day / The Commercial Appeal/Reuters Some passengers are settling in and preparing for a night spent at the airport. Air travelers could be seen camping out on the floor and napping. Luggage is slow to appear People line up to try and retrieve luggage during delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on November 13, 2026 in the Queens borough of New York City. Adam Gray/Getty Images Lines to collect luggage are also growing in some airports. It is unclear whether they are arriving passengers or travelers giving up on their flight for the day. Travelers are left sitting in the plane People wait whilst onboard a plane at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Washington, DC Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP via Getty Images Not everyone has been ordered to disembark. Photos showed some passengers sitting in unmoving planes. The FAA has not issued any updates Emmanuel Romero, relaxes on the ground as his daughters Arianne Romero, left, Hannah Romero, right, and wife, Alejandra Para, wait in the terminal at St. Louis Lambert International Airport to hear if their flight to California will be cancelled on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. The family's flight is affected by the nationwide ground stop the FAA issued to all flights Friday afternoon. The family was in Missouri to see Hannah graduate from her Advanced Individual Training (AIT) with the Army at Fort Leonard Wood. (Photo by David Carson/St. Louis Post-Dispatch via Getty Images) David Carson/St. Louis Post-Dispatch via Getty Images As of 8 p.m., the FAA has not issued any new updates on when the ground stop will end. Some exhausted passengers with canceled flights are lying down on the floor to rest. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse
events.summary: Flight 15 expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over 22 hours, before company catches it at Starbase, Texas SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket, but ultimately fell short. Starship, the world’s largest rocket, standing at 407ft, is expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase in south Texas . The rocket, which is on its 15th flight, is composed of two elements: the lower booster, with 33 Raptor engines that fired off during takeoff, and the Starship at the top. As smoke plumes wafted from the launch site, SpaceX employees erupted into cheers. SpaceX had planned for both components to return to its tower, but the booster, named Super Heavy, was aborted, and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico. The cause of that diversion remains unknown. “That certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” said Kate Tice, SpaceX’s director of quality management, but she noted the booster’s return was in line with “rigorous safety checks”. Early in the webcast, SpaceX simulated the return. The entire rocket was expected to be grabbed in the launch tower’s “chopstick” mechanical arms. Friday’s test did not rise to the double-catch mantle, which Elon Musk had described early in November as a “critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary”. Still, the flight is still poised to mark another milestone for the company. If all goes to plan, it would be the first time SpaceX has caught the rocket’s 171ft upper stage. Previous tests focused on the retrieval of the booster. The Starship, meanwhile, has continued to sail through space at over 26,000 km/h at an altitude of 270km. The launch went on as scheduled despite a nationwide ground stop that disrupted hundreds of flights. Flights to the west coast from Hawaii were temporarily paused, then resumed on Friday due to space debris from the launch, according to the island’s transportation agency. As in the past, Starship carried satellites for Starlink, SpaceX’s internet service wing, three of which were fitted with cameras to analyze the rocket’s heat shield. The data plays a role in determining if the spacecraft is ready to return. SpaceX chief executive Musk has sought to advance Starship’s “rapid reusability” as a vehicle, which he hopes will take humans to the moon and, controversially, to Mars. Nasa has contracted SpaceX, along with Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin, to provide the lunar landers that will return astronauts to the moon in 2028. Musk has cast his reusable rocket as a buffer against the enormous costs associated with future space travel. SpaceX has launched a flurry of test flights in recent years, some of which have resulted in explosions that signaled major design flaws. In September, the most recent flight test, SpaceX notched a victory, sending the spacecraft into Earth’s orbit for the first time , although its engine failed during the ascent.

events.title: Questions remain after Nvidia CEO's departure
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Despite Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, questions remain over the whole affair Jensen Huang was one of the world's most influential figures in the tech and AI industry. ( Reuters: Mike Blake ) Mounting speculation over an espionage plot against Jensen Huang and his multiple alleged affairs reached a tipping point on Friday, when the tech billionaire quit as Nvidia's CEO. The controversy centred around his relationship with Alice Huang, who US intelligence reportedly suspects to be a Chinese spy, before claims emerged he had another two extra-marital affairs. While Mr Huang's resignation puts an end to his long reign over Nvidia, questions about America's national security and the US president's knowledge of the whole saga remain. China's foreign ministry said allegations of spying in relation to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang (no relation) were "unsubstantiated" and "smears against China". ( Reuters: CTI ) When reports of an espionage plot against Mr Huang first emerged almost a week ago, top Republicans called on the tech executive to front Congress later this month. Senator Tim Scott reiterated those demands after Mr Huang's resignation, saying there were "serious concerns" to address. Separately the chairs of three House committees — the foreign affairs panel, the China select committee and the intelligence committee — wrote to Mr Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter requiring them to appear for closed-door transcribed interviews on December 1 and 2. After news broke of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset Nvidia's value plummeted. Why? Mr Huang and Mr Teter have not publicly commented on the requests, but they could face subpoenas to compel their appearances. "There are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately," the three committee chairs wrote in the letter. Mr Huang is also yet to comment publicly after reports emerged he allegedly had another two extra-marital affairs — both with Nvidia employees. His last statement was on Sunday, local time, when he admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife of over 40 years but did not name who he had been intimate with. In that statement, he said he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security". Meanwhile, Nvidia and Mr Huang are facing a ‌proposed class action accusing them ‌of ⁠defrauding ‌shareholders . Questions for the US administration Next to Mr Huang, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been called on to testify in front of Congress on concerns he did not do enough to restrict AI chip shipments to China. In December 2025 Donald Trump allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced chips to China in exchange for a cut of the sales, after Mr Huang argued that restrictions only accelerated Beijing's own AI development. That was despite concerns from both sides of Congress about China's access to the technology. Howard Lutnick is facing pressure over whether the US government was properly overseeing Nvidia's exports to China. ( Reuters: Elizabeth Frantz ) Mr Lutnick has also been criticised for the administration's refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a trade blacklist. In June, Reuters reported the Trump administration had held ⁠off adding more than 100 other companies flagged as national security risks to the list. The US ⁠has not added to the list since October 2025, the longest stretch between new postings in more than a decade. Previous reports said that Mr Lutnick's US Commerce Department had not blacklisted new Chinese companies for fear of escalating tensions between the US and China. Under-Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler has been called on to testify at a December 3 hearing as well. The Commerce Department did not respond to Reuters' request for comment. In America's pursuit to lead the AI race, Mr Huang had become a close ally of Mr Trump and was one of the few people known to have a direct line to him. He has visited the White House at least five times during Mr Trump's second term, is part of a council advising the president on science and technology, and accompanied Mr Trump on a trip to Beijing in May. The Washington Post reported in mid-October that Nvidia committed $US25 million ($36.7 million) for Mr Trump's contentious White House ballroom project, while the president disclosed buying and selling Nvidia stock earlier this year. The New York Times reported Mr Trump was briefed on intelligence findings about a suspected espionage effort against Mr Huang about a year ago, and took no action.

events.title: Regional bands say it's now cheaper to do a gig in London than interstate
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Touring Australia no longer tenable for internationally-renowned local bands as regional airfares soar It now costs Arnhem Land band King Stingray more to fly to gigs interstate than to shows in the US. ( Supplied ) Managers of internationally-renowned Aussie bands say high airfares are pricing regional artists out of the market. It comes as the Productivity Commission this week revealed a widening gap between regional and metropolitan airfares. Yothu Yindi manager Alan James says travel costs will put emerging artists out of business before their careers have taken off. With the cost of regional airfares soaring, musicians and band managers say touring has become untenable for both famous bands and emerging artists from regional Australia. An interim Productivity Commission report released this week revealed a significant price gap between regional and metropolitan flight routes. It found long regional and remote flights cost 67 per cent more on average than major city routes, while short regional flights cost 173 per cent more per kilometre. Alan James says high airfares are pricing Yothu Yindi "out of the market" for live music. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Yothu Yindi manager Alan James said the cost of travel had forced the internationally-renowned band from Arnhem Land to turn down shows within Australia. "It's $5,200 return from Gove to Brisbane, it would be cheaper for us to go do a concert in London than it would be to do a concert in a capital city of Australia," he said. Yothu Yindi bassist Stuart Kellaway — who now manages fellow Arnhem Land rock band King Stingray — said the next generation band's recent flights to shows in the United States cost less than domestic flights. Yothu Yindi played the 2025 Garma Festival but had to turn down shows interstate. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) "We've had to turn down three or four shows in the past month or so because it just wasn't going to work financially with the airfare components," he said. Mr Kellaway the sky-high airfares were affecting the ability even of artists in the prime of their careers to make a living. "With streaming and everything else, gigs are one of the last, decent income streams for bands," he said. Limited options limiting opportunities Mr James said while all bands were impacted by the exorbitant airfares, for new artists in particular, the costs could make sustainable careers in the music industry impossible. "If you're an emerging group, you've got no shot, you're out of the business," he said. "It really means for musicians, if you're not based in a capital city, then you're not in the market anymore." King Stingray manager Stuart Kellaway (third from left) says bands based outside capital cities are "not in the market anymore". ( ABC / Matt Garrick ) Both Mr James and Mr Kellaway said they had noticed a decline in the number of airlines servicing Arnhem Land throughout the course of Yothu Yindi's career. Their observations align with the findings of the Productivity Commission's report, which noted competition in regional aviation was severely limited. Skyrocketing regional airfares hurting patients Fears FIFO specialists will soon need to pass rising flight costs onto vulnerable country patients. Several airlines have reduced NT services recently, leaving flights between Darwin and capitals such as Sydney, Adelaide and Canberra serviced only by Qantas and its subsidiary Jetstar. events.title: Nvidia’s next CEO: Some prediction market traders bet Jensen Huang will make a comeback
events.summary: Nvidia has yet to name a permanent successor to Jensen Huang, with some in the industry calling him irreplaceable. Some Kalshi traders bet Nvidia may rehire Jensen Huang as permanent CEO by 2028, even after his Nov 12 resignation. Ian Buck leads the market at 33%. Huang stepped down after reports of three affairs and admitted ties to Alice Huang, who is suspected by the US of spying for China. Supporters, including Shaun Maguire, Elon Musk and Donald Trump, praised him as vital to AI leadership. Nvidia faces big risks because it has no succession plan and 60 executives report to Huang. Shares rebounded after the shock exit, but Washington scrutiny and investor concern remain. SINGAPORE – Jensen Huang has stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive , but some traders on the prediction market Kalshi are betting that the chipmaker will name him its next permanent CEO before 2029. Nvidia has yet to name a permanent successor to one of the AI industry’s most influential leaders, with some in the industry calling him irreplaceable. On Kalshi, which is regulated in the US but banned in Singapore, the implied odds of Nvidia naming Huang as its next permanent chief executive by the end of 2028 rose as high as 15% on the evening of Nov 13, before falling to around 7%. Nvidia executive Ian Buck is currently in the lead, with a 33% chance on Kalshi of becoming Nvidia’s next CEO. Buck is vice-president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing at Nvidia. He leads its multibillion-dollar data centre business, which supplies AI chips and software to major tech companies worldwide. Kalshi put the odds of Colette Kress getting the permanent job at 13%. Kress is Nvidia’s chief financial officer and was made interim CEO following Huang’s resignation on Nov 12. She is tied with Rene Haas, chief executive of British chip design company Arm Holdings. Other executives Kalshi traders are betting on include Apple chief hardware officer Johny Srouji, Palo Alto Networks chairman and CEO Nikesh Arora, Nvidia executive vice-president Jay Puri, and AMD chairman and CEO Lisa Su. Puri oversees Nvidia’s global sales, business development and partnerships. Tech executives, investors and fans have voiced support for Huang, who stepped down following reports of three affairs. He has admitted to being involved with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based, Alibaba-backed data centre firm Megaspeed . She is suspected by the US of spying for China. “Jensen is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, wrote in an X post on Nov 8. He concluded that Nvidia’s Huang is “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership”. About an hour later, Elon Musk quoted the post, noting: “I agree.” Maguire added on Nov 12 that Huang’s ousting “will leave a huge void, with the loss of a technical, aggressive, founder-CEO. “The American AI community needs to work double-time in an attempt to fill this void.” Even US President Donald Trump called Huang before he stepped down, urging him to keep fighting for his job , according to The New York Times, quoting sources familiar with the call. After Huang announced his resignation, Trump wrote in a Nov 12 Truth Social post : “Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – Tim Cook of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!” On prediction market Polymarket, trading implied a 6% chance that Nvidia would name Apple executive chairman Tim Cook as its next permanent chief executive by the end of 2028. There is also a 11% probability on Polymarket that Nvidia does not find a CEO by Dec 31, 2028. Regardless of who takes over, Nvidia’s stakes are high because so much of the AI industry relies on chips, delivered by a company that Huang co-founded, transformed and led for the past 30 years. A total of 60 executives across the firm report directly to him, and there is no succession plan. Huang’s departure therefore leaves Nvidia investors weighing several risks, Saxo UK investor strategist Neil Wilson said in a Nov 13 note. Nvidia is “about to find out whether Huang’s grip on the company and flat organisational structure was effectively storing up trouble”, said Wilson. While a successor could keep Nvidia on the same course, Huang’s detailed knowledge of its products and his hands-on management style is unique and would be hard to replicate. Wilson also pointed to scrutiny in Washington, citing reported US Justice Department inquiries involving Megaspeed and Alice Huang, and a request by three House committee chairs for a closed-door briefing on Nov 18 over national security concerns. He expects Nvidia’s relationship with Washington to become more difficult, even with US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s support. Investors, however, appear to think otherwise.

events.title: What to know about the rare nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA
events.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop for all planes due to take off in the US, delaying and canceling thousands of flights The US Federal ⁠Aviation Administration said in a statement that the nationwide halt to departures and delays to landings at all US airports that began at about 4pm ET on Friday was caused by “a temporary telecommunications outage”. “Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis,” the FAA added. Here is what we know about the rare nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. 1. What caused this? The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8.15pm ET Friday. In a White House briefing, Markwayne Mullin, homeland security secretary, and Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, appeared to suggest that the cause of Friday’s outage was that older technology became overwhelmed with data after new technology was introduced. The FAA announced three days ago that a new air traffic management tool, known as Smart, was activated at all 22 air route traffic control centers in the US. 2. How did the old technology cause this? “What it appears to be right now is”, Mullin said, “as secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology and that new equipment, new technology just wasn’t- it was overwhelming the older system, which is why secretary Duffy made it very clear the patchwork doesn’t work. We need one complete system. We need someone to come in and build the whole system. Doing it nickel- and dime-ing it together does not work. This is what happens when that takes place. ” Duffy denied the new Smart system, which incorporates artificial intelligence, had caused the problem. 3. How do we know this wasn’t a cyber-attack? Mullin said at the briefing: “We’ve seen zero evidence that this was a cyber-attack.” “Now, when we start looking at cyber threats, cyber-attacks, typically some people are going to raise their hand up and say, ‘hey, we did that.’ There’s no chatter. We haven’t seen any footprints, as you would say, or identifications of people that got into the system,” Mullin added. “It appears that this was mechanically driven.” 4. How many flights were affected? There have been 10,543 flight delays within, into, or out of the US so far, according to the website FlightAware , and 3,580 cancellations. Duffy said that more than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the ground stop was issued. 5. What is a ground stop? A ground-stop order by the FAA requires that aircraft remain on the ground and bars them from taking off. Planes already in the air are usually allowed to remain in the air. The FAA has more than 14,000 air traffic controllers who handle the more than 44,000 flights that take off from airports across the US each day, according to FAA data. 6. What is the government doing to ensure this doesn’t happen again? Duffy and Mullin used Friday night’s briefing as a chance to plead for funding from Congress. “The president for the last year has been asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system,” Duffy said. “I want Congress to give us emergency funding,” Duffy said later. “I want $50bn. President Trump is a builder. He is going to build this network, and deliver for the American people.” Both men peppered their remarks with lavish praise for Donald Trump , who was curiously quiet during the crisis that lasted for more than four hours. Last year, ​Congress ​approved $12.5bn to fix ​the FAA’s ageing communications system, and ​on Friday ‌the FAA ​and ​White House asked Congress for another $30.1bn to address other issues. 7. Has this happened before? This is just the second nationwide ​ground stop of all departures since the 9/11 attacks. The previous one came in January 2023, when the FAA paused all ⁠domestic departures for less than two hours.

events.title: Super Micro, run by Jensen Huang’s friend, says Megaspeed was ‘never’ its customer
events.summary: Super Micro Computer says that Megaspeed, the Singapore company at the center of the spy scandal that brought down Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, has never been one of its customers. The assertion by Super Micro, whose cofounder was arrested earlier this year on charges of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, comes as observers look for possible connections between two companies whose business dealings with Nvidia are under scrutiny. “Megaspeed is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer,” a spokesperson told Fortune in a statement. The company also said it “has been responsive to inquiries and has fully cooperated with U.S. and Taiwanese officials, while also voluntarily providing information and engaging with all requests from Singapore authorities to date.” Supermicro’s statement came after Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said Thursday that the Singapore Police Force and Customs had opened investigations into Megaspeed and Alice Huang, a former top executive there who had an affair with Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, and who some authorities believe was acting as a spy for China. Singapore authorities said they had asked Supermicro for information and had received only “limited cooperation.” The ministry said the Supermicro cooperation matter was first raised with U.S. authorities on July 7, 2025 and then repeatedly afterward with the Department of Justice and the FBI. Alice Huang, who isn’t related to ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, drew intense scrutiny after reports that she and the Nvidia co-founder were having an affair, which came out before his resignation on Wednesday. The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Manhattan is reportedly looking into whether entities linked to her helped smuggle Supermicro hardware with Nvidia GPUs into China. Multiple probes have been initiated into export control breaches related to Alice and her businesses, including Megaspeed. Jensen, Nvidia, and Supermicro have not been charged with wrongdoing.  However, Jensen’s downfall has cast a dark cloud over Supermicro at an intensely complicated moment for the hardware and liquid cooling tech company. One of Supermicro’s three co-founders, Charles Liang, is a longtime friend of Jensen’s and the two both hail from Taiwan. They’ve shared the stage at multiple massive Computex tech events in Taiwan, including in 2024 when Jensen was photographed having drinks with Alice. Both cofounded their companies in 1993 and Supermicro’s close relationship with Nvidia has been a boon for customers hoping to be first in line for the latest generations of high-performing chips Nvidia churns out.  Another Supermicro cofounder, Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, was arrested and charged in March along with two others for allegedly working to route about $2.5 billion in servers with Nvidia’s H200 and B200 GPUs into China through a Southeast Asian front company. Liaw has pleaded not guilty, and his trial has been pushed to March 2027. A co-defendant, Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, pleaded guilty in October. Supermicro has said it was a victim of the scheme and conducted an internal investigation finding no evidence current members of senior management were aware of the alleged conspiracy. Supermicro’s stock fell nearly 4% this week. In August, prosecutors in Keelung, Taiwan indicted nine people over 130 Supermicro servers with Nvidia B300 chips that were allegedly cleared for shipment using forged data-center inspection records . Some 74 of the servers made it to China and customs intercepted the rest. The defendants include two former Supermicro Taiwan employees and a former Nvidia Taiwan employee, who face breach of trust and document forgery charges. In Taiwan, unauthorized AI chip exports to China aren’t currently considered a criminal offense, which is why the charges relate to forgery and breach-of-trust charges. Neither Nvidia nor Supermicro was charged. The company said in a statement that it “maintains a robust compliance program and continues to work closely with authorities and industry partners to combat diversion and help protect American innovation.” The company has disclosed a grand jury subpoena and inquiries from the SEC, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and foreign authorities.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons' firm has deep ties to the chipmaker
events.summary: Cantor Fitzgerald’s reported Nvidia share count fell by nearly half between September 2025 and March 2026, a CNBC analysis found. That was the period when, according to Axios, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faced pressure from administration officials to address suspected smuggling of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China. The Wall Street firm, which Lutnick formerly chaired and is now run by his sons, maintained extensive commercial ties to Nvidia, helping arrange billions of dollars in financing for companies in its AI business universe and repeatedly hosting its top executives. Those relationships have come into sharper focus following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and revelations about Lutnick’s handling of national security concerns involving the chipmaker. There is no evidence that Cantor's business interests influenced Lutnick's decisions. In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC. The Wall Street firm liked what it heard. "We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock. Yet the firm, formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026 , according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings. The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China . Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, Axios reported Nov. 11. By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to a Nov. 10 Axios report, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina. Even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership. Those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5. An ethics expert said the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia. Richard Painter , the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota, said that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great." "His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC. There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions. "Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC. Cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick, Brandon Lutnick and Kyle Lutnick did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings. As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday. Trump is standing by Howard Lutnick. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in the commerce secretary. But cracks in the administration's unity emerged Friday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months.
