events.title: Amazon’s new Kindle Colorsoft is a premium e-reader with a premium price
events.summary: Amazon recently unveiled its refreshed Kindle lineup , introducing a new basic Kindle , Paperwhite, and Colorsoft. The new Kindle Colorsoft starts at $290, while the Signature Edition, which I’ve spent the past few weeks testing, costs $320. The base model comes with 16GB of storage, while the Signature Edition doubles that to 32GB and is available in graphite or a maroon-like Fig finish with an aluminum back. Amazon first brought color to its Kindle lineup in 2024 with the launch of the original Colorsoft. The latest model is lighter and thinner than its predecessor and features an edge-to-edge display. If you already own the first-generation Colorsoft, there’s little reason to upgrade. The core reading experience remains largely the same. Both models have a 7-inch color E-Ink display, 300ppi resolution for black-and-white content and 150ppi for color. However, if you’ve been eyeing a color e-reader, the new Colorsoft is worth considering if you can get past the hefty price tag. Unlike standard Kindles, which display everything in black and white, the Colorsoft brings your digital bookshelf to life with their original colors. This makes it a particularly appealing option for readers who enjoy comics, graphic novels, or cookbooks, where color makes a big difference. It’s also great for readers who like highlighting passages in different colors. It’s worth noting that colors on the Colorsoft are still relatively muted and not as vibrant as what you’d see on an iPad. Still, they add a welcome splash of color and make a noticeable difference compared to the black-and-white displays of standard Kindles. The Colorsoft lets you adjust the screen’s color temperature, so you can switch to a warmer, more yellow-toned display that’s easier on the eyes when reading at night. There’s also an auto-adjusting brightness option that comes in handy. When it comes to battery life, Amazon says that the Colorsoft can last up to eight weeks on a single charge, compared to up to 12 weeks for the Paperwhite. During my testing, I didn’t have to stress about charging the Colorsoft because like other Kindles, its battery lasts a relatively long time compared to other everyday electronics. One small but welcome improvement on the new Colorsoft is the repositioned power button. On the previous generation, it was on the bottom of the device next to the charging port, making it easy to accidentally press it when handling the Kindle. On the new model, Amazon has moved it to the top-right edge, where it’s less likely to get in the way. I quite like this change, and found the new location more intuitive when powering the device on and off. I enjoyed the premium feel of the aluminum back on the Signature Edition. Although Amazon provided a case with my review unit, I rarely used it, and the finish held up well. While the slimmer design isn’t a major change, I found the new Colorsoft quite comfortable to hold compared to older Kindle devices. For those who enjoy reading in the bath or by the pool, the Colorsoft is waterproof, so you don’t have to worry about accidental splashes or spills damaging the e-reader. One thing I appreciated about the Colorsoft was how infrequently the screen needed to refresh, which was something I noticed more often with the larger Kindle Scribe Colorsoft . I also didn’t experience any noticeable ghosting, where text from previous pages lingers on the screen, which is common on some e-readers. The Signature Edition supports a magnetic cover with built-in page-turn buttons that connects to the pogo pins on the back of the device, but I can’t speak to this experience because I didn’t have access to the case. The biggest drawback of the Colorsoft is its price. It’s a steep investment for a device that’s just used for reading. That said, if you really want a color display, the Colorsoft is definitely worth considering. For everyone else, it’s a nice upgrade, but far from a must-have. Many readers would be better off with the basic Kindle or Paperwhite, which start at $169.99 and $199.99, respectively. events.title: Even billionaires need human connections in AI age: Business Network International CEO
events.summary: Business Network International CEO Mary Kennedy Thompson says the world could see its first billionaire solopreneur within the next five years. SINGAPORE – While fears of AI-driven job losses persist, a new perspective on artificial intelligence is gaining ground: Workforce disruption is giving rise to more solo business owners, or solopreneurs, who will need human connections to succeed. The world could see its first billionaire solopreneur within the next five years, as AI tools take over functions such as accounting, finance, marketing and administration that once required a large organisation. But however brilliant such a one-person, billion-dollar operator may be, connections will always matter in business, said Mary Kennedy Thompson, chief executive of Business Network International (BNI), the world’s largest business referral and networking organisation. As AI continues to disrupt the workforce, this generation of solo business owners will need to master networking and find a community they can belong to, Thompson told The Straits Times in an interview. With the technology becoming more prevalent and powerful, the need for human connections becomes even more critical because people prefer to do business with those they know and trust – and face-to-face interactions build that trust, she said. Thompson said more firms from AI-related sectors have been increasingly expressing interest in joining the BNI network . As AI advances and people’s understanding of it improves, she believes BNI can help businesses establish credibility through human connections as AI makes it harder to distinguish genuine capabilities from convincing claims. “People are going to want proof points, and organisations like BNI that can provide those proof points and the human connection will grow faster.” Additionally, the organisation has observed a fall in the average age of its members over the past three to five years as more young people take the plunge into entrepreneurship. “Gen Zs are more entrepreneurial than millennials,” said Thompson. She noted that chapters consisting entirely of business owners aged 30 and below already exist in Singapore and the US, while the youngest member of the local network is a 21-year-old running an events management business. Creating a robust business referral network Founded in 1985, BNI is a membership-only organisation that helps business owners develop networks and share customer leads. Spanning 78 countries, its global footprint is organised into local chapters, each typically comprising around 35 business owners or professionals from different industries who meet weekly to share business needs and leads. In Singapore, BNI has grown from a network dominated by financial and property professionals in its first decade to more than 2,000 members from diverse industries today. Established in 2000, it now counts business development staff from several multinational companies among its members. No two professions within a chapter are the same, ensuring there is no competition within the group and that members can refer clients to one another’s businesses. Often, that results in collaboratio n , said Thompson. A chapter could include a property agent, a lawyer, a plumber and an electrician all helping one another with leads or even working together on the same project. “Every chapter meeting that we attend is a business development opportunity. That is to allow you to educate another business owner about who you are, what you do, how you value it and what businesses you’re looking out for,” she said. She noted that on average, a BNI member gets US$71 (S$91) in closed business for every US$1 spent on dues, with a one-year membership in Singapore costing around $1,700. “I don’t know any kind of marketing that has that kind of return on investment,” she added. “When you walk into a room, a lot of times what happens in networking is you and I are talking, we share greetings and pleasantries, but we didn’t get anything accomplished.” But if both parties understand the science of having a one-to-one conversation, a meaningful business lead could be developed in 30 minutes. That would be most beneficial for any business owner when developing a new connection, she noted. Over the last 12 months, the global BNI network generated more than 17 million referrals amounting to roughly US$27 billion in member-to-member business. Thompson herself has referred more than US$30,000 worth of business since the start of 2026. Beyond facilitating business development, BNI views its role as equipping entrepreneurs with the connection-building skills needed to scale their companies successfully. Thompson pointed to the weekly chapter meetings as regular practice for BNI members such that the honed skills become second nature in the real world. “It’s not just going to a meeting and talking.

events.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months
events.summary: The Trump administration announced a six-month delay Friday in enforcing the Medicaid work requirements that were scheduled to take effect in January. Why it matters: The announcement pauses a set of rules that state officials have warned they're not ready to handle — and that could cause millions of people to lose their health coverage. Driving the news: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said there will be an "optional hold harmless period" through June 30 that will give states "a transition period to further modernize systems, improve processes, and streamline the applicant and beneficiary experience. Hospitals have been so worried about the impact of the work requirements that they've created their own outreach campaign to prepare people on Medicaid, per the New York Times . The concern is not that people will be kicked out of the program for not working, but that they'll be kicked out because they don't understand the reporting rules and won't be able to prove they've met the requirements. events.title: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
events.summary: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down . “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news. Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital. Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition. “Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch. Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term. Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street. “She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.” Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said. For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal . “Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.” It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position. If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.) Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang. Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs. While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did. Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations. Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations. “When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said.

"FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them." A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement. The FAA ATCSCC advisory halts departing flights and says international flights will be dealt with individually. The notice says, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis." Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now." An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage." The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. The grounding follows on the heels of a major Microsoft outage that has affected many Microsoft-hosted services, particularly email, for more than 24 hours so far. There's no indication presently that the two incidents are related. We'll update this story as more information becomes available.® Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop. CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.” L3Harris has not responded to a request for comment. Updated to add at 2340 UTC Air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

events.title: Nvidia stock suffers longest weekly losing streak since 2012 as market value sinks by $1.7 trillion
events.summary: Nvidia shares plunged 13% this week, and just wrapped their sixth straight weekly decline. That's the longest losing streak since 2012. The chip giant has lost roughly $1.7 trillion in market cap since the slide began in early October. Nvidia investors turned bearish before this week's Jensen Huang saga. But the selling on Wall Street accelerated in the past few days, sending the stock to its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012. The chip giant, which spent most of the year as the world's most valuable company, has lost 30% of its value during the losing streak. That's a drop of roughly $1.7 trillion in market cap and it pushed the company below Apple . Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led it for 33 years, resigned on Thursday after two separate extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with an employee — were made public. The board named finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a full-time successor. Nvidia shares fell 13% this week, the most since April 2025. News of the first reported affair hit the front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife." The board convened late Wednesday after The New York Times reported on the other affair , this one with the company's vice president of health care. By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder, who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump's top allies in the corporate world. "With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months," Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report on Thursday. Luria lowered his price target to $200 from $300, but maintained his buy rating. "We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition," he wrote. Last week, prior to Huang's departure, Nvidia shares dropped about 9%. Much of the decline came after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the artificial intelligence buildout. In the weeks before the election, Nvidia's stock was sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is wildly profitable, big customers like neoclouds are reliant on the debt markets. Heading into next week, the pressure is on Kress. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. Analysts are projecting 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era. Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report on Thursday that, even though they see the company reporting solid earnings, "we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term." "The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang," they wrote.

events.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq end lower as Nvidia uncertainty weighs on tech shares
events.summary: A ticker shows Nvidia trades as futures-options traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange's NYSE American in New York City, on Nov 13. NEW YORK - The S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed lower on Nov 13, as concerns about Nvidia pressured technology shares , while a reading on inflation failed to alter expectations for more rate hikes from the Federal Reserve. Nvidia’s shares fell 2% and recorded their sixth straight week of declines, their longest streak since October 2012, after CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation on Thursday. He stepped down after revelations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with a businesswoman suspected by the US of spying for China . The Financial Times reported that Nvidia’s board has approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Huang. The uncertainty about leadership at the chipmaker has raised concerns about the durability of the AI trade, given Nvidia’s primary role in the industry’s boom and its financial ties to a host of companies in the sector, which has been a pillar of the bull market in equities. “The tech trade, the AI trade, Nvidia is going to go through a period of volatility, and you’re going to see the bulls and bears kind of wrestle on where this narrative goes through the rest of the year ... there’s been a loss of confidence,” said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial in Troy, Michigan. “The market and investors are trying to navigate what does the AI theme look like when we have the absence of Jensen Huang, who was basically the AI champion and willing to use Nvidia’s balance sheet to fund a lot of this AI expansion. That’s gone.” Sweeping Democratic victories in the midterm elections last week also raised concerns about government regulations potentially slowing growth among AI-related companies. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 50.46 points, or 0.10%, to 52,347.55, the S&P 500 lost 30.73 points, or 0.40%, to 7,561.67 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 229.82 points, or 0.91%, to 25,136.27. Despite the recent volatility, the major indexes recorded weekly gains, as the Nasdaq and S&P 500 both snapped a four-week streak of declines. For the week, the S&P 500 gained 2.51%, the Nasdaq rose 2.27% and the Dow climbed 2.07%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 3.4%, with Advanced Micro Devices dropping 8.8% and Broadcom down 4.8% as the biggest drags on the index. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius also ended lower, while data center-related firms IREN lost 6.7% and Applied Digital fell 5.8%. The losses come ahead of AI company Anthropic’s much-anticipated IPO next week, which could test investor appetite for established AI heavyweights as money potentially shifts toward the new entrant. The S&P 500 technology index shed 1.7% and was the worst-performing of the 11 major S&P sectors. But Microsoft ended 0.2% higher, as it erased earlier declines after a global outage that included its Outlook and Teams products began to ease. Airlines dropped in the final minutes of trading with the NYSE Arca airline index closing down 1.4% after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop of all departing flights on Friday. The agency said this was “due to extraordinary circumstance and reasons for safety” after it earlier reported serious air traffic control communications issues. On the economic front, the Labor Department said US producer prices were slightly cooler than expected in October, but still shot up 6.5% year over year, the largest annual gain since November 2022. The data kept expectations for a rate hike of at least 25 basis points at the Fed’s December meeting completely locked in, with markets pricing in a roughly 10% chance for an outsized 50-basis-point increase, according to CME FedWatch. Comments from multiple Fed officials earlier this week suggested the US central bank was open to a more aggressive path of rate hikes as price pressures worsen. The sentiment for additional rate hikes was echoed by more Fed officials on Friday, including San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly, who said her “bias” is that the central bank will need to increase its policy rate, while Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins said tighter monetary policy is coming because of high inflation. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.28-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange and by a 1.61-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 9 new 52-week highs and 1 new low, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 37 new highs and 340 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 16.38 billion shares, compared with the 18.52 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

events.title: Airlines scramble to get flights in air after planes grounded across US — as it happened
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts US officials lift order grounding flights after thousands of travellers affected — as it happened Here is a summary of the day's key events: US officials have lifted a national ground stop order for all departing flights hours after thousands of travellers, including Australians, were impacted. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has blamed an "old air traffic control system" for an outage that led to the ground stop. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says there is not yet any evidence suggesting a cyber attack was the cause. More than 7,000 flights were cancelled during the order. The halt is just the second ground stop issued by regulators since the September 11 terror attacks in 2001. Choose what information you see below by using filters Thank you for sticking with us throughout our coverage of today's US air traffic control centre outage . We're ending our live updates here but, as always, you can keep up to date with the latest information on this story and other news via the ABC News website and mobile app . Until next time, have a fantastic afternoon! How Australians were caught in the mayhem of a nationwide US flights ground stop As we've been reporting to you throughout the day, Australians have found themselves among the thousands of people whose travels have been halted due to the US ground stop order. My ABC News colleague Kristy Sexton-McGrath has collated some of their stories in the link below. 'The line-up is huge': Australians caught up in US flight chaos 📷: US airspace, flights and airports come to a standstill Everything you need to know about the US air traffic ground stop In the hours after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued an immediate pause of departing flights across the country due to "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety" , air traffic ground to a halt. If you're looking to catch up on everything that happened following that order and the impact it had on national and international air traffic, my colleague Audrey Courty has covered it all in the link below: What we know about the US air traffic communications outage Safety investigators heading to earlier ship crash affected by air traffic outage In other news from the US today, more than 100 people were rescued after a tanker collided with a river cruise boat near the port of New Orleans . In the aftermath of that accident, the US's National Transport Safety Bureau (NTSB) announced it was launching an investigation and sending a team to Louisiana . While initially unrelated to today's nationwide halt on flights, both news stories have since merged. The NTSB has released a statement in the past 20 minutes saying the ground stop order has impacted its earlier plans. "Due to the residual delays from the nationwide ground stop, the NTSB will no longer send a board member and will instead send a team of investigators by ground to the scene of the vessel collision in New Orleans," it said in a statement on X. Passengers stuck on tarmac for more than 5 hours after cross-country flight Frustration is continuing to grow for travellers who are still impacted by the fallout of today's ground stop order. Among them is Ruth Coles , who jumped on an Alaska Airlines plane from Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey and flew five hours across the country to Los Angeles . But, after her plane landed on the tarmac at Los Angeles International Airport , that is where she currently remains. She has told The Associated Press she was flying to visit her sister and attend a festival when she learnt about the ground stop order mid-flight. Passengers on her plane have been told they are waiting for a gate to open up, she said. "The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line," Coles said, but that was more than five hours ago . Coles said they have been given soft drinks and cookies and been allowed to use the restroom. Frustrated, she posted on X multiple times asking the airport for help and messaged Alaska Airlines support. The airline told her they were trying to park the flight in a remote area and provide bus transportation back to the terminal. FAA systems 'reliable' after earlier disruptions With flight services resuming across the US, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has released its own message to assure travellers the country is safe for air travel. It's worth pointing out that while thousands of planes were grounded and many more pulled out of the skies over the US, Donald Trump was mostly silent.

events.title: Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance—2 habits that take 'a few seconds' can help you avoid similar traps
events.summary: Work AI is making a mess of how humans interact at work Psychology and Relationships Using AI chatbots mainly for companionship can lower feelings of wellbeing Psychology and Relationships 5 ways to be more yourself and stop worrying if you're ‘good enough’ Earn Are you richer than you think? How to find out—and what to do if you are Work Some job seekers are refusing to do AI interviews, even in a tough market The biggest heist in cryptocurrency history began with small mistakes many internet users make. A hacking group tied to North Korea recently stole $6.3 billion from the crypto exchange Binance. The operation was sophisticated, involving fake job interviews and malicious code. But it was also mundane. Although artificial intelligence played a role in the hack, this was not a cyberattack of the future, propelled by swarms of AI agents. Rather, it relied on humans who made some basic errors, like clicking a link because it appeared first on a search results page or trusting strangers at a fake company without taking a few seconds to look them up. We work at the Digital Inquiry Group , a nonprofit that researches how people evaluate online information and creates free, evidence-based curriculum that helps people decide what to trust. In over a decade of research, we've found that people frequently engage in online behavior that makes them more likely to get duped. Two simple strategies can help you better navigate today's information landscape, from traditional phishing to misleading social posts to AI fakes. Here's how. When searching online, the first result is not always the best or the safest The Binance heist began when one of the company's engineers downloaded compromised software. That engineer, according to the Reuters investigation of the hack , clicked on a sponsored search result that appeared higher on the results page and directed them to the malicious code. Our research at the Digital Inquiry Group suggests internet users frequently behave as if first is best. They click on the first thing they see. They incorrectly associate a higher placement with vetted content, ceding judgment to tech company algorithms. Students have gone so far as to tell us "Google is almost never wrong" or "AI is always right." Professional fact-checkers commonly practice click restraint . They understand that whether you're searching on the internet or querying a chatbot, first isn't always best. If you're researching an organization, the first link will often be to its own site, which is hardly likely to disclose anything that's wrong with it. So the next time you search for something online, be wary of links to sponsored content, the organization you're investigating, or to open platforms where anyone can post and information isn't verified, such as Quora or Reddit. Read the brief snippets beneath each link, and make a more informed choice about what to open. Always ask yourself: Who is behind this information? What makes them credible? Look for people and organizations that have direct expertise on the topic at hand, or have processes to ensure the accuracy of information, such as news outlets that employ editors and fact-checkers. 'The internet is a precarious place'—always get external verification Binance says it caught that first malicious download, replaced the device and changed passwords. But later, another engineer downloaded compromised code as part of what they thought was a job interview, which included a virtual meeting with the supposed CEO of a fake company. It's tempting to think that the engineer should have seen something was off. But the internet is a precarious place because bad actors know how to make content feel legitimate. Binance says its employee was snared by a hacker posing as an HR rep who "shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust." When they encounter a piece of unfamiliar content, professional fact-checkers don't just read it closely — they read laterally . They open new browser tabs to see what other, credible sources have to say. Fact-checkers know that bad actors make themselves look good on their home turf, but that it's a lot harder to fake a good reputation across the internet. The next time you encounter something unfamiliar online, look for authoritative sources that can shed light on the person or organization. You might find a news article that confirms the claim you're looking into, or a report that identifies a supposedly neutral source as biased. In some cases, you may find nothing at all, which is a signal in itself: if you look up a company that reached out to you and find no external confirmation of its existence, that should be an immediate red flag. Had that first Binance engineer engaged in click restraint and verified the source of the software, they might have avoided the malicious download.

events.title: ‘The machine doesn’t stop’: Abu Dhabi’s wartime plan for keeping its cultural ambition alive
events.summary: The Signal Interview “We have plan A’s all the way to plan Z’s, from our best-case scenarios to our worst-case scenarios,” Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak says, when asked how the culture, tourism, and property groups he leads are preparing for what might happen next in the conflict that has shaken the Middle East. Many of those plans are contingent on the US-Israeli conflict with Iran ending, but “if this conflict gets worse, we also have a very clear route,” says the chairman of the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi. The manga-loving 44-year-old member of Abu Dhabi’s Executive Council, whose other interests include sneakers, rap music, and basketball, has spent more than a decade at the heart of the city’s strategy to diversify its economy using museums, UFC fights, and theme parks. Last year alone, the city opened five museums and welcomed a record 26.6 million visitors. Culture and tourism are “the building blocks of our future,” he says. But the conflict has forced him to craft a response that combines a strategic pivot, reassurance to local staff and foreign partners, and continued commitment to his city’s long-term aims. When the Iran war started in February, flights and events were canceled and the number of Western tourists to the Gulf plunged, emptying local hotels. “We had to basically rethink how we’re…promoting ourselves,” Al Mubarak says. But, he adds, “We always understood that, no matter what happens… the machine doesn’t stop.” A pivot to new growth markets Before the conflict, Abu Dhabi was working toward a goal of attracting 39.3 million visitors a year by 2030, up from 24 million in 2023. It projected that those tourists would contribute AED 90 billion a year to the city’s economy. Al Mubarak is still sticking to his 2030 goals, but he says the assumptions underlying them have changed. He now expects a 10-15% drop in visitors from the US and Europe compared to its original estimates, for example, with growth from other parts of the globe making up the difference. So he has changed the focus of Abu Dhabi’s marketing, looking to pull in far more visitors from its own region, and from Eastern Europe, India and the rest of Southeast Asia, and Africa. The city is already seeing 5-8% growth in visitors from “some of our Eastern geographies,” he says, and much larger numbers from around the Gulf. On Yas Island this summer, he says, “Some days I felt I was in Saudi, some days I felt I was in Qatar, some days I felt I was in Moscow.” He recalls talking to two tourists as they watched the smoke from a drone attack on a French navy base in the first week of the conflict: when he asked if they were alright, they replied: “We’re Russians, so this is nothing.” Abu Dhabi has been a magnet for wealthy Westerners, with its Formula 1 track and outpost of the Louvre. But Al Mubarak wants to use the current crisis to broaden its appeal to other parts of the world whose populations’ economic power is growing. Under his worst-case scenarios for the war’s outcome, his plans would focus Abu Dhabi’s culture and tourism strategy much more on its immediate region and the Global South. That grouping of poorer countries comprises more than 70% of the world’s population, he notes, and its people want “to experience a lot more than they have.” Westerners have been more put off by news coverage that he says exaggerates the security threat, but he has not stopped marketing to them, too. “We haven’t stopped acknowledging that they are a traveler and they are a future potential traveler,” he says. “We’ve kept [at the] front of their mind that the UAE is here and Abu Dhabi is here, and it’s going to continue to develop, it’s going to continue to grow. So when the time is right for you as a traveler, our doors are wide open.” Three-quarters of Abu Dhabi’s hotel rooms were full again by August, Al Mubarak notes. At Aldar Properties, the commercial real estate developer he also chairs, new sales dropped 34% in the first nine months of this year, but at AED 18.9 billion were still higher than for the same period in 2024. Overseas buyers — from China, the UK, Russia, and elsewhere — made up 28% of the total. After the first day of Iranian attacks, he maintains, “business has really been as usual.” Projecting normality, and an alluring vision Informed by its experience during the pandemic, Abu Dhabi kept cultural institutions open throughout the conflict to give residents places to connect and “a sense of comfort,” Al Mubarak says. To reassure his own teams, he set up daily management group meetings, and a stream of video conferences, emails, and helplines for employees. What mattered most was to show that leaders were listening rather than just talking, he says. “Small things like that make a difference,” he notes, adding that his strategy starts with Abu Dhabi’s own residents. The city wants to be a “home away from home” for the world’s culture-lovers, he says, but “we did not develop our cultural strategy and our cultural infrastructure for people to come [to Abu Dhabi]. We developed it for people that are here.” But Al Mubarak is equally keen to project a sense of normality for potential visitors who are contemplating Abu Dhabi from afar. “Imagine yourself in Abu Dhabi today,” he says. The weather’s good this time of year, so “you’d wake up in the morning and you’d sink your feet in beautiful white sand,” then maybe go for a swim, he suggests. Then a tourist could go for an AI-personalized museum tour, a round of golf, some shopping, a concert at the Sphere (a $1.7 billion entertainment venue opening in 2029), or a comedy show. It’s “an imaginary story,” he says, but one “that could be a reality” for a visitor. The next step in realizing that vision will come on Dec. 11, when a branch of New York’s Guggenheim Museum opens on Saadiyat Island. Some of Abu Dhabi’s partners have expressed fears about the region’s suitability as a home for their artwork in a period of conflict — “our French partners raised concerns on some of the loans that they’ve had at the Louvre,” Al Mubarak acknowledges — but he was able to reassure them that its buildings are “built to withstand things of this sort of nature.” The opening of the Frank Gehry-designed Guggenheim will be a symbolic and emotional moment for Abu Dhabi, he says, but also one that “highlights our aspirations.” The case for not outgrowing your imagination What outsiders looking at Abu Dhabi’s transformation often miss is what has powered its economic growth, Al Mubarak says. “What they don’t see is that just three generations ago — my grandfather and my great-grandfather — they lived a very, very difficult life. They went days where they couldn’t find food.” The city’s ambition “comes from hunger and it comes from struggle,” he says. Even as it builds ever more glittering projects, he adds, “That struggle I’m talking about, we feel it. That taste is still in our mouth.” Abu Dhabi is still “the new kid on the block,” he says — an underdog

events.title: ‘Chinese companies are born to make money’: AI pioneer Kai-Fu Lee on the 3 biggest myths about China’s AI race efforts
events.summary: Despite years of U.S. efforts to gain an edge over China in the AI race by restricting its access to the most advanced chips, one AI pioneer says America’s efforts have instead helped create a new generation of Chinese AI models that are quickly catching up to their American counterparts. Kai-Fu Lee, an AI entrepreneur and former president of Google China, said in a Fortune Daily interview that U.S. export restrictions on the most powerful American chips have shaped Chinese companies’ strategy of building competitive AI models with fewer resources. In response to these limits, which American companies don’t face, Chinese AI developers have built open-weight models that Lee estimates are now just six to 12 months behind those created by some of the biggest American AI companies, including OpenAI as well as Anthropic—which is reportedly preparing to go public as early as next week. Yet when Americans think about China and the motivations of Chinese companies, they’re often getting some key things wrong, Lee said. In an interview with Fortune Daily published this week, he detailed three of the biggest misconceptions about China’s AI industry that he says have taken hold in America. Profit motive One of the biggest misconceptions about Chinese companies is that they are more focused on winning the AI race and becoming the first to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI)—widely considered the ultimate goal of AI development—than on building profitable businesses. That assumption is incorrect, Lee said. “Chinese companies are born to make money. That’s the primary purpose,” Lee said. “It’s not so much to win AGI or win the race.” He compared questions about the profitability of the current wave of Chinese AI developers like DeepSeek with those surrounding other Chinese tech companies like Pinduoduo, Meituan, and ByteDance. These tech giants’ business models were also initially questioned before they became some of China’s biggest companies. “You may reasonably doubt China’s ability to do a breakthrough, which is valid. [The] U.S. is way ahead on that, but never doubt Chinese ability to find a way to make money,” he said. Motives and competition A second misconception, Lee said, is that China’s embrace of open-weight models and open-source technology is part of an organized government effort to compete with America. Instead, Lee said, market competition has driven the shift. He pointed especially to DeepSeek, a Chinese startup that stunned American AI companies in early 2025 by releasing a highly capable AI model by the same name that it claimed was trained using significantly less computing power than its American competitors. “Chinese companies are venture funded just like the American companies,” Lee said. “They just want to serve their investors.” Beijing has played a significant role in shaping the country’s AI industry. Investors with ties to the government participated in more than 140 Chinese AI deals in 2025, Fortune reported earlier this year, citing a Pitchbook analyst note.  China’s president, Xi Jinping, has also encouraged AI development in China. In 2025, Xi called for the country to develop “an independent, controllable, and collaborative artificial intelligence basic software and hardware system.” Lee said in the interview that American companies have good reasons to spend more, including attracting the world’s best researchers and giving them enough computing power to experiment. A different playbook The third misconception, Lee argued, is that U.S. export controls are the main reason Chinese companies have shifted toward models that require less computing power, while American companies pour billions into data centers . He argued that Chinese companies are naturally more frugal because they have different priorities than their American counterparts. “The Chinese companies are naturally parsimonious; not just the startups,” he said, adding that “prudence and survival instinct” are more important to them than the pursuit of AGI. That contrasts with the American approach, which emphasizes spending heavily on computing power to attract top researchers and accelerate AI development. Because of their resourcefulness, Chinese companies can develop and operate models for as little as one-tenth the cost of their American competitors, making their products attractive to businesses that don’t want to pay premium prices for AI services. Despite the growing competitiveness of Chinese AI developers, American companies still produce more top-tier models and higher-impact patents, according to a Stanford University study . OpenAI and Anthropic are also the world’s most valuable AI companies. OpenAI was valued at $1.25 trillion in a November funding round and is eyeing a potential IPO in 2027. Anthropic, meanwhile, is preparing to go public as early as next week in what could be one of the largest IPOs in history, seeking a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion . Still, when DeepSeek showed it could compete with America’s leading AI developers, it helped boost the hopes of Chinese AI developers. Before DeepSeek, these developers believed their country was years behind the U.S. After DeepSeek showed off its model in 2025, sentiment shifted, he said. “It’s a national pride thing, so people say, ‘Okay, we thought we were never going to catch up. Now we have a shot.’ So, it was quite a special moment,” he said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy
events.summary: The Campaign Legal Center is calling for an investigation into whether Alicia Jackson, director of the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, violated ethics laws. Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health A nonpartisan ethics watchdog group has asked for an investigation into whether a top Department of Health and Human Services official violated ethics laws after a recent ProPublica investigation revealed actions experts called “alarming” and an “obvious conflict of interest.”  Alicia Jackson, who heads the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, publicly endorsed a change to federal health policy on hormone replacement therapies while owning stock in a company that provides access to menopause treatments.  In a letter to the department’s inspector general , the Campaign Legal Center also questioned whether Jackson properly identified up to $400 million in underlying assets held by her husband’s investment firm. The center’s review identified an additional potential conflict — investments in a second firm that provides hormone treatments for menopause.  Jackson, who heads the HHS agency that invests taxpayer money in medical technology and research, was recently placed on administrative leave, though health officials have not publicly explained why. In its letter, the Campaign Legal Center cited the ProPublica investigation that found Jackson spoke at an HHS press conference last November and was quoted in a department news release announcing the decision to remove “black box warnings” from hormone replacement therapy products.  At the time, Jackson owned at least $115,000 in stock and an unknown amount of stock options in Evernow, a company she founded that connects women to hormone replacement treatments, according to her financial disclosures . Read More Top U.S. Health Official Backed a Medication Policy Shift That Benefited a Company She Has Stock In It’s unclear what role, if any, Jackson played in the decision to drop the requirement to display a black box warning, the most serious type of federal safety warning. The Food and Drug Administration regulates drugs. And an FDA panel of experts had recommended ending the requirement months before Jackson became her agency’s director in October 2025. Still, ethics experts noted that federal law prohibits government employees from participating “personally and substantially” in matters that could influence their personal finances — even making statements at a press conference or in a news release.   The Campaign Legal Center asked the inspector general to examine whether Jackson broke federal ethics laws by failing to recuse herself. Neither Jackson nor the HHS will say whether she obtained a conflict-of-interest waiver before participating in the policy announcement.  “Americans have a right to know that government decisions are not being made to benefit a federal employee’s financial interests,” the organization wrote. The center also asked the inspector general to determine if Jackson failed to fully and accurately disclose her and her spouse’s financial interests in private investment funds. ProPublica’s investigation found that Jackson reported she and her husband owned more than 60 venture capital and private equity funds that she said do not disclose their holdings to investors. These include at least 13 funds managed by 137 Ventures, a venture capital firm co-founded by her husband, Alex Jacobson . The company invests in a wide range of industries, including healthcare, digital health and medical device companies. Ethics experts said the funds could pose a serious conflict of interest if the underlying businesses received grants or contracts from her agency.  137 Ventures founders Alex Jacobson, left, and Justin Fishner-Wolfson Kimberly White/Getty Images for 137 Ventures The Campaign Legal Center’s review of Jackson’s disclosures identified one of those funds — 137 Ventures IV LP — as an investor in Thirty Madison Inc., a virtual healthcare company. Thirty Madison owns a subsidiary that provides hormone replacement treatments for women experiencing menopause symptoms. Jackson’s disclosures do not show her divesting from the fund before the black box warning announcement, the center said. Under federal law, financial disclosure forms filed by federal officials like Jackson must then be certified by ethics staff as complying with the law. But Jackson’s two financial disclosures — filed last October and two months ago — remain uncertified.  HHS’ inspector general’s office would not confirm or deny whether it is investigating Jackson. The inspector general, T. March Bell, was one of nearly 100 appointees confirmed by the Senate in a December 2025 party-line vote . President Donald Trump fired the previous inspector general just days into the president’s second term. ProPublica also requested responses from HHS, Jackson, Jacobson and 137 Ventures, but none commented. In a statement to ProPublica last month, an HHS spokesperson said that while Jackson was on leave the agency would “assess the facts before determining any change in her status. HHS requires all officials to comply with federal ethics laws, regulations, and policies.”  Jackson was appointed by Trump as her agency’s second director and sworn in on Oct. 20, 2025. The agency, created three years earlier to spur revolutionary biomedical research and technologies, has a $1.5 billion budget. It has issued numerous contracts and grants, including $160 million for genetic medicines combating rare diseases and $144 million to study existing treatments for age-related illnesses. Jackson’s disclosures are among 2,400 added last month to ProPublica’s Trump Team Financials database , a searchable tool launched in March. The records detail the finances of more than 2,300 officials appointed by Trump. Since last year, we’ve requested disclosure records from 127 federal agencies and the White House. Disclosures from roughly 1,500 appointees remain unreleased. events.title: US government grounds all flights across the United States ‘due to extraordinary circumstances’
events.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday afternoon that it has grounded all flights across the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances” and issues related to safety. The FAA’s website said the cause is an “equipment outage.” The site itself was down for a brief period at the time of publication, with a note that the website was “experiencing technical difficulties.” Per an alert sent by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center , or ATCSCC, the FAA said the ground stop means that aircraft cannot take off from departure gates. The message said that the disruption was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” but did not specify further. The alert was not visible on the ATCSCC website at press time. The alert stated that all departing flights must remain on the ground “until further notice.” Inbound international flights will be “managed on a case-by-case basis,” it said. A spokesperson for the FAA told TechCrunch that it issued the ground stop “following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” which manage the airspace across the United States. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a post on X : “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.” It’s not clear what caused the ongoing FAA equipment outage. The outage comes in the same week that the administration rolled out an AI-powered tool for air traffic controllers to save aircraft flight time and fuel costs — though it’s unclear if the ongoing outage is related. Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that there is “no indication yet that this was a nefarious act,” but warned that the recovery “is going to take some time.” Updated with comment from the FAA, and remarks from Homeland Security. events.title: The Big Fly Swat unleashed after bar flies' inspired idea
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tiny outback town builds world's biggest fly swat It's hoped The Big Fly Swat will encourage "big thing" tourism and give others a reason to detour off the highway and visit Kingoonya. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) A seven to eight hour drive into the outback north-west of Adelaide brings you to a micro town so small it's almost a ghost town. Kingoonya, with its population of roughly 13, offers an authentic slice of Australian country life rarely glimpsed by outsiders. That is, until now. It's hoped that the installation of Australia's latest "big thing" will draw more people to venture off the highway, visit the local pub or cafe and take a selfie to say they have seen the world's biggest fly swat. The official opening of The Big Fly Swat took place this week at Kingoonya. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) Once a railway maintenance town for the tracks that criss-cross Australia from Sydney to Perth and Adelaide to Darwin, Kingoonya once had a population of over 100. The trains still come — as many as 70 a week pass through — but few stop. While the railway workers and their families are long gone. Up until the 1980s Kingoonya was still a busy petrol stop on the main road that travels up the middle of the country from Adelaide to Darwin. But then the highways department decided to shift it 40 kilometres to the east, to Glendambo. Kingoonya was a busy petrol stop on the highway between Adelaide and Alice Springs before the road was shifted 40km to the east in the 1980s. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) Overnight, the town nearly disappeared, with even the pub closing for a time. "The population went down to one for a while," said Leesa Carty from the Kingoonya and Area Progress Association. These days, visitors come in the form of four-wheel-drive adventurers and those en route to local stations. It has brought revenue for the pub, cafe and caravan park. And also more carrots and apples for the retired horses who freely roam the dusty streets, mooching treats and seeking out shady spots. The idea for the swat was thought up on the verandah of the Kingoonya Bush Hotel, where fly swats are always on hand for the customers. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) Throughout all the ups and downs for Kingoonya over the many years, there has always been one constant: the flies. Ms Carty was sitting on the front porch of the Kingoonya Bush Hotel one night with former publican Johnny Brett when the idea for the swat was born. The tables were scattered, as they always are, with beers, ashtrays and fly swats. Leesa Carty runs the caravan park and cafe in Kingoonya and is also a member of the Kingoonya and Area Progress Association. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) The question was how to best spend a $30,000 grant from the Outback Communities Authority to bring people to town. "I think I just went 'flies' and he went 'fly swat' and we just went, 'Yes!" she recalled. "That's the one. We could do a big fly swat." Many months later, the Big Fly Swat, with its accompanying fly (the eyes made from red kitchen strainers), is complete. The fly on the fly swat now looks back over the town. ( Supplied: Grayson Cooke ) Painted blue, the metal swat was 8 metres long (or in South Australian parlance, about one Stobie pole high). With its location decided on, it was cemented in place between the main street and the railway track. At the official opening this week, Ms Carty, holding one of the pub's plastic swats, was invited by Marg Howard of the outback authority to "bash the crap" out of the ceremonial red bow placed on the big swat for the occasion. Leesa Carty was invited to "bash the crap" out of the ribbon on the big swat at the opening ceremony. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) A cheer went up from the gathered crowd of Kingoonya and surrounding residents as The Big Fly Swat was declared open. Ms Howard was enthusiastic about the project and the town, which is one of the many little populations the authority oversees. "I think some people will come to see it because it's a Big Thing and big things are big things in Australia." Paul Willis watches over the resident three free-roaming horses which amble through town and wait under the shade in the heat of the day. ( ABC News: Caroline Horn ) The new owner of the 89-year-old Kingoonya Bush Hotel, Jeff Verning, was among those in the crowd at the swat opening. A frequent visitor to the region for many years, he and wife Catherine took over the pub this year. After the celebrations died down, they joined their customers on the verandah for a drink and a smoke as they did most nights, watching the sun go down and the trains pass by.

events.title: Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank
events.summary: Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to bring shoppers back The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap? Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing. Central to this, the study says, is trying to banish, or at least tame, motor traffic, because too often urban centres are places “designed to be driven through, not for time to be spent in”. As well as citing a lack of imagination, the report, which is co-produced by bike storage company Cyclehoop, blames planning regulations that favour conformity and clutter and too often treat speeding cars as a given, to which everything else must adjust. “The default high street is engineered for traffic and furnished from a catalogue: a tarmac pavement, guardrails penning people at the kerb, litter bins ordered from a procurement catalogue, a row of plastic planters – public investment that is joyless,” it says. While planners have traditionally focused on car access as a metric for thriving town centres, calculations for the Create Streets report suggest that replacing parking with other kerbside infrastructure, including bike spaces or outside drinking and dining areas, creates more economic value. It found that one parking space in the high street of a market town is typically used by about 3.5 vehicles a day, bringing in just over £73,000 a year in spending to nearby shops. But the same 12 square metres, if used to hold nine share e-bikes, generates an average of 13 trips a day, with over £146,000 a year in spending, even taking into account the lower average spend per person. In a busier city, where share bikes would be used more frequently, the estimated total annual spend rises to more than £300,000. Repurposing the space for outside dining brings less dramatic gains, but in a city centre it can still amount to about £120,000 in extra annual spending. The report calls for a cultural rethink involving low-cost tweaks that rip away ugly and unnecessary street furniture and make better use of kerbsides. Calling use by families “the indicator species of a healthy high street”, the report cites what is known as “the wrist test” – whether it feels safe to let go of a young child’s wrist so they can roam with some freedom. This is best done, it argues, by removing the threat of speeding motor vehicles and not by trying to mitigate their impact. It calls the removal of pedestrian guardrails next to roads “the most cost-effective upgrade for the majority of high streets”, saying they are an eyesore with minimal safety benefits. The report says “the absurdity of modern public realm management” is exemplified by Secured by Design, policy guidelines on cutting neighbourhood crime. These can, critics point out, mean benches and plants are removed on the advice of police, supposedly to discourage antisocial behaviour. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has pledged to try to reverse the decline of high streets, announcing in September a £210m regeneration fund. However, the bulk of the money will go into buildings: turning old shops into shared workspaces or community cafes, or keeping pubs and clubs in business. The report argues that renovating buildings is pointless if the street outside is unappealing. To reduce clutter, it says, there should be “a presumption of removal where an item cannot be justified”. The effects can be dramatic, the report says, pointing to examples including Altrincham in Cheshire, where the creation of a walkable, car-free urban area helped see retail vacancies fall from over 30% to 7% in less than a decade. Such initiatives do not have to be expensive, it claims, noting the example of an unused patch of land next to a church in Grimsby which was turned into a park for less than £20,000. “Streets that are ugly are not so because councils lack the desire to change them, but because the system is counting the maintenance liabilities, not the benefits,” said David Milner of Create Streets. “What works is cheap: trees in the ground, benches people want to sit on, clutter taken away. “So much of what is built now seems to be temporary, looking more like road works than public realm improvements, so we encourage the concept of permanence; more trees in the ground, not in giant plant pots, for example.” A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We support local leaders to make decisions on pedestrianisation based on their communities’ needs.

According to Sean Duffy, U.S. Secretary of Transportation, the issue stems from communication issue impacting “all Air Route Traffic Control Centers” nationwide. “The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” Duffy posted to X Friday afternoon. “FAA technicians are investigating the issue. Federal officials have yet to publicly identify what triggered the problem, and it is unclear if the incident is linked to a cyberattack. The FAA directed departing flights to remain on the ground until further notice and said it would handle inbound international flights case by case. events.title: US aviation administration resumes flights after grounding
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts US Federal Aviation Administration says flights can resume after national ground stop It is only the second time flights have been grounded in the US since the September 11, 2001, terror attacks. ( Reuters: Joshua Lott ) Flights in the United States have resumed after the US Federal Aviation Administration earlier issued a national ground stop due to safety. It was only the second time flights have been grounded in the US since the September 11 terror attacks in 2001. The grounding had been called due to a communication issue affecting 22 regional air traffic control centres. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says flights can now resume, after it earlier issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstance and reasons for safety". US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed the ground stop was due to a communication issue affecting all air route traffic control centres. Look back on our live blog for the latest on the issues affecting flights in the US and Australia. Mr Duffy said there was a communications issue affecting 22 regional air traffic control centres that direct planes en route between airports nationwide. He said FAA technicians were investigating the cause of the issue. US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication yet of a nefarious act behind the communication issue. "It's just a telecommunications outage … everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying." Mr Mullin said investigators would look at whether there was any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But the system operates out of one location near Washington DC, and only sends recommendations to the air traffic control centres. What we know so far about why US flights were grounded Aviation authorities cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for the outage. Shortly before the announcement, the FAA halted traffic in Chicago due to air traffic control issues. The agency said: "All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice." The FAA said international flights would be managed on a case-by-case basis. According to the Eurocontrol website, all US-bound traffic from its member states were suspended at the FAA's request because of technical issues. There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including Israel. FlightAware, an online aircraft-tracking website, is reporting that about 10,500 flights in and out of the US have already been delayed today. The website also said more than 1,800 flight services had been cancelled. Traveller Jeff Dubner was still waiting to disembark from his plane an hour and a half after leaving the gate at Los Angeles International Airport. "It's frustrating. This certainly sounds like it's going to be more than the usual run-of-the-mill delay. I look forward to finding out why," he said. This is only the second nationwide ground stop in the US since the September 11 terror attacks in 2001. The last one was in January 2023, when domestic departures were paused for less than two hours. The task force wants Congress to reauthorize cyber and information-sharing related bills and is still assessing whether it wants to recommend the passage of new bills. Notably, the ongoing Nvidia scandal was not discussed during the meeting, the official said.

events.title: What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs
events.summary: Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO raises questions about the company's role in AI financing. Investors are watching whether a leadership change alters Nvidia’s role in backing AI companies. Smaller AI infrastructure companies may be more sensitive to any pullback in Nvidia’s support. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny. Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive. Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change. "Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday. The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier. On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers. It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July. Neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday. CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress. It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li. "We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said. "However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday , before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person." "There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us." Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted. The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions. "Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies." — CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

events.title: AI risks are the biggest threat to the financial system, Fed survey finds
events.summary: A financial stability report that the Federal Reserve released Friday showed respondents most concerned about threats from artificial intelligence. AI was cited by 87% of respondents in the latest view from a variety of participants, up from 50% during the last survey in the spring of 2026. Threats from artificial intelligence topped the list for greatest risks to the financial system, far exceeding any other dangers, according to respondents who participated in a Federal Reserve survey released Friday. The central bank's twice-yearly look at a variety of dangers saw a surge in respondents saying that the biggest danger comes from AI along several fronts including debt, stock market valuations and security risks. "Respondents noted three distinct areas of concern: (1) elevated equity valuations and the possibility that lower-than-expected earnings could result in lower valuations and a market correction; (2) cybersecurity risk, stemming from either a malicious attack by sophisticated state actors or damage caused by frontier AI models themselves; and (3) risks associated with complex forms of AI-related financing," the report stated. The report comes with Wall Street on edge over high-flying AI hyperscalers, while communities are on alert for the rapid spread of data centers used to power the technology. Some 56% of voters in this month's midterm elections said data centers were of crucial or major importance in their choices, according to exit polling. Respondents to the Fed survey released Friday include a variety of market participants, economists, analysts and institutional sources. The report covers the period up to Oct. 28, just a few days shy of the election. Of the group, 87% cited AI as a "salient risk" to the system. That was up from 50% in the survey during the spring of this year and well ahead of the next most-cited danger, a risk asset correction, which was mentioned by 52% of those surveyed. Other leading risks were higher long-term rates (48%), cyberattacks (43%) and fiscal debt sustainability (43%), the latter coming with the U.S. debt over $40 trillion and the budget deficit near $2 trillion. The report otherwise found the system fairly stable, though it mentioned that hedge fund leverage is at its highest since 2013 and concentrated on a relatively small group.
