events.title: Activists call for Pressley to launch House speaker bid against Jeffries
events.summary: House Democrats are all but certain to elect House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries as their speaker designate next week. There could still be some turbulence, though , with progressive activists calling for Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., to launch a bid against Jeffries. Ricardo Sanchez, a Pressley spokesperson, said she was in “active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment, and deliver for the people. She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership.” Most Democrats don’t believe Pressley will actually launch a bid ahead of next week’s leadership elections. She’s privately denied interest in running to other lawmakers, according to people familiar with her comments, and she hasn’t laid the groundwork for a bid by sounding out support from other lawmakers. House Democrats are staring down brewing fights as younger lawmakers jostle for power and influence ahead of the party assuming its largest majority in decades. Once their leadership slate is set, the caucus will weigh major changes like implementing term limits, shaking up panel leaders, and standing up select committees on controversial policy issues. “We can have the fight about how many terms should be the limit, but I think the time is right — with all these new members coming into the caucus — to set some limits,” said Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt. At the “What’s Next” conference on Friday, Jeffries said discussion about term limits was the “right conversation to have.” And Rep. Janelle Bynum, D-Ore., launched an effort this morning to change the seniority system for subcommittee leadership positions. Jeffries and Democratic leaders could face an influx of new members who aren’t as beholden to caucus traditions when it comes to picking leaders based on seniority. “I think it’s going to be important for the Democratic Caucus to make sure that the voices of this large, energetic, new class of members are included at the table, and in general, I think we, as a party and as a Congress, are healthier when we allow for new perspectives and more renewal,” said Rep.-elect Luke Bronin, who’s coming to office after unseating a longtime Democratic incumbent. Democrats are also weighing the future of the select panel on China and whether to stand up a select committee on AI. Some Democrats have argued for changing the China committee, keeping it as is , or sunsetting it altogether. Top House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., who is close to Jeffries, has advocated for folding the China committee into his panel, and for standing up a separate Foreign Affairs subpanel on AI and chips. Doing so could set off a turf war with other powerful committee leaders.

events.title: Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer
events.summary: US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, according to a report from a former OpenAI engineer. Will DePue, who left the AI giant earlier this year to launch Unemployment Labs, an AI research consultancy, published forensic evidence showing that "DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models." "This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it," said DePue in a social media post . "When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern – a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model." It doesn't sound that insane. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang followed from revelations that he had an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who, in 2023, founded Singapore-based Megaspeed International. That company is reportedly under investigation by US authorities for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China. Huang's departure coincides with a renewed push to tighten US chip export controls. House Speaker Mike Johnson supports the idea . And there are at least four bills awaiting consideration that aim to limit China's access to leading edge AI tech: the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, Match Act, and the Cloud Security Act. On Monday, US Senators Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) cited Jensen Huang's "relationship with a suspected Chinese spy" as a justification for passing the AI Overwatch Act, which would codify the Trump administration's existing chip export controls. The Trump administration on Thursday said it's not sure whether Alice Huang was a spy, an allegation denied by Beijing and currently under investigation by the FBI. Whatever the case, the current rules clearly are not working. Only a few weeks ago, Lava, an Israel-based security company, said it had found "32 Nvidia B300 GPUs, part of Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra generation, through publicly exposed monitoring endpoints with IP addresses geolocated to China." These GPUs, Lava noted, are subject to US export controls [PDF]. The security biz said its findings followed from the exposure of monitoring systems intended for internal infrastructure management that were publicly exposed. How DePue reached his conclusion The analysis published through DePue's consultancy, "Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled Nvidia Blackwell GPUs," takes a different approach: analyzing the published weights of various models from Chinese AI labs. As described in the report, model weights – the parameters that change in relation to training data – must be initialized with some value. One method for doing so involves a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox. The algorithm starts with a seed value that produces the same set of initial values whenever it's run. Using PyTorch, initialization can be done by creating multiple GPU threads that work in parallel, with the help of Nvidia's cuRAND library. And because this process is not truly random, it's possible to select a chip and a seed value, generate the initial weights for that hardware and compare that pattern to a model's published weights. "I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models," said DePue. "In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models – including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3 – were initialized on Nvidia Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in Nvidia's flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems." Noting that this is the first time MiniMax and Ant Group have been publicly linked to usage of Nvidia's Blackwell, he also cited several limitations to his approach. One is that usage of Blackwell GPUs doesn't prove where the GPUs were located, so it's possible some of these Chinese labs used this hardware through US providers – a loophole the Cloud Security Act aims to close. DePue's report includes initial seed values that linked DeepSeek-V3 to Nvidia's Hopper and DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Blackwell, for those who wish to attempt to reproduce the results. DuPue claims that multiple senior researchers, both independent and inside frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, have confirmed the result. Coincidentally, OpenAI and Anthropic have each complained about Chinese labs copying their models through distillation, a pastime also noted by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. ®

events.title: Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance
events.summary: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Office of the Comptroller of the Currency National Credit Union Administration The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Federal Reserve Board, the National Credit Union Administration, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that they will extend, until December 16, the comment period for proposed guidance on managing risks associated with third-party relationships. Comments on the proposal were originally due November 16. The proposed guidance reflects the agencies' supervisory experience and lessons learned from examining financial institutions' third-party risk management practices. It is intended to help banks and credit unions tailor their risk management practices to the risks associated with individual third-party relationships. The proposed guidance takes a principles-based approach and, like all supervisory guidance, is non-binding. When finalized, the federal bank regulatory agencies plan to rescind existing third-party risk management guidance and replace it with the finalized guidance to promote consistency and prudent innovation in the banking industry. NCUA also plans to rescind its existing third-party risk management guidance and will conduct its own reviews to update related guidance as needed. Also today, the Federal Reserve Board separately announced that it will extend, until December 16, the comment period on a proposed third-party risk management guide specifically for Federal Reserve-supervised traditional community banks. events.title: They train people to avoid 'honeypot' scams—here are the common red flags they spot: 'It feels so good to be wanted'
events.summary: Psychology and Relationships ChatGPT for Teens makes safety strides, says expert, but do they work? Psychology and Relationships Parenting expert Emily Oster on navigating anxiety around tech and AI Psychology and Relationships Emotionally intelligent couples ask 1 question every morning: Psychologist Work Forcing workers to use AI can be counterproductive—3 tips for a better approach Raising Successful Kids Harvard- and Stanford-trained child psychiatrist: 5 habits of parents who raise highly resilient kids Shawnee Delaney often kicks off a training session by telling a room full of corporate workers: "OK, raise your hand if you've ever gotten a flattering message on LinkedIn just complimenting your background and your profile and your experience." "Every hand goes up," she says. Then, she tells attendees how responding to a simple adulatory message could unwittingly open the door to a potential romance scam. Delaney is a corporate security expert, well-versed in teaching people how to avoid “honeypot” schemes, in which a bad actor uses romantic or sexual interest to build trust and gain information, access or leverage over a target. The term is currently making headlines in the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation from the company, following reporting on his admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Honeypots, also known as "honey traps," are a very human form of social engineering attack, a category that also includes various forms of phishing and use of deepfake technology. And you don't have to be a billionaire tech CEO to possess information that scammers may value. As competition in the global artificial intelligence race heats up, OpenAI is reportedly training employees to recognize espionage tactics including bribery, romantic manipulation and blackmail, according to The Wall Street Journal . On Nov. 3, cryptocurrency exchange Binance revealed that a recent cyberattack — which saw roughly $6 billion of digital assets stolen — was partially made possible by a fake job interview scheme that infected an employee’s work computer with malware. "People can get solicited, bribed, romanced, etc.," says Kevin Tian, co-founder and CEO of Doppel, an AI-powered platform meant to help identify and deflect social engineering attacks. He adds: "If you've got access to sensitive IP [intellectual property] — it's not just AI companies — you can be a target." Increasingly, scammers can use AI to scour websites ranging from Reddit to Pinterest for an individual's personal information and customize a ploy designed specifically for them, Tian says. Once they have relevant data points, attackers tend to use "the oldest tricks in the book: elicitation, flattery, ego," says Delaney, a former intelligence officer with the Defense Intelligence Agency and the founder and CEO of Washington, D.C.-based corporate security consulting firm Vaillance Group. In many cases, Delaney notes, targets have an inkling that something is suspicious — but they'd rather allow themselves to believe the interest is legitimate. So how do you keep yourself from falling victim? Trust your self-awareness, common sense and ability to identify situations that feel too good to be true, she says. "The bottom line is, we're all human," says Delaney, adding: "It feels so good to be wanted, or to be respected, or to be appreciated, or loved." How to spot red flags and do some vetting Delaney, who has worked with Fortune 500 companies such as Uber and Merck, advises corporate clients on cybersecurity risks and develops training programs to improve employees' awareness of security threats. Her sessions aim to build awareness of manipulative connections, such as romance scams, from how they begin to the natural progression they often take. "Introduction, then repeated contact, favors, sensitive requests — the secrecy, the pressure," she says. Bad actors may tap into any information you post online to find an interest that can be mirrored and exploited, or an acquaintance who can be infiltrated and make an introduction. If someone you know and trust makes an introduction, you might be less likely to "go do due diligence" on the new person, even if they're a stranger, Delaney says. One of Vaillance's services includes building a "targeting package" around an executive or C-Suite member, says Delaney. "We can show how they are vulnerable and how we would target that organization just by leveraging the people around them in that circle: spouses, friends, kids, parents, administrative assistants, neighbors," she says. "That's when people's eyes open." From there, she discusses red flags to spot. Conversations that begin with flattery and seemingly innocuous small talk can gradually shift toward digging for information, introductions to colleagues or access to documents, says Delaney. It's human nature to want to be helpful and fulfill friendly requests, she adds.

events.title: This year’s bug count just passed 100K
events.summary: Chalk up a new record for vulns. The number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) found and disclosed so far in 2026 surpassed 100,000 on Friday - more than double 2025’s total - and the reason can be summed up in two letters: AI. “It’s kind of wild,” Josh Bressers, VulnCheck’s director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure, told The Register . “The thing that almost scares the bejesus out of me is while 100K sounds like a lot, in a couple years we're going to say, remember when it was only 100K?” As of the time of our interview, about 4 pm UTC on Friday, VulnCheck counted 100,222 CVEs, he said. Microsoft alone added 1,094 security flaws to the total count on Tuesday, following 1,474 vulnerabilities the month before. “There's no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we're seeing.” All the major CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) - these are the organizations authorized by the CVE program to assign unique identifiers to security vulnerabilities - like VulnCheck, Microsoft, Oracle, GitHub, and other large enterprise IT vendors “are just screaming into the atmosphere right now,” Bressers said. “It’s AI.” Meanwhile, the percentage of these bugs that are exploited in the wild remains relatively consistent. About 1.4 percent (1,363) of the CVEs published this year have been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. “But obviously, as the number of CVEs grows, [1 percent] of 1,000 is a lot different than [1 percent] of 100,000,” Bressers said. Plus, as other security researchers have documented, the window between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits – often by reverse engineering the patch while end users are still applying the fix – is rapidly shrinking. This is also thanks to AI . From CVE to KEV From January to June, 88 percent of the exploitation observed by CrowdStrike using public proof-of-concept (PoC) code occurred within 48 hours of the code's release. The security firm said China-linked groups such as Vault Panda and Genesis Panda moved even faster, launching attacks within 24 hours of disclosure. Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026. This window has closed even further during the second half of the year, which also seems to coincide with the AI-induced vulnpocalypse . “It’s often just hours,” Bressers said, noting 14 make-me-root vulnerabilities that VulnCheck disclosed on Friday in Copeland refrigeration controllers. Two are under active exploitation. These are the devices that Iranian hackers abused to spoil food and spark fires in supermarkets across Europe . “We published those CVEs, and literally minutes later, we were seeing hits on our honey pots,” Bressers said about the Copeland device vulnerabilities. “We’ve hit a point where with anything that looks interesting, someone is taking that information and seeing what they can do with it. Is it AI driven? Probably. It'd be hard to say it's not, because we've seen it really ramp up recently.” This influx of software bugs requires a sea change in how the entire industry approaches vulnerability disclosure and patching. “We don't have a security problem anymore,” Bressers said. “We have a data problem now. Instead of obsessing over vulnerabilities, we need to start looking at things like heat maps for infrastructure, and figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you. The CISA BOD helps with that.” What to prioritize in a patchpocalypse The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) in June issued a cybersecurity directive that replaces flat-deadline vulnerability management policies. Instead of prioritizing patching based solely on CVSS severity scores, the directive instructs organizations to prioritize based on specific risk criteria, including whether the asset is internet-exposed, under active exploitation, and whether an attacker can automate the exploit. “It's telling people to figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you, and then put those at the top of the list, instead of just saying we're going to fix all the criticals,” Bressers said. AI-generated vulnerability disclosures also create huge headaches for open source software developers and maintainers, which Bressers describes as a security problem “ super close to my heart .” “You've got individual developers that are drowning in vulnerability reports,” he said. “You have foundations being crushed by AI agents scraping their data or downloading their packages, millions of times a day, and it's straining the seams absolutely everywhere you look. The one thing I can say with certainty is: The way we currently do things has to change, and it's going to have to change fairly soon.” Different open source projects have taken different approaches to solving this issue. The Eclipse Foundation, which houses the Open VSX Registry , in April launched a “managed tier” for enterprise customers and other organizations running Open VSX at scale. Instead of using the free, open source version, the managed version guarantees a 99.95 percent uptime SLA backed by service credits. Its customers include AWS, IBM, Google, Cursor, and Windsurf. This paid option means commercial users who rely on the registry help fund its ongoing maintenance - and their own platforms’ security and performance. Meanwhile, curl’s maintainer, Daniel Stenberg, citing an “ avalanche of vulnerability reports ," updated its bug reporting rules last month. As of October 26, all low- and medium-severity reports go directly into the public GitHub repository, with only the high- and critical-flaws receiving private handling. Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty program this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team. “A lot more needs to happen, and I think it is going to be a challenge to enact some of this change,” Bressers said. “When a package registry drastically changes something, people start freaking out, and the world is going to end, and people on LinkedIn are complaining - a lot of people are hesitant. No one wants to be the first to jump into the alligator-filled pool. That's one of our challenges.”®

Morgan Securities. The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to hear a case in which Robinhood seeks to block a class-action lawsuit over the omission of interim financial data from the online broker's initial public offering in 2021. Robinhood wants the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling by the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals that revived a lawsuit by investors against the company and firms involved with the IPO, including Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan Securities . A San Francisco federal court judge had previously dismissed the lawsuit. The Trump administration and the Securities and Exchange Commission had urged the Supreme Court to hear Robinhood's appeal. "We are pleased the Supreme Court has agreed to hear our case and look forward to presenting our argument," a Robinhood spokesperson said in a statement. CNBC has requested comment from the attorneys representing the plaintiffs in the case. Trump's successors already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout China panel chair demands answers on Huang's alleged affair with a Chinese spy Pete Hegseth decries impeachment push, defends Iran war handling Robinhood's IPO came on the heels of a surge in investor interest during the Covid-19 pandemic in so-called meme stocks, and trading in the crypto asset dogecoin. In July 2021, Robinhood conducted its IPO, "for which it prepared a registration statement" that "contained only limited information about Robinhood's performance during the second quarter of 2021," the 9th Circuit panel that heard the case noted. "After the initial public offering, Robinhood reported financial results from that second quarter, and its stock price dropped," the panel wrote. The investors who sued Robinhood and the other defendants alleged the registration statement omitted material information it was legally required to disclose.

events.title: Noosa startup's solution to tackle burping cattle's methane emissions
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Methane-reducing supplement made in Noosa commercialised for cattle industry Nusqe Spanton says Provectus Algae has made an affordable methane-fighting supplement. ( ABC News: Jessica Ross ) A Noosaville-based company has developed an affordable feed additive for cattle designed to reduce methane emissions from cow burps by about 65 per cent. The Queensland government has granted $3.8 million to help commercialise the supplement. Affordably reducing methane emissions from Australia's 30 million burping cattle is a step closer, researchers say, after reaching a milestone at an industrial estate minutes from Noosa's Main Beach. In a shed stacked high with self-cleaning tanks, swirling red algae is being mass-produced under strobing lights. Nusque Spanton takes a walk through the algae growing room. ( ABC News: Jessica Ross ) Founded eight years ago, Provectus Algae has developed what it describes as a library of photosynthetic microbes. Among its work, it's using algae to make granular and liquid cattle feed additives for feedlots, paddocks and dairy farms. Now a $3.8 million Queensland government grant will help the company commercialise its cattle feed supplement. The recipe was built on CSIRO's 2011 discovery that native Asparagopsis seaweed could significantly reduce methane emissions from livestock. However, a 2024 Murdoch University study found cattle avoided feed with higher Asparagopsis concentrations, and there was evidence of ulceration and inflammation in cows' stomachs. Asparagopsis seaweed growing in the Provectus Algae laboratory. ( ABC News: Jessica Ross ) Provectus Algae CEO Nusqe Spanton said his company swapped the native seaweed out and recreated its processes using other algae and photosynthetic microbes. "It's a bioidentical product to what's found in the Asparagopsis itself," he said. "We've been able to bio-mimic the exact constituents we found in the algae species that was originally developed by the CSIRO." Mr Spanton said livestock happily ate the supplement. The algae has been turned into a dry cattle feed supplement. ( ABC News: Jessica Ross ) "We have done extensive safety testing, and we've proven that there is no residue within the animal, and we've proven safety throughout the animal supply chain." The CSIRO has estimated ruminant animals, including cows, sheep and goats, which produce methane through digestion, are responsible for more than 10 per cent of Australia's total greenhouse gas emissions. Scientists have fitted cattle with unusual-looking high-tech headgear to quantify exactly how much methane they produce, mainly through their burps. A 2025 study found Australia's grain-fed cattle emissions were 56 per cent lower than previously believed . The technology to measure methane emissions involves tight-fitting headgear strapped to cows' heads. ( Credit: Supplied ) Provectus Algae has run pilot trials with more than 3,000 cattle, including on Mort and Co feedlots on Queensland's Darling Downs. "We target a range in the feedlot industry, pastoral and dairy applications of around 65 per cent emissions reduction," Mr Spanton said. He said the supplement worked by targeting microbes in the guts of ruminant animals. "It's extremely effective … it doesn't affect the broader digestibility microbes that are found in the rumen and therefore doesn't impact the ability for that animal to grow or be healthy in its life cycle," he said. Nusqe Spanton showed state minister Tony Perrett around the factory. ( ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols ) Queensland Primary Industries Minister Tony Perrett said the state contained half the national cattle herd, worth more than $14 billion to the Queensland economy. "That's why we're continuing to back smart research, smart people and taking those opportunities into commercialisation," he said. The Victorian, Tasmanian, South Australian and Western Australian governments have also invested in businesses to accelerate efforts to lower livestock emissions. University of Melbourne carbon farming professor Richard Eckard said additives worked better in feedlots, where supplements were continuously eaten. "If you had to deliver it in the northern grazing industry — where we measure our properties in hundreds of square kilometres — well, it's a different challenge," he said. "It's why we need a mixture of options." Richard Eckard would like to see the costs of the supplements come down to less than 10 cents per animal.

events.title: How Nvidia’s Jensen Huang – and Trump – jumped the guardrails
events.summary: The Scoop In January, the general counsel for what was then the world’s most valuable company delivered a blunt directive on chip export controls to more than a dozen government officials: What Donald Trump and his friend Jensen Huang want, goes. “I was with the president when he and Jensen discussed this so I want to let you know what the president wanted,” said Nvidia’s Tim Teter, according to people with access to a detailed account of the call. “He wants this to go fast.” People on the call fell silent. At issue were proposed conditions on licenses to export Nvidia’s H200 chips to China, which included requirements that chipsellers know who their cloud customers were before shipping and conduct know-your-customer checks on any buyers purchasing more than a few thousand chips. Nvidia objected, with Teter calling the cloud-customer requirement a “poison pill” for the company, the people said. Nvidia also wanted the threshold for the know-your-customer checks to be in the tens of thousands (the equivalent of billions of dollars of chips) and pushed for end-of-life conditions to only apply to chips that were facing export controls. While it’s not unusual for big corporations to work with US government agencies and Congressional staffers on legislation or agency rulemaking, or even to see draft regulation in advance, people familiar with Nvidia and its former CEO’s Washington connections say the chipmaker wielded an unprecedented level of influence in shaping guidelines with far-reaching global security and business implications for the entire industry. The previously unreported discussions have only taken on greater significance since Huang stepped down from the company he co-founded decades ago after media reports of extramarital affairs with two subordinates and one with a customer and suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia declined to comment. Spokespeople for the White House didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. A spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security, which is housed within the Department of Commerce, said it was “completely routine” for the department and other agencies to work with individual companies in this manner and that “often the conditions change in response to legitimate commercial considerations” raised by corporations. The final version of all license conditions are reviewed by the state, defense, energy, and commerce departments.“Nvidia would have gone through the same process for license conditions as any other license applicant. Nvidia consulting with non-political experts at multiple US government agencies regarding its proposed changes to the conditions is consistent with standard practice,” the spokesperson said. Invoking the president If Trump was Huang’s friend in the White House, Teter was his muscle in Washington. After more than two decades at law firm Cooley LLP, Teter joined Nvidia in 2017, soon after the chipmaker announced the beginning of the “ AI computing era .” Nvidia’s GPUs had sparked the “big bang” of modern AI, Huang wrote at the time, years before Nvidia would turn into the world’s most valuable company. But as Nvidia became a bigger geopolitical force — and Huang became a fixture alongside Trump at meetings, dinners and the Oval Office — Huang and Teter developed a “scorched earth, adversarial attitude,” according to a former government official familiar with their Washington presence. “They make things more personal, going after think tankers, government officials, and the like,” the former official said, referring to reports of Nvidia targeting critics of the company and proponents of export controls. As he bulldozed through Washington, Teter regularly invoked President Trump’s name to push Nvidia’s agenda. In one exchange viewed by Semafor, Teter accused government officials who were developing export restrictions of misrepresenting Nvidia’s products and President Trump’s policies, chiding them for not carrying out Trump’s agenda and insisting that Trump deserved their support. Teter and the team of Nvidia lobbyists would often capitalize on their implicit White House backing and on the fact that most Hill staffers didn’t have the technical expertise to fight back on the company’s claims that certain restrictions weren’t technically feasible, even if later they were proven wrong, current and former congressional staffers told Semafor. Staffers “were kind of just believing whatever they were told,” and Nvidia would get all sorts of bills watered down, one staffer said. Nvidia’s “MO has largely been gaslighting,” creating an “intense trust deficit between the government and the Hill and Nvidia,” a former staffer said. And “obviously, the canonical example at this point is Nvidia denying” improper chip sales to China, this person said. Huang has said there’s no evidence chips were getting diverted to China, but Bloomberg has reported that Nvidia undercounted the Megaspeed sales it reported to the US government by 50,000 chips, worth billions of dollars. Companies tied to Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy, have purchased at least $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips since 2023, The Information reported . But well before Nvidia came under fire for its relationship with Megaspeed, Nvidia told staffers that a provision in the 2025 Chip Security Act, which would require chipmakers to be able to locate their chips, was a nonstarter. “They basically said it was not technically feasible” the former staffer said, “they were like, ‘we would need completely new technology to do this, and even if we did it would be very easily spoofable.’” In meetings with committee staff, Nvidia lobbyists argued location verification would create security holes. They “ran this line of bullsh-t on how the Chip Security Act was going to create all these cyber vulnerabilities,” a second former staffer said. “We spent six months going behind them and having to unpack all of the bullsh-t that [they were] telling to other offices.” Then in December, Reuters reported a new location verification technology feature, which Nvidia had been demonstrating privately for months. The feature was launched in May, meaning the company had been “lying to Congress about the technical feasibility while you were literally baking it into your next chip generation,” this person said. Nvidia declined to comment on the location-verification technology. Willing partner Nvidia, though, found a willing partner in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who appeared to be more concerned with avoiding another painful trade war with China, as Trump was, and with staying on the president’s good side than with combing through the innards of chip regulations, according to people familiar with the matter. “Lutnick was fine with the H200s [being sold]. I think he’s just tried to be very careful to not rock the boat, and also it’s been convenient to make friends with industry allies like Jensen, especially since Trump likes Jensen as well,” a former Commerce official told Semafor

events.title: Why a new court ruling matters for press freedom and privacy
events.summary: Protecting privacy and press freedom: An important Fourth Circuit ruling Nov 11, 2026 | Jon Palmer, Corporate Vice President and Chief Legal Officer, Microsoft The free press in America depends on the ability of journalists to protect confidential sources. On November 10, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit underscored that principle. The court placed limits on secret government demands for journalists’ online data, and upheld the rights Microsoft and LinkedIn went to court to defend. LinkedIn, a Microsoft subsidiary, challenged two government orders: one, seeking journalists’ online data, and another that prevented the company from informing the journalists or their news organizations of the demand. The opinion, authored by Judge Harvie Wilkinson III, opens with the statement that “[i]t is part of the audacity of the American project to believe that collective security can coexist with individual freedom.” Writing that “[c]onfidentiality of sources is the lifeblood of a free press,” the court remanded the case to the district court to consider narrowing both the scope of the government’s demand for information and the restrictions on LinkedIn’s ability to disclose the demand. In a world where journalists routinely use digital platforms to identify sources, communicate privately, and gather information, this case provides key legal guidance. Overbroad requests for online data can expose confidential sources, including individuals who may have no connection to the investigation itself. As a technology provider, we believe we have an important responsibility both to follow the law and to protect the people and organizations that rely on our services. When users are unaware that the government is seeking their information, technology providers are the last line of defense. They alone are in a position to challenge overly broad demands and ensure users’ rights are protected. We were proud to be supported in this case by amicus briefs filed by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, the American Civil Liberties Union, and other technology providers including Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta, and X. Microsoft has a long history of standing up for these protections across administrations led by both political parties. Our position has remained consistent: government demands should be appropriately tailored, secrecy is the exception, not the rule, and customers should receive notice unless the government demonstrates a specific need for nondisclosure. For well over a decade, we have challenged unnecessary secrecy orders, pressed for changes to Justice Department practices, and advocated for stronger legal safeguards regarding government access to customer data. We recognize the government’s legitimate responsibility to investigate crime and threats to national security. As the Court here recognized, those investigations must be conducted within appropriate legal limits and must still protect privacy and First Amendment rights. This ruling reinforces that balance, concluding with the statement: “Serious security and speech claims are in tension in this case. There is space under law for both.” Now Congress should finish the job. As Brad Smith, Microsoft’s Vice Chair and President, argued in calling for Congressional reform of nondisclosure orders. Favorable court decisions and changes in government policy are important, but they are no substitute for durable legal protections. Congress should strengthen the laws governing nondisclosure orders by ensuring that secrecy is appropriately limited, justified by specific circumstances, and subject to meaningful judicial review. These reforms would help protect the privacy of individuals and organizations while preserving the government’s ability to investigate crime. The Fourth Circuit’s decision is an important reminder that privacy, press freedom, and public safety need not be competing interests. Our laws should protect all three. Microsoft and its subsidiaries will continue to stand up for these principles and the rights of the people and organizations that rely on our services. Protecting customer privacy means standing up for transparency Keeping secrecy the exception, not the rule: An issue for both consumers and businesses DOJ acts to curb the overuse of secrecy orders. Now it’s Congress’ turn. events.title: From the first console to the next chapter, XBOX celebrates 25 years
events.summary: Tokyo Game Show Xbox Stream 2022: News and Updates on 22 Games From Majority Japanese Developers, Deathloop Coming to Xbox Next Week, and More Stories Untold Is Now Available For Xbox One Dungeon Defenders: Awakened Available Now on Xbox Series X|S and Xbox One Minecraft Dungeons II’s New Dimension Coming to Minecraft Java & Bedrock Edition Fable: Deep Dive Into New Gameplay With Playground Games | Official XBOX Podcast Gears of War: Reloaded Multiplayer Beta Begins This Weekend – Preorder Now for Access This message was just sent to Team XBOX employees globally. Microsoft was founded on the belief that computing could put extraordinary capabilities in the hands of ordinary people. Gaming has been part of that story since the company’s beginning. In 1979, we released Microsoft Adventure , a text-based game that looked more like MS-DOS than an early version of Minecraft . Adapted by a single programmer, Gordon Letwin, one of Microsoft’s first 13 employees and later an architect on OS/2, the game let players explore a digital world, collect treasure, solve puzzles, and encounter mythical creatures. A few years later, Bruce Artwick brought the magic of flight to the 16-bit IBM PC, making it possible to fly a plane from your desk. Over the following decade, Microsoft published dozens of other titles including Minesweeper , Age of Empires , and another four Microsoft Flight Simulators , while Windows helped usher in 3D gaming with partners such as id Software (which would join XBOX some 24 years later). In the mid-1990s, a small team working on DirectX, the technology that helped developers make games for Windows, had a big idea: using PC architecture to power the first American video game console in decades. Shortly thereafter, work began on the secret “Project Midway.” When the original XBOX launched in 2001, it was impossible to miss. It was 2-3x larger than rival consoles, with a giant X molded into a black enclosure and a bright alien green jewel at the center. It shipped with a hard drive when competitors asked players to buy standalone memory cards and an Ethernet jack when 9 in 10 households still used dial-up. It also boasted more than twice the processing power of the PlayStation and GameCube and pioneered dual analog controllers. A year later, Xbox Live revolutionized online play with persistent friend lists and matchmaking, as well as a common service for developers to build connected experiences. And bringing all of this together was Halo: Combat Evolved , a launch title that not only defined XBOX but proved its first advertising campaign: “Games Will Never Be The Same.” Twenty-five years later, XBOX has grown into one of the world’s largest gaming businesses. We’ve built four generations of XBOX consoles, with a fifth on the way. Today, our games reach more than a billion players every year spanning beloved and iconic franchises such as Call of Duty, Candy Crush, Diablo, Doom, Fable, Fallout, Forza, Gears of War, Halo, Minecraft, Overwatch, Sea of Thieves, The Elder Scrolls, StarCraft, Warcraft, Wolfenstein, and many more. XBOX has been built by generations of employees, studios, developers, and partners who believed in what gaming could become. To all of you, thank you. I especially want to recognize the 111 people across XBOX and our studios who have been here for 25 years or more. You’ve helped shape the history we’re celebrating today, and each of you will receive a special engraved console to commemorate what you’ve helped build. Since joining XBOX, I’ve heard stories of friendships that began over a session and lasted a lifetime, of people who met the person they would marry, and of parents now sharing the games they grew up on with their children. I’ve also heard about people who are no longer with us, and how much those hours spent playing together still mean to those who love them. Ultimately, this is why we exist. The story of XBOX has never been ours alone. Our fans have challenged us, cheered us on, held us accountable, and stuck with us. We’ve been celebrating this anniversary with fans around the world and special launches. Today, we are bringing the celebration home to Seattle. Gaming has always been an industry driven by dreams. Not just the desire to bring something imagined to life, but to share it with others. Sometimes that dream is of a game, other times a console, a character, or an entire universe. The history of XBOX is a testament to the power of these dreams and how they can grow over time. The first Microsoft Flight Simulator was just 160 KB, with 2D graphics, 16 colors, and 20 total airports. The 2024 version draws on more than 2.5 petabytes of data (more than 15 billion times the size of the original game). Its 200-million-square-mile map recreates almost every city, road, and landmark across the planet, with trillions of individually rendered trees and real-world weather reproduced in near real time. While modern games demonstrate the heights of human craft in ways unimaginable just decades ago, the cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown just as dramatically. As a result, too many ideas never become games, and too many games fall short of what their creators imagined. For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition. We must change this. Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today’s games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982. I believe the future of gaming will look more like its beginning, when a small team with a big idea could change how the world plays. Our responsibility is to deliver great games, unmistakable hardware, and give more people the chance to make something the world has never seen.

events.title: Hassett denies report he's leaving White House: 'Not true'
events.summary: National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett poured cold water on a report that he's expected to leave the White House in the coming weeks. That report is "not true," Hassett told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a text message. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett on Friday poured cold water on a report that he's expected to leave the White House in the coming weeks. Semafor reported earlier Friday afternoon that Hassett "has been inquiring about roles outside the administration," even before Republicans' drubbing in last week's midterm election. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , and his counselor David Zervos , are among the names being floated to replace Hassett, according to Semafor, which cited unnamed people familiar with his plans. But a White House official told CNBC in a statement later Friday, "There is no factual basis for this reporting." "Kevin Hassett is a key member of President Trump's economic team and will continue working to advance President Trump's economic policies," the official said on condition of anonymity to discuss the matter. Zervos, reached by phone after Semafor's story published, declined to comment. While Hassett denies he is departing the White House, several other Trump administration officials have stepped down since Democrats' staggering wins in the Nov. 3 midterm, flipping Congress blue and overhauling President Donald Trump's plans for the rest of his term. White House chief of staff Susie Wiles left her role Friday and was succeeded by Stephen Miller. Multiple Department of Justice officials have also left since Election Day, including Harmeet Dhillon, a leader in the DOJ's civil rights division, and John Eisenberg, who headed the national security division.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters What, you didn't actually want to fact-check it yourself, did you? Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer 10 hours ago Another Linux kernel developer steps back from some duties due to overload 16 hours ago Alibaba's Qwen3.8 re-educated with a more Western worldview 1 day ago Google promises its new smart specs won't give creeps their ideal view 1 day ago A third of US AI chatters are hot at bots, hurling insults at LLMs 1 day ago The internet is full of schlock, from biased news and dubious hot takes to false factoids. LogicLens aims to separate fact from fiction using the very same technology behind some of that slop: AI. It’s a simple premise, really: LogicLens, which lives in Chrome as a browser extension , or on iOS in the form of a mobile app called Receipts , combs through articles, social media posts, and other content to check it not only for factual inaccuracies, but also for bad reasoning. LogicLens and Receipts claim to identify logical fallacies , flag reports that misrepresent information, detect content that attempts to polarize an issue, and the like. It also cites sources, so if, for example, you need to call someone out on their BS, you’ll have ammunition. Or, if you’re trying to fact-check something before sharing it, you can get a more accurate view of the situation, and maybe post something else instead. Using the Chrome extension is as simple as clicking on its icon in the list of extensions in the browser. On iOS, the Receipts app is found as a share option. Once it starts, LogicLens scans an article, post, video, etc. to find potential issues of factual or logical inconsistency and flags them for review. If the facts of the matter turn out to contradict your worldview, LogicLens’ creators say they’re not trying to be partisan - you may just not be as informed as you need to be, which hopefully their tool will assist with. “We're not trying to be the referee of truth,” the company’s about page states. “Instead, LogicLens helps uncover the context, so you can decide for yourself without the spin." Of course, AI is increasingly used for online analysis and content review, and LogicLens is no exception. LogicLens doesn't identify the AI models powering its service in its publicly available documentation, but AI is definitely the backbone of the system. According to LogicLens, it's using an AI system that's “Research-backed and custom designed to outperform general models like ChatGPT & even trained experts.” We’ll leave that up to anyone willing to give the tool a spin to decide, but one thing’s for certain: The world needs something. Large language models and image generation tools are increasingly being used to generate internet content slop, and not all of it is as harmless as poorly made commercials for drop-shipped garbage: Some of it is being used to craft very convincing misinformation. A 2024 study found that AI-generated misinformation was even more convincing than stuff crafted by humans - and that was two years ago. Just think how much worse it’s likely become since then. To make matters worse, concerns have been raised about critical thinking skills being on the decline , potentially making it harder for people to identify falsehoods on the internet. AI users are reportedly less likely to admit they don’t know something, even though use of AI has been found in studies to l essen brain activity , leading to poorer retention of facts and worse performance on tests. Is using more AI the solution to the problem? In an ideal world, we’d all just put the computers down and go touch grass, but we’re not in an ideal world: We’re living in the age of AI. LogicLens is free but requires sign-up and restricts nonpaying users to 15 analyses a day and 100 over the course of a month. A $4.99 monthly subscription removes those analysis caps.

events.title: The senators who could join Van Hollen's insurgency against Schumer
events.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen is picking up endorsements in his challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader. Why it matters: The leadership fight exposes divisions within the Democratic Party days after its sweeping midterm victory , with some demanding a new direction and others crediting Schumer for the historic blue wave. Driving the news: Van Hollen (D-Md.), a senator since 2017, announced Thursday he's challenging Schumer because "we need new leadership." "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people." The other side: Schumer has far more public endorsements than Van Hollen. "Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?" Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said in a statement of support for Schumer. Van Hollen has disputed Schumer's claim to credit for the party's midterm performance, arguing that the wave was powered by voters rather than leaders in Washington. By the numbers: Schumer has public support from 14 senators, including himself, compared with five for Van Hollen. A candidate will need 28 or 29 votes to win, depending on the outcome of Alaska's Senate race, where votes are still being counted. Senators backing Van Hollen State of play: Van Hollen told MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side, though only four have publicly endorsed him. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) endorsed Van Hollen on Thursday night, saying he will fight for working families. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) threw his support behind Van Hollen when he announced his challenge Thursday. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) issued an endorsement for Van Hollen Friday afternoon. Incoming Sen. Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) endorsed Van Hollen Friday morning after previously calling for new leadership. Who wants new leadership? Some sitting senators have called for a leadership change without endorsing Van Hollen. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) has called for change but hasn't endorsed either candidate. Before Van Hollen announced his candidacy, Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) told NBC 5 Democrats "absolutely are committed to change," but didn't rule out supporting Schumer. Several Democratic senators-elect have also called for new leadership, including: Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.). Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Ill.). Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine). Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.). Sen.-elect Chris Pappas (D-N.H.). Context: Progressive critics say Schumer hasn't fought hard enough against President Trump and his agenda. Schumer's decision to help advance a Republican-backed government funding bill in March 2025 fueled the progressive backlash against his leadership. The progressive Working Families Party urged Schumer "not to seek another term as Senate Democratic Leader" in a letter, as first reported by Axios . Another labor group has also opposed Schumer and endorsed Van Hollen. Who's backing Schumer? Schumer entered the leadership fight with broad support among Senate Democrats. "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader," Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement this week. Schumer's public supporters include Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and King , along with Schumer himself. Also backing Schumer: Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Tammy Baldwin (Wis.) and Jack Reed (R.I.). Schumer also received pre-election endorsements from Sens. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), though neither has publicly reaffirmed that support since Van Hollen entered the race. Senators who haven't picked a side Several sitting senators have yet to publicly back either candidate. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) and Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) have not publicly committed to either candidate. Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) have called for a caucus debate over leadership. Sens. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) have expressed openness to a leadership change without endorsing either candidate. Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) hasn't committed to Schumer and wants to hear his vision for the Senate. The 2028 factor Several potential 2028 presidential contenders face a choice over who should lead Senate Democrats. Ossoff and Booker , both possible 2028 presidential contenders, have yet to pick sides — leaving them to choose between the party's longtime leader and a changing of the guard. Meanwhile, Gallego and Kelly , also seen as possible 2028 contenders, have backed Schumer. Zoom out: Schumer himself is up for reelection in 2028 and could face a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who has also been mentioned as a potential presidential contender. Schumer could also retire rather than seek reelection . What's next: Senate Democrats will hold a secret-ballot leadership election Dec. 1. Incoming senators will participate, and members can cast their ballots differently from their public endorsements.

events.title: Trump to rule on tariffs for Australian lamb after trade commissioners disagree
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Trump to rule on tariffs for Australian lamb after US trade commissioners disagree Some trade experts believe Donald Trump is likely to put new tariffs on Australian lamb as a result of the decision. ( Reuters: Leah Millis ) A US trade investigation has left the door open to putting tariffs on lamb imports. Australia argued against tariffs during the probe. US President Donald Trump will make the final decision, likely early next year. A US trade panel reviewing Australian lamb imports into the United States has been unable to agree on whether the American industry has been hurt by the imports. The rare tie-vote at the US International Trade Commission (USITC) means US President Donald Trump will ultimately decide whether to place tariffs or other trade restrictions on the Australian meat. "A tie vote … means the president can decide which vote (affirmative or negative) he chooses the 'winning' vote," Georgetown University's Jennifer Hillman, a former USITC commissioner, told the ABC. Australia has been warning the US that any new tariff would just push up prices for American lamb-eaters. Most of the lamb imported into the US comes from Australia and New Zealand. More than 100,000 tonnes of Australian lamb was exported to the US last year. It was valued at more than $1 billion. The next step in the process is a public "remedies hearing" to debate possible tariffs or other measures on December 1 . Commissioners will then produce a report for Mr Trump by January 11. "They will make recommendations to the president, but tariff decisions are always political decisions in part," said Alan Wolff, a former deputy director-general at the World Trade Organization. "In this administration, that's no different, except we know the president does, in fact, like tariffs. The USITC has been investigating the issue since July. The probe was requested by US trade ambassador Jamieson Greer, one of the key architects and strongest proponents of Mr Trump's tariffs policy. Australian lamb exports are already subject to a 12.5 per cent tariff, along with many other Australian products. Republicans call for Australian lamb tariff probe Republicans write to Donald Trump's top trade officials to request an investigation into Australian lamb, as several members of Congress sponsor a bill for a 30 per cent tariff on Australian sheep products. Australia has been arguing against that tariff, saying it goes against the countries' free trade agreement. It has also argued against any prospective new tariff on lamb. Mr Trump has not publicly commented on the issue. But he recently angered US cattle farmers by publicly supporting an increase in beef imports to push down prices — a possible sign he could be persuaded by affordability arguments against tariffs on lamb. Australia's ambassador in Washington, Greg Moriarty, told a recent USITC hearing that Australian lamb was important to keeping prices low in the US. '"Any action to restrict lamb meat imports would only increase costs for US con­sumers, reduce product avail­ab­il­ity and risk revers­ing the steady growth in US demand for lamb to the det­ri­ment of the US industry," he told the trade commission. The American Sheep Industry Association described today's decision as "an important step toward securing trade relief for US sheep producers". The investigation followed years of campaigning by the sector, which argued "surging low-priced imports" from Australia and New Zealand were hurting the domestic industry. Dozens of Republicans in the US Congress backed their campaign. In a letter to trade officials in January, they argued foreign producers, "particularly Australia and New Zealand, have consistently taken advantage of our relaxed barriers and used them to undercut and infiltrate the US lamb market". events.title: This young startup wants to power floating data centers with the ocean’s heat, and investors are already on board
events.summary: Anyone who has weathered a hurricane can tell you that the oceans — which fuel the storms — contain a tremendous amount of energy. Thanks to global warming, they’re holding more than ever. A new startup wants to harness that energy to power data centers. Drogue , which has kept a low profile until now, is building a system that harvests heat from the ocean to power data centers on board floating vessels. According to founder and CEO Sam Sipe, the first prototype should be bobbing around the ocean, crunching bits, less than two years from now. The goal, Sipe said, is to help data center developers deploy servers in AI-friendly timelines. “The data center industry is a real estate game, and so they’re playing on 8- to 10-year timelines, including interoperability with utilities and [independent system operators]” that manage regional power grids, he said. “AI demand has increased 10x in just the last three years. It’s completely incompatible.” Drogue was founded just six months ago in Washington, D.C., and the startup told TechCrunch exclusively that it has already raised $20 million, including from XYZ Venture Capital, Toyota Ventures, Tamarack Global, Dream, FDVC, Garuda Ventures, Flexcap, Boost VC, and Slow Ventures, among other investors. In those six months, Drogue has designed a multi-megawatt prototype that will be installed on a traditional oceangoing ship and sent out to sea in early 2028. Future versions will be built on floating structures that more closely resemble offshore oil platforms. To Sipe, the decision to turn to the ocean was obvious. After years flying E-2D Hawkeyes off U.S. Navy aircraft carriers, he had an appreciation for the ocean’s immense power. “Most people think, oh, ocean — hard waves, storms, corrosion, biofouling. And I just see this majestic place and resource that we just ignore,” he said. As the planet warms, the oceans have been absorbing an additional 5.8 million terawatt-hours of energy every year. By comparison, all of human civilization uses about 180,000 terawatt-hours each year. If Drogue were to take some, surely the ocean wouldn’t miss it. The startup’s technology works like a heat pump run in reverse. A heat pump uses electricity to move heat from one place to another; Drogue’s system instead uses a difference in temperature to generate electricity. This approach, known as ocean thermal energy conversion, or OTEC, was first developed in the 1950s. Surface waters are warmer, heated by the sun, while down-deep temperatures are much colder, about 39°F on average (4°C). “There’s basically no amount of heat we can pull out of that that will collapse that temperature differential,” Sipe said. To leverage the temperature differential, the startup’s system draws in warm surface water, uses it to cool the data centers, and then sends the now-warmer water to boil ammonia, a chemical that turns to gas at -28°F. That ammonia gas is then sent through a turbine to generate electricity. Once through the turbine, it courses through a condenser, which turns the gas back into a liquid. There, cold water drawn from 1,000 meters deep passes over the condenser’s fins to absorb the heat. The warmed water is then released, and dissipates into the ocean. The ammonia gets sent back to the start of the sealed loop, and the cycle repeats. The basic idea was tested in the 1980s but tossed aside. “A lot has changed since the ’80s, specifically manufacturing techniques around the pipe and the heat exchangers,” Sipe said. To find out why, Sipe sought out people who had worked on those early efforts. “I just talked to everyone, basically interviewed them and figured out what went wrong, what went right, what would you do next. And everyone was like, dude, this stuff works. It’s just a matter of being able to raise enough capital to build something big enough, because there’s a sweet spot,” he said. There also had to be customers who could use that power while still at sea. Sending power to shore would require lengthy, expensive cables, and manufacturing on board would require similarly expensive shipping of materials and finished goods. Data centers are ideal — the servers are compact relative to other equipment, and shipping data off the platform is incredibly cheap. Each vessel would live at sea for about a decade, Sipe said. Drogue already has “approval in principle,” a preliminary sign-off, from the American Bureau of Shipping, which sets and checks safety standards for ships. Now it’s in the process of buying its first ship to start building a prototype ready for the open ocean. In many ways, Drogue’s concept is similar to Elon Musk’s plan for orbital data centers : find a cheap source of power, and get the data centers as close to it as possible. Except unlike orbital data centers, Drogue’s don’t need to launch expensive rockets to get there. They can just sail a ship on the ocean, something humanity has been doing for millennia.

events.title: Senate Dems break 32-year drought on leadership challenges
events.summary: As House Democrats barrel toward a speakership coronation , Senate Dems are getting their first contested race for leader in over 30 years. Why it matters: Democrats have spent years tearing themselves apart over the party's direction — without forcing their leaders to win a head-to-head vote. Senate Democrats will get that fight this year for the first time since Tom Daschle vs. Chris Dodd in 1994 — courtesy of Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) challenging Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.). But no one's challenging Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) for speaker. The last contested Democratic House leader race was in 2016, when Tim Ryan failed to beat Nancy Pelosi for minority leader. Between the lines: House Democrats are being bombarded with calls and emails urging them to oppose Jeffries, but the two most frequently floated alternatives — Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) — don't appear to want the job. Raskin told Axios that chairing the Judiciary Committee is his "dream job" and that he's "absolutely ... not a candidate for speaker in any way." "I am supporting Hakeem and voting for Hakeem," Raskin added. Pressley has privately told colleagues she isn't interested, multiple House Democrats told Axios. "Congresswoman Pressley is in active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment and deliver for the people," spokesperson Ricardo Sanchez said in a statement to Axios. "She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership." The big picture: Since the last contested Democratic leadership election, Republicans have endured the rise of MAGA, former Senate GOP leader Mitch McConnell's fall from power and a revolving door of House GOP leaders. In 2018, Kevin McCarthy drubbed Jim Jordan 159–43 to become House minority leader. In 2022, McConnell had to beat Rick Scott after the Florida Republican challenged him for Senate GOP leader. In 2023, McCarthy needed 15 ballots to become speaker and was ousted later that year. Republicans burned through nominations on Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan before settling on Mike Johnson . In 2024, John Thune had to beat two challengers — Rick Scott and John Cornyn — to succeed McConnell as Senate GOP leader. In 2026, Jim Jordan ... well, you know what happened. It was Tuesday. The intrigue: Van Hollen told reporters in Denver on Friday he's stopped "pursuing" a 2028 presidential bid because the "size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call with the American people." Van Hollen is up to five public votes (himself included) ahead of the Dec. 1 secret ballot. Schumer's at 14. The winner will need 29. Over in the House, the real question at this point feels like whether any House Democrats will oppose Jeffries on the House floor on Jan. 3. Jeffries has enjoyed unanimous support from his caucus since becoming leader in 2022 and is "confident that we're on a positive trajectory" but takes "nothing for granted," he told reporters yesterday. The bottom line: For once it's the Senate, not the House, providing all the drama on Capitol Hill.

events.title: How the Microsoft outage impacted courts and governments
events.summary: Courts and governments worldwide felt the impact of this week's Microsoft outage, which sidelined work and stymied communication. Why it matters: When Microsoft's popular workplace software went offline Thursday, it meant an extended lunch break for some offices — but for the courts and governments, it raised questions about the vulnerabilities of the technology underpinning justice and governance. Case in point: The state of Maine's judicial branch warned in a Thursday alert that requests for protection orders filed by email — urgent requests to keep parties safe from harm — may not have been received. Multiple court documents reviewed by Axios show lawyers requesting deadline extensions or alerting judges to the outage impacting their work. That includes DOJ lawyers: Government attorneys asked for an extension in the case brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over President Trump 's Kennedy Center takeover , saying the outage prevented them from "completing the necessary coordination." In a separate filing, Beatty's team acknowledged they were impacted as well. Zoom out: The impacts were also felt in courtrooms and offices internationally. The AP reported that a U.K. criminal trial was delayed as a result, with a Manchester judge saying, per BBC's reporting , "We are learning of the dangers of relying on computers and data systems." U.K.-based police forces also urged the public Friday to call first responders for aid, rather than using online forms. The Supreme Court of the Philippines said it, too, was affected by the outage. What they're saying: "We obviously need backup methods to keep the wheels of justice turning," says Gissou Nia, the founder and director of the Atlantic Council's Strategic Litigation Project. She pointed to a prior incident that previewed international reliance on U.S. tech: Though not exposed by an outage, the Trump administration's sanctions on the International Criminal Court prompted the Netherlands-based court to move off of Microsoft software to avoid its work being paralyzed. While court deadlines can be pushed back, service disruption for individuals seeking urgent injunctive relief is more critical, she notes. "If the only way to communicate ... is through these servers, and the request wasn't reached, it can result in somebody having left the country or having moved money out of an account," Nia says. Reality check: Shay Cleary, a National Center for State Courts consultant who specializes in tech and cybersecurity, emphasizes that courts typically have manual back-up plans in place. "Many of the people who work in courts are dedicated public servants, and they can figure out how to do things right," he adds. With Congress back in session, Hill communications were also left in a holding pattern Thursday — with one staffer writing on X, "Hope nobody needs Congress for a little while, your Legislative Branch is currently paralyzed by the Outlook outage." Municipal governments in Austin , Texas, and Jacksonville , Florida, among several others , warned that their emails — and in some cases, phone systems — were impacted. What we're watching: A page providing updates on the suite of Microsoft tech tools said in a Friday morning post that it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress." That statement came some 22 hours after the page first said the company was investigating reports of issues with email access. The bottom line: The very tools that connect us digitally can also divide us when things go wrong — underscoring the importance of preparing old-school backup plans to fill the gaps. events.title: IMF says more progress needed on Lebanon's banking sector reform
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund on Friday said Lebanon's bank restructuring law remains a key sticking point as Beirut looks to secure a new economic reform programme with the multilateral lender. The fund said progress was made in discussions on the country's banking sector restructuring strategy during a November 11-13 staff-level visit to Lebanon and that further engagement is expected to continue. "However, further work is needed to reach an agreement on a strategy for an effective and durable restructuring of Lebanon’s banking sector, leading to a sound and resilient system," said Ernesto Ramirez Rigo, IMF mission chief to Lebanon. The IMF in particular pointed to the implementation of the Bank Resolution Law and the Financial Stabilisation and Deposits Recovery Law - or the financial gap law - as "essential to restore financial stability and maximise deposits recovery" once they are adopted. Lebanon reached an initial staff-level agreement with the IMF in 2022 after the country's economy collapsed, although the government at the time was slow to implement the fund's recommendations. Lebanon defaulted on its debt for the first time in March 2020, leading to hyperinflation, high unemployment, a surging poverty rate and depositors frozen out of their savings. Its financial collapse generated losses of roughly $70 billion, a figure used in official estimates since 2022, although that number is now expected to be higher. The fund said further talks are needed to maximise deposit repayments while ensuring consistency with the central bank's and the banking sector's liquidity positions, and public debt sustainability and the restoration of the central bank's solvency. The IMF also said it remains critical the Financial Stabilisation and Deposits Recovery Law "upholds the hierarchy of claims in the allocation of losses, thereby maximising protection for depositors". Lebanon's Parliament passed a bank resolution law in August, although President Joseph Aoun appealed it to the Constitutional Council over an amendment concerning the central bank's independence and power. The fund at the time said it would assess any changes to ensure they were consistent with international standards. "The mission looks forward to continuing the engagement with the authorities to make further progress on these fronts in the coming weeks and remains fully committed to supporting Lebanon in its efforts to design and implement a comprehensive economic reform program, in line with the IMF’s policies and mandate," Mr Ramirez Rigo said.
