events.title: Pressure grows on Trump's Commerce Secretary Lutnick in fallout from Nvidia scandal
events.summary: How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security? US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet. Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions. Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but was not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with. Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months". "But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added. Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said some parts of the administration wanted more controls on trade with Megaspeed Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China. "President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said. Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment. There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but the Financial Times separately reported that the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included. However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia. "The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC , external . "The real story here should be: did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? "It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that." Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past. In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, according to US media. How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House Published 19 hours ago How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions Published 1 day ago Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X. Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Huang. Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips. They say Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into the US for inspection. A 25% tariff - a levy paid by US importers to the federal government - was imposed on those chips under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security. "Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said. events.title: After Jensen Huang’s exit, what top financial advisors are doing with Nvidia: Exclusive CNBC poll
events.summary: In a CNBC flash poll of its Financial Advisor 100 and Financial Advisor Council, most respondents said they were holding their Nvidia positions steady; none said they were selling at the time of the poll. AI demand, valuation and Nvidia’s leadership or governance were the most-cited factors that could change respondents’ approach. Advisors said investors should weigh their Nvidia concentration, time horizon and risk tolerance before reacting to short-term volatility. To gauge how wealth managers are responding, CNBC polled members of its Financial Advisor 100 and Financial Advisor Council. Thirty of the 122 firms and professionals contacted responded to the online, multiple-choice flash poll, conducted between 11 a.m. and 5 p.m. EST on Nov. 12. The poll is a snapshot of respondents' views, not a measure of all financial advisors. Most advisors polled are holding steady Most respondents, 19, said they are holding their Nvidia positions steady. Another four said they are increasing their stake, while seven said they do not own the stock. None said they were selling at the time of the poll. "Most of our clients are in a position to hold; the reason is because it makes up a smaller percentage of an overall diversified portfolio," Winnie Sun , managing director and founding partner of Irvine, California-based Sun Group Wealth Partners, said in an interview. Sun is a member of the CNBC Financial Advisor Council. More from CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors: CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor for 2026 takes a family-office approach CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 FAQ: Who is eligible and how rankings work Roth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisor After Jensen Huang's exit, what top advisors are doing with Nvidia: CNBC poll In open responses, several advisors wrote that they are taking a "wait-and-see" approach before changing their investment strategy with Nvidia and are telling their clients to do the same. "Don't react to short-term headlines," wrote certified financial planner Peyton Jamison, president of Jamison Private Wealth Management in Alpharetta, Georgia. "The company's valuation is extremely attractive, and the focus should remain on its underlying fundamentals and long-term investment potential." His firm is ranked No. 78 on the 2026 CNBC Financial Advisor 100 list. What would change advisors' positions Asked what factors could change their approach to Nvidia, 13 respondents cited the outlook for AI demand, 11 pointed to valuation, and 10 mentioned company leadership or governance. Some said the decision depends on the client, with eight citing risk tolerance and seven mentioning portfolio concentration. Seven said they do not expect to change their approach. Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results Tuesday, after the market close. In poll remarks, advisors said the company's fiscal third-quarter earnings will help determine their course of action. Advisors said that for investors, what to do may depend on how much Nvidia stock they already own, when they expect to need the money and how comfortable they are with volatility. "If this is a company that's going to keep you up at night and you just feel really uncomfortable with these unknown risks, then there was always the option to sell and move that capital to another stock or another portfolio," Sun said. How investors can check Nvidia exposure Nvidia exposure can also come through mutual funds and ETFs . Nvidia's large market value makes it a significant holding in many broad-market funds, including funds that track the S&P 500, as well as target-date funds in retirement-plan options. Investors can check their Nvidia exposure by reviewing the fact sheets for the funds in their 401(k) or brokerage accounts, which typically list a fund's largest holdings. A stock's decline does not translate one-for-one into a fund's decline. However, investors with dedicated technology, semiconductor or growth funds may have more Nvidia exposure than they realize, advisors say. "Nvidia is a big part of virtually everyone's portfolio whether they take an active or passive index approach," wrote Andy Pratt, a partner and director of investment strategy at Burney Wealth Management in Reston, Virginia, which is ranked No. 34 on the 2026 CNBC Financial Advisor 100 list. He said he advises clients not to overreact to short-term news and to let the dust settle before making decisions. — CNBC's Stephanie Dhue contributed reporting to this article.

events.title: How Microsoft outage has affected key public services in the UK
events.summary: Hospitals, GPs, police forces and property agents have had to find a workaround for Microsoft packages Hospitals, GPs, police forces and property agents across the UK have been hit by the global Microsoft outage . Here’s how the disruption to email and other IT facilities has affected key services. The NHS experienced “serious” and “widespread” disruption across the UK on Friday as a result of the Microsoft outage, with hundreds of hospitals, GP surgeries and community health services affected, senior health sources said. While some doctors, hospital workers and NHS night staff told the Guardian they first noticed problems accessing emails during the early hours of Friday morning, the severity of the problem became apparent to most from about 6am. The NHS.net Connect system – which more than 1 million NHS staff use for emails, meetings, calendars, file access and other tasks – is powered by Microsoft. The outage meant many could not log in, perform basic duties, or send and receive patient data needed for the delivery of healthcare. NHS sources said the outage caused disruption to a range of Microsoft 365 services relied upon by staff, including Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive and Copilot. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) also said it was experiencing problems sending and receiving emails. Some staff resorted to using patients’ paper records after being unable to access email and other IT facilities. An NHS England spokesperson said: “Local NHS services are enacting longstanding measures to manage IT outages and ensure critical services and appointments can continue for patients today.” Patients were urged to attend appointments on Friday unless advised otherwise, and to continue using 999 for emergency situations. Inevitably though, some operations and appointments were cancelled. Some staff said they were unable to send urgent messages about referrals for cancer and other serious conditions. NHS community services staff expressed concerns that patients who usually contact them via email, sometimes with very urgent needs and requirements, were unable to do so. Some local NHS organisations posted on social media requests for patients to contact them by phone. However, some GP surgery staff told the Guardian they were inundated with patients calling on Friday to check if appointments were going ahead. By Friday afternoon, some NHS doctors reported being able to send and receive emails again. The full extent and impact of Friday’s disruption on the NHS will probably not be clear for some days. Cases at magistrates, crown and civil courts were cancelled or delayed, as the Courts and Tribunals Judiciary relies on Microsoft platforms, including Outlook, for email. Minshull Street crown court in Manchester was among those affected, with Judge Maurice Greene sending jurors home for the weekend on Friday morning as their case, in which nine men are on trial accused of raping a woman who was drugged by her husband , was abandoned for the day. Greene told the jury that staff had been hunting for a fax machine as an alternative to email. “Many institutions rely on Microsoft 365, as do the court and various institutions connected to the court, so there have all been sort of delays because of this,” he said. The outage affected all levels of the court system, right the way up to the supreme court, the highest court in the land. “The Court is currently not receiving emails, but the Portal and contact forms are still functioning as normal,” it said in a post on X. Civil court cases, including in the family courts, were also affected, with planned judgments unable to be handed down. These are normally sent remotely, by email, meaning that some judgments have been delayed until Monday. The Scottish Courts and Tribunals Service said all civil and criminal courts were running, but that “some hearings are subject to delays”. A Downing Street spokesperson said people should “continue to attend courts and tribunal systems where they are able to”. The main reported casualty for policing was the service for people to report crimes or concerns online. Forces said emergency calls to 999 were unaffected. Back office roles, including communication departments, HR and some internal email systems, were worst hit. One senior source in a southern English force said: “It was more of an inconvenience rather than an operational challenge.” A spokesperson for Durham constabulary, in north-eastern England, said: “Frontline services and our ability to respond to incidents remain unaffected. Although our online crime reporting service has been down for several hours, our 999 and 101 lines have remained in constant operation for the public. “Our primary issue has been around the loss of email, which means we anticipate a potential backlog of non-urgent demand once the outage is fully resolved.

events.title: Scott Bessent says Treasury wanted to blacklist Megaspeed ‘for months,’ blaming Howard Lutnick as Nvidia fallout widens: ‘Commerce has the pen’
events.summary: Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick is now facing public pressure from his fellow Cabinet members over his decision to not blacklist Megaspeed, the cloud computing company at the center of Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The Treasury Department, among other federal agencies, were in favor of placing trade restrictions on Megaspeed, but the decision ultimately lay with Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on Friday. “There was coordination. Treasury, War, USTR, and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” he said. “But Commerce has the pen….You will have to ask them about their internal processes.” Megaspeed is under investigation by the Justice Department over the suspected violation of U.S. export controls, which prohibit certain U.S.-made chips from being sold and shipped to China. Helmed by Alice Huang, the alleged spy, Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatric shipped at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to China over two years, The Information reported . Lutnick under pressure Lutnick is facing intensifying scrutiny over reports he took action to protect Nvidia from the Trump administration’s export controls of U.S. AI hardware to China. The commerce secretary reportedly spent months “undoing” efforts to hold Megaspeed accountable for potential export control violations, Axios reported . Bessent confronted Lutnick in the Situation Room following the midterm elections over not placing Megaspeed on the entity list, according to the outlet. Bessent told CNBC, “We don’t repeat conversations in the Situation Room.” According to the New York Times , when Trump officials approached Oracle about cancelling a $7 billion deal to lease chips to Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent , Lutnick’s top deputy Jeff Kessler spoke up and said Lutnick had issues with a cancellation, as it would halt the shipment of 100,000 advanced Nvidia AI chips. Lutnick reportedly said he didn’t understand the rush to scrap the deal. The Commerce Department and Nvidia did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment. Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers want to hold Lutnick accountable for not placing Megaspeed on the blacklist. “The obvious question is why did he choose to sell advanced chips?” Republican Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy told Politico . “Secretary Lutnick needs to answer that in front of God and country.” Lutnick agreed to testify alongside Huang before the Senate Banking Committee to address national security concerns on Dec. 10.  Meanwhile, senior White House officials are now weighing whether to oust the commerce secretary from his position, Reuters reported . Even before news of Huang’s affair broke, Lutnick’s decision not to add 100 companies , including China’s DeekSeek, to the entity list put him in hot water. Lutnick’s potential conflicts of interest Lutnick argued with senior White House officials that export regulations against China would stoke the trade war with China and he insisted on having conversations with Trump about China’s restricted access to U.S. chips, the Times reported. The commerce secretary also had a friendly relationship and financial ties with Nvidia, bolstering concerns about favoritism toward the tech company. “Howard is the person I talk to most in the administration—he’s on top of the technology and learning the industry quickly,” Huang said in September 2025.  Before Lutnick became commerce secretary, he was the CEO and chairman of investment bank Cantor Fitzgerald, which held about $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock prior to President Donald Trump’s second term. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation
events.summary: Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday. That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago , led by IVP. LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence. With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use. True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well ( case in point is newcomer Mintive ). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce. events.title: Are you team car door or car bonnet? This town's history depends on your answer
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Lightning Ridge opal history dispute plays out on car doors and bonnets Blow the layer of dust off Lightning Ridge and you will find a town as rich in colour as the precious black opal mined here. The stone’s dark undertone is the marriage of carbon and iron oxide, brought together over millennia beneath the earth’s surface. It brings colour to life in a way that no other precious stone can. It is an exceptionally rare find, with more than 90 per cent of the world’s supply located beneath this outback moonscape. Great fortunes have been made and lost here on Yuwaalaraay Country in Northern NSW, where stories have become facts and truth can be just as elusive as the black opal itself. Among the corrugated iron shacks and the long-abandoned mine shafts that pockmark this land, the past is everywhere. Exactly what that history is, however, depends on who's telling it. Barb Moritz is waiting for us in front of an old miner's cottage on the main street. Built in 1932, its warped pinewood beams and lopsided tin roof resemble an abstract painting. It's the headquarters of the Lightning Ridge Historical Society, and the seat from which Barb holds court. She emerges from the shadow of the verandah awning whirring with facts and directions, her dark eyes glowing. Barb cuts a strikingly vibrant figure amid a palette of rusted metal and aging wood. When she smiles, the afternoon sun catches her opal dental filling and it flashes with brilliant greens and blues. Introductions are swift before Barb leaps into her opening stanza, fine tuned over decades of leading tour groups. She points towards the local pool, opened by Dawn Fraser in 1990. The Opal Miners Hall of Fame is further out, just a few minutes' drive from the cottage. Then there's the Lightning Ridge Cemetery, or as Barb refers to it, the "dead end of town". She casts us a deadpan glance and pauses for effect. Barb is a long way from the cornfields of Iowa in the American mid-west, where she grew up. She still isn't quite sure if she chose to move to Lightning Ridge, or if the black opal lured her. "From the very beginning, I feel I was directed to opal," she says, her accent still thick. Barb arrived in Lightning Ridge in the summer of 1990. Three years later, she was working for the historical society. "I met the people who lived here, the old-timers who built this community," she says. It wasn't long before Barb was the society's secretary. Tucked away behind the old miner's cottage is an aging demountable filled to the brim with miners' ledgers and newspaper clippings dating back more than a century. It is the engine room of the historical society. And it's here, among the records, that Barb pieces together a version of Lightning Ridge's opal-mining evolution. In the late 1990s, this history was translated onto a conspicuous canvas unique to the town's identity, the "car door tours". Across the featureless landscape, car doors mark out four colour-coded routes (green, red, yellow and blue) to sites the society deems significant to the town's history. "People lock their car doors because they're afraid maybe one will go missing," Barb says with a glimmer in her eye. The doors have become much more than a tourist attraction for the droves of travellers and grey nomads who pass through. They are now part of the landscape. They're also used by locals and emergency services to help locate people living on claims that are well and truly off the beaten track. The population of Lightning Ridge is a bit of a mystery. Officially, it has about 2,000 residents. Unofficially, it's more like 5,000 because many people move to this outback town to disappear. We follow Barb's car as she navigates the dirt roads, tracing the green car door tour as it winds its way up to McDonald's Six-Mile opal field. Perched on an ironstone ridge above the town, facing the western horizon, it's a moonscape of colourless rock, sheet metal and dozens of deserted mine shafts. You can't miss the monument to Charles Nettleton. Protected by a wire fence, the jagged rectangular stone slab and its plaque look lovingly maintained, but resemble a tombstone. There is pride in Barb's eyes as she takes stock of the monument, pale yellow under the midday sun. It would not be here without her ability to move heaven and earth for her adopted home. "[Charles Nettleton] was the first professional opal miner who came to this country" Barb explains. "And we decided … we needed to have a monument — a historical reserve — to where he had sunk his first shafts for the syndicate of businessmen who hired him.

events.title: The 4 types of people Dario Amodei said he won’t hire — and what Anthropic looks for instead
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said talent and culture "are the most important things" for a company. Bloomberg/Getty Images Dario Amodei said Anthropic doesn't hire jerks or people who can't get along with others. He said talent and culture are the company's top priorities, and he spends 40-50% of his time on it. Amodei said that focus has helped with retention. Don't bother applying for a job at Anthropic if your goal is to be the star of the show. That was one of the first things Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized on Friday, in a live-streamed interview with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon ahead of the AI startup's hotly anticipated IPO . Amodei said the company has been "very disciplined about turning down people who are deeply technically talented," but don't fit its culture. The company's recent IPO filing stated that its workforce grew from about 940 employees at the end of 2024 to about 5,300 as of late September. "We don't want people who are jerks. We don't want people who try to steal the show and don't work well with others. We don't want people who aren't oriented towards the public benefit," Amodei told Dimon. Amodei, who worked as vice president of research at research at OpenAI and was a senior research scientist at Google Brain, said talent and culture "are the most important things" for a company. He said he now devotes 40% to 50% of his time to focusing on those priorities. 'High-trust, low-ego' The CEO said that talent and culture create technology, and the company's presence and how it's viewed by the public comes from the talent and intentions of the people who build that technology. Amodei said he and his six cofounders decided at the company's founding that talent and culture would be their priority. "If you stick to that consistently, it's painful in the short run. But you get a team where everyone works together, and everyone is on the same side," Amodei said. Anthropic describes itself as a "high-trust, low-ego organization" on its website, and in its IPO filing said that "teams operate in a truth-seeking environment where the best argument wins, not the loudest voice or the most senior title." Amodei told Dimon that he encourages other leaders to demonstrate honesty and trust. He said that every two weeks he holds a "Dario Vision Quest," an all-hands meeting where he said he speaks to the company about what's going on. Amodei said he tries not to hide things from staff and doesn't rely on corporate jargon. That creates an environment where employees can trust leaders and leaders can trust employees, he said. "Everyone feels that we're being honest with them," Amodei said, adding that this carries "enormous value." A focus on retention Amodei told Dimon that the approach works because employees share the same values and a common goal. Whether the task is training a model, meeting a safety objective, building a product, or advancing a policy priority, "the whole company comes together to make it happen," he said. Amodei said that maintaining that kind of environment has helped with retention, which is critical given the company's dependence on senior leaders and key technical team members. Amodei said that all seven cofounders, including himself, are still at the company, along with over three-quarters of its first 100 employees. In its IPO filing, Anthropic said it experienced only about 1% "regrettable attrition" in a 12-month period. Amodei added that it's a "relatively frequent" occurrence for employees to come back after leaving. He said two major product employees left and came back after two weeks. "They said, 'Sorry, we didn't appreciate what we had,'" Amodei said about their return. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process
events.summary: Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse. However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists. Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options. Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds. This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual. This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time. By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI. events.title: Microsoft says affected services fully recovered after more than 24 hours of global disruption
events.summary: The US tech company was not aware of any malicious activity and ruled out AI as the cause. Microsoft on Nov 13 said that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook, Copilot and other applications, ending a global outage that crippled online communications across businesses and governments for over 24 hours. Microsoft blamed server issues for the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and said that a broader roll-out of software fixes was stabilising the system. It was not aware of any malicious activity and ruled out artificial intelligence as the cause. Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending e-mails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings. It affected government agencies from Australia and Japan to the US, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements. Organisations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared. The outage, reports of which started climbing around 5.25pm GMT on Nov 12, according to Downdetector’s parent company Ookla, is one of the longest in Microsoft’s history and the second disruption to its services in 2026 . Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online – its cloud-based e-mail and scheduling hub – leaving unconnected applications operational. The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it. It also highlighted the dependence on Microsoft’s workplace software, with outage reports spiking as employees began their workdays across Asia and Europe, according to Ookla. Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels. “It shows how much of the working day now runs through one provider’s e-mail and collaboration tools,” said Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Ookla. Microsoft shares closed flat at US$523.88 on Nov 13 . The stock has gained roughly 8% so far in 2026 . Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, said Mario De Cicco, vice-president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS. De Cicco estimated global insured losses at between US$300 million (S$386 million) and US$500 million – well below the US$400 million to US$1.5 billion toll from the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that crashed more than eight million Windows-based computers and caused widespread disruptions. Microsoft also faced an outage with its 365 services in January 2026 and in October 2025 . In October , it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software and industries worldwide. “The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage in 2026 ,” said Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro. “If reliability starts to look like a recurring problem, it hands every IT department a reason to think twice before putting even more of their business in one provider’s hands.” Still, some analysts have questioned whether such incidents can push customers on to rivals due to the steep switching costs of replacing tools embedded so deeply in daily operations. A spokesperson for the British government said it was working with Microsoft to find a solution for the outage that hit organisations such as the National Health Service (NHS) and London’s Metropolitan Police. Lack of access to e-mails and other services impacted the Metropolitan Police’s ability to report some crimes online, though its ability to respond to calls was not affected. The NHS said its local services were turning to alternative measures such as IT systems or paper records. For businesses, the fallout was widespread. European exchange operator Euronext reported e-mail disruptions, British insurer Aviva activated backups for its earnings calls and Danish shipping giant Maersk warned customers of delayed updates. American AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic also faced issues with Microsoft connectors, while Indian airlines IndiGo, Akasa Air and Air India said e-mail support services were impacted. The outage also disrupted fund management at Taiwanese securities firms, life insurers and investment trust companies. One of the companies even cancelled a bond repurchase transaction, a source familiar with the situation told Reuters. Another Taiwanese financial company resorted to using fax to confirm trades, a second source said.

events.title: ‘The easiest way to penetrate a billion-dollar company’: Ex-FBI operative on how spies target CEOs
events.summary: Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia has put a rarely discussed risk in plain view: for a CEO, a new business contact or a budding romance may come from someone more interested in the company’s secrets. “Sometimes the easiest way to penetrate a billion-dollar company is to get close to the person running it,” Eric O’Neill, a former FBI counterintelligence operative, told Fortune . For O’Neill, protecting executives should include teaching them to recognize manipulation—and giving others a way to intervene when the boss won’t listen. Huang stepped down Thursday as president, CEO, and a board member of Nvidia, No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500, amid scrutiny of his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China. The company named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor. In a message to employees Sunday, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and said he would cooperate with the board’s investigation. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials believed Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, had been recruited by China’s intelligence service. The Chinese government has denied the allegations . Nvidia’s board said Sunday that it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security had been compromised, but that its independent investigation , led by a committee of independent directors, would examine all available information. The company has lost about $450 billion in market value since Huang’s admission. How trust becomes a security risk O’Neill, whose undercover work helped catch FBI spy Robert Hanssen, founded NeXasure AI and wrote Spies, Lies, and Cybercrime . He said an intelligence-gathering attempt often looks, at first, like an ordinary relationship. He said an approach rarely begins with someone asking an executive to hand over company secrets. It may start at a conference, through a business introduction, over drinks, or even on a dating app. The operative finds common ground, builds trust, and makes the executive feel important. Romance can speed things up. Using romantic or sexual interest to gain information, access, or leverage is known as “ honey trapping ,” a tactic far older than dating apps. The warning signs can be subtle, O’Neill said: a relationship that moves unusually quickly, persistent questions about sensitive business matters, requests to meet influential colleagues, or encouragement to keep secrets. The goal may be information, influence over a business decision, or compromising material that could later be used for blackmail. Those signs are harder to recognize when the person under scrutiny is someone the executive trusts. “By the time a security professional raises concerns, the executive may already be emotionally invested and unwilling to listen,” O’Neill said. CEOs have access to information others want, from intellectual property and strategic plans to government relationships. O’Neill argues their security training should teach them how someone might use a personal relationship to get closer to those assets. Peter Warmka, a former CIA senior intelligence officer who now trains executives through his Counterintelligence Institute, told Fortune his sessions cover who might target a company, what they want, and how they approach employees and contractors. Senior executives are prime targets because of their access, he said, but their attitudes toward security can also leave them exposed. “Unfortunately, they are also perceived as more vulnerable because many believe not all security measures imposed on lower-level employees also apply to them,” Warmka said. Much of his training focuses on overseas travel, including the risks of electronic eavesdropping in hotel rooms and on the way to meetings, intelligence collection targeting their devices, and interpreters who may work for intelligence services. Even with that preparation, recognizing an attempt to extract information can be difficult. “Well-trained operatives know how to elicit information without raising suspicion,” Warmka said. How boards can intervene when the CEO won’t listen When a CEO dismisses a warning, someone else needs a way to act. Chief security officers, general counsel, and chief information security officers should have a confidential route to independent directors, O’Neill said. If the CEO will not cooperate, the board can bring in outside counsel and investigators to assess a credible threat and recommend protective measures. Where warranted, the company should involve federal authorities. A romantic relationship alone does not prove espionage, O’Neill emphasized. Any investigation should be objective and discreet, balancing the executive’s privacy with the company’s security. That requires someone outside the relationship to assess the risk. “No executive, regardless of wealth, reputation, or brilliance, should be the final authority on investigating a threat in which that executive may be personally compromised,” O’Neill said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump bought Nvidia stock as he helped chipmaker with change to export rule
events.summary: President purchased up to $5m of stock before revoking Biden-era rule that limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to China Donald Trump bought Nvidia stock worth millions of dollars as he made decisions on America’s China policy that would benefit the chipmaker, an analysis has found . In May 2025, Trump’s administration rescinded a Biden-era rule designed to prevent the most advanced US-made AI chips from being exported to China. This rule aimed to strengthen the US’s own chip industry and to protect America from what was widely regarded as a national security threat: the possibility that China might develop superior AI. In the days before he rescinded the rule, Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate that he bought between $1m (£760,000) and $5m worth of Nvidia stock – a purchase noted in an analysis by the anti-corruption group DeKleptocracy. He also bought shares in other tech companies, including Apple, Meta and Microsoft. The diffusion rule would have limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to what has been one of its largest markets: China accounted for about a quarter of the company’s sales between 2010 and 2022. Nvidia’s shares rose in value just after Trump announced the rescission of the rule, and after he had bought the stock. In December 2025 Trump said he would allow Nvidia to sell H200 chips to China, a decision that was greenlit by the Department of Commerce in January 2026. This was a controversial move. H200s were one of the company’s most advanced chips – six times better than what was available in China at the time, said experts. The Council on Foreign Relations suggested selling H200s would “supercharge” China’s future AI factories and strengthen the US’s rival. Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate he made at least three purchases of Nvidia shares in the days after announcing this, all of them between $250,001 and $500,000. These trades are among Trump’s larger purchases of Nvidia stock, although he appears to have made dozens of transactions involving the chipmaker’s shares since taking office. DeKleptocracy wrote in its analysis: “While the country debates how a possible Chinese spy may have manipulated White House policy for one AI company, it must grapple with how Trump’s corruption may have motivated him to deliver the entire AI industry’s technology to China.” Get the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning The US – and the global economy – have been grappling with revelations that Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s former chief executive, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang. Reports have suggested this relationship allowed Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed, to obtain billions of dollars worth of Nvidia’s chips, even as other companies struggled. Trump was twice briefed by US intelligence officials on their conclusions that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset. He did not act on this assessment. Jensen Huang has been described as a close Trump ally and has met the president a number of times. Nvidia made a $25m contribution to Trump’s ballroom in October 2025, with Huang saying he was “delighted to be a part of it”.

events.title: Hassett expected to depart White House
events.summary: National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett is expected to depart his role at the White House in the coming weeks, three people familiar with his plans told Semafor. Hassett has been inquiring about roles outside the administration since well before this month’s midterm elections, some of the people said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who could hold both jobs, and his counselor, David Zervos, are among those being eyed to replace him. Hassett’s plans haven’t been officially announced and, like much in the Trump administration, there’s always the chance they could change. The Treasury Department did not comment for this story. A White House official told Semafor that “there is no factual basis for this reporting,” adding that “Kevin Hassett is a key member of President [Donald] Trump’s economic team and will continue working to advance President Trump’s economic policies.” “Under President Trump, Americans have received more than $82 billion in individual tax relief, over 70 million children have been enrolled for a Trump Account, nearly 20 fair trade deals have been secured, poverty is at an all-time low and real wages for hardworking Americans have increased,” the official continued. “The Trump administration will continue delivering results for hardworking families.” Hassett later denied he planned to leave in a text message to CNBC. Trump tapped Hassett, who served in the first Trump administration, to return as his top economic adviser nearly two years ago. Since then, Hassett’s served as the face of everything from the economic fallout from the Iran war to the president’s campaign against former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell. Hassett, who was in the running to replace Powell, saw one of his top priorities advance in February, when the president signed an executive order that sought to expand access to retirement plans for workers whose employers don’t provide one. The order, first reported by Semafor , followed Hassett’s longtime advocacy for recreating the government’s Thrift Savings Plan for private-sector workers — but ultimately took a less ambitious approach, creating a website where workers can shop existing plans. Hassett’s expected departure, while not tied to Republicans’ lackluster midterm results, would be the latest in a series of staffing changes hitting the Trump administration in recent weeks. Hassett’s deputy, Ryan Baasch, left the White House at the end of September . More recently, Trump replaced his then-chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s strict immigration policies. Roles under Miller have been shifting in recent weeks, as Semafor reported . Multiple people inside and close to the administration say they expect further staffing changes and departures as the year comes to a close. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is currently in the crosshairs amid scrutiny over his handling of export controls on AI chips.

events.title: Who is Anne Jakrajutatip? Here's what to know about the former Miss Universe CEO
events.summary: Anne Jakrajutatip bought Miss Universe in 2022. Josh Brasted/Getty Images Anne Jakrajutatip became the first woman to own Miss Universe in October 2022.  She said she was inspired by Angela Ponce, who was the first trans woman to compete in the pageant. Jakrajutatip ushered in big changes, including allowing all women 18 or older to compete. Anne Jakrajutatip made history when she purchased Miss Universe in October 2022, making her the first woman to own the organization since it began in 1952. Jakrajutatip brought big changes to the pageant, including allowing all women 18 or older to compete. But her time at the top of the world's biggest pageant was frequently shadowed by controversy, and she ultimately stepped down in June 2025 following an investigation into her company, JKN Global, by Thailand's Securities and Exchange Commission. A Bangkok court issued a warrant for Jakrajutatip's arrest in relation to an ongoing fraud case in November 2025. Jakrajutatip hasn't publicly discussed the allegations and did not respond to Business Insider's repeated requests for comment. Her whereabouts remain unknown. Here's what to know about Jakrajutatip. Anne Jakrajutatip was born and raised in Bangkok, where she struggled with her gender identity from an early age. Anne Jakapong Jakrajutatip was born in Bangkok, Thailand. Courtesy of Miss Universe During a January 2023 interview on "The Journal" podcast , Jakrajutatip said she had known she was "trapped in the wrong body" since age 5. Jakrajutatip also told Them in June 2023 that she was bullied as a child and didn't find her voice until she took a public speaking class in high school. "I wanted to have the weapon that is the microphone to express my attitude and exhibit that leadership to everyone," she said. "No more bullies. You cannot do anything harmful to me because I'm clever and smart and I can be successful." Jakrajutatip attended university in Sydney before returning home to take over her parents' video-rental business. Jakrajutatip is the third richest transgender person in the world. Courtesy of Miss Universe Jakrajutatip graduated with a degree in international relations, paying her tuition with money she earned working at a gas station, according to Them. At this point, Jakrajutatip said she knew she was a transgender woman, but she didn't feel comfortable coming out in Thailand. Jakrajutatip turned her parents' store into a content distribution empire. Hector Vivas/Getty Images Jakrajutatip's first major deal was with the BBC, she told The Guardian in 2023. She said she had spotted the documentary "Walking With Dinosaurs" at her parents' store and offered to distribute the BBC series in Thailand. The outlet reported that she sold a million copies and soon began distributing content from India, Japan, the US, and South Korea as well. Jakrajutatip expanded JKN Global as she launched beauty lines and bought TV channels in Thailand. Jakrajutatip counts Oprah Winfrey as her biggest inspiration. Courtesy of Miss Universe Them reported that Jakrajutatip's profile rose in Thailand as she appeared on the country's version of "Shark Tank" and "Project Runway," and she continued to expand her business portfolio by launching drinks and food supplements. Jakrajutatip previously told The Guardian that Oprah Winfrey served as her main source of inspiration as she pursued a career in media. To this day, Winfrey is the only person that Jakrajutatip follows on Instagram. In 2018, Jakrajutatip launched a nonprofit to support transgender people. Two years later, she underwent gender-affirming surgery. Anne Jakrajutatip has two children. LILLIAN SUWANRUMPHA/AFP via Getty Images According to Them, Jakrajutatip underwent surgery in 2020 and became a mother six months later. She had a second child the following year. Jakrajutatip knew she wanted to own Miss Universe after seeing Miss Spain 2018, Angela Ponce, make history. Miss Spain Angela Ponce during the national costume competition at the 2018 Miss Universe pageant. LILLIAN SUWANRUMPHA/AFP via Getty Images Jakrajutatip told Them that she was in the audience when Ponce became the first transgender woman to compete at Miss Universe. "I stood up and applauded for her. I cried, and she also cried on the stage," Jakrajutatip said. "When I turned back, everyone just stood up after me and applauded her big time." "That moment, I thought, 'This is it. This is a pageant I can turn into a platform, and it must be a women's empowerment platform,'" she added. Jakrajutatip bought Miss Universe for $20 million in October 2022. Jakrajutatip with Miss Universe R'Bonney Gabriel. Roy Rochlin/Getty Images for Empire State Realty Trust Jakrajutatip acquired the Miss Universe brand just weeks after the Miss USA organization descended into chaos as contestants claimed the 2022 pageant had been rigged in favor of R'Bonney Gabriel , who went on to win Miss Universe months later. In a statement sent to Business Insider after the announcement, Jakrajutatip said she was proud to take over the organization. "We seek not only to continue its legacy of providing a platform to passionate individuals from diverse backgrounds, cultures, and traditions, but also to evolve the brand for the next generation," she added. During her first Miss Universe as the owner in January 2023, Jakrajutatip told pageant fans that she was ushering in a new era. "From now on it's going to be run by women, owned by a trans woman, for all women around the world," she said. Jakrajutatip's company filed a "business rehabilitation" petition with Thailand's bankruptcy court in 2023. Jakrajutatip with Miss Universe President Paula Shugart (left) and Miss Universe CEO Amy Emmerich (right) during the Miss Universe Extravaganza in Bangkok on November 7, 2022. LILLIAN SUWANRUMPHA/AFP via Getty Images JKN Global had missed a payment on a multimillion-dollar loan in September 2023. The company said in a letter to Thailand's stock exchange president that its financial liquidity management was "not in line with the expected forecast" and that it intended to restructure its debt. After the news broke, Jakrajutatip told Miss Universe fans on Instagram that the pageant was her "first priority in life." "No matter how joyful or painful it's gonna be…. Our universe must go on, must be great and must stay on top as the legendary Beauty Olympics in the World! I will sacrifice and do everything for the great success of OUR UNIVERSE!" she wrote in the post shared on November 9, 2023, which has since been taken down. events.title: Retirees sometimes tap savings for one-off expenses. Here’s what advisors say to consider first
events.summary: Withdrawing money from a traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account is not as simple as taking the amount you need, advisors say. There are tax implications to consider that go beyond owing taxes on the money you withdraw. You may be able to strategize how you tap your nest egg to mitigate the potential tax impact. It's also worth considering other ways to cover your unplanned expense. Retirees facing a large expense that's not in their regular household budget may turn to their traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account balances to cover it. While retirement savings may be the easiest place to turn for the money, financial advisors say there are a few things worth considering before making one-off withdrawals. "Be aware of the fact that it's not as simple as just taking out the amount of money that [covers] what you want it for," said certified financial planner Victoria Trumbower, managing member of Trumbower Financial Advisors in Bethesda, Maryland. The firm ranked No. 19 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026. More from CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors: CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor for 2026 takes a family-office approach CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 FAQ: Who is eligible and how rankings work Roth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisor After Jensen Huang's exit, what top advisors are doing with Nvidia: CNBC poll At the same time, research shows that many retirees aren't even spending their nest egg . About a third still have 100% or more of their initial assets when they reach their mid-80s, according to a May study by the Employee Benefit Research Institute, a nonpartisan research group. "Retirement savings are meant to be spent," said CFP Alex Canellopoulos, director of wealth and a partner with Vista Capital Partners in Portland, Oregon. "A one-time withdrawal isn't necessarily a bad decision, as long as it fits within a sustainable retirement plan." Unplanned withdrawals often go toward debt In 2025, about 15% of 401(k) owners ages 60 to 72 with balances of at least $100,000 who had left their employer made an ad hoc withdrawal from their account, according to Vanguard's How America Retires 2026 report, which analyzed more than 125,000 ex-plan participants. This age group falls between the onset of penalty-free withdrawals — age 59½ — and the threshold for starting required minimum distributions — currently age 73. RMDs are amounts that retirees must withdraw annually from traditional 401(k)s and IRAs. Not all 401(k) plans allow occasional withdrawals from ex- employees — about 43% did in 2025, up from 16% in 2015, the Vanguard study says. If a plan doesn't offer such ad hoc distributions, a former employee who wants to tap that money would have to withdraw or roll over the entire balance. Typically, they roll it over to an IRA and take withdrawals from there. The most common reasons for retirees taking irregular distributions, based on a 2025 Vanguard survey of 8,000 clients noted in the recent report, are paying off debt , with 31% of respondents citing it; covering unforeseen expenses such as medical care and home repairs, noted by 23%; and discretionary spending, with 22% citing it as a reason. Regardless of why you take the money, advisors say a key consideration is the impact on your tax situation. Distributions from a traditional 401(k) or IRA are generally taxed as ordinary income. If you don't have other means to cover the tax bill, you may have to withdraw extra from your retirement account to compensate — which creates a tricky situation. "It's like a double whammy because you have to pay income tax, but you don't have any money to pay income tax , so you've got to withdraw more money to pay the tax, and then you've got to pay taxes" on the extra amount, Trumbower said. For illustration: If you need $50,000 after taxes and assume a combined federal and state income tax rate of 25%, the math says you would need to withdraw about $66,667. That's because the money withdrawn to cover the tax bill is itself taxable. A $66,667 withdrawal taxed at 25% would result in about $16,667 in taxes, leaving $50,000 after tax. "It's going to cost you a lot more than you think," Trumbower said. There may be an undesirable ripple effect A taxable withdrawal from retirement savings can also trigger additional costs elsewhere. For example, if you're receiving Social Security retirement benefits, the added income could cause a larger portion of that money to become taxable. Depending on how much other income you have, 0%, up to 50%, or up to 85% of your Social Security benefits may be subject to federal income tax . A large retirement-account withdrawal can increase that other income and make more of your benefits taxable.

events.title: How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI
events.summary: Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics , governance , and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges. “AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance. Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union , the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology , and the International Organization for Standardization . The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias , security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap. Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies. Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust. Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance. The benefits of microcredentials Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program. Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment. For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles. Translating standards into microcredentials Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards , most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle. The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust. To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert .

events.title: Homes with architectural designs that cost just $1 near completion
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts First Corrimal homes with $1 plans from NSW Pattern Book nearing completion Topic: Housing Construction Industry The four row homes in Corrimal will be the first in the state built using a Pattern Book design. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) A set of row homes in Corrimal will be the first of the NSW government's $1 pattern book designs to be completed. The government has sold more than 25,000 designs from the book, with 22 being built. The opposition says the low numbers show the scheme is a "failure", but builders say it is working. Construction costs might be soaring across the country but on a building site at Corrimal, north of Wollongong, no-one is complaining about the price that was paid for an architect's plans. Builder James Forrest and his team are putting the finishing touches on four new row homes, following designs purchased for just $1 from a pattern book launched by the NSW government in July 2025 . If he meets the November deadline, he will be the first in the state to complete a home under the scheme. Mr Forrest said using the design saved him an extraordinary amount of time, because it included planning controls and a 10-day complying development pathway. "All the rigours of the design work have been done already. It's just matching it to the site, and it's approved," he said. James Forrest aims to complete the project by the end of November. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) The Corrimal development used one of eight low-rise designs available for the nominal fee of $1 in the first six months of the scheme. The program was sold as a way to get more high-quality housing built faster and cheaper. So far, 25,000 designs have been purchased and 22 are being built. Harry Catterns says the designs can be adjusted to different sizes and configurations. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Architect Harry Catterns co-owns the company that designed the row homes. "We thought it would be a more helpful contribution to the housing mix if we could provide small house-like dwellings with their own front door, their own garden, rather than the typical apartment you might see on a site like this," he said. Mr Catterns said the design could be adjusted to one, two or three bedrooms and offered different bathroom configurations. All are two-storey, with balconies and sliding glass doors. The builder is hoping to have the homes ready for tenants, and owners, by Christmas. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Mr Forrest said he hoped to have three homes occupied by Christmas, and the fourth, larger home on the market shortly after. "These will be cheaper for buyers than ordinary builds for a number of reasons, but primarily because of its speed and cost-saving," he said. Mr Forrest estimated the Corrimal build was around $600,000 cheaper than an ordinary project. The Pattern Book now offers 17 designs after nine mid-rise options were added in November 2025. They cost up to $2,500 and do not have the same planning controls or fast-track as the low-rise designs. Tom Forrest says the scheme has been a "dud". ( ABC News: Sam Foster ) The Urban Taskforce's Tom Forrest said the mid-rise developments would still need final development approval from councils and faced the same planning timelines as a typical build. "Nobody is building and it hasn't improved the number of new dwellings brought to the market," he said. So far, the entire Housing Pattern Book program has translated to fewer than 60 applications, with 45 of them approved. The Housing Industry Association does not agree, with NSW chief executive Brad Armitage saying it was working for builders. "When you take those [economic] factors into consideration, so many approvals with this relatively new pattern book is actually quite strong," he said. Brad Armitage says the pattern book is a success. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) The NSW opposition has promised to overhaul the scheme with new designs and review planning controls if it is elected next March, describing it as a "failure". "We want to see a lot more builders like this one at Corrimal rolling out a lot more housing as part of the pattern book and clearly it's not working at the moment," Shadow Housing Minister Chris Rath said. "We need to make it much easier to actually build the pattern book designs. "It's just far too slow and far too restrictive." NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully defended the outcome. "We're seeing challenging economic conditions for new home building, higher interest rates, higher building costs, shortages of skilled labour," he said.

events.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its 'dots' AI agents to make purchases for users
events.summary: OpenAI announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" AI agents to make purchases on behalf of users. ChatGPT Wallet will initially be available to OpenAI's Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are over 18 years old. OpenAI built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, and it allows those customers to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. OpenAI on Friday announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users. The company built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express , Mastercard and Visa , and it allows cardholders to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check. OpenAI said its dots agents will never actually access a user's card details. Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a "payment token," which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction. "Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview. ChatGPT Wallet comes as a growing number of consumers are exploring how to use personal AI agents to manage their calendars, book travel and complete other day-to-day tasks. OpenAI introduced the dots agents during its annual developer conference in late September, shortly after Meta's Muse offering topped the App Store charts . Purchases made through ChatGPT Wallet could eventually kick-start a new revenue stream for OpenAI, but the company said it is not taking a cut of transactions to start. With the initial launch, OpenAI is working to build relationships with merchants and position itself as a serious platform for shoppers, especially as vendors are beginning to experiment with personal agents. OpenAI has pushed deeper into AI-enabled commerce over the last year, but some of its early attempts failed to take off. The company introduced an " Instant Checkout " feature last fall, which it quickly pivoted away from. By March, it had rolled out a revamped shopping experience that aimed to make it easier for users to find and compare products. Nayak said ChatGPT Wallet builds on OpenAI's previous efforts, particularly around product discovery. "We think that this is the next step, where if someone found something they're really excited to buy, then we want to be able to get them through to that endpoint," she said. Nvidia live updates: CEO Jensen Huang resigns, Colette Kress named interim chief CoreWeave CEO Intrator tells CNBC he has canceled his planned share sale program Meta head of infrastructure will leave and be succeeded by former AWS cloud exec Amazon’s Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses ChatGPT Wallet is initially available to OpenAI's Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are over 18 years old. The limited rollout is intentional, and the "right approach to make sure things are working," said Luke Gebb , executive vice president and global head of innovation at Amex. OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot supports more than 1.2 billion weekly active users and nearly 100 million paying users as of the end of the third quarter. With such a broad user base, Gebb said OpenAI can decide to "turn up the volume" on ChatGPT Wallet when it wants to. "It just makes sense to watch it, start it in a contained environment, and then keep rolling from there," Gebb told CNBC in an interview. Merchants and vendors are still reckoning with the rise of personal AI agents, and some companies have opted to forgo them entirely. United Airlines said Wednesday that it will block agents from accessing its systems to book tickets, and Amazon prevents the agents from purchasing products on its platform. OpenAI said Friday that agentic commerce is still in its "early days," and it published tools and guidance alongside its ChatGPT Wallet announcement to help businesses start to navigate the transition. The company explained how merchants can make sure their websites aren't inadvertently blocking OpenAI's agents, for instance. "It's going to take time for the ecosystem to build the right infrastructure to be able to make this experience really amazing and seamless across all of their sites," Nayak said. "Really, who we are speaking to here is the networks and the merchants." WATCH: OpenAI raises $15B at a $1.25T valuation, sources say. What it means for the IPO

events.title: Nvidia approached Arm CEO Rene Haas to succeed Jensen Huang, report says
events.summary: Rene Haas is among several candidates being considered, and there is no guarantee he will be offered the job or accept it, the FT reported. Nvidia’s board has approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings chief executive Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang, the Financial Times reported on Nov 13, citing sources familiar with the matter. Huang stepped down on Nov 12 after revelations of extramarital affairs , including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, plunging the chipmaker into crisis and sending shockwaves across an artificial intelligence industry he helped bankroll. Haas’ name has been making the rounds among analysts since Huang’s exit. He spent seven formative years at Nvidia, rising to vice-president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He is among several candidates being considered and there is no guarantee he will be offered the job or accept it, the FT reported. Nvidia’s finance chief Colette Kress is currently interim CEO. Nvidia’s board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the CEO role and had not formally engaged any potential candidates. “Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature,” the board said in a statement. Prior to Huang’s resignation, a long-time Nvidia engineer had urged the board in an internal post to consider employee sentiment before taking any action, Wired reported late on Nov 12. The post has since drawn more than 1,600 comments, with several urging the board to find a way to bring Huang back, the technology news platform said, citing internal correspondence it reviewed. Nvidia has about 42,000 employees worldwide. Billionaire Elon Musk separately said on X that a petition was under way to reinstate Huang and that he would sign it. It was not immediately clear whether Musk was referring to the internal effort reported by Wired. Nvidia declined to comment on the Wired report as well as Musk’s post, while Arm also declined to comment. Reuters could not independently verify the reports. Haas became Arm CEO in 2022, overseeing the company’s Nasdaq listing in 2023. Arm designs processor architectures and licenses them to other companies that develop chip designs. Historically, its strength has been in mobile phones and it is expanding into computers. Haas’ combination of familiarity with Nvidia and experience running a publicly traded chip company could make him an unusual fit for the role, said Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities. “Rene is one of few external candidates who wouldn’t need to be brought up to speed on Nvidia,” Boloor said, adding that Haas’ understanding of the company’s culture alongside his experience running Arm was “a combination you don’t find very often”. Arm’s US-listed shares pared losses after the report and were down more than 5%. Nvidia’s shares were down over 3%. Some analysts expect the next CEO to break from Huang’s three-decade reign as the hands-on “chief conductor” who personally steered engineering road maps, geopolitical negotiations over China exports and massive investments across the AI ecosystem. A potential shift towards a more institutional leadership structure would come as Nvidia faces heightened regulatory scrutiny and growing consensus among US lawmakers to further restrict the company’s chip exports to China. Insiders and tech titans in the running Analysts view Kress as a steady financial authority, while veteran engineer Ian Buck is seen as a top candidate after leading development of CUDA, the software platform that powers Nvidia’s AI chips. Apart from Haas, external names discussed by analysts include AMD chief Lisa Su, who has navigated the key China market, and Micron chief Sanjay Mehrotra, whose memory chips power Nvidia servers. Other candidates cited by industry watchers include Marvell head Matt Murphy and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who oversaw the iPhone maker’s in-house silicon development. Former Apple chief Tim Cook was floated by US President Donald Trump , as Nvidia’s board evaluates whether to prioritise financial continuity, deep technical expertise, or experience running a global tech heavyweight.
