events.title: Johnny Depp has reportedly earned $650 million throughout his career. Here's how he makes and spends his money.
events.summary: Johnny Depp. Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images Depp has earned over $650 million in his career, including paydays averaging $20 million per film. He's also been known to spend money on things like an island and $30,000 a month on wine. He reportedly took a smaller payday for his latest movie, "Ebenezer," in exchange for back-end profits. Johnny Depp has been a superstar since the 1980s, and he's been paid like one. From the "Pirates of the Caribbean" franchise, which paid him tens of millions, to a seven-figure deal with Dior, Depp has used his paydays to live a lavish life: He once bought an island in the Bahamas and spent $30,000 a month on wine. Here's a breakdown of Depp's wealth and how he's reportedly spent it. Over a 13-year span, Depp earned $650 million, according to his former management firm. Getty/Atsushi Tomura After finding fame on the hit late-1980s TV series "21 Jump Street," Depp became a bona fide movie star thanks to performances in offbeat Tim Burton movies like"Edward Scissorhands" and "Ed Wood." Depp was paid handsomely for his efforts. According to his former management firm, The Management Group, Depp earned over $650 million in the 13 years they worked together from 1999 to 2016. A large portion of that is paydays he received playing Captain Jack Sparrow in the "Pirates of the Caribbean" franchise. After the success of "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl," Depp started routinely banking $20 million per movie. Disney The first "Pirates" movie, "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl," made over $650 million at the box-office worldwide. With that, Depp's asking price soared. On top of taking in $20 million pre-picture in the franchise, he got around 20% of the back end per picture, according to The Hollywood Reporter. So not only was he paid upfront, but Depp was cut another check after the movie broke even. Depp earned more than $40 million on each "Pirates" movie thanks to his back-end deal. Johnny Depp and Captain Jack Sparrow in Disney's "Pirates of the Caribbean." Disney Thanks to the success of the "Pirates" sequels, including 2006's "Dead Man's Chest," which earned over $1 billion worldwide , Depp's earnings from the movies became astronomical. The actor brought in north of $40 million per sequel on the back end of the movies alone, per THR. Again, that doesn't count the $20 million base pay for each. But not all of that went directly into Depp's pocket. His agents got 10%, managers took 5%, and there are deductions for taxes and expenses. However, the paydays only got bigger from there. The back-end deal for "Alice in Wonderland" was even larger: $55 million. Walt Disney Studios Taking a pause from playing Captain Jack in 2010, Depp teamed up with Tim Burton again for the latest adaptation of "Alice in Wonderland." On top of his $20 million base, THR reported that he took in $55 million on the back end thanks to the movie's successful box office run, which brought in over $1 billion . Thanks to the "Pirates" movies, "Alice in Wonderland," and 2014's "Into the Woods," in which he played the Big Bad Wolf, all getting prime home entertainment releases and cable play, Depp took in $25.7 million in residuals in 2016 and 2017 thanks to his profit participation deals on those movies. In 2016, he even landed on Forbes' list of highest-paid celebrities . He reportedly took in $48 million that year. Depp has earned millions as the face of Dior's Sauvage fragrance for men. Dior advertisement featuring Johnny Depp in Milan, Italy in October 2021. Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto/Getty The actor has been the face of Sauvage for years. Depp was reportedly taking in $3 million to $5 million in the deal . In August 2022, Business Insider confirmed that Depp signed a seven-figure, multi-year deal with Dior. Depp was paid $16 million for just one scene in "Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald." Johnny Depp as Gellert Grindelwald in "Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald." Warner Bros. Depp was asked to step down from "Fantastic Beasts 3" days after losing a libel case against the publishers of the UK newspaper, The Sun, over a 2018 article that described him as a "wife beater." However, because he had a "pay-or-play" deal on the movie , meaning he would get paid regardless of if he appeared in it, he was paid his $16 million fee. Depp only filmed one scene as Grindelwald. Mads Mikkelsen took over the role for 2022's "Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore." Depp bought an island in the Bahamas for $3.6 million. BELGRADE, SERBIA - OCTOBER 19: US actor Johnny Depp attends the promotion of the animated series "Puffins" in Belgrade on October 19, 2021. Srdjan Stevanovic/Getty Images The actor first set eyes on the 45-acre island located 60 miles from Nassau in 2003 while filming "Curse of the Black Pearl." He purchased Little Hall's Pond Cay for $3.6 million in 2004. He's since outfitted the island with solar-powered buildings, including a house with stunning 360-degree views . He spent $5 million to shoot the ashes of his friend, author Hunter S. Thompson, out of a cannon. (L-R) Hunter S. Thompson and Johnny Depp in 1997. Rose Hartman/Archive Photos/Getty Depp befriended famous gonzo journalist Thompson around the time he played him in the 1998 movie "Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas." They stayed friends until Thompson's death in 2005. Thompson had spoken about wanting his funeral to be an extravagant affair involving his ashes shot out of a cannon and a red, white, and blue fireworks show to end the event. Depp said he spent $5 million to fulfill his friend's wishes. Depp had $2 million in monthly bills, including $100,000 a month for addiction issues. Actor Johnny Depp appears in court during his defamation case against ex-wife Amber Heard at the Fairfax County Circuit Court on April 14, 2022. Shawn Thew/Pool via REUTERS Depp had huge daily spending habits to live a lavish lifestyle, which led to him spending $2 million a month on bills, according to his former management firm. At one time, the actor reportedly paid : $300,000 a month for a 40-person staff $10,000 a day to his former security manager $350,000 monthly to maintain his 156-foot yacht (which he has since sold to J.K. Rowling for $27 million ) $30,000 monthly for wine (Although Depp told Rolling Stone this was a conservative estimate.  "It's insulting to say that I spent $30,000 on wine," he said. "Because it was far more.") $100,000 a month for a doctor to treat his addiction issues Depp commented on his spending in 2017, telling the Wall Street Journal , "It's my money." "If I want to buy 15,000 cotton balls a day, it's my thing," he said. events.title: Noelia Voigt was the first Miss USA to give up her crown. Here's what to know about the pageant queen.
events.summary: Noelia Voigt was the first Miss USA to ever relinquish her crown. Courtesy of Miss USA Noelia Voigt won the Miss USA pageant in September 2023. She became the first woman to relinquish her crown when she resigned in May 2024. Voigt has returned to the Miss USA organization since Thom Brodeur replaced Laylah Rose as CEO. Noelia Voigt spent seven years working to become Miss USA . She won first runner-up three times at state pageants before making it to the national stage, where she took the crown in 2023. That made it even more shocking when Voigt became the first Miss USA in the pageant's history to relinquish her title, giving up the crown just months before her reign was set to end in 2024. This is her story. Noelia Voigt began watching pageants at an early age, but her mother didn't allow her to compete as a child. Noelia Voigt of Utah. Courtesy of Miss USA Voigt was born and raised in Sarasota, Florida. Her mother, Jackeline Voigt, is from Venezuela, and her father, Jack Voigt, is an American former Major League Baseball player. He played for the Baltimore Orioles, Oakland A's, Texas Rangers, and Milwaukee Brewers during his 14-year career, according to his website . After winning Miss USA in September 2023, Voigt told Business Insider that she grew up watching pageants with her mother. "My mom is from Venezuela, and over there, pageants are their Super Bowl and Olympics — it's a huge deal," Voigt said. "So I had always wanted to do pageants from a really young age." Voigt said she began asking to compete in pageants before she was 10, but her mother was "really protective" and made her wait. "Depending on the pageant that you're entering at that age, it can be potentially damaging to a young girl if they don't end up winning," Voigt said. "Then they have this negative association with it, and they think that it has something to do with them." "My mom didn't want that for me," she added. "So she waited until I was old enough to understand that, if I didn't win, it's not a reflection of me or who I am." Voigt won her first pageant when she was 16 years old. Vogit volunteering with Smile Train as Miss USA 2023. Courtesy of Miss USA Voigt was named Miss Sarasota Teen USA in 2017. She went on to compete at Miss Florida Teen USA that year and placed first runner-up. Although she found early success in the world of pageants, Voigt said her friends made fun of her newfound passion . "I was really hurt and confused as to why people I thought were my friends were making fun of me for doing something that I was really excited about and that I was doing good things with," Voigt told Business Insider. "At first, it really did sting. But it was clear to me that it was an attempt to steal the joy I had from this accomplishment." Voigt made anti-bullying part of her platform and authored a children's book on the topic called "Maddie the BRAVE." Voigt credited pageants with helping her get out of an abusive relationship in high school. Courtesy of Miss USA Voigt told Business Insider that competing in pageants was an eye-opening experience as she navigated an abusive relationship during her teenage years. "When you're in pageants, you're surrounded by women who are really uplifting of one another," she said. "They all have a really good sense of self-respect, and they know their worth, and a lot of times if you find yourself in an abusive relationship, that might be something that is lacking." "Once I broke into the pageant world and started to get involved in a lot of community service, I started to realize that anybody that was toxic in my life was simply holding me back," she added. "Pageants absolutely helped me realize my worth." Voigt moved to Alabama for school and continued to compete in pageants. Miss USA 2023. Courtesy of Miss Universe Voigt competed in Miss Alabama 2022 and Miss Alabama 2023 , placing first runner-up in both competitions. "A lot of people ask me if it hurt that I kept getting first runner-up, and I just told them the honest truth — that I was really proud of myself for getting that placement," Voigt told Business Insider after her win. "I always felt very honored that the judges still felt I could do the job if something happened and I needed to step in." "Every year that I hadn't won the pageant, it gave me another year of opportunity to do good things for my community, so I really wouldn't have traded it for anything," she added. Voigt moved to Salt Lake City in April 2023 and won Miss Utah 2023 three months later. Courtesy of Miss USA By winning Miss Utah, Voigt had finally accomplished her dream of making it to the Miss USA stage. "It could have been very easy for me, all those times getting first runner-up, to just say, 'I can't do this anymore, I'm so frustrated,'" Voigt told Business Insider. "But instead, every time I got first runner-up, it was more fuel to the fire for me to keep on going." Voigt was crowned Miss USA on September 29, 2023. Miss Utah Noelia Voigt was crowned Miss USA in 2023. Miss USA Voigt became the first Venezuelan-American to win Miss USA after she was crowned at the Grand Sierra Resort and Casino in Reno, Nevada. She was also the first Miss Utah to win the title since 1960. "This is something I've worked toward for a really long time," Voigt told Business Insider. "It's been a journey of perseverance and not giving up." Voigt went on to compete at Miss Universe 2023 in El Salvador, where she placed in the top 20. On May 6, 2024, Voigt announced she was stepping down as Miss USA. Miss Teen USA 2023 UmaSofia Srivastava and Miss USA 2023 Noelia Voigt. Chance Yeh/Getty Images for Supermodels Unlimited Voigt said she was relinquishing the Miss USA crown to focus on her mental health, but a cryptic message was hidden inside her Instagram statement. It read "I AM SILENCED." Two days later, Miss Teen USA 2023 UmaSofia Srivastava resigned as well. The pageant queens said they couldn't speak publicly about their experience due to strict nondisclosure agreements they had signed under the leadership of Laylah Rose , who became the CEO of Miss USA in August 2023. Jackeline Voigt and Barbara Srivastava, the pageant queens' mothers, told Business Insider their daughters had endured "eight months of torture and abuse" from Rose. "The woman who was supposed to be all about empowering and bringing women together and pushing them to speak for their causes and charities, she did quite the opposite," Barbara Srivastava said during the May 2024 interview. In her official Miss USA resignation letter, Voigt detailed the "detrimental mental and emotional toll" of her time as Miss USA and said she had to be prescribed two anti-anxiety medications. "I've never ever in my life been on anti-anxiety medication," Voigt told Business Insider during an exclusive August 2025 interview . "It wasn't something that came out of nowhere. events.title: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh-oh, Jensen!
events.summary: The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims. The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service. While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang. U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff. Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips. White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination. That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025. However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed. “If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer. Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and S i ngaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai. In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “ China problem ” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips. Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry. If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven’t been cleared for import. Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips. events.title: Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost?
events.summary: Watch: What we know so far about the Microsoft outage A major Microsoft outage has impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world. Services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot, are being restored almost 24 hours since issues first surfaced. Microsoft said the outage was not a cyber-security incident and was caused by a technical issue. It has apologised for the disruption. Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong. Schools, GPs and businesses hit by global Microsoft outage as company scrambles to solve issue Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries. From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps. But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America. The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues". In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels". The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade. "We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday. Will emails affected by the outage ever arrive? Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery". In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away. Earlier, Microsoft said it would be extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up". The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email. When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent. Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time. Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues. "What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said. "The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs. "One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in. "You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit." The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online. Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time". He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal. Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences. "Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is. "Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said. In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services." How many people have been affected? More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed. Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services. Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.

events.title: Nvidia CEO’s exit marks pivotal moment for African AI
events.summary: Alexis’s view Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia could prove to be a turning point in the rollout of AI in Africa. The technology offers the potential to turbocharge economies across the continent, but chips form the backbone of this revolution. And, as our San Francisco Bureau Chief Reed Albergotti put it, “ Huang was Nvidia’s one-man, long-term moat .” Without Huang’s singular vision, there’s uncertainty. The questions swirling in the wake of his exit are a reminder that the development of African compute still relies on hardware and software supplied by US companies. Huang’s resignation raises questions, for example, about the US chipmaker’s relationship with Cassava Technologies: Nvidia last year became an investor in the pan-African digital infrastructure company, which it supplies with chips. The partnership is central to Cassava’s push to expand services in the more than 30 African countries in which it operates. Nvidia’s financial commitment and supply of hardware offered an opportunity for African companies to access the compute needed to train and run their own AI models. If Huang’s successor takes a different approach, the Cassava partnership may not be replicated elsewhere on the continent, limiting the access African firms have to cutting-edge technology. The implications extend to the public sector, too. Only last month, the World Bank named Nvidia and Cassava as partners in an initiative aimed at expanding digital access in Africa to improve services and create jobs. Any change in Nvidia’s strategy would, in the long term, have the biggest implications for South Africa. The continent’s largest economy is home to about 40% of its roughly 160 data centers. So next week’s visit by South African President Cyril Ramaphosa to the US is well-timed. Ramaphosa, who will speak at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event , will be accompanied by a delegation that includes his ministers for finance, trade, and energy. He plans to meet tech executives, researchers, and investors during his trip, which will focus on AI infrastructure. Ramaphosa’s team has described it as an attempt to position South Africa as a “ competitive AI hub ” on the continent — but it’s shaping up to be a first peek at Silicon Valley after the departure of one of its central figures. Notable The proliferation of data centers across Africa is creating new pressure on the continent’s resources, reported Aaliyah Vayez for Al Jazeera.

events.title: Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that caused chaos for businesses
events.summary: Microsoft 365 is suffering an outage affecting services including Outlook and Teams. Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Microsoft's 365 outage entered a second day, affecting services like Teams and Outlook. Microsoft says its services are recovering. The outage disrupted governments, businesses, airlines, and some AI tools. Microsoft has apologized for a massive outage that dragged into a second day and disrupted access to email, Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 tools. The company said late Friday morning that services were recovering and stabilizing. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," the company said in an X post. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously." The cause of the outage, which disrupted businesses around the world, was "technical" and "not related to cyber or AI / agents," Microsoft added. The company said it has addressed the underlying issue, which stemmed from an earlier network upgrade, and is continuing to restore services. It did not provide a timeline for a full recovery. What happened? Microsoft first flagged the outage on Thursday around midday ET, writing in an X post that users in the Americas were having trouble accessing Exchange Online mailboxes. In a follow-up post, it said the issue could affect users "in any region." Later on Thursday, Microsoft said on X that some of its infrastructure was under elevated load across multiple regions. It said the strain was not caused by an increase in customer traffic, but because a number of servers had unexpectedly become unavailable. By Friday morning, Microsoft's public service status page was still showing "service degradation" for both Microsoft 365 business customers and consumer products. It also had a knock-on effect on some AI tools . Anthropic and OpenAI said in status update pages that their connectors to Microsoft 365 tools had been disrupted. Anthropic said late Friday morning that it was seeing some recovery, but "Microsoft's incident remains open, so errors may return." What was the impact? The outage caused significant disruption for businesses, with many workers unable to use systems such as email or Teams. Downdetector recorded more than 130,000 reports of Outlook problems in the US at the outage's peak on Thursday. That figure reflects user reports, not a confirmed count of affected people or businesses. Other Microsoft services were affected too. It said in its service advisory that the disruption could affect Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, Microsoft Defender, Intune, Power BI, and other Microsoft 365 products that rely on Exchange Online. Reuters reported on Thursday that the US House of Representatives said the outage had affected its users, while electric-truck maker Workhorse Group postponed its quarterly earnings call because of the disruption. Air India said in a Thursday X post that it had rerouted email services, while IndiGo said in an X post on Friday that its email support channel was disrupted. Both airlines said their flight operations were unaffected. AP also reported that government agencies in Singapore, the Philippines, and Japan had reported knock-on effects. Is this unusual? Microsoft and other Big Tech companies have been here before. This outage, however, is unusually long. It lasted more than 22 hours — longer than a major Microsoft 365 disruption in June 2022, which took 16 hours and 27 minutes to recover from, according to a Microsoft service alert , potentially making it the company's longest 365 outage ever. Microsoft also suffered a separate outage for Azure, its cloud service, on September 30 and October 1, affecting customers across several regions. Microsoft said it rolled back a change after some customers had trouble using its cloud networking services. Other cloud providers have faced similar problems. Google said a global Google Cloud and Workspace outage in June 2025 lasted three hours. Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud computing arm, also had a major disruption in Northern Virginia in October 2025. It said it fixed the initial problem in about two and a half hours, though some services took longer to return to normal. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Nobody wants to run against Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
events.summary: The movement to prevent House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) from becoming speaker is struggling to get off the ground due to a fatal flaw: Nobody else wants the job. Why it matters: Despite the phone calls and online petitions, the demands from progressive holdouts, Jeffries' ascent has become a self-fulfilling prophecy. The House Democrats most often floated as potential challengers don't appear to be interested: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) told Axios on Thursday his "dream job" is to chair the House Judiciary Committee. "I am not a candidate for speaker in any way. ... I am supporting Hakeem and voting for Hakeem," said Raskin. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) has privately told colleagues she doesn't want the role despite an online movement seeking to draft her, according to multiple House Democrats who have spoken directly with her. "Congresswoman Pressley is in active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment, and deliver for the people," spokesperson Ricardo Sanchez said in a statement to Axios. "She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership." "He's the only one running," Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.) told Axios on Thursday when asked if she plans to vote for Jeffries as speaker. Said Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.): "I am really encouraging our leadership to make it easy for me to vote for the one person that's running. But as of right now, there's ... no one else that has put their name forward." "As far as I've heard, Jeffries is the only person running," said Rep.-elect Randy Villegas (D-Calif.). Jeffries said in a NY1 interview : "Someone could always emerge in the next week or so, but right now there are no declared challengers, no indication that anyone may put themselves forward." The intrigue: For once it's the Senate, not the House, providing all the drama on Capitol Hill. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) launched his bid to replace Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Thursday night. Yes, but: The progressive grassroots have continued this week to swamp sitting and incoming House Democrats with calls and emails urging them to oppose Jeffries, according to lawmakers and aides. Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) told Axios he has gotten an "avalanche of messages." Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said she is getting "hundreds" of calls "every day" urging her to oppose Jeffries. A senior House Democrat who is supporting Jeffries told Axios the callers into their office have suggested "like 10" different members as possible alternatives. Jeffries has pushed back on Axios' reporting that members are being flooded with calls, saying in his NY1 interview: "There's no indication that members of Congress have been overwhelmed by any calls." State of play: Jeffries has begun meeting with skeptics ahead of House Democrats' Nov. 18 leadership elections. He is expected to easily win the nomination for speaker, determined by a simple majority vote of the caucus. The real question is whether any House Democrats will oppose him on the House floor on Jan. 3 and deny him the unanimous support he has enjoyed from his caucus since becoming leader in 2022. "We're going to continue to talk to every single member of the House Democratic caucus, both current members and incoming members, about what we all can do together for the American people," Jeffries told reporters at a press conference on Thursday. The Democratic leader said he is "confident that we're on a positive trajectory" but takes "nothing for granted." Between the lines: Several Democratic House members and members-elect predicted that, given the grassroots pressure bearing down on progressives right now, at least a handful are likely to openly oppose him. What they're saying: Leonard told Axios he sat down with Jeffries on Wednesday and shared what he has heard from callers, including "that the Democratic establishment brand is in the toilet and that the leader's name is synonymous with the Democratic establishment." Ramirez said she has "begun conversations" with Jeffries and intends to "have more next week." Asked if Jeffries has met with the Jeffries-skeptic "Bloc" of incoming progressives, she said: "It is my understanding that that they're scheduling time to meet with them." Reps.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) and LaKesha Womack (D-N.C.) said Jeffries met Wednesday with members of the North Carolina delegation, many of whom are holdouts in the speaker election. "We're still having conversations, we're still listening ... at the end of the day, we're going to all sit together, we're going to listen to everything and we're going to move forward like that," said Ojeda. The bottom line: "I mean, right now, I don't even know if there's anybody that's stepping up against him," Ojeda added.

events.title: Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch
events.summary: (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.) Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question. First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago. The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began. Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area: The uptrend line extending from the early 2025 low through the early 2026 low. The 38.2% Fibonacci retracement of the entire 2025-2026 rally. The former 2025 highs, which represented resistance before becoming a key breakout zone earlier this year. This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline. For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse. The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025. Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights). The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective. The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now. That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market? One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses. Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend. We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed. The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off. From here, it's all about the follow through. We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum. events.title: My Dubai Salary: 'I said goodbye to two husbands to focus on my business'
events.summary: Madiha Abaida came to Dubai for a holiday. She ended up buying a property , opening a factory and never leaving. That was in 2018. She had been living in Monaco for a decade before that – a resident for tax reasons , as she puts it plainly – but after her marriage ended, she wanted a fresh start somewhere new. It was not straightforward, though. She launched a fashion brand in Dubai in 2020 and then the pandemic cancelled everything. So, she opened her own textile factory instead. She brought in staff, bought the machinery and worked 16-hour days. The fashion brand – originally conceived in Milan – became a Dubai operation born of necessity. Since then, she has pivoted again. Pink Madi, her beauty salon in Dubai, opened recently. Before that, she spent years building a real estate portfolio across the UAE and Spain's Golden Mile in Marbella, where she buys old homes, renovates them and sells them for $2 million to $3 million. She counts more than 25 properties in total. Today, she describes herself, without hesitation, as a millionaire . And she wants to go to Mars. What was your first job and first salary? When I was 16 or 17, I was selling Coca-Cola and noodles in order to study. People see me as a woman with power, but they don't know the price I paid. I was very hard-working from the beginning. I was a model first, when I was 17. And I studied to be a lawyer because my mother, she was married to a judge. I wanted to make my mother happy. But honestly, I never wanted to be a lawyer. I don't have this kind of personality. One day I said, “OK, I'm sorry – I need to do what I really believe I'm good at.” Then I started my fashion brand, and it was a big success in Milano. I had over 17 magazine covers. My first ever salary was €200. Then at 22, I also opened salons in Marbella – I had three salons there. And now? Now I have my real estate and my Dubai salon. My salon opened only recently – but I bought the salon seven months before that. I believe in energy. I do Reiki. When I entered the salon, it was all blue, and I didn't like the energy. I said, “I need a full renovation.” It took me six months. I was paying my staff throughout that whole time. It's the first salon, but not the last one. I am honestly very hard-working. I don't sleep. That is my secret – I sleep three hours a night. Because I need to watch everything. I'm very picky. Living in Monaco, I learnt luxury. Living in Miami, too, I learnt a lot. I travelled the whole world. With my experience in the fashion industry, I try to create something unique for women. What do you invest in? I have bought very good homes, old homes, in great locations in Marbella. I give them facelifts because I'm good at renovation. I sell them for $2 million or $3 million. I have over 25 properties total. Over six in the UAE. I also invest in stocks, crypto – all of this. That's also why I don't sleep. Money doesn't sleep. Do you have any debt? No, no, no. I always work with my own money. I don't take any credit from the bank. I calculate everything because the interest is high, and I don't like to pay interest. That's also why I divorced twice. When my two exes made me choose between them and my business, I said, "Habibi, bye bye." Madiha Abaida Growing up, were you taught how to handle money? No. My mother, she's very traditional. But I believe when you want something, today we have the platforms, you can learn everything. I don't lose my time watching stupid Netflix. I prefer to invest my time to learn. I paid for courses to learn about all this, because I come from a normal family, and my dream was to have a beautiful life. I wanted to be a millionaire by myself. That's also why I divorced twice. When my two exes made me choose between them and my business, I said, “Habibi, bye bye.” Financial independence is very important to me. Nobody will control me. I believe in this. I'm a feminist. I believe in hard work. And then people, they respect you. What are your major monthly expenses? For myself and my family, I just spend what I want – because they deserve it. When it comes to business, of course, as a businesswoman, I need to know how much I expect. That's how we make money. But when it comes to myself – I spend around Dh100,000 a month. I love myself too much, because I was hurt in the beginning. I learnt to love myself. I learnt to take care of myself. I have very deep experiences. I only trust myself. What are your financial goals? A lot. I want Pink Madi to go global – not only here, but America, everywhere. I have projects to launch my own make-up. I also have a charity for animals. events.title: The folly of just-in-time supply chains | Letters
events.summary: The folly of just-in-time supply chains Hannah Walker says systems designed to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can end up less capable of fulfilling their actual purpose The article by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend on the dangers of excessive optimisation identifies a problem extending far beyond mathematics and artificial intelligence ( The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly, 8 November ). The widespread adoption of just-in-time supply chains illustrates it perfectly. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses reduced costs and improved efficiency, but frequently transferred those savings into risks that remained invisible until something went wrong. The disruption of global manufacturing during the pandemic exposed the consequences. The same thinking has shaped public services and national defence. Hospital beds, experienced staff, strategic stockpiles and redundant infrastructure can all appear wasteful when measured against immediate demand. Yet their value lies precisely in their availability when circumstances cease to be normal. Europe’s dependence on American military capabilities provides a particularly troubling example. What appeared financially efficient in peacetime has created strategic vulnerabilities as the reliability of US commitments comes into question. The fundamental error is not optimisation itself, but optimising the wrong objective. A system designed to minimise expenditure may succeed brilliantly at doing so while becoming progressively less capable of fulfilling its actual purpose. Resilience is not inefficiency. It is a form of insurance. Like all insurance, the value only becomes apparent when it is needed – usually in a crisis. Hannah Walker Wymondham, Leicestershire Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

events.title: Microsoft outage: company scrambles to fix global issue that took down Outlook and Teams
events.summary: Microsoft scrambles to fix global outage affecting Teams and Outlook Tech firm says it is ‘deeply sorry’ for disruption that took services down and has now addressed the underlying issue What caused the outage and when will it be fixed? Microsoft outage hits UK hospitals, GPs, schools and police Tell us: have you been affected by the outage? Microsoft has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”. The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services. The outage of Microsoft’s services, which began Thursday evening, lasted roughly 18 hours before services started to recover just before midday GMT on Friday. Microsoft said it was bringing back services gradually to ensure a stable restoration. Earlier on Friday, it said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels” as it brought back services. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, and more than 90% of Fortune 500 companies use Copilot, Microsoft’s AI chatbot, according to the company. On Friday, government agencies worldwide, from municipalities in France to the US House of Representatives, reported problems with Microsoft services. The issues were patchy, with some but not all users reporting problems with services including Microsoft Teams and Outlook email. The outage website Down Detector showed an increase in Microsoft 365 problems at about 6pm GMT on Thursday, with nearly 130,000 reports of problems in 74 countries affecting access to Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams as well as enterprise services such as SharePoint and OneDrive. Copilot was also affected. Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running. Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.” The Microsoft outage also hit connectors used by ⁠OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI ⁠services. OpenAI said it was investigating a problem with Microsoft connectors in which new connections might be broken and tools were not working as ⁠expected. Anthropic said it had identified an issue with an upstream provider ​affecting its Microsoft 365 ​connector. The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products. In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several British police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead. Some schools in the UK notified parents that reporting attendance or absence issues had to be done via phone. National Rail, which provides information across the UK network, warned people might not be able to access tickets that had been emailed to them. US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffers on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported. Multiple cities, including the City of Tampa, Florida, posted notices on their municipal websites to say that they were affected by the outage. Law enforcement offices across the US were also affected, with one sheriff’s county in Colorado saying it was unable to process bond payments because Outlook email was down, and requesting that anyone who needed to post bond do so in person. When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86. In Australia, the financial impact of the outage was expected to cost billions of dollars , according to the risk advisory firm, RSM Australia. Several government agencies, including national security sevices, were unable to access or send emails. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Hospitals and health clinics were affected , although the Australian Medical Association on Friday said had been no impacts for patient care. Courts and schools also struggled to operate as normal. The Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were affected, and Taiwanese security firms, life insurers and investment trust companies said fund management services had been disrupted. In financial markets some portfolio managers have been unable to check emails, making it hard to access on some trading platforms. In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.

events.title: Gen Z hasn’t made up its mind on AI, survey finds
events.summary: Gen Z is often cast as souring on AI, but they’re no more negative about the technology than their parents and grandparents. A new survey from Milltown Partners, shared first with Semafor, found that 73% of Gen Z adults haven’t made up their minds on AI, while half said they expect AI to harm society. That matches baby boomers (50%) and Gen Xers (48%), while millennials were the most upbeat, with 39% expecting harm. Companies and politicians are all eager to understand the generation’s stance on AI, given how much they drive tech trends and how AI and data centers played an outsize role in the US midterm election. The report also pointed to a paradox that seems to define young people’s relationship with AI: Many say it makes them worse at thinking for themselves and harder to find a job — but 46% said they use it every day, the second-highest rate behind millennials. Young people are also less worried than older generations about the existential risk that dominates much of the AI safety discourse. And they are more conflicted about their own use: 30% of Gen Zers said they sometimes feel guilty using AI, more than double the rate among respondents over 30.

events.title: My partner moved in with me — and my 30-year-old daughter. It hasn't always been easy, but it's worked for 9 years.
events.summary: Living together hasn't always been easy for the three of us, but we've built some great routines. Samantha Priestley In 2017, my partner moved in with my adult daughter and me. At first, we all had to make compromises and adjust to some growing pains. Viewing each other as adult roommates helped, and the three of us still live together now. I'd been dating my partner for a couple of years before we decided to move in together. He'd been staying over often, at first for just a night at a time, and then for few-day stretches. One time, he was setting off for work from my house, duffel bag in hand, and I said, "This is stupid. Why don't you just move in?" And so he did, but he didn't just move in with me. My adult daughter lives at home , so "moving in" meant joining both of us. There have been challenges, but nine years later — with my daughter now 30 — this is still our setup. We all had to make some compromises when my partner moved in My daughter moved back in with me after she finished school. Samantha Priestley I got divorced when my daughter was a teenager, and started dating again once she was an adult. Although she had left home for university, she came back to live with me after finishing her studies. When my partner moved in with the two of us, it was into the home I'd shared with my ex-husband. It didn't feel right, so we quickly decided to get a place of our own, and the three of us moved into our four-bedroom Edwardian terrace house a few months later. By this time, my daughter and I had both been pretty set in our routines … like sharing a bathroom. My daughter was used to taking as long as she liked to get ready, but with an extra person, she had to account for three people's schedules instead of two. Meanwhile, my partner was clearly used to leaving his things lying around when he lived alone, but now, he was with two women who liked things to be tidy. If he were moving in with just me, the two of us might have tried to compromise, but he definitely felt some pressure to fit into our world, rather than asking me and my daughter adjusting to suit him. For me, the biggest compromise I've had to make is with my time. My attention was only required by my daughter when I was at home, but now I had to split my time with the two of them, which could be tiring at times. I felt constantly conscious of not leaving either of them out. Take cooking, as one example. My daughter and I always enjoyed cooking together, so I made sure we kept doing it — to this day, we prepare dinner together almost every evening. But my partner likes cooking, too, so we made a new habit of making a big breakfast together every weekend. I've had to prioritize alone time with both my partner and my daughter My partner and I make sure to plan plenty of date nights. Samantha Priestley The biggest problem I've found is one that shows up in almost every family and housing dynamic: Cohabitation can be hard, and sometimes we bug each other. It's not uncommon for me to feel like I'm in the middle. It's not that my partner and my daughter argue or don't get along, but inevitably, there can be tension over who didn't take out the recycling or who used the last of the milk, and I feel the pull in both directions when there is. I've found that the best way to avoid this is to make sure we all get some space. My daughter and I go on vacation together three times a year, plus day trips , to give my partner time to himself. Meanwhile, my partner and I go out on date nights, leaving my daughter alone. Even just taking a walk by ourselves when we need air is a good way to get some alone time. We each have our own rooms in the house — my daughter has her own bedroom, and my partner and I both have home offices — which really helps. We don't have a traditional family setup, but we're still a unit I encouraged my partner to treat my daughter like an adult roommate. Samantha Priestley My daughter will always be my little girl in many ways, but she contributes financially to our home and has always split household chores , tasks, and responsibilities with me. So, when my partner moved in , I had to help him understand that yes, she's my daughter and I'll always look out for her — but she's also an adult, and neither of us expected him to take on a father-like role. "Talk to her like any other adult," I remember telling him. "Think of this like a house-share with a friend." That attitude helped our dynamic click into place and went a long way in helping the two of them build a friendship. Given my daughter's age, they were never going to view each other as father and daughter, but they do see each other as family. When my daughter announced she wanted to watch a bunch of old movies, we immediately decided that every Saturday would be movie night, and it's become our own little tradition. The three of us go out for dinner together, spend the holidays together, and even take trips together. Things are always changing in families, but for now, we're making this work. My daughter is currently saving up enough money to get her own place. In some ways, it will be great to have the space and time to live as a couple, because we never have. But I'll also miss living together as the three of us. It might not be the living setup any of us would have chosen, but sharing our home like this has created a bond between the three of us that's unique and beautiful. events.title: Jensen Huang’s biggest mistake was getting too involved in DC
events.summary: Reed’s view Jensen Huang made a lot of mistakes, but the one that really brought him down was getting too involved in DC. The skillset of a great technologist is the opposite of someone who’s great at politics. Technologists have to think years, sometimes decades in advance. When they figure out a winning formula, they bet everything on it. That’s a really bad way to operate in Washington, where things move on two-year election cycles and commitment to any one idea, faction, or ideology is a liability if and when the political winds change. When Donald Trump was elected president for a second term, it seemed like the world was suddenly a fundamentally different place. The White House was open for business in a way never seen in history. It was irresistible for a lot of tech people (Elon Musk and Marc Andreessen also fell into this trap). For a while, it seemed like Huang was one of the few technologists to find success in DC. His friendship with the president helped advance his worldview — that America should export its technology around the world, even to China. But it was all a mirage. Political people understood this would never last, and it would end in hearings, investigations, and prosecutions. This has all come as a shocking surprise to many in the tech industry. Nvidia was aggressive in its policy positions in part because it had the backing of the president. It should have used that influence sparingly, and not just to get what it wanted but to make more allies on both sides of the political aisle. So far, the underlying allegations against Huang are unproven. The alleged spy who led to this mess may not even be a spy . And many in the tech industry are angry and want to fight back. That’s the wrong instinct. In the tech industry, the relentless will to win is perhaps the most redeeming quality of every operator. In DC, you can’t ever really win. You can only lose. The Nvidia scandal and the post-midterm tech industry peril are exactly the reason we came up with the idea for our convening, Silicon Valley & The World, which takes place next week in the heart of the industry. We’re bringing leaders in from around the globe to burst Silicon Valley’s bubble and make it a more worldly place. We have what I think is the best lineup of speakers ever assembled at a media industry convening and I hope Jensen Huang, who was supposed to speak, will reconsider. If you’d like to tune in, register for a virtual broadcast pass , or watch live on YouTube and at Semafor.com . Notable Palantir CEO Alex Karp, another CEO that developed close ties to Trump and Washington , told Politico Playbook that he is a “ progressive ” and a lifelong Democrat.

events.title: At 40, I moved my family of 4 to Spain. We spent that first year abroad learning from our mistakes.
events.summary: Moving from the US to Spain has meant embracing culture shocks and making a few mistakes. Courtesy of Brian Hodge About a year and a half ago, my family of four left the US and moved to Spain . We've adapted in many ways but still sometimes struggle with late mealtimes and limited store hours. Locals take their time at cafés and restaurants, and it's pushed us to embrace a laid-back attitude. I should've known that we were too early when we had to duck under the partially closed metal awning. We'd arrived after the restaurant's posted opening hours, but my suspicions were confirmed when we were greeted by a hostess who was still taking off her motorcycle helmet. Definitely too early. She suggested we come back later, with a reservation. Welcome to the struggle of finding dinner in Spain before 8 p.m. About a year and a half ago, my family and I made the bold decision to leave the US, sell most of our belongings — including our home — and move our lives to Spain . Although it's absolutely been a dream come true, there are still some cold-water-on-the-face moments that snap us awake and remind us how far we've come. We've gradually adjusted to new business hours and norms Restaurants are a little different in Spain than they are in the US. Courtesy of Brian Hodge Even simple things like dining out and shopping at local stores have required some readjusting. Restaurants typically open later and stay open later than they did back in the US, especially during Spain's languid, sunny summers. This all sounds very romantic until you have hungry children looking for dinner at 7:30 p.m. and most local restaurants don't open for another hour. Then dinner becomes a mish-mash of ham, cheese, and olives back home. It's possible to find inexpensive wines at the local market ... just check their hours first. Courtesy of Brian Hodge And don't count on stopping by the local supermarket on Sundays — ours is closed. Fish at the Mercado Central on Mondays? Forget it. Picture instead dozens of fish stalls, row after row of shops usually spilling over with squid, shellfish, swordfish, tuna, and more, all shuttered. I've also stopped counting how many times I've tried to pick up a few items at a local store in the middle of the day, only to be greeted by closed doors because the whole street has shut down for "siesta" (also known as a post-lunch rest). These breaks are common throughout Spain, and often last for two or three hours in the middle of the day, but can vary depending on the region. We like to look at fresh produce at the Mercado Central when it's open. Courtesy of Brian Hodge Although these shops often stay open later in the evening to help balance things out, we do miss the simple reliability of many local businesses being open all day. On the bright side, in Spain, restaurant and business hours seem to intentionally force us to slow down and plan ahead. Dining and café culture have also pushed us to slow down and enjoy meals more Café culture is alive and well in Spain. Courtesy of Brian Hodge In Spain, café culture is alive and well. The sidewalks frequently fill with workers, families, and neighbors of all ages, making the chairs and tables a lively extension of the neighborhood. They take their time sipping, chatting, and sharing food. Diners rarely seem to be in a rush — and it's considered poor form to eat while walking or commuting. We've found ways to adapt to our new country. Courtesy of Brian Hodge We've learned to budget more time for quick meals and the art of flagging down the waiter for the check — otherwise it simply won't arrive. It took a bit of getting used to, especially coming from a country where rushed meals are more normal, and the check can sometimes arrive at the same time as the food. However, there's no rushing you out of restaurants here. In fact, the Spanish even have a word, sobremesa , for the idle chatter and company that follows a meal. Allow extra time accordingly. Sometimes, ordering mishaps have actually worked in our favor One time, I thought I asked for the menu. Instead, I got three courses of food. Courtesy of Brian Hodge One of our first meals in Spain was at a local restaurant in our neighborhood. Buoyed by a healthy mix of overestimating our level of fluency and underestimating just how quickly waiters can talk, we were excited to experience a more authentic, truly Spanish experience. So when I thought I was simply asking for the menu, we could only laugh when we received a "menú del día" ("menu of the day"), heaping plates and platters as part of a three-course meal. In retrospect, the fact that the waiter talked for so long and in such detail about each dish should have been a sign, but it turned out to be an error in our favor. The multicourse meal was delicious, priced at only about 14 euros per person, and one of the best we've had. We now actively seek out menús del día whenever we're out. All in all, living here has meant planning more but also embracing a laid-back attitude In Spain, we've learned to embrace life at a slower pace. Courtesy of Brian Hodge Ultimately, we've learned to take things more slowly and make plans in advance when it comes to meals and errands — things we probably should've been doing anyway. And we've especially learned to appreciate our little adventure and the fact we were actually able to pull it off, despite all the bumps and bruises along the way. I'm not sure how long my family will stay in Spain , but we set out on this path to push ourselves outside our comfort zones and learn new things. On that count, even the mistakes have been a success. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The best pumpkin pie I've ever made uses a surprisingly easy recipe from Bobby Flay
events.summary: I'm a pretty big fan of Bobby Flay's recipe for pumpkin pie. Paige Bennett I previously tested three celebrity chefs' pumpkin-pie recipes, and Bobby Flay's was my favorite. Overall, Flay's recipe for pumpkin pie was easy to follow, and the dessert turned out delicious. The graham-cracker crust was sturdy, and the flavorful whipped cream really made this dish. I've baked more than 100 recipes from celebrity chefs , often putting them head-to-head to find the best dishes out there. When testing out star-studded takes on pumpkin pie , Bobby Flay's version of the seasonal dessert blew me away. The chef's " Throwdown Pumpkin Pie " recipe, found on the Food Network website, features a sturdy graham-cracker crust, creamy spiced filling, and decadent bourbon-maple whipped cream. Even better, it's pretty easy to make. Here's how I put it together and why I plan to keep this pie recipe in my rotation year after year. Most of the ingredients are pretty basic I already had a lot of the ingredients for Bobby Flay's pumpkin pie in my pantry and fridge. Paige Bennett Flay's recipe is a no-fuss option for people who love a homemade dessert but don't want to spend a full day making a flaky pie crust , as it uses a graham-cracker base instead. The recipe also doesn't require carving and roasting fresh pumpkin. Instead, canned pumpkin purée gets mixed with butter, eggs, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, granulated sugar, dark-brown sugar, heavy cream, salt, and fresh vanilla-bean seeds. Of course, this dish wouldn't be complete without the flavorful whipped cream made with heavy whipping cream, maple syrup, vanilla-bean seeds, and bourbon. The steps are easy to follow, too I crushed the graham crackers with a mallet. Paige Bennett Before baking this pie, I measured out all of the ingredients and organized them in groups for the crust, filling, and whipped cream. This made following this recipe a quicker, simpler process. Although the recipe calls for a food processor, I didn't have one when I first made this dish. Instead, I used a mallet to crush the graham crackers, which I'd sealed in a plastic bag to avoid making a mess. I then combined the crumbs with butter, sugar, and cinnamon in a small blender. The graham-cracker crust had to bake. Paige Bennett From there, I firmly pressed the graham-cracker mixture into a pie tin and baked the crust for 10 minutes at 350 degrees Fahrenheit to set it. Once the pie crust had been prebaked, I set the oven to 275 degrees Fahrenheit as instructed and got to work on the filling. Making the filling was also simple. Paige Bennett I started by whisking the eggs and sugar together before adding in the pumpkin, heavy cream, salt, vanilla, spices, and sugars.  Once I had the creamy filling ready to go, I strained it and poured it into my cooled pie crust. I ended up with far more filling than I needed for one pie. According to the recipe, this is intentional, and extras can be used toward more pies or frozen for later use. The crust wasn't perfect, but it held the filling just fine. Paige Bennett Luckily, Flay's whipped cream can be thrown together while the pie finishes baking. To do so, I combined heavy whipping cream, bourbon, vanilla-bean seeds, and maple syrup in a stand mixer. The recipe calls for Grade B maple syrup, but that's no longer a classification, so I use a dark Grade A syrup instead. It added a nice rich flavor to the whipped cream. My pie ended up baking for about an hour and a half. The pie and whipped cream paired together perfectly There's hardly a greater combination than pumpkin pie and whipped cream. Paige Bennett Flay's whipped cream beautifully balanced the pumpkin pie's pumpkin flavor and spices and was tasty on its own, thanks to the maple syrup, bourbon, and vanilla. The pumpkin pie itself had a great texture. Although the bottom of the crust was slightly too soggy, it still held together well. Plus, the dish maintained a good height and sported crispy edges. I wish the crust was just as tasty as the filling and whipped cream, though. In the future, I plan to add more sugar and cinnamon to the graham-cracker mix to boost its flavor. Even so, this pie was surprisingly easy to put together and utterly delicious. I'll definitely be making it again. events.title: Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both | Jonathan Freedland
events.summary: Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both The environmental and economic dilemmas he faces are formidable but, with a bold plan, he could set an example for leaders around the world F or politicians of the centre-left especially, it’s the great dilemma of the age. How do you do what everyone can see is essential to save the planet from boiling – even as your voters demand action to get the economy growing and to make life more affordable? Plenty of activists will tell you there’s no contradiction, that tackling the climate crisis makes economic as well as ecological sense and, in the long term, you know they’re right. But you don’t live in the long term. You’re running the government right now and facing several unavoidable, binary choices. Andy Burnham is a prime example. This week, he addressed the Cop summit in Antalya , promising “a new era of British leadership” in the struggle against global heating. It’s important to him to talk that way: his political strategy relies on shrinking the appeal of the Green party, whose electoral success earlier this year helped remove his predecessor. But talk only takes you so far. Eventually the words have to be matched by action. That’s where things get tricky. Last month Burnham’s government approved the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, dismaying climate activists. Soon there will have to be a decision on Rosebank, the much bigger proposed new oilfield northwest of Shetland. There are also signs that ministers are preparing to weaken the targets set for the car industry to shift to electric vehicles. And this week, the chancellor, John Healey, declared himself fully “behind building a third runway at Heathrow”. Small wonder that campaigners are talking of hypocrisy and the government’s “crumbling” credibility. What is Burnham to do? He has Healey in one ear, telling him that a thriving airport is an engine for economic growth, doubtless alongside the oil, gas and car industries. And in the other he has the climate scientists, reminding him that global carbon emissions are at record levels and the planet is getting hotter every year. What option does he have, except to keep putting off the moment of choice, buying himself time by saying, for example, that Rosebank is a “quasi-legal decision” that cannot be hurried? Naturally, there are advocates for each of the binary options, whether it’s green activists demanding he put the planet first, regardless of the impact on jobs or prices, or business leaders insisting it be the other way around. But he is in a different position from each of those warring sides – because he has to come up with something both can live with. The answer might just be an arresting blend of pragmatism and radicalism – both, and at the same time. Such an approach would begin with saying a couple of things campaigners might not want to hear. First, that the most reliable route to reducing the use of fossil fuels lies not with curtailing supply – blocking production – but with slashing demand. Or as Michael Jacobs, who served as the climate and energy adviser to Gordon Brown in Downing Street, told me this week: “We need to destroy the demand for oil and gas.” On that goal, there has been remarkable progress, whether measured in the shift to renewable sources of power, such as wind and solar, for the generation of electricity or the move to electric vehicles: last month just under one in two new cars registered in the UK were either fully electric or plug-in hybrids . The second message Burnham might deliver to a wary, green audience would be: symbols matter, but they should not obscure the thing they are meant to symbolise. In that context, and given that destroying demand is more important than curbing supply, he could argue that the green light he gave to Jackdaw should not be overplayed. That project is relatively small and has an expected lifespan of only about 10 years. Yes, it became a signifier, but the bigger picture is what matters. It would be much harder to make that argument for Rosebank, which is bigger than Jackdaw and set to last for 25 years, and harder still for Heathrow, not least because emissions from aviation are stubbornly difficult to reduce: you can’t shrink demand for aviation fuel, because, as of now, there are few readily available alternatives. So a third runway means a serious increase in the UK’s emissions of CO 2 . But what if Burnham felt he could not rebuff the growth lobby on Heathrow and Rosebank, especially if he also stands firm on his electric vehicle targets despite the howls of protest from UK carmakers? Is there a bone he could throw them, while not enraging the climate-concerned voters he needs to keep on side?
