events.title: Meet Colette Kress, Nvidia’s New Interim CEO
events.summary: Nvidia’s CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang is officially out , and longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress is in. The chipmaker’s board of directors announced Thursday that Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, has been named interim CEO following Huang’s resignation amid a scandal over his extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman believed by US officials to be an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Harvey Jones, the newly appointed chair of Nvidia’s board, said in a statement that Kress “has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position.” He added that Kress will be supported by an “experienced leadership team” and that the board has “full confidence” in her. Kress was among the most obvious candidates to fill the void after Huang’s departure, according to multiple tech executives and industry analysts who follow Nvidia closely, given her long tenure at the company, credibility on Wall Street and across the tech industry, and, perhaps most importantly, her deep familiarity with Nvidia’s business and finances. “She’s extremely strong-willed, professional, and whip-smart. She doesn’t tolerate nonsense. She can be friendly and gracious too,” says a former Nvidia executive who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “She obviously has a keen sense for how Jensen thinks.” “Colette is the logical choice,” says Patrick Moorhead, founder and chief analyst at Moor Insights & Strategies, who has tracked the chip industry for decades. “She has credibility with investors because she answers hard questions directly.” Moorhead says Kress has operated as much more than a “numbers” CFO. “In my conversations with her, she goes deep on the product road map, from rack-scale systems to networking and software,” he says. Nvidia’s board said on Sunday it was launching an independent investigation into Huang’s activities following a report by The New York Times that he had an affair with a woman named Alice Huang, who US officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. WIRED reported on Monday that Huang quietly hired a crisis communications firm sometime last year to handle matters related to his personal life. By October of 2025, the firm was being looped in on all press inquiries involving Huang at Nvidia, around the same time The New York Times reported that US authorities were investigating whether a company linked to Alice Huang had helped Chinese firms evade US chip export controls through its subsidiaries. While Huang has long been the public face of Nvidia, Kress has been responsible for managing the chipmaker’s relationship with Wall Street. On earnings calls, she often details Nvidia’s financial performance, customer demand, supply constraints, and other key metrics. “One of the things we don’t focus on is the stock price. We focus on our investors and how we would like to innovate,” Kress told the Israeli business newspaper Globes in 2023. Before joining Nvidia, Kress spent more than two decades in finance roles at Microsoft, Cisco, and Texas Instruments. Huang personally recruited her in 2013, when Nvidia was still best known for its gaming graphics cards, according to Globes. Huang laid out his vision for the company’s future on a whiteboard, explaining how Nvidia could become a major supplier of computing infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Other potential successors to Huang included Ian Buck, an Nvidia veteran of more than 20 years who created the company’s software platform CUDA and now oversees its high-performance computing business, and Jeff Fisher, who joined Nvidia in 1994 as the head of software sales and later became senior vice president of its GeForce unit, where he led Nvidia’s strategy for bringing GPUs to market. However, Nvidia’s unusual corporate structure has long meant that dozens of executives reported directly to Huang. The company lacks a traditional chief operating officer. Even executive vice presidents aren’t necessarily given direct control over budgets, sources have told WIRED. As a result, few people within the organization have the same level of understanding of the company’s financials as Kress. The former Nvidia executive who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity said that while Kress is incredibly sharp and “can step into the [CEO] role immediately without needing any guidance,” she doesn’t have the same engineering and technical expertise that Huang brought to the role. She has also shied away from being “at the center of public attention,” the person said. Given the intense scrutiny surrounding Huang lately, that leadership style might be a welcome temporary change for Nvidia. events.title: The end of the 'Nvidia put' that powers the AI ecosystem
events.summary: Liz’s view Jensen Huang is out, and with him goes the “Nvidia put” that has underpinned the entire AI ecosystem. Huang, who resigned from his post Thursday, was the AI world’s central bank chairman and human security blanket, always there with a checkbook to backstop, acquire, hire, invest in, or otherwise underwrite the least underwritable corners of AI. That “put” — finance speak for a guaranteed buyer on the other side of a trade — has kept the AI financing and fundraising markets lubricated, even as it invited criticism of their circularity. It’s also helped prop up the stock market and padded 401(k)s for the last couple of years. Nvidia guarantees more than $100 billion of data-center leases , owns $51 billion worth of stock in privately held companies, and another $63 billion in listed ones. Its balance sheet was a sponge that absorbed the market’s growing AI fears and put a floor under deal prices. Whoever replaces him will face much higher stakes, akin to Tim Cook after Steve Jobs at Apple. They’ll also be on a tighter leash from a board of directors I suspect will get a much-needed refresh by the time this saga is over. (It’s hard to imagine the former president of Taco Bell or the former chief marketing officer of the NFL probing Huang too deeply on off-balance-sheet lease guarantees for next-generation data centers.) Not only will that change the fabric of one of the world’s most valuable companies, but it will also push up the price of AI debt and equity — making the AI buildout more expensive for everyone — by taking a huge buyer off the table. Notable Unlike with the 2008 financial crisis, “this time we can see it on a blue-sky day: Nvidia is officially too big to fail, ” I wrote in October. “What would be revealed by a stress test of Nvidia that contemplated a rise in the cost of AI-linked debt, a decline in venture-backed startup values, and a slowdown in data-center construction?” What happens under new leadership will determine the future of the company.

events.title: Jensen Huang's ouster triggers an AI earthquake
events.summary: Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia has plunged the AI industry into uncharted territory — a corporate earthquake that dwarfs even the chaos unleashed by Sam Altman's temporary firing from OpenAI in 2023. Why it matters: Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy , with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars. At the center of that vast financial flywheel is Huang, who spent 33 years making himself synonymous with Nvidia — and Nvidia synonymous with the AI revolution. "This is no ordinary CEO. This is no ordinary company. This is no ordinary sector. This is no ordinary time," economist Mohamed El-Erian wrote on X , warning of contagion across the AI industry. The latest: Huang resigned from all his positions at Nvidia, the company's board of directors said Thursday, following allegations of two affairs, including one with a woman accused of being a spy for China. The board named Nvidia's CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. Zoom in: As recently as two weeks ago, the notion of Nvidia without Jensen was unthinkable. Even after his affair with Alice Huang — the woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — came to light, President Trump and Nvidia's board stood behind him, Silicon Valley's elite rallied to his defense and betting markets suggested he would survive. It took revelations of a second affair — this time with an executive who reported directly to Jensen Huang — to shatter that consensus and bring his storied reign to the brink of a stunning end. Driving the news: After that second affair came to light Wednesday night, Nvidia's board reportedly met to settle Huang's fate. The White House was read in. The market reaction has been brutal. Nvidia had already shed more than $1 trillion in market value since the initial scandal erupted, and shares plunged further in after-hours and pre-market trading overnight. One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang. Zoom out: Huang's rise was the stuff of Silicon Valley legend: The Taiwanese immigrant went from cleaning toilets at a Kentucky boarding school and waiting tables at Denny's to building one of the most valuable companies in history. Huang and two fellow engineers hatched the idea for Nvidia at a Denny's booth in 1993, launching a chipmaker that would revolutionize gaming, transform modern computing and ultimately power the AI revolution. Clad in his trademark black leather jacket, Huang became a global AI rock star — with a cult of personality that drew adoring crowds, calmed markets and commanded the attention of world leaders. The big picture: Huang's apparent downfall comes amid mounting anxiety over the AI industry's future, as new financial, political and regulatory risks threaten one of the largest infrastructure buildouts in history. The timing is especially fraught for Anthropic , whose historic IPO — backed by a $10 billion commitment from Nvidia — looms as a referendum on Wall Street's faith in the AI trade. Huang spent years defending the industry's soaring valuations and dismissing warnings of a speculative frenzy. Now his own scandals could help burst the bubble he insisted didn't exist. What to watch: The blast radius could extend far beyond Silicon Valley and Wall Street, threatening to engulf the Trump administration in a scandal over its handling of sensitive technology exports to China. Huang forged a close alliance with Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who loosened restrictions on chip sales even as other officials raised concerns about Chinese espionage and smuggling. Top Senate Democrats are already demanding that Lutnick and other senior officials preserve records of their dealings with Nvidia and Huang, laying the groundwork for a sweeping investigation. The bottom line: As veteran China watcher Bill Bishop wrote after Huang acknowledged his first affair: "There is rarely just one lie." events.title: A new AI model wants to read between the lines
events.summary: The Scoop New York-based AI startup millionways on Thursday launched its new AI model that claims to offer insight into human intent and motivations. The company also told Semafor it has raised $6 million in US funding, with investors including football stars Jason Kelce and DK Metcalf. The Thorsten-4 model was born out of a research project in Germany in which dozens of psychologists interviewed more than 7,000 people about their personal lives and aspirations. That data — which the psychologists labeled by hand to capture what people’s words revealed about their motives and thinking — was used to train the model. Millionways cofounders Martin Cordsmeier and Max Weidemann argue that understanding is missing from regular AI models, which are trained on internet text. They see the model as particularly useful in sales and executive hiring, where a search firm could prompt it to evaluate an interview transcript to gauge how a candidate will behave under pressure. “We can add a level of human understanding that the language models cannot get to by themselves,” Weidemann said, adding that the model should be “a decision-making support tool rather than the ultimate decision-maker.” J.D.’s view Enterprises are increasingly injecting task- and industry-specific models into their tech stacks, rather than defaulting to the frontier models for every task. Just this week, leading voice AI company ElevenLabs, for example, announced a healthcare-focused version of its new transcription model. This gives CIOs more choice and customization, but it also adds the burden of testing whether specialized models actually beat fast-improving frontier ones. Cordsmeier and Weidemann ran our conversation for this story through Thorsten-4, which deduced that I was most focused on relationship-building and being conscientious: “You move between logic and intuition, and tough questions energized you.” (I’ll take the compliment!) I ran a transcript of the same call through Anthropic’s new Claude Fable 5.2 model and asked for a psychology analysis: Claude also gave a solid assessment, though it was less sure of itself, focusing more on the job I was doing than on me as a person. It (correctly) noted that my “unstated goal was source cultivation.”

In our latest Short-Term Energy Outlook , we expect a 23,000 barrels per day (b/d) (6%) increase in 2026, followed by a 60,000 b/d (13%) rise in 2027. At a forecast 505,000 b/d in 2027, output would be the most since 2014. If realized, these annual production increases will be the largest since the 1980s, when Alaskan crude production peaked at 2.0 million b/d. The recent growth is attributable to two projects on Alaska's North Slope: The Nuna project, owned by ConocoPhillips, started production in December 2024 and is expected to produce 20,000 b/d at its peak. So far this year, it has produced an average of 10,000 b/d, partially offsetting existing production declines. The Pikka Phase 1 project, jointly owned by Santos and Repsol, began production in May 2026 with initial average monthly production of 2,000 b/d and reaching 38,000 b/d as of September 2026, according to data from the Alaska Oil & Gas Conservation Commission . We expect peak production of 80,000 b/d by winter 2026–27, nearly 20% of total Alaskan production in 2025. Notably, our STEO production data indicate that third-quarter 2026 production grew 4% as Pikka Phase 1 came online, marking the first third-quarter production increase in more than 40 years. events.title: Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO
events.summary: Jensen Huang stepped down as the chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday, four days after the company announced its internal investigation into an affair he had with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. “Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately,” the Nvidia board said in a statement. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will serve as interim CEO. The board said it “will consider internal and external candidates” for a permanent replacement. The board’s investigation was announced on November 8, slightly less than two weeks after The New York Times reported that the chief executive had been the target of a Chinese intelligence operation facilitated through his relationship with Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen. The pair have been spotted in public together at least twice, in June 2024 and May 2025 . On November 11, The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also allegedly had a relationship with a direct report at Nvidia. The alleged relationship with a subordinate, along with Huang’s business dealings with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI company where Alice Huang previously held a senior position, likely played a greater role in the board’s decision to oust Huang than the Chinese espionage allegations, a source familiar with the matter tells WIRED. US intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump on Huang’s relationship with Alice last year, but the president did not act on it. On November 6, The New York Times and Financial Times reported that Alice was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security and that she had been recruited to collect information on the Nvidia executive. (The Chinese government has rejected all claims that Alice was a spy for the country. ) Huang sent a companywide email on Sunday acknowledging his affair, apologizing to his family and Nvidia employees, and pledging cooperation with the internal investigation. The executive has been married to his wife, Lori Huang, since 1985 , and both of the couple’s two children work at the company. On Monday, WIRED exclusively reported that last year Huang began working with a crisis PR firm to manage his personal communications. In October 2025, those PR consultants started to be looped in on all press inquiries involving Huang, whether those inquiries were personal or professional in nature. The timing lines up with a New York Times report that month that the US Commerce Department was investigating whether Alice Huang’s Megaspeed was helping Chinese companies get around American export controls with the help of a vast web of subsidiaries. The investigation was reportedly halted and transferred to the Justice Department after Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter inquired about it. Huang has been a vocal critic of these export controls, which he argues unnecessarily constrain the market for American chips, create discrete Chinese and American tech ecosystems, and spur China to build competitive chips of its own. Huang has worked to develop a relationship with Trump in order to advocate for policies that are advantageous for Nvidia, including the idea of opening its markets to China. Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 with friends Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. The trio reportedly brainstormed their vision for the company in a Denny’s diner and aspired to bring realistic 3D graphics to personal computers. For the first few decades of its existence, Nvidia was primarily known in the gaming community for creating chips powerful enough to render high-quality in-game graphics. In 2012, after a new kind of neural network known as AlexNet won a high-profile prize in computer vision, Nvidia pivoted from high-speed computer graphics to building chips that would support artificial intelligence. Huang has repeatedly said that the introduction of AlexNet, which was developed by AI engineers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton, was a “Big Bang”–like event for computing. Because its new GPUs proved highly effective at powering AI models that require massive amounts of processing power, the value of Nvidia shares soared in 2023 and 2024, in lockstep with the broader AI boom that began sweeping through the world economy. In the summer of 2025, Nvidia became the first company in history to cross $4 trillion in value. As of September 2026, the company controlled about 90 percent of the GPU market. Much of Nvidia’s epic rise over the few decades has been attributed not just to its cutting-edge chips and its software “moat,” CUDA, that keeps developers locked into those chips, but also to the fast-thinking, controlling, charismatic, and often bombastic leadership style of Huang himself. Now, that critical part of the company’s success is out.

events.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after affair with suspected Chinese spy
events.summary: Embattled Nvidia co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned, marking a stunning fall from grace for the leader of a vital US computing giant that has long helped to fuel the artificial intelligence boom. Mr Huang’s departure came days after he admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. In a statement, Nvidia's board of directors thanked Mr Jensen for his "profound" contributions to the company. "The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry," the statement read. Colette Kress, current executive vice president and chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive, Nvidia announced. Nvidia stock was closed down 4.44 per cent, much steeper than the Nasdaq's drop of 0.39 per cent. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors, said Ms Kress had helped lead the company through a “period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position”. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia's strategy and advancing its technology road map." Political fallout US President Donald Trump , a long-time ally of Mr Huang, posted about the AI tycoon's departure on Truth Social, the US President's social media platform. "Now that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place: Tim Cook of Apple," Mr Trump wrote. "A legend replaces a legend." Mr Huang's many meetings with Mr Trump, however, often brought controversy. He would lobby Mr Trump to try to relax US chip export policies affecting China, which caused an uproar with both Democrats and Republicans. Jensen Huang’s decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws. They still owe Congress answers. — Elizabeth Warren (@SenWarren) November 12, 2026 Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren on Thursday claimed Mr Trump and those he appointed to the Department of Commerce enabled some of the controversies that engulfed Nvidia. " Secretary Howard Lutnick and undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fuelling China’s military," she said, referring to reports of Nvidia's dealings with China. Alice Huang affair Mr Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, sparked a crisis this month when he admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a technology executive. US officials and investigators said they believe Ms Huang, who is not related to Mr Huang, to be a spy working on behalf of China, the top US rival in the tech and AI field. To maintain its edge in the AI race, the US introduced export policies designed to keep some of the most powerful US-made semiconductors and computers away from adversaries. But Mr Huang and Nvidia openly opposed the export policies. He said the restrictions hampered US influence and prevented American technology from becoming a global standard. Proponents of the export policies, however, said they strengthened the US lead and made it difficult for countries such as China to catch up, particularly in the need for computing power to train large language models. Some of those supporters of the export policies accused Nvidia and Mr Huang of wanting to boost revenue at all costs, even if detrimental to US national security. As the overall mood towards AI, Big Tech executives and unregulated technology began to sour among US voters, politicians increased scrutiny of Nvidia. Infidelity By the time Mr Huang admitted to the affair, media reports had accused his company of ignoring various products entering China. Mr Huang’s admission of infidelity expedited and amplified calls for further inquiries. Shortly after his confession, Nvidia’s board of directors announced an independent investigation to address reports of whether he had been the target of a foreign spy operation and what, if anything, had been compromised. Company representatives initially insisted Mr Huang would remain chief executive but pressure grew. He founded Nvidia, with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, in 1993, as the personal computer sector was booming. A major part of that was gaming but many computers were not designed for gamers and Nvidia saw an opening in the market. The company designed special graphics cards and video boards that, while popular, did not make Nvidia a household name. As a result, its name was mispronounced by many for a long time. Profits steadily grew, however, and the company methodically expanded. As progress in AI started to hit its stride, Nvidia soon found its custom graphics processing units and boards in unprecedented demand. Stuff of legend Nvidia could hardly build its products fast enough to keep up with demand, yet it knew how to make them to perfection. Revenue and profits soared, and Mr Huang’s presence became almost impossible to ignore, even among those who had no interest in AI. His work ethic and management style became famous. At one point, CBS did an interview inside a Denny’s restaurant where he had spent many late nights founding the company. It was the sort of story that exemplified the American dream, But as Nvidia and Mr Huang enjoyed unprecedented success, some US officials raised concerns that Nvidia’s profits were being generated at the expense of national security, with its products potentially being used by hackers and hostile governments. Mr Huang’s fuelled more questions about Nvidia’s governance. His exit probably eclipses Apple’s dismissal of Steve Jobs in 1985, which was mainly caused by a boardroom power struggle. Who is interim chief executive Colette Kress? Within a few hours of being named Nvidia's chief executive, Ms Kress told the company’s more than 42,000 employees that she believes in Nvidia's future. "I recognise that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication," she wrote. Ms Kress said a company-wide meeting would take place on November 18, where more announcements would be made. "We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the Al revolution, and we have important work ahead of us," she wrote. Ms Kress was previously chief financial officer for US technology company Cisco, and before that was a corporate vice president of Microsoft, from 2006 to 2010. According to her LinkedIn profile, Ms Kress earned a master's from from the Southern Methodist University's Cox School of Business in Dallas, Texas. For undergraduate studies, she attended the University of Arizona.

events.title: Trump orders Vance to focus on "corruption" in Democrat-run areas, not Iran
events.summary: President Trump directed Vice President JD Vance on Thursday to turn his "complete and total attention" toward alleged corruption in Democrat-run cities and states, contending that "[w]e don't need a deal with Iran." The big picture: After Vance concluded that the Iran war drove Republicans' stunning midterm walloping, Trump is reorienting his No. 2's focus — and directing him to go after Democrats the president labeled as "CORRUPT AND EVIL." Oil prices surged, and stocks sank after Trump's post reinjected a note of uncertainty into a market that was acting like the Iran war was all but over. Driving the news: "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Also on Truth Social Thursday, he threatened new tariffs on Mexico and criticized GOP senators for failing to pass the Save America ACT — adding that failure to do so was "devastating" for Republicans during the midterms. He said that he had asked Vance to "focus his complete and total attention" on so-called "Corruption and Crime" in Democrat-run cities and states, naming Minnesota, California and Illinois. Vance has chaired Trump's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud since the president created it via executive order earlier this year. Throughout the first half of his administration and federal crackdown on U.S. cities, Trump has repeatedly framed blue areas as hotbeds of crime and corruption, even when the stats haven't necessarily backed up those arguments. Catch up quick: Vance was recently heavily involved in a push to reach a new ceasefire with Iran and resume nuclear negotiations, Axios' Barak Ravid reported. Vance was a skeptical voice in Trump's inner circle about the war, Ravid reported, and led U.S. negotiating delegations after it began. Vance's office and the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Between the lines: Vance offered a surprisingly candid assessment of the midterm shellacking, writing in an X post last week that "[t]he reason we lost is the war." He continued: "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest." "But everyone knows why we lost." What we're watching: Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with his G7 counterparts in Paris on Tuesday, where he said Trump had considered resuming the war or cutting a deal but instead settled on strangling the Iranian regime, Axios previously reported . Rubio has signaled skepticism of a diplomatic breakthrough — and Trump's post indicates that door is closed, for now. Editor's note: The story has been updated with additional information. events.title: Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries – that hurts the companies, too
events.summary: When multinational companies decide where to build a factory, open a mine or establish a regional office, they have to consider whether the investment will still be profitable years into the future. Making that decision increasingly means thinking about risks, like whether surrounding roads will flood, worker safety will be compromised by extreme heat in the summer, and clean water will be available. As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events around the world, these effects can be especially severe in poorer countries that lack the resources to prepare for disasters or recover quickly after they hit. I study how political and environmental risks affect international business . In my new book, “ Multinational Corporations and Climate Change: Risks, Responsibilities, and Resilience ,” I explore how disaster risk is affecting the ways global companies see these climate-vulnerable markets, and how those views are leading some foreign investors to avoid these developing nations altogether. Low- and middle-income countries aren’t the only ones that suffer when multinational corporations pass them by. The companies themselves also stand to lose out on business opportunities in emerging markets if they pull away. How climate risk affects foreign investment Evidence from several studies suggests that multinationals are systematically avoiding investing in the most climate-vulnerable countries. These include my own analysis of 159 countries. Although these studies focus on different samples, they identify the same trend: Countries characterized by greater climate vulnerability received less foreign investment . The results are not trivial. My book identifies a 12% reduction in foreign direct investment for each 1-point rise in climate vulnerability on a 100-point scale, while holding other relevant factors constant. This vulnerability data measures countries’ exposure to climate hazards as well as their capacity to adapt. Companies rarely say why they’re avoiding a particular location, but their climate-related concerns occasionally become visible. For example, Google halted plans to build a US$200 million data center in Chile after an environmental court revoked its construction permit over the likely effects on water supplies and the environment. Similarly, a $1 billion data center proposed in Kenya by Microsoft and the Abu Dhabi-based artificial intelligence company G42 was delayed and ultimately suspended amid concerns about water stress in the area. Companies have reason to be cautious about climate risks. One analysis of 71 large publicly traded companies found that firms reporting major flood losses experienced a 5% average decline in shareholder value over the following year, after accounting for broader market movements. In Vietnam, typhoons and floods caused an estimated $475 million in damage to energy and transportation infrastructure in 2022. Unreliable infrastructure cost companies there about $280 million . An aerial view shows scores of vehicles submerged at a flooded Honda factory in Thailand in November 2011. Paula Bronstein /Getty Images Severe flooding in Thailand in 2011 forced several companies, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, to temporarily suspend production as factories flooded, shutting down production of parts or vehicles made there. Costs like those shape where companies choose to invest next. While climate risk does not stop all investment in climate-vulnerable markets, it does make projects in these nations relatively more expensive, less attractive and more difficult to finance than less risky locations. Who loses from investor avoidance? For developing countries, less foreign investment means fewer jobs are created . These countries also have fewer opportunities to benefit from exposure to the new technologies that multinationals bring when they invest abroad. Those results highlight another way climate change is deepening global inequality. It reduces the economic activity that could support future development, while simultaneously damaging physical infrastructure and threatening human health and well-being. Developing countries are especially vulnerable to the effects of rising global temperatures, whether for their dependence on agricultural markets, geography or relatively fragile infrastructure . A report from the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago projects that 90% of heat-related deaths in the coming decades will take place in low- and middle-income countries. Similarly, a 2022 study found that around 90% of people exposed to flooding live in developing nations. Yet poor countries have contributed only a tiny fraction of the emissions that are causing climate change, even as they face the brunt of the damage. For example, African countries are responsible for less than 4% of greenhouse gas emissions globally. But they stand to experience the greatest negative effects of climate change. Lost opportunities for multinational companies When a company avoids investing in climate-vulnerable countries, that may reduce its exposure to floods, droughts or extreme heat, but the decision also carries potential costs for the company. Many of these countries have growing consumer markets, energy resources or critical minerals that multinationals need. Companies that dismiss them as too risky may lose out on promising opportunities. For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world’s cobalt , while Indonesia has become the dominant producer of nickel . These countries are highly vulnerable to climate change , which is likely scaring some companies away . Yet companies with a greater tolerance for risk have established strong positions in those countries’ mineral industries . Thus, more cautious firms may reduce their risk exposure, but they are also surrendering access to important resources and growing markets. Reducing investor avoidance There are ways to help companies overcome their climate-risk avoidance so more investment can pour into these countries: Foreign aid from wealthy countries can help developing countries shore up their roads, ports, electrical grids and water systems before extreme storms or droughts occur. My 2025 study found that climate-vulnerable countries that received more aid for climate adaptation also received more foreign direct investment than those receiving less aid. The result suggests the funding may reassure companies that climate risks are being addressed. International development banks can share some of the risks by providing climate risk insurance to multinationals. This would offer a safety net to absorb some of the losses if a covered disruption prevents a project from operating as intended. The World Bank already offers similar coverage against political risk incidents, which has given companies confidence to invest in countries such as Kenya , Mozambique and Nigeria . events.title: While California’s wealth tax failed, states are taking other steps to collect more revenue from the rich
events.summary: State efforts to tax the rich did relatively well in the 2026 midterm elections, following a series of state legislative moves in that direction in recent years. That might come as a surprise because a majority of voters rejected California’s Proposition 40 . The much-publicized ballot initiative would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. Google co-founder Sergey Brin and several other billionaires spent nearly $400 million trying to persuade voters to reject it. Emmanuel Saez, a University of California, Berkeley economist who studies inequality and helped design Proposition 40, lamented the loss, saying: “ Today oligarchy has won .” As a law professor who recently wrote a book about wealth inequality , I have been monitoring the results of these efforts aimed at taxing the rich. Despite Proposition 40’s failure, I think it’s important to observe that many Americans expressed support during the midterms for hiking income taxes on the rich, and to a lesser extent, taxes on the second – or third or fourth – homes the very wealthy possess. Taxing the rich at the ballot box Taxing income is proving a more successful strategy than taxing wealth. Major changes to income taxes were up for a vote in five states during the midterms. Three of those ballot initiatives were proposals that sought to boost income tax rates on the rich or maintain those rates. All three prevailed. In Washington state , for example, voters backed a measure that will preserve its new 9.9% income tax on household income above $1 million. This “millionaire’s tax,” signed into law earlier in 2026, is the state’s first personal income tax. Meanwhile, Colorado voters rejected Proposition 136 , which would have capped the state’s income tax rate at 4.4%. They also approved Amendment 87 , a new graduated income tax that raises rates on households and businesses with incomes over $500,000. And even though California’s voters rejected Proposition 40, they did approve Proposition 3 . That measure makes permanent the income tax rates enacted in 2012 for the state’s highest earners, which were set to expire in 2031. The surcharges, adjusted annually for inflation, start at 10.3% for incomes of $360,000 and go up to a 12.3% surcharge for taxpayers earning over $721,000. And in August 2026, Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have required the state’s lawmakers to eliminate its income tax. This would have meant losing $8.5 billion in revenue annually. The change would have let rich income taxpayers off the hook and replaced lost revenue through an increased sales tax that would have hit low-income taxpayers hardest. The two losses were in North Carolina and Iowa . Neither state voted directly on a tax to be levied on the rich. But both approved constitutional amendments that will make it harder for the state legislatures to enact these kinds of taxes in the future. North Carolina’s governor, Josh Stein, called the amendment in his state a “ millionaire protection cap .” People visit the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco, on Feb. 21, 2026, months before a ballot initiative that would have introduced such a measure failed to garner enough support. AP Photo/Jeff Chiu State legislatures raising income tax rates on high earners Ahead of the midterms, new taxes on the rich introduced via state legislatures , rather than ballot initiatives, also emerged. In Maine, legislators voted in April 2026 for a tax surcharge of 1% on income over $1 million. The following month, Hawaiian lawmakers created a new 13% income bracket for single taxpayers earning above $500,000 or couples filing jointly who make over $1 million. This change is paired with a reduction in rates for lower-income brackets. And one month after that, Rhode Island enacted a surcharge for millionaires’ income to be phased in over the next three years, reaching a maximum 3% rate. In 2009, New York became one of the first states to pass one of these high-earner income taxes . Washington, D.C., Massachusetts and Maryland also enacted these “millionaire taxes” in 2022, 2023 and 2025, respectively. Taxing additional homes Another way that state and local governments are boosting the tax revenue they get from wealthy constituents is by levying special taxes on pricey homes that aren’t the owners’ primary residences . These initiatives have succeeded both in state legislatures and voting booths. Montana lawmakers, in April 2025, approved a new tiered property tax system , which took effect on Jan. 1, 2026. It raised property tax rates on vacation homes and short-term rentals to 1.9%, while primary residences and qualifying long-term rentals pay lower, tiered homestead rates . New York City rolled out its “ pied-à-terre tax ” in July. The new tax imposes an annual surcharge of 0.8% to 1.3% on single-family homes valued at $5 million or more, and 4% to 6.5% on condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. The surcharge only applies to homes that are not a primary residence . Rhode Island has a similar property tax that took effect at the same time as New York City’s. It’s an annual surcharge of $2.50 for every $500 of assessed value above $1 million that applies to non-primary residences. And on Nov. 3, voters in Boulder, Colorado, approved a residential vacancy tax on homes that sit empty more than half the year. The surcharge, which goes into effect in 2028, will be roughly $4,000 a year for each vacant property. It applies across the board, but homes that aren’t primary residences are the clear target. However, just west of Boulder in Crested Butte, Colorado, a second-home tax failed. So did an effort to levy a similar surcharge in San Diego, California. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks about the fiscal year 2027 budget in New York City on May 12, 2026. Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images Why income taxes are attractive to voters and lawmakers There is a good reason why taxing the income of rich people is easier to pull off than taxing their wealth: Income taxes are much easier to calculate . Income taxes can be based on annual income tax filings, whether state or federal. It requires no extra work to value someone’s net worth. There are no such filings for wealth, except after death, if a large estate is left behind . Wealth taxes also require the annual valuation of businesses, farmland, artwork, intellectual property and other assets – many of which are hard to estimate. The downside of taxing income instead of wealth is that it limits how much revenue can be raised from the people most able to pay taxes. Most wealthy people convert little of their wealth into income. One common exception occurs when they sell some of their stock . Property taxes, like income taxes, are an exception to this rule. events.title: Quantum leap: IBM plans to scale beyond 1,000 qubits in 2027 with Nighthawk r3 processor
events.summary: IBM has unveiled the Nighthawk r3, an upcoming next-gen quantum processor that will feature 520 qubits, as another step towards a planned fault-tolerant quantum system it hopes to launch in 2029. Big Blue's current Nighthawk r2 was only made available in September and features 120 quantum bits (qubits) capable of handling circuits using 7,500 operations. Its successor, IBM claims, will have more than four times as many qubits and execute 10,000 quantum operations to tackle larger, more complex problems while maintaining the same speed and accuracy. Nighthawk r3 is slated to arrive in 2027, when Big Blue plans to link two of the quantum processors into a single system with more than 1,000 qubits. IBM said applications increasingly require circuits executing thousands of quantum operations on approximately 100 qubits or more, speeding up collection of the millions or billions of samples needed to perform complex computations. Speed determines whether such demanding workloads can be completed in practical timeframes and at a reasonable cost. The new quantum processor will feature 10 chip-to-chip interconnects, called l-couplers, designed for linking together processors that it will use to enable a single 1,040-qubit system. This tech was tested using Nighthawk r1 processors . IBM previously outlined its goal of reaching reliable error correcting territory in 2029 with a quantum processor codenamed Starling. Now it intends for this to be the world’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer , capable of running quantum circuits comprising 100 million quantum operations on 200 logical qubits. This is an ambitious goal, considering fault-tolerant quantum technology always seems to be at least a decade away, despite numerous breakthroughs and technology introductions. However, some in the technology industry believe the odds on a working system are shortening , given the increased activity around making encryption ready with support for quantum-resistant algorithms. Then again, a professor at the University of Auckland New Zealand famously claimed last year that quantum computers hadn't so far managed to factor any number greater than 21 without cheating. IBM presented a framework for Starling in a 2025 paper outlining hardware to implement the improbably named bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) error correction codes. These significantly reduce the number of physical qubits needed to store and process quantum information, compared to existing surface codes. Using the architecture in the paper, Big Blue intends to assemble Starling from modules that each contain a quantum memory and logical processing unit (LPU), allowing logic operations on the memory. The modules will have universal adapters letting them connect using l-couplers. IBM is also preparing the way ahead by combining its quantum processors with classical high-performance compute (HPC) systems to research better quantum error correction. Last week, Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) in the US announced such a system , combining an IBM Quantum System Two with Nighthawk r2 quantum processors and Umbra, powered by AMD 5th Gen Epyc CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators. IBM also has a partnership with Japan's RIKEN scientific research institute under which an IBM Quantum System Two has been integrated with the Fugaku Arm-based supercomputer, once the most powerful system in the world. ®

events.title: Washington risks misinterpreting Iran's 'peacemaker', according to analyst
events.summary: Washington is at risk of mistaking Mohsen Rezaei’s new prominence for a willingness to make concessions, Iran analyst Alex Vatanka argues. The former Revolutionary Guards commander, now secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, has received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance and is reportedly seen by American intelligence as the figure best placed to deliver a deal across Tehran’s factious institutions. But Rezaei’s comeback owes little to public legitimacy — he lost four presidential bids and his economic ideas were widely mocked — and much to a leadership vacuum left by the war and a network of IRGC loyalists built over decades, Vatanka writes for the Saudi-owned magazine Al Majalla. Rezaei has already shown the limits of his flexibility. He welcomed the letter’s tone, then insisted Washington accept Iran’s conditions first. Yesterday he went further, telling Al Mayadeen that not “ a single speck ” of enriched uranium would leave the country because Iran needs it to build nuclear-powered submarines — a rejection of the core US demand. His appointment was itself a product of hardline frustration: Rezaei was elevated by people close to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei who were unhappy with parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf’s handling of the talks, a Crisis Group analyst told Radio Free Europe . — Ed Clowes

events.title: First Abu Dhabi bank raises 15 billion dirhams for postwar boom
events.summary: First Abu Dhabi Bank, the UAE’s largest lender, will raise 15 billion dirhams ($4.1 billion) through a rights issue to fund its “next phase of growth.” The bank told analysts it sees higher organic growth opportunities rather than acquisitions ahead, positioning itself for a postwar investment boom in the country. Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund Mubadala, which owns a nearly 40% stake in FAB, is backing the deal. It’s the latest bank in the emirate to raise money through an equity sale after Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank raised 6 billion dirhams last year and Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank is raising 1.75 billion dirhams. Banks have been tapping equity more as they seek growth; loans increased faster than new deposits. They have also faced higher provisioning and higher impairments as banks build buffers due to the war. — Matthew Martin

events.title: UAE billionaires optimistic about foreign investment despite eight months of war
events.summary: UAE officials and billionaires had a unified message to foreign investors today: After eight months of conflict, the country has emerged as an even more attractive destination for global capital. They can be forgiven for talking up their own book, but foreign investors seem bullish too. At the Bloomberg Invest Dubai conference on Thursday, Blackstone executives said the firm had deployed more capital in the region over the past year than ever before, and opened a DIFC office for its growing private wealth business. Meanwhile, PIMCO highlighted opportunities to finance infrastructure projects. UAE Investment Minister Mohamed Hassan Alsuwaidi said the country plans to draw more foreign capital into energy, industry, infrastructure, AI, and logistics. He also pointed to shortages of offices and warehouses as opportunities. Real estate has gone through multiple boom-and-bust cycles over the past two decades, but when viewed over the long term, the trend line has clearly been up. Mohamed Alabbar, founder of Emaar Properties — which built the world’s tallest skyscraper — was characteristically upbeat. The developer recently unveiled a $3.3 billion business district at Dubai Creek Harbour, with 300,000 square meters of commercial space. And while the war has taken a toll on its hotel business, Emaar’s hospitality unit was able to boost profits last quarter by cutting costs. Alabbar acknowledged rising construction costs, but dismissed concerns that the property market was set for a sharp decline. Though the eight-month Iran conflict was a test, “I would say that if there was a bubble, it would have burst.” — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Fallout from Nvidia CEO’s likely ouster could slow Gulf AI buildout
events.summary: The fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s likely ouster will reach the Gulf, where ambitious AI buildouts depend on advanced US chips. Fear over China’s access to American technology through intermediaries has forced local AI champions like PIF-owned HUMAIN and Abu Dhabi-backed G42 to fight hard for chip access. Huang’s affair with a woman US intelligence officials allege is a Chinese spy will no doubt sharpen that scrutiny. Lawmakers are already pushing for new curbs on chip diversion, a move that could threaten the speed of development here. A friend-of-the-Gulf in Washington is also under pressure as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who greenlit the supply of tens of thousands of advanced GPUs to Saudi Arabia and the UAE, faces allegations that he stalled action against the Singapore firm tied up in the Huang scandal; Commerce denies the account. Still, the region’s relationship with the world’s largest chipmaker has long been one of customer and vendor: Great fortunes are tied to Nvidia, but the loss of the company’s leader shouldn’t undermine its ability to produce silicon. The question for the Gulf is, as it’s always been, about access. Dubai real estate tycoon Hussain Sajwani — who is building data centers around the world and expects his early investments in Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX will yield a “few billion dollars of profit” — said at the Bloomberg Invest conference in Dubai that “Nvidia is the most important company today in the world. It is by far. It has a genius CEO … I think if he’s forced to depart, it will be a big loss for the whole. This guy has done a great job.” — Kelsey Warner

events.title: Saudi oil production rebounds to near prewar levels
events.summary: Saudi oil production rebounded in October, driving up overall output by OPEC members to near prewar levels for the first time and helping keep down crude prices even as Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz have picked up. OPEC production rose by 1.97 million barrels a day, the majority of which was accounted for by higher Saudi output, according to the latest data from the cartel. Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said last week that the company aimed to “maximize production” in the fourth quarter, with the expectation that demand will be bolstered by efforts to replenish global oil inventories drained during the initial months of the Iran war. US military escorts, ship-to-ship transfers, and pipelines to ports away from the Strait of Hormuz have all helped restore output, although Saudi Arabia has stepped up shipments through its eastern ports as Houthi militias in Yemen threaten the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Iraq and UAE output also hit fresh highs for the year. Boosting oil flows is essential for Gulf states as they look to restore public finances bruised by the war and higher spending on new trade routes and defense. In contrast, Iranian production was almost half of prewar levels, according to OPEC. — Matthew Martin

events.title: Hackers exploiting ScreenConnect plugin flaw to spread malware across hundreds of PCs
events.summary: Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments. Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing. ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015. Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes. Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected. The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control. Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console. Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA. Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity. The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe. ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access. In a security advisory , the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family. It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit. ConnectWise stressed that the 400 environments were identified because they had the extensions installed, not because they were necessarily compromised. The company said: "At this time, we have found no evidence of a compromise of ConnectWise infrastructure or a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself." There's another nasty trick buried in SCKit. According to Huntress, the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it. If the technician connects through ScreenConnect, the toolkit attempts to transfer malware back to their workstation, steal authentication cookies, and use their access to infect other machines. That could give attackers a route from one compromised customer into others managed by the same IT provider. However, Huntress says it has yet to see that part of the attack succeed. "We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far," the researchers wrote. Huntress also suspects that some of the malware's C# code was generated using an LLM, pointing to unusually detailed comments explaining what the code is supposed to do. Apparently, even malware authors appreciate a little help with their homework. Both Huntress and ConnectWise are urging administrators not to investigate suspected infections by remotely connecting through ScreenConnect, since doing so could put the technician's own machine at risk. Administrators are being advised to use other security tools to investigate affected machines, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients, and check what commands have been run. Any malware left behind will also need to be removed before the machines are brought back online. Huntress warned on Reddit that some machines were becoming reinfected within minutes of being taken out of isolation because the malware had not been properly removed. Simply disabling the vulnerable extensions won't necessarily undo the damage, either. As ConnectWise warns, "Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints." And with the attackers already able to install their own remote access software, kicking them out could prove considerably harder than closing the door they came through. ®

events.title: Emaar’s mall footfall down 10 per cent due to Iran war, says Alabbar
events.summary: Footfall and retail sales at Emaar’s malls have fallen by about 10 per cent and hotel occupancy has dropped sharply as the Iran war weighs on tourism and consumer spending in Dubai, Emaar founder Mohamed Alabbar said on Thursday. “In our mall business, we are 10 per cent less in traffic. We were growing 10 per cent per year for the last five years,” Mr Alabbar told the Bloomberg Invest event in Dubai. He did not specify which malls were affected or over what period. He also said retail was down about 10 per cent after growing by a similar percentage annually in recent years. The hospitality business was affected too, with occupancy levels falling to about 65 per cent from 80 per cent, he added. The war, which started in late February with attacks by the US and Israel on Iran, has affected sectors in the UAE including property, tourism and aviation. The countries have yet to reach an agreement to end the war, now in its ninth month. However, US President Donald Trump has hinted that he is not planning to resume the bombing campaign as he faces calls to wind down the conflict after his party's defeat in last week's midterm elections. Mr Alabbar said the company was not slowing down its development activity, with construction continuing and projects being delivered ahead of time. “Development contractors are moving on time … material coming in … cost increasing about 5 per cent, which is OK,” he said. However, the company is “holding back” on tendering a big tower until the regional situation cools down. He did not provide further details on the new project. In June, Emaar Properties announced an “extraordinary” Dh200 billion ($55 billion) megaproject in Dubai , set to house nearly 150,000 people. The master plan, spread across more than 4.5 million square metres, is to feature residential towers, villas and mansions, Grade-A commercial offices, shops, luxury hospitality and other amenities. “It will all depend on what happens between Donald Trump and the Iranian leadership. That's really the key to everything, and [if] that happens in one month, I think the market will take 12 months, and then [it] will be in good shape,” Mr Alabbar said. He is also betting big on India, which he said “will be a major [market] for us” in the next five years as part of the company's global expansion plans. Emaar already has a presence in the country with projects in Gurugram, Mohali and other cities. The company will continue to grow in the Middle East, including the UAE, Egypt and Syria. Mr Alabbar’s developer Eagle Hills is working on two major projects in Syria, including a residential and tourism development, as part of a framework agreement the company signed with the Syrian government in October. Data centres and Anthropic investment Damac Properties founder and chairman Hussain Sajwani also spoke during the Bloomberg Invest event, outlining global expansion plans of the company. Damac is looking to expand in the UK and Australia with new data centre projects, after announcing $20 billion of investment in US data centres last year. The company is present in 14 countries and “we are in serious negotiations in the UK for a big parcel of land. We are in serious negotiation in Australia for a big parcel of land”, Mr Sajwani said. The company hopes to reach 10 gigawatts of capacity by the end of next year. “Our focus is on large data centres, which are 100MW and above. We go into where the large populations are, so the US, the EU and Asia.” The company also has investments in AI firm Anthropic and is making a lot of money from them, he said. “What I have made in 30 years [since starting his business], I made in Anthropic in less than two years. At [an] $18 billion valuation, it is going public at $1.4 trillion.” Last week, Anthropic reported revenue of nearly $17 billion in the period ending September 30, as investors brace for its potentially record-breaking IPO . The maker of Claude , a family of large language models and an AI chatbot, reported $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ending on September 30. “Between only three companies, OpenAI, SpaceX and Anthropic, we're making [a] few billion dollars a month.” Mr Sajwani also spoke about Nvidia and its chief executive Jensen Huang, who is embroiled in controversy over alleged extramarital affairs. “If he is forced to depart, it will be [a] big loss for the world, not for America, for the world. This guy has done a great job.”

events.title: Nvidia board prepares to oust CEO, name interim chief
events.summary: The Scoop Some members of Nvidia’s board favor appointing Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO at the beleaguered chipmaker if CEO and founder Jensen Huang is ousted, according to people familiar with the matter. The board met on Wednesday evening, though it has not yet announced its decision. Nvidia’s board has debated whether, as part of its potential replacement of Huang, to introduce a chief operating officer to serve alongside the interim chief executive, some of the people said. Semafor earlier confirmed that Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust Huang as soon as Wednesday, after media reports detailed that he had a second extramarital affair. The Nvidia board briefed the White House on its planned meeting, according to a senior administration official. Nvidia has tapped an outside search firm to find the company’s next CEO, Bloomberg reported. One person being considered for the top job is Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who was among the executives considered for Intel CEO in 2019, according to another person familiar with the matter. Whirlwind Saga Nvidia’s stock fell more than 8% in after-hours trading, hitting a 52-week low. Spokespeople for the company didn’t immediately provide a comment. Huang’s firing would cap a whirlwind saga that’s seen the global frontman for the AI boom admit to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The $4 trillion company’s long-tenured board announced a Wachtell Lipton-led probe into whether Huang may have divulged corporate secrets or endangered US national security. In addition to providing many of the most advanced chips for hyperscalers, Nvidia has entered into billions of dollars worth of financing deals underwriting the AI buildout. Democrats Move In Sens. Chris Coons, D-Del., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., sent a letter to members of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet on Wednesday asking them to preserve documents related to Nvidia’s chip exports to China or entities that could divert such chips to the country. They also asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller to preserve documents and communications concerning Huang and the suspected Chinese operative he had an affair with, as well as the correspondence between Huang and Trump. “This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote in the letter . “Reports suggest that officials within the government — including at the White House, State Department, and Commerce Department — were aware of concerns about NVIDIA, its relationship with Megaspeed, and the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips.”

events.title: The latest FreeBSD report is here, and the AI debate is ongoing
events.summary: The FreeBSD project's status team has published FreeBSD's third status report of 2026, showing plenty of ambitious work underway and a community still undecided on how to treat code from AI coding assistants. The FreeBSD Status Report Third Quarter 2026 is a substantial document, with 51 entries from five teams covering 16 projects, plus six other sections with more detailed reports. There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. Another covers the new AppJail effort – a containerized app distribution system for FreeBSD, including for GUI apps, which aims for something broadly comparable to Snap, Flatpak and AppImage on Linux. In other words, interesting and quite radical stuff is happening in the FreeBSD space. What this particular LLM-skeptical vulture was most interested to see, though, was an update on the internal discussion about how to handle code generated by AI coding assistants in the project. We first reported on this vexed subject back in September 2025 and no final answer has yet been published. NetBSD banned AI-generated code in 2024 and although the bot-boosters say this will doom it to irrelevance, as we reported last month, the project is thriving . Also back in October, we looked at OpenBSD 8.0 , whose launch materials are full of mockery for AI users. Under the FreeBSD Core Team section , there is a subsection headed "FreeBSD Developer AI survey." The survey was created by Baptiste Daroussin, and received 140 responses. Although the percentages show that there is some resistance to AI, there are hints here as to why it’s taking so long. Some project committers are against it, yet many more are proponents. Since there are only seven bullet points, we thought we would quote them in full: Policy: 88 percent want the Project to adopt a policy, either a formal, written policy (49 percent ) or light guidance and best practices (39 percent ). Six percent said that AI should be explicitly discouraged, and three percent that the existing contribution rules are sufficient. AI-assisted code: 35 percent said it must be disclosed, 25 percent that it must be reviewed more strictly than human code, 22 percent that it should be treated like any other contribution, and 16 percent that it should be rejected outright. Safeguards: mandatory human review (78 percent ) and mandatory disclosure (69 percent ) were requested most often, followed by provenance or licensing documentation (47 percent ) and mandatory testing (39 percent ). Disclosure: 84 percent want AI use disclosed, either always (48 percent ) or when its involvement is significant (36 percent ). 79 percent want AI-assisted commits marked in the commit log, and 56 percent prefer a tag that names the tool. Concerns: the main concerns about quality are correctness and subtle bugs (39 percent , licensing and provenance (26 percent ), and maintainability (21 percent ). 75 percent are somewhat or very concerned about copyright and licensing. Principles: accountability, meaning that a human remains responsible (91 percent ), and transparency (78 percent ) were selected most often, and preserving code quality was the top-ranked goal for a policy. Other uses: 65 percent would allow AI-generated documentation with human review. 54 percent would allow AI tools on Project infrastructure, most of them with restrictions, and 29 percent would not. Only six percent for explicit discouragement, 16 percent for outright rejection, and 35 percent against LLM-generated documentation. This plus the usual sort of calls for responsible use and disclosure, concerns about copyright issues, and so on. The Reg is strongly reminded of the Debian developer poll we reported on in August . This had no fewer than four slightly different AI-refusal options out of eight, and despite the Condorcet voting method it uses, the result was giving permission to use bots . With such relatively weak opposition, we suspect that FreeBSD will go the same way as Debian: tell developers to be careful, but allow bot usage, resulting in LLM-extruded code being committed into the project. ®

events.title: UAE has come out of the war 'exceptionally well', investment minister says
events.summary: The UAE has come out of the war “exceptionally well” and the continued economic momentum despite uncertainty is driving the government to open new sectors for foreign investment, a senior official has said. “I think we have to show investors the positive side of this, which is there is opportunity in every crisis, and [we are looking into] how do we present those opportunities to investors, how do we open up sectors that previously weren't open to investors, especially around infrastructure projects,” Mohamed Alsuwaidi, Minister of Investment, told Bloomberg Invest on Thursday. The UAE is investing heavily in infrastructure with new pipelines and ports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. It is also looking to expand port capacity on its eastern coast, including at Fujairah, projects that are expected to cost billions of dollars. The scale of the financing needs was underlined by First Abu Dhabi Bank's plan to raise as much as Dh15 billion ($4 billion) in the country’s largest rights issue, which will help support the country’s infrastructure expansion and diversification beyond oil. “I don't see a slowdown in what we're doing. We see more opportunities for investors, bigger projects coming to life,” Mr Alsuwaidi said. “AI is booming, logistics is booming, air freight is becoming a bigger business. Multiple sectors are opening up, and we need to help our investors see that and follow those trends.” The UAE continues to grow despite the impact of the Iran war. The country was attacked with hundreds of missiles and drones after the conflict broke out in late February, with damage to civilian infrastructure and energy sites. The UAE's real gross domestic product grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of the year, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the war's impact . Foreign direct investment into the UAE rose by about 6 per cent last year to a record $48.24 billion, the ninth highest total in the world, according to UN Conference on Trade and Development data. The Emirates was also the top recipient of FDI in the Middle East, ahead of Saudi Arabia, which ranked 13th, Unctad said in its World Investment Conference 2026 report released in July. There is no dearth of capital or talent in the country and the government is moving towards new capital models to fund the massive infrastructure needs, Mr Alsuwaidi said. “I don't see a challenge in the UAE on the funding front. I see opportunity to attract third-party capital in ways we haven't in the past,” he said. “More and more projects around energy, around industries, around infrastructure in general, are being open to the public through either public-private participation, but also through partnerships with governments or local governments, but also privatisation of certain government assets.” There's also a high demand in the housing market because people are interested in coming to the UAE, and “we can't keep up with the demand, so we keep building”. Some parts of the property market, particularly offices and warehouses, were facing shortages, he added.
