events.title: Fertiglobe boosts UAE exports to 95% of production but logistics costs hit profit
events.summary: Fertiglobe, the world’s largest seaborne exporter of urea and ammonia, said it has restored UAE exports to 95 per cent of production in the third quarter, despite continuing disruption at the Strait of Hormuz . That is up from 56 per cent in the second quarter, it said in a statement on Thursday to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, where its shares trade. Reaching that figure involved extensive efforts by Fertiglobe's production and supply-chain teams as well as working with majority shareholders XRG and Adnoc, and even the government, Ahmed El Hoshy, chief executive of Fertiglobe, told The National , without disclosing the specifics on how it was achieved. The company, however, said UAE exports were supported by active inventory, logistics management and a “focused commercial approach”. The effective closure of Hormuz, through which about one third of global seaborne fertiliser passed before the Iran war began on February 28, has significantly affected the supply chain. While Fertiglobe has been transporting the stocks it had stored during the peak of the war, “we still have inventory left over, so I'd even like to export more than we've produced”, Mr El Hoshy said. However, higher freight and logistical costs have affected earnings. Net profit attributable to the owners of the company for the third quarter dropped by 90 per cent to $22.7 million. Revenue for the period, however, rose by 19 per cent to $904.5 million, driven by higher ammonia prices and sales volumes. Along with the higher logistics costs, “sometimes the logistics to get product out also made it a little bit challenging to know the timing of exports”, Mr El Hoshy said. The company also carried out a turnaround at its EBIC plant in Egypt, and during that process had to use inventories to continue selling products. “When you use inventory to sell in Q3 instead of actual production, you end up getting charged with the fixed cost for the product … [and] you end up paying a larger amount,” he said. And while ammonia prices were higher, the lower cost of urea also brought down margins, he added. Urea, the most commonly used chemical for fertiliser, recorded a significant price increase to about $720 a tonne in mid-April from about $465 a tonne on the eve of the war, according to Trading Economics. Prices have now cooled to about $430 a tonne. Fertiglobe is the largest producer of nitrogen fertilisers in the region, with a production capacity about of 6.6 million tonnes of urea and ammonia through subsidiaries in the UAE, Egypt and Algeria. Last year, it also established Fertiglobe Australia to operate assets it acquired from Chinese-based company Wengfu. Gas price impact While Fertiglobe uses long-term contracts for gas that are not linked to European gas prices, the benchmark acts as a bellwether for the industry, Mr El Hoshy said. High European gas prices have caused about 35 per cent of European ammonia capacity to remain offline, he said. Dutch front-month futures, which tracks European gas prices, was at about €90 ($100) per megawatt-hour on Thursday, more than double annually. “There's 19 million tonnes of ammonia capacity that sits in Europe today,” Mr El Hoshy said. “Their cash cost today to produce ammonia is $1,000 a tonne, and the price that is in Europe today is $750 a tonne. So there's some mismatch. Either their cost needs to come down, or the price of ammonia needs to go up to justify them restarting their plant.” Given the current situation and how low the inventories are, “we continue to be relatively constructive on the outlook for the market for ammonia and urea because the Europeans are now operating at a rate where they're not able to make money unless the price of ammonia goes up”, he said. Robots cleaning up Fertiglobe, which has implemented its initial $55 million cost optimisation target, has launched FIT3, a new programme aimed at achieving a further $30 million of annual non-gas cost savings by the end of 2028. “Together with maintenance capex normalising from 2027, this will strengthen our competitiveness and cash generation through the cycle,” the company said. The turnaround programme in Egypt and the UAE is expected to deliver strong results, Mr El Hoshy said. At the EBIC plant, production has increased by more than 20 per cent on a run rate basis. Outside of regular maintenance, the programme in Egypt used artificial intelligence to go through data from every single interruption the plant has had since it started in 2009 and it came up with a list of things needed to be done. “We discovered things and took care of it. We also used robotics for the first time to clean areas in the plant that humans couldn't get to, never been touched in 17 years, and that has allowed us to remove dust and debris,” Mr El Hoshy said. “Since we started up in September for our plant in Egypt, we have achieved rates not achieved ever in these plants, so record daily production.” Outlook The company is preparing for different scenarios and aiming to see how it can reduce costs when faced with issues such as higher temporary logistics costs. “What we've done internally is looked at … how we procure things, how we do things logistically, how we load product, where it's basically across all functional groups, [we are looking for] ways that we can reduce costs using simplified processes,” he said. Looking ahead, if the war continues, “I still think that we're in a very tough position having the Strait of Hormuz compromised for exports of sulphur, which is a which is a very important input for fertiliser, urea, ammonia and natural gas”, Mr El Hoshy added. The products must get to global markets because it's in a “very vulnerable position”. Any impact will be felt mainly in low to medium-income countries in terms of not being able to secure the adequate fertilisers they need to increase the crop yields to feed their populations, he said.

events.title: Bracing for Nvidia's impact
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's apparent fall from grace is a shock to a company at the core of the U.S. markets and the AI ecosystem that he did much to create. Why it matters: CEO scandals happen at companies. Their stocks fall. But there is no other company quite like Nvidia. Its size, financial resources and strategic position in the AI boom have made both the chipmaker and Huang, personally, pillars of the industry that has come to drive both the stock market and the economy. Catch up quick: Following revelations this week that Huang had admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman believed by the U.S. government to be a Chinese intelligence asset, the New York Times reported Wednesday evening that Huang also had a romantic relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal and other outlets are reporting that the company's board of directors was preparing to oust Huang. Nvidia shares plunged in the after-hours trading session. Context: The uncertainty surrounding Huang's position comes as the AI trade is going through one of the crises of investor confidence that have periodically hammered AI shares in recent years. The concern this time centers on the ability of the AI build-out to continue, as rising interest rates and a saturated market curtail the sale of bonds to pay for data centers. Chip makers like Nvidia have been particularly hard hit by this recent AI slump. Its shares were down roughly 30% from their recent high through Wednesday's close, vaporizing nearly $1.59 trillion in shareholder wealth. There have been market drawdowns around AI before, says Eric Sheridan, a research analyst at Goldman Sachs, in a big new report on the investment cycle. "The stakes are undoubtedly higher now as we're further along in the cycle and the dollars being spent have grown considerably, which may be adding to investor skittishness." Stunning stat: Since the end of last week, the company lost over $600 billion in market value through Wednesday's after market session. Zoom out: Those losses will touch a lot of portfolios. With a market capitalization of roughly $4.18 trillion — through Wednesday's close — Nvidia is the world's second-largest publicly traded company, behind Apple, giving it significant sway in market capitalization-weighted indexes, such as the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100. Yes, but: If anything, a focus on Nvidia's massive size obscures how important the company is. It dominates the market for the graphics processing units, or GPUs, that are the costliest input into AI data centers — about 75% of a data center's total cost, per Goldman. It also finances and backstops significant chunks of AI computing power. That means Nvidia is bankrolling a small army of AI firms: AI coding companies, data center operators, neoclouds. For example: Nvidia has put more than $2 billion into CoreWeave, the troubled neocloud that's seen its borrowing costs soar in recent weeks. It has equity stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI. Follow the money: Such was Nvidia's — and Huang's — stature in the tech world that in recent years, the mere mention of a company by the Nvidia CEO could create big market winners and losers . In June, for example, positive comments from Huang about Marvell Technology sent the company's stock soaring nearly 33% in a single day. State of play: Now, it's Nvidia shares that might need words of encouragement. On Wednesday the stock received a downgrade to "market perform" from "outperform" from Bernstein Research. "We admit to struggling mightily with this call, and can sympathize with the case to buy the dip," Bernstein's analysts wrote. "But our gut tells us that we probably haven't yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here; we've had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines." Morgan Stanley also removed the company from its list of "top picks" earlier in the day, after the stock had declined more than 25% since it was named top pick last month. What's next: Whatever comes next for Nvidia, the company is likely to be in an extended period of strategic paralysis. "Decisions about acquisitions or investments or product roadmaps, those are the kinds of things that will now have to be paused, if — again — if this happens, all these things are going to have to pause," Gil Luria, an analyst covering Nvidia for the brokerage firm D.A. Davidson, tells Axios. "So it just slows the company down when it can't make the most important, biggest decisions." The big picture: Huang has presided over one of the most remarkable explosions of wealth creation in market history. From the closing price on its first day of trading, Nvidia's total compound return with dividend reinvestment is 462,906%, according to FactSet. He has been at the helm of the company since he co-founded it in 1993. The bottom line: But depending on how the situation plays out, shareholders may be about to find out what an Nvidia without its charismatic leader looks like.

events.title: UK appoints climate security envoy as Thunberg criticizes COP31 leaders
events.summary: The United Kingdom has appointed a special envoy to address climate change security threats ANTALYA, Turkey -- The United Kingdom on Thursday announced the appointment of a special envoy to tackle security threats from climate change while small island leaders called for urgent action, describing planet heating as a life-or-death issue for their people at the climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya. Alix Sebastien Pillay, the vice president of Seychelles, a 115-island archipelago in the Indian Ocean, said his country's very survival is at stake. “It is time to move past the talking,” Pillay said. “For Seychelles, climate action is not simply an environmental priority.” Pillay was speaking on the second day of the leaders' summit at the U.N. climate talks, where government leaders addressed the state of a warming world and what they plan to do about it. While the entire globe is threatened by souped-up storms, hotter heat waves, worsening droughts and floods, island nations are among the hardest hit by climate change as they also have to deal with rising seas swallowing up their land. Pillay said Seychelles is experiencing millions of dollars of damage as a result of storms and floods, despite contributing little to increased global warming. He said a U.N. fund created for compensating for climate-related loss and damage needs to be urgently strengthened. “Climate recovery must not come at the expense of our development or push vulnerable nations further into unsustainable debt.” Speaking at the talks, Dalton Tagelagi, prime minister of the small Pacific Island of Niue, said the El Niño conditions which have driven up global temperatures are a warning of what might happen if planet heating is not controlled. “Sea temperatures in the central Pacific are more than three degrees above normal. It is a warning of what is coming if we do not cut emissions now," Tagelagi said. The comment came as a report said the world has failed to slow global warming trends in the past five years because plans weren’t realized and efforts that would have helped were canceled out. “Aggregated climate action has now essentially stalled for five consecutive years with positive and negative actions canceling each other out,” the independent Climate Action Tracker said in its report. The first five years after the 2015 Paris Agreement, the world did so much that it trimmed an entire degree Celsius (1.8 degrees Fahrenheit) from warming projections, but nothing has changed since, the report said. Climate change is caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases, which happens when fuels like gas, oil and coal are burned. Confronting climate change means finding ways to drastically cut the amount of emissions put into the atmosphere each year. Countries establish plans to reduce emissions, called nationally determined contributions. The speed of reductions and ways to achieve them are different by country. Because collective efforts of countries haven't significantly reduced global emissions, the world is now “headed toward an irrecoverable overshoot of 1.5 degrees Celsius” (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures, which is the warming threshold the world adopted during the Paris Agreement, according to the report. The report said if the nations of the world fulfill all their climate promises — which is a big if — the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than preindustrial times. On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the appointment of a special representative to deal with security risks from the climate crisis, one of the first such appointments anywhere in the world. “Climate is a national security issue,” Burnham said at the summit. “The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is upon us all now devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere." He said Britain would place climate resilience high on the agenda when it assumes the G20 presidency next year. Climate activists said, however, that Burnham’s policies do not fully align with the sense of urgency he expressed in his speech. “Burnham needs to start bridging the widening chasm between words and deeds on climate action,” said Ami McCarthy of Greenpeace UK in a statement. “The future we feared has become the present we are living. events.title: Microsoft admits SQL Servers might wobble after October update
events.summary: Encountered some odd SQL Server connection behavior since the October update? There might be a culprit… Microsoft has admitted that a change has caused linked server queries to fail to close connections. Linked servers via OLE DB providers have been around for years and are a useful way of, for example, using additional data sources in queries. Once a provider is added, SQL Server can open a connection to grab data, and close it again when the query is complete. Or, at least, that's the theory. The problem is that after the October 13 (KB5126646) update, connections created by SQL Server linked server queries might remain open. According to Microsoft, "As additional queries are performed, connections to external databases can accumulate instead of closing as expected. "This can slow or degrade server performance after prolonged run time." You think? Administrators will likely have already noted a suspicious number of open connections to external databases on affected systems. Microsoft said the issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. It gave PostgreSQL and Oracle as examples of connections known to be affected. And the fix? "If idle connections can be identified, it is possible to manually close them to temporarily relieve server load. "It is also possible to temporarily restore system stability by restarting the SQL service." The Windows behemoth went on to state the obvious: "However, these steps can also interrupt active queries or transactions, and the problem can resurface again after sufficient operation time." Bouncing a SQL Server to deal with connection leakage is less than ideal, although it would at least be a good failover test and, let's face it, having to restart Microsoft services regularly is something many administrators will be all too familiar with. There is a mitigation available, although only through Microsoft support for business. Otherwise, an out-of-band update should be along within the next few days to deal with the problem. According to Microsoft, the technical glitch affects every version of Windows except Windows 11 26H2, stretching back to Windows 10 1809 and LTSC 2019, and Windows Server from 2025 back to 2012. Microsoft, or rather the unfortunate souls responsible for administering their server products, has not had the best time of late. The October 2026 Windows Server update left some Exchange Servers wobbling until either a Registry edit was made or a fix was applied as part of the November update. ®

events.title: Gulf business leaders rally behind Nvidia's Jensen Huang as board weighs his future
events.summary: BREAKING: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia chief executive Gulf business figures have rallied behind Jensen Huang as Nvidia's board weighs whether to remove its co-founder and chief executive over two alleged affairs. "If he is forced to depart, it will be big loss for the world, not for America, for the world. This guy has done a great job," Hussain Sajwani, founder and chairman of Damac Properties, said at Bloomberg Invest in Dubai on Thursday. Saudi investor Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed, founder of KBW Ventures, was more blunt. "If Nvidia board fires Jensen Huang, that would be the dumbest thing they've ever done," he wrote on X. If Nvidia board fires Jensen Huang, that would be the dumbest thing they've ever done. — خالد بن الوليد Khaled Alwaleed (@KhaledAlwaleed) November 12, 2026 Their comments come as the world's most valuable chip maker faces a leadership crisis. Mr Huang admitted on Sunday that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman whom US investigators accuse of spying for China. Nvidia's board launched an investigation into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Mr Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, a senior Nvidia executive who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal reported that the board was preparing to oust him. Nvidia shares fell about 7 per cent in pre-market trading on Thursday, as the turmoil weighed on technology stocks. Mr Huang has close ties to the Gulf, where Nvidia's chips underpin ambitious artificial intelligence plans. He has championed "sovereign AI", the idea that countries should build their own AI infrastructure, a pitch that has resonated with governments in the UAE and Saudi Arabia. In July, Washington eased export rules to allow UAE companies, including G42 and Core42, to receive Nvidia's advanced chips without a licence. The scandal has also drawn scrutiny in Washington, where House Republicans are pushing for Mr Huang to testify and lawmakers from both parties are calling for tighter controls on chip exports to China. Nvidia has not commented on the board's deliberations.

events.title: European tech buyers add digital sovereignty to cyber shopping list
events.summary: European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology. Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked. According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent. That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent. The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more. Context stopped short of assigning blame. It said organizations are reviewing their reliance on third-party tech in light of EU compliance regimes: the NIS2 Directive and Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA). NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024 , requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to critical infrastructure. DORA, introduced in January last year, is designed to strengthen cyber security in the financial sector. "Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision. As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored," said Context veep of research Joe Turner. "We're seeing a measurable shift in the EMEA channel. EU vendors gained nearly three points of sales share in two years. An organization can keep its existing identity platform and still choose a European supplier to manage its security logs. That's the kind of decision that gives European vendors an opening." The stats indicate that EU-HQd vendors comprised 92 percent of tracked sales in security awareness training, 82 percent in vulnerability management, and 52 percent for SIEM and log management. US-headquartered companies held into 74 percent of identity and access management sales and 54 percent of cloud security sales. The Reg has asked Context for UK-specific figures to see whether British customers are also voting with their wallets for European alternatives. That certainly isn’t the case for tech purchases in the British public sector, despite Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s professed desire to buy British. Data released yesterday by the Institute for Public Policy Research showed just £1 in every £6 spent by government with the biggest technology suppliers goes to Brit businesses. Still, Burnham only came to power in July so there is time yet for him to put his money where his mouth is. Sovereign AI is another area of concern for enterprise customers. Analyst Omdia said last month that despite the marketing adjective meaning "local assets," almost a third AI providers disclose no proof of sovereignty, and some "expect enterprise to pay for audits to verify their claims." Omdia also found that 80 percent of contracts say network resilience is "out of providers control or responsibility," and "US-headquartered AI providers offer better service transparency and contract terms than a majority of local sovereign AI providers, with providers in India a notable exception." Sovereign services in Omdia's classification include data residency, operational autonomy, jurisdictional sovereignty, and technological autonomy. "Local hosting is not sovereignty. Serious providers must demonstrate their credibility through transparent operations, fair contracts and proof of competence. That includes the network, because data in transit must be sovereign too," said Camille Mendler, research director for telco B2B at Omdia. Someone should tell Microsoft and Anthropic . ®

events.title: Rockstar workers vote on union recognition as GTA VI launch looms
events.summary: More than 1,600 Rockstar Games employees in the UK will begin voting on union recognition on Thursday, with the ballot kicking off just a week before the long-awaited launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. The ballot, which opens on November 12 and runs until November 26, will determine whether Rockstar formally recognizes the Rockstar Game Workers Union, part of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB). Nearly all UK employees below director level are eligible to vote. If successful, the union would become the largest recognized union in the UK games industry, giving workers a collective voice. The proposed recognition agreement follows four months of negotiations between Rockstar management and employees. It would allow workers to negotiate over pay, overtime, pensions, bonuses, leave and other employment conditions, while securing consultation rights over HR policies and AI. The vote comes at a particularly busy time for Rockstar, with GTA VI finally due to arrive on November 19, more than 13 years after its predecessor. The game is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches in history, although the people responsible for making it have rather more immediate concerns than sales records. "I am incredibly proud of the work we've put into making this game. I'm also proud of the union we've built here. For me, those two things are connected," said Nestor Uriate, an animation programmer and Rockstar Game Workers Union representative. "We care deeply about the games we make, and we want to make sure we can continue doing that work in an environment where we're respected, have a meaningful say over our conditions and can feel secure about our futures." The vote follows a year of bad blood between Rockstar and the IWGB. The union accused the GTA developer of union busting after it fired 31 members in October 2025, claiming they had been singled out for taking part in a private Discord group. Rockstar denied the allegations, insisting the workers were dismissed for gross misconduct rather than their union activities. The dispute subsequently reached an employment tribunal, where Rockstar unsuccessfully attempted to have blacklisting allegations struck from the case . Closing submissions are expected on November 17 and 18, meaning the legal proceedings will reach their final stages just as GTA VI prepares to hit shelves. Despite the ongoing dispute, Rockstar's head of publishing, Jennifer Kolbe, recently indicated that management would respect the outcome of the recognition vote, telling Bloomberg : "We go where the team goes. So if they want a union, they will have a union." The union campaign has also attracted support from elsewhere in the games industry, including SAG-AFTRA and the Communications Workers of America (CWA), which represents workers at Blizzard. Alex Marshall, president of the IWGB, said the vote was an opportunity for Rockstar employees to take greater control over their working conditions. "What happens at Rockstar matters beyond the studio. Workers across the games industry are watching, and this ballot is an opportunity to show what can be achieved when people come together, organize and build the collective power to shape their own working lives." For Rockstar, November was already shaping up to be a big month. By the time GTA VI has been in players' hands for a week, the company should also know whether its UK workforce has voted to secure a formal seat at the negotiating table. ®

events.title: Arada and Alya target $1.63bn property pipeline across UAE and Saudi Arabia
events.summary: UAE developer Arada has teamed up with Alya Developments to explore co-investment opportunities in premium property in the Emirates and Saudi Arabia, following the former's entry into the kingdom. Arada's newly established investment management platform, Arada Capital, and Alya signed a preliminary agreement to explore premium developments in the Emirates and Saudi Arabia under a potential Dh6 billion ($1.63 billion) pipeline, they said in a joint statement on Thursday. The companies will initially pursue two projects in the UAE, with Abu Dhabi's Yas Island and Downtown Dubai earmarked as potential areas, they said in a joint statement on Thursday. It did not provide plans for Saudi Arabia. Arada Capital, the investment management platform of Arada Group, was announced in July and is aiming for $5 billion in assets under management within four years. Arada Group is jointly owned by Saudi businessman Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed’s KBW Investments and Sharjah-based Basma Group. Alya is backed by Canada's Brookfield , which manages about $1 trillion in assets, and Abu Dhabi-based Lunate , a global investment firm with more than $125 billion in assets. The move follows last month's launch of Arada's Dh14 billion residential project in Riyadh, as the developer expands into the kingdom. Arada's group chief executive has separately outlined plans to build 100,000 homes across Saudi Arabia over the next three to five years. Arada also has operations in Australia, Syria and the UK. “This partnership represents an important milestone in Arada Capital's ambition as a fund manager … we see significant potential to bring forward premium residential projects distinguished by their quality, thoughtful design and disciplined delivery,” said Moustafa Fahour, chief executive and managing director of Arada Capital. “Our shared ambition is to create homes of enduring quality and value, for the people who live in them and those who invest in them,” added Otto Dreyer, chief executive of Alya. Property developers are continuing to launch projects in the UAE despite concerns about the slowing of the market as the Iran war continues. This week, Dubai’s Nakheel unveiled the new Palm Springs master development next to Palm Jebel Ali, while Abu Dhabi’s Aldar Properties last month said it plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE. In September, Arada and Aldar teamed up to build new housing projects on Yas Island and at Seih Sdeirah in Abu Dhabi, representing a combined value of about Dh15 billion. Arada also unveiled plans for a $7 billion “UAE-style” development in Damascus. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, has boosted its real estate sector as it continues its economic diversification strategy. In January, the kingdom began implementing an updated property ownership law for non-Saudis, allowing foreign individuals and companies to acquire real estate subject to regulatory and geographical restrictions. The authorities expect the changes to attract international developers, stimulate investment and support economic diversification. “The UAE and Saudi Arabia continue to present compelling long-term opportunities and our focus is on bringing together the right partners, capital and expertise to deliver sustainable value for investors and communities alike,” Mr Fahour said. Second Australia approval secured Separately on Thursday, Arada said it has received approval for its Dh1.6 billion Wattle Green residential community in Castle Hill, New South Wales, Australia. The 14,000-square-metre project is planned to feature 445 residences across three buildings. The approval is Arada's second major planning consent in Australia within a little over a month, after securing a similar decision for the 33-storey London Place residential project in Campsie, south-west of Sydney, early last month. “We are pushing ahead with our pipeline of projects at a time when we know delivery in this market demands real conviction,” Arada group chief executive Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said.

events.title: From Emmett Till to Robert Johnson, the Delta powered Scott Colom's historic Senate bid
events.summary: Scott Colom 's path to a historic U.S. Senate upset ran through the Mississippi Delta — where Emmett Till was abducted, Fannie Lou Hamer fought for the ballot and the blues became an American art form. Why it matters: Nearly 150 years after Reconstruction, Mississippi sent a Black American to the U.S. Senate for the first time since 1881. The votes pushing Colom toward that milestone came from communities where Black residents spent generations fighting for the ballot. Driving the news: The Associated Press projected the race for Colom on Wednesday, handing Democrats a historic upset over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. By the numbers: An Axios analysis of AP county returns found Colom ahead in 16 of the 18 counties in the Mississippi Delta National Heritage Area . Colom collected roughly 100,000 votes to Hyde-Smith's 62,000 — a 38,000-vote advantage. In 2020, Democrat Mike Espy carried 15 of those counties by about 25,000 votes, according to Mississippi's certified county returns . Colom's share of the two-party vote climbed from about 56% to 62%. Statewide, Colom led Hyde-Smith by about 4,700 votes out of more than 962,000 counted when the AP called the race Wednesday — a margin of roughly half a percentage point. What they're saying: "Mississippi voters made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out," NAACP president Derrick Johnson said in a statement. Johnson said Mississippi voters showed up despite efforts to remove voters from the rolls . Zoom in: Colom's electoral map traces some of the most painful and defining chapters of Black American history. Coahoma County: Home to Clarksdale and the famed crossroads associated with the legend that bluesman Robert Johnson sold his soul to the devil. Colom led with about 4,700 votes to 1,300. Leflore and Tallahatchie counties: Emmett Till was abducted near Money in Leflore County in 1955. His body was recovered from the Tallahatchie River in Tallahatchie County, where an all-white jury acquitted his killers. Colom led by about 4,200 votes in Leflore and 1,300 in Tallahatchie, according to AP returns . Sunflower County: Fannie Lou Hamer, who lived in Ruleville, challenged Mississippi's racist voting restrictions. As late as the spring of 1965, only 155 Black residents had registered to vote in the county, according to the Mississippi Department of Archives and History . Colom led with about 5,300 votes to 1,700. Washington County: Robert F. Kennedy visited Greenville during his 1967 tour of Delta poverty . 29.4% of Washington County is still in poverty per the Census Bureau's 2020–2024 estimate . Colom led with about 8,700 votes to 2,400. Zoom out: Colom didn't suddenly turn the Delta blue. Espy won most of it in 2020. But Colom widened the Democratic margin. In DeSoto County, which falls within the heritage area but outside the Delta's historic heartland, Colom led by about 3,300 votes. Hyde-Smith won there by roughly 12,100 in 2020. Colom also swept the Golden Triangle counties of Lowndes, Oktibbeha and Clay, his home region in northeastern Mississippi. He won all three by double-digit margins and improved on Espy's 2020 performance. Between the lines: The historical symbolism stretches beyond the Delta. Colom led with about 12,100 votes to 9,700 in Forrest County, named for Confederate Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest, the Ku Klux Klan's first grand wizard. Hyde-Smith faced criticism during her 2018 race against Espy after saying she would sit in the front row if invited to a public hanging . She later apologized to those offended. The bottom line: The region where Black Mississippians fought some of America's fiercest battles for voting rights helped elect the state's first Black U.S. senator in 145 years — and raised a new question. Can political representation finally bring economic change to the Delta?

events.summary: Saudi Arabia's annual international investment and economic conference, the Future Investment Initiative, has been postponed to 2027 after it was stopped this year because of attacks on the kingdom by the Houthi rebels in Yemen The 10th iteration of the flagship investment conference will take place from October 25 to 28 next year in Riyadh, the Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute confirmed. The annual gathering has attracted senior policymakers, global investors and business leaders, with previous events focusing on investment opportunities and economic growth . At last year's summit, the kingdom called for greater private sector investment in its major development projects, while its sovereign wealth fund has since outlined plans to increase its domestic investment allocation . The postponement also affected a major gathering for the kingdom's technology sector, which continues to pursue large-scale artificial intelligence investments . Ahead of FII10, the institute will host its FII Priority Miami summit from March 31 to April 2, 2027, followed by an Asia summit, with dates and location yet to be announced.

events.title: Democrats debate taking a page from Trump's economic playbook
events.summary: President Trump is turning the federal government into an investor in dozens of private companies, and some Democrats are considering following his lead as their party emerges emboldened from the midterm elections. Why it matters: Democrats are gaining new power to scrutinize Trump's corporate investments, even as his approach gains traction within their own party. They're looking at investments and aid for clean energy and other priorities, like support for energy infrastructure. State of play: The Trump administration's investments in energy, critical minerals and other industries are already drawing calls for congressional investigations . "The Trump administration has widened the aperture for industrial policy," Jennifer Granholm, who served as President Biden's Energy Secretary, said at a gathering of energy and climate experts Axios attended in Berkeley, Calif., last month. "You're not going to have state ownership of enterprises," Granholm told Axios in an interview afterward. "But maybe you do take a little bit of an ownership slice" for national security or global competitiveness reasons, she said. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) has also expressed openness to federal ownership stakes, while raising concerns about the Trump administration's lack of transparency and accountability, he told Semafor . Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) has argued that the U.S. needs to consider a more aggressive industrial policy to compete with countries like China, while warning against direct government ownership. "We are long overdue for having a conversation about, 'should the United States even have an industrial policy?'" Casten said at a recent University of Chicago event . "For a long time, we viewed industrial policy as something that socialists do." Casten said he would support the U.S. ensuring domestic manufacturing of certain parts of supply chains, like electronic control systems that operate energy infrastructure, and even pursuing "smart tariff policy" to have competitive markets. The big picture: The Biden administration spent billions subsidizing clean energy and semiconductor manufacturing. Trump has taken government intervention a step further by acquiring ownership stakes in companies ranging from Intel to critical mineral producers. It's been a striking reversal for a president who has repeatedly criticized Democrats for government overreach. How it works: The Trump administration has announced more than $30 billion in investments across nearly 50 deals involving government ownership and related financial arrangements, according to a Council on Foreign Relations tracker . The investments span semiconductors, critical minerals and energy — strategically important industries where high costs and long development timelines can make private financing difficult. Flashback: Washington has taken ownership stakes in private companies before, including during the 2008 financial crisis. But those investments were intended as temporary measures to rescue struggling businesses, unlike Trump's national security-focused investments. What they're saying: "Equity from the U.S. government can act as patient capital that helps derisk an investment with a long time horizon or technological risk that would otherwise not attract sufficient private investment," said Jonathan Hillman, a Council on Foreign Relations fellow behind the tracker. Hillman said the deals announced since January 2025 have also mobilized $28.5 billion in private capital. Yes, but: Some politicians and energy leaders warn that direct government ownership could open the door to political favoritism and market distortions. "Government is not a venture capital fund. It's not a private equity fund. It's not well suited to pick winners and losers in the marketplace," said Tim Pawlenty, former Republican governor of Minnesota who now leads the Solar Energy Industries Association, at the same University of Chicago event. "If it starts to go down the slippery slope of 'it's just the flavor of the day company because we like it' or they're well connected or whatever, then you got problems." Threat level: "Buying stakes in public companies is so, so, so dangerous," Casten said. "I have no idea how a future president unwinds our stake in Intel without totally tanking Intel stock," he added, referring to the administration's roughly 10% stake in the semiconductor giant. To avoid such concerns, Hillman suggests creating a federal chief investment officer to oversee investments and eventual sales. The other side: The White House defended the investments as a way to rebuild American manufacturing and secure critical supply chains, emphasizing that companies participate voluntarily, spokesman Matthew Middleton said. What we're watching: Democrats could spend the next two years scrutinizing Trump's investments — while debating whether a future Democratic administration should make similar deals of its own. events.title: Democrats unite against Big Health Care
events.summary: Newly elected Democrats from ruby red states are leading a charge to take on corporate health care and some business practices that they say drive up health care costs. Why it matters: Democrats may not be anywhere close to agreement on Medicare for All, but they're relatively united around confronting Big Health Care after campaigning hard on the populist theme. Driving the news: While expanding Medicare, reversing GOP Medicaid cuts and reviving enhanced Obamacare subsidies are getting most of the attention, there's a subtle shift in rhetoric and policy positions toward blaming big health companies for the affordability crisis. It reflects the reality that a substantial expansion of the federal government's role in health care isn't in the cards while President Trump is in office, but populist themes could unite the rank-and-file and even draw in some Republicans. Even candidates who didn't constantly rail about drugmakers or insurers have adopted policy ideas that, until recently, were confined to left-leaning think tanks. Case in point: Incoming Texas Sen. James Talarico ran on breaking up big health care companies and "stop[ping] hospitals and insurance companies from overcharging patients." (He also supports allowing Americans under 65 to join Medicare.) South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews ran on limiting insurer profits per enrollee, expanding the number of drugs subject to Medicare drug price negotiations and banning private equity-owned hospitals. Incoming Kansas Sen. Adam Hamilton supports expanding Medicare drug price negotiations and extending the negotiated prices to private health plans, as well as addressing Medicare Advantage overpayments from the federal government. Other targets include medical debt, pharmacy benefit manager practices and caps on out-of-pocket drug costs. Many of these ideas already have buy-in from more-senior progressives. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) has sponsored the Break Up Big Medicine Act, which is co-sponsored by Republican Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, which would prohibit common ownership of health plans and providers. Incoming Michigan Sen. Abdul El-Sayed, an avid Medicare for All supporter, ran on support of the Warren-Hawley bill, as well as expanding Medicare drug price negotiations. The House's health care working group , made up of both progressives and moderates, pitched capping "excessive" hospital prices and enacting site-neutral payments. The big picture: Voters have made clear that they want lower health care costs. So while a broad overhaul of the health system may not immediately be on the table, Democrats are looking for ways to deliver. Powerful health industry groups are poised to push back, arguing that the populist policies would threaten patient care and access in some communities. But the ideas under discussion could gain favor with some Republicans. What they're saying: When asked at an Axios event on Tuesday whether Congress should address ownership ties between insurers, PBMs and pharmacies, Rep. Morgan Griffith — the top Republican on the House Energy and Commerce's Health Subcommittee — said, "I've only heard the case for breaking them up." "There's just something in your gut that bothers you when your pharmacy, your PBM and your insurance company are all owned by the same people," he added. What we're watching: Forcing drugmakers to lower prescription drug prices could be a particularly compelling target, given Trump's demonstrated interest in the topic. He has previously called on Congress to codify the "most-favored-nation" deals he made with pharmaceutical manufacturers that require the companies, in some cases, to offer Americans prices on a par with what's paid abroad. The Senate Finance Committee's top Democrat, Ron Wyden of Oregon, told reporters this week that he's open to a deal codifying those agreements in exchange for an expansion of the number of drugs Medicare can negotiate on, according to InsideHealthPolicy . The bottom line: It was only four years ago that Democrats struggled to find enough votes for the modest drug price negotiations that exist today, marking the first successful legislative attempt to directly lower health care costs in any sector by either party. Now, they're more willing to push for change and confront big industry players.

events.title: Scoop: AOC shakes up team again as 2028 decision looms
events.summary: New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is shaking up her team for the second time in the past few months as she prepares to make the biggest decision of her political life. Why it matters: The overhaul comes as the democratic socialist leader is debating whether to run for president in 2028 — or Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's seat, which is up the same year. Zoom in: Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with her longtime digital fundraising firm, Middle Seat, according to three people familiar with the decision. At the same time, sources said, she's brought on Aisle 518 Strategies — the company led by Democratic strategist Tim Tagaris, who oversaw Bernie Sanders' record-breaking online fundraising strategy in his two presidential campaigns. Middle Seat has been key to Ocasio-Cortez's operation. Over the past two years, she has paid the firm more than $6 million — about a quarter of her operation's disbursements during that period. AOC is close with Sanders, and if she decides to run for president, progressives say, she would be able to quickly staff up with his former advisers. But Ocasio-Cortez's latest move doesn't necessarily signal that she's leaning toward a presidential run or a Senate bid. Tagaris' firm has helped power the small-dollar fundraising operation for California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who's widely expected to run for the White House. It also has worked with other Democrats who are potential contenders for president — Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Vice President Kamala Harris, according to the company's website . Middle Seat, the firm AOC is leaving, has Sanders roots as well: It was founded by alumni of the Vermont senator's 2016 campaign. Flashback: Ocasio-Cortez's reorganizing follows several changes she made to her staff this year, as Axios previously reported . They included parting ways with her longtime campaign manager and creative director, as well as bringing aboard a few former aides. The Washington Sun reported this week that AOC had hired Freeland Ellis, a Sanders alum, as a communications aide. What they're saying: A spokesperson for Ocasio-Cortez declined to comment. Tagaris declined to comment, and Middle Seat partner Kenneth Pennington did not respond to a request for comment.

events.title: How the midterms swing each party's economic feelings
events.summary: Note: Figures compare average daily sentiment readings over the seven days before each election with the five days after. Election Day is excluded; Data: Morning Consult; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios There was an unusually sharp partisan mood shift in the wake of the midterms, according to sentiment data from Morning Consult that was shared exclusively with Axios. Why it matters: While big partisan swings in consumer sentiment are typical after a presidential election, they have been much smaller in midterm races. The latest numbers show just how tightly Americans' views on the economy are now intertwined with politics. By the numbers: Democratic consumer sentiment rose 6.5 points in the five days after the election compared with the week before, while Republicans' mood fell 6.4 points. How it works: Morning Consult's index considers survey responses from approximately 5,000 U.S. adults. They're asked five questions, including on people's personal finances and financial outlook, as well as their views on overall business conditions. Zoom in: The biggest shifts in sentiment were in respondents' feelings about the future. Republicans' outlook across all five metrics fell after the election. Their confidence in business conditions over the next five years plummeted 12 percentage points. Democrats, meanwhile, had a jump of 9 percentage points in confidence about business conditions (although they remain negative about it) and an even bigger increase — 12 percentage points — in optimism that their own finances would improve over the next year. Of note: Both sides were more negative about their own finances compared with a year ago. Zoom out: Overall sentiment, which includes Independents, barely moved — ticking up less than one point, per Morning Consult. The opposing partisan shifts appear to have canceled each other out. Reality check: It's early days, and sentiment could shift quickly. Between the lines: Consumer sentiment was once a telling measure of how people would actually spend their money: Good vibes meant more spending. Lately, it's looked more like a political measure. "Sentiment matters because it's vibes," says Eli Yokley, a U.S. politics analyst at Morning Consult.

events.title: Alex Karp Said He’s a ‘Progressive.’ OK! Here’s Some Other Stuff He’s Said Recently
events.summary: When Palantir chief executive Alex Karp sat down with Politico this week, he reportedly used the word “progressive” eight times to describe both his political philosophy and his company . “I’ve been a Democrat my whole life,” Karp told Politico, which noted that he called the Democratic Party “ totally irresponsible ” in the distant time of October 2025. “I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.” This isn’t the first time Karp has called himself a progressive. In 2018, The New York Times reported that Karp described himself as such. In the same article, he claimed to have voted for Hillary Clinton. Karp has also donated money to Democratic candidates. In 2023, for instance, he donated $360,000 to a joint fundraising committee for Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. The next year, he donated $1 million to MAGA, Inc. Palantir has a share of supporters from the Democratic party. However, it’s not necessarily clear how the products of Palantir—a company that built the technology that underpins much of the Trump administration's brutal arrest and deportation campaign, sold tools to the US military that can use generative AI to help plan and execute drone strikes, and partnered with the Israeli military to assist in its devastating war on the Gaza strip, among other things—could reasonably be seen as progressive. It’s instructive, then, to look at what else Karp has said in recent weeks, and how it lines up with his idea of what’s “progressive.” In his most recent quarterly letter to Palantir shareholders, Karp actually doubled down on his basic premise. In it, he argued that Palantir employees are “the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement.” “We are all, in no uncertain terms, living through what John Lewis Gaddis, the professor of naval and military history at Yale, presciently described decades ago as the long peace ,” Karp wrote, despite the fact that the US and Iran are currently engaged in direct warfare. During Palantir’s corresponding earnings call on November 2, Karp was asked to clarify the statements in his letter. “Our products are built to avoid war, meaning the adversary knows that they will have such pain inflicted upon them that in fact it's not worth going to war,” Karp said. He did not, however, address the relevant possibility that the US is the party that initiates war. “I grew up as a lefty,” Karp continued. “I don't actually like war. I want to avoid war. I don't support wars.” But he said, “Sometimes they are necessary, and when they are necessary, America and its allies need the very, very, very best tools.” Karp went on to say that Palantir has both a “moral imperative” and a “mission reason” for having the “somewhat crazy aspiration” of dominating its market. That mission, Karp said, is supporting the war fighter. Conveniently, it’s also very profitable. “We are delighted that we can support the war fighter even more because we're making so much money,” Karp said. Karp’s recent comments in Politico could also be seen through the lens of convenience. Democrats will have a majority in both chambers of Congress next year, and since about half of Palantir’s revenue comes from government work, it’s pragmatic to sow goodwill. Palantir has seen continued success, after all, across Democratic and Republican administrations. However, Karp doesn’t care about cultivating favor with everybody. He pointedly excludes anyone who has criticized Palantir in what he calls “ridiculously stupid and malicious, incredibly hard to understand attacks.” (Karp didn’t name examples, although many critiques of Palantir have come from the American left.) “What motivates me is helping to make sure we are fighting for you,” Karp said, addressing Palantir investors, “and quite frankly, making sure that the people that made fun of you and made fun of us are suffering.” In your inbox: Inside WIRED’s newsroom with Katie Drummond They war-gamed dimming the sun —it went worse than you think The Big Interview: Nathan Fielder tells us everything Live tracker: Elon Musk’s America PAC is spending big on the midterms Introducing the app: More ways to make the most of WIRED © 2026 Condé Nast. events.title: Murders plunge 17% in America's biggest cities
events.summary: Data: Major Cities Chiefs Association (MCCA) ; Note: Tulsa Police changed crime-reporting systems, which may affect year-over-year comparisons.; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios Homicides fell 17.3% across major U.S. police jurisdictions through the first nine months of 2026, extending a retreat from pandemic-era violence that began under President Biden and continues under President Trump . The big picture: A new Major Cities Chiefs Association report found declines in all four major violent-crime categories among 66 reporting U.S. large law enforcement agencies from January through September, compared with the same period last year. Homicides dropped 17.3%. Robberies fell 13.3%. Rapes declined 3.8%. Aggravated assaults decreased 4%. State of play: Combined, the four categories fell 6.3% — or 17,940 fewer reported offenses, an Axios analysis found. Fifty-two of the 66 agencies reported overall declines. Homicides dropped in 50 jurisdictions, increased in 14 and remained unchanged in two. Zoom in: Some of the nation's largest cities recorded striking homicide declines. Memphis: Homicides plunged 36.5%, from 156 to 99. San Antonio was down 36.5%, Indianapolis down 33.6%, Philadelphia down 21.2%, Aurora, Colorado down 65.2% and Newark, New Jersey down 59.1%. The intrigue: New York City, the nation's largest city, also recorded declines across all four violent-crime categories, according to the updated MCCA figures. Homicides fell 19.7%, from 239 to 192, while robberies dropped 12.5%, from 11,413 to 9,990. Rapes declined 1.5% and aggravated assaults fell 1.9%. Taken together, the four categories fell 4.9% — or 2,059 fewer reported violent crimes. Yes, but: The declines weren't universal. San Diego reported 45.2% more homicides, while Las Vegas recorded a 23.4% increase. Washington, D.C., saw homicides fall 29.9%, but robberies surged 41.1%, pushing its combined violent-crime total up 9.7%. Between the lines: The decline spans presidential administrations. The Council on Criminal Justice dates the homicide turnaround to the second half of 2022, underscoring that falling crime predates Trump's return to office. The caveat: The figures remain preliminary. Houston reported no data because of a records-system transition, and Tulsa recently switched crime-reporting systems, complicating year-over-year comparisons. MCCA corrected its New York City figures on Nov. 12, resulting in revised national totals. This story was corrected after the Major Cities Chiefs Association updated its statistics to show a decrease (not an increase) in all four major violent-crime categories in New York City during the first nine months of 2026. Nationally, homicides declined 17.3% (not 15.2%) and the combined violent-crime declined 6.3% (not 4.9%).

events.title: Orbit Global Menu: A working global menu addon for GNOME
events.summary: A new extension brings a working global menu bar to the GNOME desktop, even for some apps that don’t have menu bars at all. Orbit Global Menu is a new GNOME extension that gives the GNOME desktop a feature it was intentionally designed without, and one that some users miss very badly – this vulture being one of them. It adds a working global menu bar to the GNOME top panel. We suspect this is something that will cause strongly contrasting opinions among many GNOME users: some will by puzzled why anyone would bother, while others may think "at last!" and rush to try it. There have been other attempts to do this before, and the Reg FOSS desk has tried several of them, but we never found one that worked with the majority of applications. Our fondness for this UI feature was visible in the two-part series we wrote in September on how to customize Xfce and then in part two how to get the global menu working with more apps. The problem is getting worse over time, as in recent versions (since GNOME 40 and Gtk4), the GNOME human-interface guidelines encourage smartphone-style hamburger menus, replacing the traditional horizontal menu bar. It is tricky to add global menu bar support to apps that lack a menu bar, but Orbit's developer "Unmade" found a rather labor-intensive solution. The menu bar applet contains maps of keyboard controls for 292 different apps, so it can show a menu all on its own and then send those apps simulated keystrokes to operate it. It's not the programs' full menu trees, just a subset of them, but it works. It's also not the most elegant solution, but it is a solution and it works. We tried it on Ubuntu 26.10 and every app in the full install worked to at least some extent. If you are willing and able to build and install a small additional connector, it lets the global-menu applet talk to lots more applications. The GNOME shell is unusual among open source desktop environments, to an extent that we have criticized before. GNOME Shell was designed with a distinctive look and feel of its own, unlike almost all other desktops. It has a minimalist, stripped-down layout that doesn't look or work quite like anything else, and it's intentionally not very customizable. To change how GNOME works means writing new Javascript code, then packaging it as an extension that users can install from the GNOME Extensions website. This requires both a browser extension and a "native host messaging" connector to be installed into the underlying OS – or a purpose-written app. By default, the desktop comes with neither. The end result is that GNOME lends a visual identity to the Linux desktop, one that is clear and distinct from either Windows or macOS. (Back in 2013, this vulture argued that when Microsoft threatened to sue multiple Linux vendors over infringing Windows UI patents, some 20 years ago, this UI fragmentation was just what the company wanted .) GNOME 2 was the Linux world's default desktop. GNOME Shell was controversial in its early days, and lost pole position, but it has since won it back. Today, GNOME is the default desktop on all the major distros: Ubuntu, Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the RHELatives, as well as Debian and SUSE, all default to GNOME. GNOME does away with a lot of features that are significant functional parts of other graphical desktops. For instance, it has no desktop icons, no system tray or defined place for status indicators, and neither GNOME nor GNOME-compliant applications have menu bars, either inside windows (Microsoft style) or in the top panel (Apple macOS style). This is disorienting and confusing for those used to controlling software mainly using their menus – but now, that's mainly older hands. This design suits those who grew up on smartphones and tablets, or who feel more comfortable with their stripped-back keyboardless UI than a full desktop WIMP, which can be overwhelming to newbies and non-techies. If you've followed the evolution of graphical desktops for some 40 years, as this gray-plumed vulture has, some trends are very apparent that aren't so clear if you came in once evolution was underway. Apple introduced the first global menu bar in the Lisa, and improved on that in the Macintosh. DR GEM copied it very early on , but Apple sued and DR changed the PC version of GEM to be less Mac-like. Microsoft's Windows came along after this, and moved menu bars inside windows instead. When Apple acquired NeXT in 1996 , it moved NeXTstep's patent-avoidant vertical menus back to a global bar at the top, along with the clock and some status indicators. There they remain, 30 years later. In 2007, it launched the iPhone, containing a very cut-down OS based on OS X, replacing the Finder with a cut-down version of the Dashboard layer from OS X 10.4 . The panel remained, shorn of its menus, which were too fiddly for a small screen. As The Register mentioned in 2017 , in its preliminary releases, Android started out as a keypad-driven Java phone that looked and worked very much like BlackBerry. When the iPhone appeared, Google changed course . The new Android UI resembled iOS, complete with that top panel, still without menus. GNOME 3.0 was not far behind: in 2009 the team promised a revamp of the user experience, and in 2011, launched GNOME 3.0. It too has the fixed top panel — now huge on a laptop or desktop landscape screen – and mostly empty. Now that top panel regains its original 1983 function. We're rather impressed by the Orbit global menu. It does the job, and it even works with apps that don't have menu bars. It's not perfect: for instance, over-long menus have to scroll, and may fail to do so if new submenus appear. The GitHub repository has extensive instructions, including how to build and install the optional connector module that lets more apps export their real menus to the extension. It also tells you how to instruct some apps, notably Firefox, that there is a global menu for it to use. We are saddened to note that, as is so often the case, Wayland gets in the way here. It works rather well with some other extensions, too. With a menu bar, GNOME's strangely centered clock seems out of place, but several extensions, such as F rippery Move Clock , shove it over to the right where we still feel it belongs. If you prefer a lighter-colored panel and dock, it also plays nicely with Blur my Shell . ®

events.title: FCA proposes greater pension investment flexibility to support long-term value for savers
events.summary: Workplace pension providers could have greater flexibility to invest for the long term under proposals from the FCA, helping them deliver better outcomes for savers while ensuring savers' interests remain protected. The FCA is consulting on excluding certain performance-linked fees from the charge cap for default funds in workplace pensions it regulates.Performance-linked fees are common in private markets, including private equity, venture capital and private credit. The proposed change would give providers greater flexibility to access a broader range of investments where this could help improve long-term returns and value for savers.The FCA is clear that greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Providers should carefully weigh potential returns, risks and costs when making investment decisions, and any higher charges should be justified by the additional value delivered to savers.Alongside the proposed flexibility, the FCA is proposing safeguards covering transparency, fair allocation of fees between savers and scrutiny of how private assets are valued. Providers and Independent Governance Committees would need access to the information necessary to assess whether performance-linked fees offer value for money.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market integrity at the FCA, said: 'People's pension savings should work hard for them. We want providers to have greater choice over how they invest for the long term where this can deliver better outcomes for savers.'But greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Any higher charges must be justified by additional value, with firms carefully weighing returns, risks and costs when deciding what is in savers' best interests.'The proposals would bring FCA rules more closely into line with the regime for trust-based pension schemes, where certain performance-linked fees have been excluded from the charge cap since 2023.Greater alignment would support competition and choice and reduce unnecessary complexity for providers operating across both parts of the market.The proposals would give providers an option, not an obligation, to use the exemption. Providers should do so only where it is in savers' interests, and they can meet the relevant protections.The FCA is seeking responses by 14 January 2027 and currently expects to make final rules in summer 2027 following consideration of feedback.Notes to editorsThe consultation is open until Thursday 14 January 2027. Read CP26/40: Exempting performance fees from the workplace pensions charge cap.This work is a priority under the FCA's Pensions Regulatory Priorities (PDF) and forms part of the wider pensions reform.In 2023, the Government changed the rules so certain performance fees sit outside the limit on charges, with protections for members. The proposals build on changes made for trust-based schemes in 2023, while reflecting developments in private markets and strengthening protections in areas such as how investments are valued.The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA .

events.title: More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
events.summary: The Department of Homeland Security says it’s not detaining Americans.  In written statements, it has said that “allegations that ICE is arresting and deporting U.S. citizens is FALSE.” It has said that “when individuals are briefly questioned under ‘reasonable suspicion’ and are found to be U.S. citizens, they are immediately released.” And it has said that “U.S. citizen agitators are only held while they actively remain a safety threat to our officers and the public.” But ProPublica has identified more than 500 citizens detained since President Donald Trump returned to office. They are not just numbers.  Among them is an elderly car wash owner whom agents repeatedly knocked to the ground as they detained several of his workers. A 6-year-old whose mother says still has nightmares after agents pointed guns at him and his siblings. A high school senior who was detained after she tried to stop officers from questioning her autistic younger brother. A dad who was held for several days and missed his daughter’s third birthday.  Over the past year, several of these people shared the lingering effects of what happened to them with ProPublica. Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan In their own neighborhood Photographed at their home in a Boston suburb “We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held.” Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan In September 2025, Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan learned that ICE agents had intercepted members of her family as they drove one of her uncles to a court hearing. Ramirez Sanan, then 17, said she rushed to the scene and discovered agents had broken the car windows and pulled her two uncles, her mother and her younger brother out. Video of the incident showed agents kicking and slamming Ramirez Sanan’s mother to the ground and then twisting her arms to handcuff her. Ramirez Sanan said she saw other agents questioning her brother against a fence, threatening to arrest him if he couldn’t prove he had legal status. Both she and her brother are citizens. “Him being a 13-year-old with autism, he doesn’t understand these things like we do. He didn’t know what ‘a legal status’ is. He’s not able to tell them: ‘Yes, I have a legal status. I’m born here,’” Ramirez Sanan said. She said that when she rushed toward her mom and brother, begging agents to let them go, they detained her. “It was really scary thinking that they might have taken us and deported us to Guatemala, where we don’t have anything.” DHS said that its agents intercepted the car in order to detain the uncle who was going to court that day, and that they “used the appropriate force necessary.” He was facing charges of sexual assault on a child and remains in ICE custody. He has pleaded not guilty.  As for Ramirez Sanan, her mother and her brother, they were released the day of the incident. Her mother, who has lived in the United States for 20 years and has a green card, was treated at a hospital for a concussion, bruising and nerve damage in one of her arms.  DHS denies that they were ever detained. “We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held,” said Ramirez Sanan, who struggled with anxiety and depression after the incident. “I lost my whole senior year fighting this. My brother isn’t the same either.” Andrea Velez On her way to work Photographed in Los Angeles In June 2025, Andrea Velez was dropped off at work at a shoe company in downtown Los Angeles and inadvertently walked into an immigration raid on street vendors. She said one of the masked agents rushed toward her, grabbed her and slammed her to the pavement. Velez said she attempted to shield herself with her work bag.  “Throughout the whole time, I kept saying I was a U.S. citizen,” Velez recalled, saying that agents called her an “alleged U.S. citizen” even after they checked her ID. “They kept saying how many ‘bodies they got’ that day.” Velez said that she was detained for two days, and that she was denied an opportunity to call family or a lawyer for most of that time. The government charged Velez with assault. DHS said she “made physical contact” with agents and tried to impede them. A judge ultimately dismissed the case.  After her arrest, Velez said she was so afraid of being detained again that she worked remotely and avoided going outside. Williams said that agents began confronting students and staff. At some point during the commotion, he said, the agents threw him to the ground and choked him so hard he couldn’t breathe. “They didn’t even know what they were doing — just kind of being reckless [with] assault rifles out and pepper-spraying staff after they took me down,” Williams recalled.  Agents drove Williams to the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building, where they detained him for several hours. Later, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi published his photo on her social media accounts, describing him as a “Minnesota rioter.” Federal authorities issued a warrant for his arrest for assaulting officers. The charges against him were eventually dismissed, and he’s filed a claim against the government for damages over his arrest.  Williams said he’s still haunted by the idea that he came close to meeting the same fates as Good and George Floyd, who was killed by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020. “I didn’t leave the house for at least up to a week,” he said. “I felt lucky to be alive.” Anabel Romero, John Carter, Juana Rodriguez and their children Attending a horse race In October 2025, some 200 federal agents and local police officers in armored vehicles, a helicopter and on horseback conducted a raid on a racetrack in Wilder, Idaho, and detained hundreds of people, including dozens of children . Among them ProPublica identified at least 30 U.S. citizens. Photographed at a park in Meridian, Idaho Anabel Romero had left her kids eating in the car while she went to look at the horses. They were on opposite sides of the track when the raid began.  Romero said the agents wore camouflage and had their guns drawn. She had no idea who they were. So she ran and tried to hide. “They didn’t identify themselves,” Romero said. “I didn’t know who they were.”  She said unidentified officers tackled her, zip-tied her and threatened to “fucking blow your head off.” On the other side of the track, Romero’s 14-year-old daughter, SueHey Tello, said officers surrounded their car, pointing guns at her brother, 6, and sister, 8. events.title: Some Democrats push to keep House’s China committee
events.summary: As House Democrats debate the future of the select committee on China, some in their party are arguing for keeping it around. “If you want to be able to look at the comprehensive issues facing the US-China relationship, there is not a single committee that covers all of it. It’s spread all over. So this puts it in one single committee,” said Rep. Greg Stanton, D-Ariz., who hails from a more centrist wing of the party and sits on the select panel now. Some progressive groups led by Just Foreign Policy are mobilizing to defend it, too, after Semafor reported some lawmakers were lobbying to kill it . A letter from the groups shared with Semafor praises the “different approach” from Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., its current top Democrat. “We believe Democratic leadership now has an important opportunity to build on this progress and demonstrate a more responsible and constructive approach to US-China relations,” it states. There’s a bipartisan push to save the committee as members consult House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries on its future. He told reporters Wednesday the discussions with committee leaders and the caucus on the future of the China select panel and a proposed AI select committee were “ongoing.” Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat, who favors folding the select panel under his committee, has been pushing to make it a “special” committee under House Foreign Affairs, a person familiar with the talks said. That would mean it would resemble a Foreign Affairs subcommittee that off-committee members could still join. Republicans made a similar move last Congress, putting a committee on the “Weaponization of the Federal Government” under the Judiciary Committee rather than standing up a separate panel. “We will follow the lead of the incoming speaker on how he wants to handle the China select committee, but the Foreign Affairs Committee is well poised to conduct oversight of this administration’s China policy,” a spokesperson for Meeks said.

events.title: Some Democrats want to pump the brakes on Hegseth impeachment
events.summary: Some top Democrats want to pump the brakes on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth next year after this week’s attempt came up short. “We have a very difficult set of decisions to make and I don’t think we should hastily make them,” said Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the top Armed Services Democrat. He worries the party could get stuck in internecine conflict after a sizable number of Democratic absences on the impeachment procedural vote caused hand-wringing this week, which could take attention away from cost-of-living issues that powered their midterm gains. “Strategically and tactically, what’s going to best advance our agenda? And I worry that what you saw yesterday is a preview of one of our biggest challenges,” Smith added. With plenty in the caucus pushing for a Hegseth impeachment, though, another lawmaker could force a vote next Congress — whether Democratic leaders want it or not. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark told Democrats in a closed-door meeting Wednesday morning that the party had disappointed the American people by not having all of the members there for the impeachment vote, and that it was their job to show up for the people who sent them there, according to people familiar with her comments. Still, Democrats, including Clark, note that they likely couldn’t have won the vote, given the lack of GOP defections beyond Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who introduced the resolution. Nearly a dozen Democrats missed the vote Tuesday referring the impeachment articles to the Judiciary Committee, with Democratic lawmakers blaming traffic and scheduling conflicts , among other issues. Looking ahead to the next Congress, top Democrats plan to conduct investigations into Hegseth on their own terms, rather than letting their hand be forced early. “I think we should do oversight and investigations under our own timetable, not Tom Massie’s,” said Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., the top Intelligence Committee Democrat. “And I’d really like to see affordability stay at the center of the agenda.” Still, others wanted to keep impeachment in mind. “Everything’s on the table there. I don’t think there’s a single Democrat or a lot of Republicans that think that Hegseth is qualified for the job and has done the job well,” said Rep. Greg Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Foreign Affairs Committee Democrat.
