events.title: Introduction To FP8 Formats: Part 1
events.summary: The industry is moving from high-precision formats (FP32, FP16, BF16) to lower-precision data types for Machine Learning (ML) inference and training. In cloud and data center environments, lower-precision data types deliver higher throughput by packing more compute per cycle from the same platform. On edge and mobile devices, smaller formats reduce model size, memory footprint and bandwidth, which directly affects power consumption and latency. Arm, Intel, and NVIDIA published an OCP 8-bit Floating Point Specification (OFP8). It is an interchange format that allows software systems to share the models easily. FP8 is not a future concept, it is being deployed today. It is already supported by NVIDIA’s Hopper H100 GPU, with software deployment appearing in major ML frameworks. Arm added the FP8 support to the Arm v9 ISA and is exploring the best way to integrate the FP8 across all the ML platforms. This blog post explains the FP8 data formats, the new Floating-point Mode Register (FPMR), and the instruction set that makes FP8 practical on Arm CPUs. FP8 data format Unlike IEEE FP64, FP32, and FP16, FP8 is not a single format, it is a family. The whitepaper FP8 Formats for Deep Learning proposes an FP8 format consisting of two encodings: E4M3 and E5M2. Why a family of formats? With only 8 bits available, FP8 makes a trade-off between precision and dynamic range. A single encoding cannot fit all tensors equally well. Activations and weights usually have a smaller and more stable value distribution after training or calibration. They can therefore benefit from more mantissa bits, which help represent nearby values more precisely. Gradients can change much more during forward and backward passes. They can therefore benefit from more exponent bits and a larger dynamic range, which helps avoid overflow or underflow. The two encodings enable software to choose the right format for each tensor role. Use E4M3 when precision is more important and use E5M2 when dynamic range is more important. This is the key idea from FP8, and Arm reflects the same idea in the FPMR register. With FPMR, each source operand can independently select which FP8 format it uses. Supported data types E4M3 E5M2 Exponent bits 4 5 Mantissa bits 3 2 Bias 7 15 Max normal value 448 57344 Special values NaN only Inf and NaN E4M3 uses 1 sign bit, 4 exponent bits, and 3 mantissa bits, with a bias of 7. E4M3 uses most bit patterns for normal finite numbers instead of saving many of them for special values. This helps E4M3 extend dynamic range, which is more useful for deep learning workloads. E5M2 uses 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, and 2 mantissa bits, with a bias of 15. E5M2 follows IEEE 754 conventions for the exponent field and special values, including infinities and NaNs. Because of this, it can be viewed as IEEE FP16 with fewer mantissa bits, like how bfloat16 and TF32 can be viewed as IEEE FP32 with fewer bits. This makes conversion between E5M2 and IEEE FP16 straightforward, while still providing a wider dynamic range than E4M3 FPMR: The Floating-Point Mode Register When hardware executes an FP8 instruction, it must know the format of each source operand, the format of the destination result, and the scale factors to apply. Because FP8 modes can change per tensor, software may need to update the format and scaling settings frequently inside performance-critical code. For this reason, Arm introduced a dedicated control register – FPMR. FPMR is separate from FPCR. Hardware can recognize and rename FPMR writes more efficiently, making per-tensor FP8 mode changes closer to a normal register write rather than a pipeline-serializing control update. FPMR contains the following fields: Field Bits Description F8S1 [2:0] Format of 1st FP8 source. 0b000 = E5M2, 0b001 = E4M3. F8S2 [5:3] Format of 2nd FP8 source. Same encoding as F8S1. F8D [8:6] Destination result Format for instructions that convert other floating-point formats to FP8. Same encoding as F8S1. OSM [14] Overflow Saturation for FP8 multiplication instructions. OSC [15] Overflow Saturation for FP8 convert instructions. LSCALE [22:16] Unsigned Log2 down-scaling factor. Result × 2^(−LSCALE). NSCALE [31:24] Unsigned Log2 up-scaling factor for widening FP8 sources. LSCALE2 [37:32] Second down-scaling value for dual-source convert instructions. FP8 instruction set on Arm The 2023 and 2024 architecture extensions add FP8 instructions across Advanced SIMD, SVE and SME. The following table summarizes the architectural features and the instructions they provide. Architectural features Supported category Instructions Description FEAT_FP8 Advanced SIMD/SVE/SME FCVTN, FCVT, F1CVT, F2CVT, BF1CVT, BF2CVT, FSCALE FP8 convert instructions; a floating-point scale instruction. FEAT_FP8FMA Advanced SIMD/SVE FMLALB, FMLALT, FMLALLBB, FMLALLBT, FMLALLTB, FMLALLTT FP8 widening multiply-accumulate. FEAT_FP8DOT4 Advanced SIMD/SVE FDOT (.S) FP8 → FP32 4-way dot product. FEAT_FP8DOT2 Advanced SIMD/SVE FDOT (.H) FP8 → FP16 2-way dot product. FEAT_SSVE_FP8FMA SME FMLALB, FMLALT, FMLALLBB, FMLALLTT FP8 widening multiply-accumulate in Streaming SVE mode. FEAT_SSVE_FP8DOT4 SME FDOT (.S) FP8 → FP32 4-way dot product and accumulate in Streaming SVE mode. FEAT_SSVE_FP8DOT2 SME FDOT (.H) FP8 → FP16 2-way dot product and accumulate in Streaming SVE mode. FEAT_SME_F8F32 SME FMOPA, FDOT, FVDOTB, FVDOTT, FMLALL FP8 outer product and accumulate into FP32 ZA tile; FP8 dot product and accumulate into FP32 ZA array; FP8 widening multiply-accumulate into FP32 ZA array; FEAT_SME_F8F16 SME FMOPA, FDOT, FVDOT, FMLAL FP8 outer product and accumulate into FP16 ZA tile; FP8 dot product and accumulate into FP16 ZA array; FP8 widening multiply-accumulate into FP16 ZA array. FEAT_F8F32MM Advanced SIMD/SVE FMMLA FP8 matrix multiply-accumulate to FP32 FEAT_F8F16MM Advanced SIMD/SVE FMMLA FP8 matrix multiply-accumulate to FP16 All FP8 compute instructions read the source format from FPMR (F8S1/F8S2) and apply scaling via LSCALE/NSCALE. These widening instructions always use FP8 data as the input format. Accumulation uses a wider type, such as FP16 or FP32. This keeps the bandwidth advantage of FP8 inputs while preserving numerical stability during accumulation. Further reading For more detailed information about FP8, see the Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile architecture and the FP8 Formats for Deep Learning paper . Part 2 will explore FP8 instructions, from conversion and scaling to dot products, matrix multiplication, and outer products in Advanced SIMD, SVE, and SME. events.title: AWS distills its cloud into a local emulator that runs on your PC
events.summary: AWS has released an emulator that kind-of-almost lets you use its cloud on a PC. As explained in the GitHub repository for the prosaically named “AWS Emulator,” the tool “is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint.” The emulator doesn’t replicate the whole AWS cloud, instead offering its APIs. “You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI),” the repo explains. Because those tests never touch the AWS cloud, the tool is free to use. AWS wrote the emulator in Rust, a choice that senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib wrote helps to ensure the tool “stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop.” The emulator tool doesn’t replicate the entire AWS cloud. Abib said it supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub . The Register found over 1,300 items on that page. While the tool lets developers test APIs, it doesn’t replicate anywhere near all the features of the Amazonian cloud. “It doesn’t evaluate IAM [Identity and Access Management] policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior,” Abib wrote, adding “How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature.” AWS publishes “fidelity scores” that detail how closely the emulator works on different AWS services. Amazon tries to achieve full fidelity, so the emulator produces the same results as AWS for valid API calls, and the same errors for invalid ones. Coding agents can also drive the Emulator, an option The Register mentions because AWS advises the easiest way to check if a project will work with the tool is to use the aws-emulator skill for AI coding agents. “With the skill, your agent finds the AWS operations and resources that your project depends on. It checks them against the fidelity tests and fidelity scores for the emulator. It then tells you which parts of your project you can rely on the emulator for, and which ones might behave differently from AWS,” according to AWS documentation. AWS has made the emulator available as an RPM or Debian package. Mac and PC users will need to run Docker and an image of the Emulator. “You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint,” Abib instructed. “When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ . You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.” “From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment.” The cloud colossus’s intent appears, as ever, to encourage more use of its cloud – in this case by satisfying developers their code will run well when deployed there, and making it easy for them to test for that. ®

events.title: Jensen Huang faces second affair claim as Nvidia board considers his future
events.summary: BREAKING: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia chief executive Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is facing new allegations of a second affair, this time with a senior executive at the chipmaker, as the company's board meets to decide whether he should keep his job. The New York Times has reported that Mr Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care and one of his about 60 direct reports, quoting five people who have worked at the company. Ms Powell has been with Nvidia for more than 18 years. Nvidia has declined to comment on the allegation and has not said whether its board inquiry, launched on Sunday into Mr Huang's relationship with Alice Huang and led by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, will be widened to cover it. The company's code of conduct addresses conflicts arising from personal relationships and requires reported misconduct to be investigated. The allegation came days after Mr Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife , following reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman whom US investigators accuse of spying for China. Nvidia's board opened an inquiry into whether he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation, while expressing confidence in his leadership. China has called the allegations “entirely groundless”. The Wall Street Journal reported late on Wednesday that the board was preparing to oust Mr Huang. Directors have also hired an outside firm to identify possible replacements, according to reports. Under Nvidia's bylaws, a majority of its 11 directors, all of whom, except Mr Huang, are independent, can remove the chief executive “with or without cause”. Nvidia shares, which closed 2.9 per cent higher at $173.73 on Wednesday, fell more than 8 per cent in after-hours trading . The fallout extends well beyond the boardroom. Nvidia's chips underpin the global AI build-out, from US technology giants to sovereign projects in the Gulf, and the scandal has emboldened lawmakers seeking tighter controls on where those chips can be sold. Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives has estimated the company's value at $300 a share with Mr Huang as chief executive and $225 without him. Mr Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has no obvious successor. Analysts have suggested chief financial officer Colette Kress as a possible interim leader. Pressure is also building in Washington as House Republicans are pushing for Mr Huang to testify and have raised the possibility of a subpoena. Legislators from both parties are calling for tighter curbs on chip exports to China. US President Donald Trump has called Mr Huang “an honourable guy”. Mr Huang remains listed as the keynote speaker at Nvidia's GTC event in Washington from December 1 to 3.

events.title: Disgraced former CA eMudhra blames buggy script for hopelessly weak certificates
events.summary: Former certification authority eMudhra has claimed a buggy Python script is the main reason it issued laughably insecure digital certificates. The company posted its account of the matter on Bugzilla where a user with the handle “Naveen Kumar ML” wrote “During a single key‑generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, sixteen subordinate (issuing) CA key pairs in eMudhra’s ‘B’ and ‘C’ series were generated correctly on a hardware security module and then processed through an approved wrap/unwrap round‑trip using a custom python key‑handling script.” eMudhra aimed to create eight ECDSA P-384 private keys which should have been 48 bytes long. But the script contained what Kumar described as “a bug/defect in the import code [which] resulted in a read‑back from the unwrapped object that truncated the private value, so the certified public keys correspond to private scalars below the expected range and are recoverable from public information.” The truncation is the key problem here, because it appears that eMudhra ignored 47 of the 48 bytes, producing its infamously insecure single-byte keys such as the number four. Whatever the nature of the bug, Kumar asserts it was “a custom script run only on an isolated ceremony host and was not a function of the emCA software.” eMudhra needed that script because “global supply chain constraints” meant it couldn’t acquire the hardware security modules (HSMs), devices that generate and store cryptographic keys, that it wanted to use when creating a set of certificates for use in the USA. It therefore used HSMs made by a company called Utimaco to generate keys and planned to transfer the keys it produced to a different set of HSMs from a company called Crypto4A. Kumar explained that eMudhra decided on that move, which is unusual, because changes to policy about provenance of certificates meant it had to generate new certs by the end of May. The plan went sour when the company didn’t notice the errors in its script and didn’t test the keys it created. The rest is history: a Mozilla team member noticed that the company’s keys were woefully weak and pointed out that attackers could therefore issue fraudulent certificates that allowed them to impersonate servers, observe traffic, or even modify data in transit. Browser-makers quickly tweaked their software so it would not recognize certs from eMudhra. The Indian business then quit the SSL/TLS certification business, which it said was never a major source of revenue but had suddenly become a severe source of embarrassment. Kumar’s new post lists three steps eMudhra will take to wind up its certification business, one of which will see the company “Put in place improvements motivated by findings of [an] independent review to strengthen our general PKI operations.” Sounds like a plan. ®

events.title: Outgoing Trump foe Massie forces new Epstein files showdown
events.summary: Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) secured the 218 signatures needed to force another House showdown over the Jeffrey Epstein files Wednesday, just one day after fellow Republicans blocked his attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Why it matters: Congress overwhelmingly voted last year to force the release of the Epstein files, but survivors and lawmakers say the Trump administration has still withheld records. The new bill would give them the power to sue the DOJ and help state prosecutors pursue investigations. Driving the news: Massie announced Wednesday afternoon that his discharge petition for the Epstein Files Transparency Act II had reached the required 218 signatures. Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.) provided the final signature Wednesday, according to the House clerk's records . Just four Republicans signed the petition: Massie, Nancy Mace of South Carolina, Ralph Norman of South Carolina and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania. The other 214 signatures came from Democrats. What he's saying: "I'm working closely with @RepJayapal, @RepTeresaLF and @RepRoKhanna to get this to the floor for a vote soon," Massie wrote on X . The other side: The White House didn't answer questions about the bill. In a statement, spokesperson Lauren Bis said President Trump has "been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein. And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House Oversight Committee's subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein's Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein's victims than anyone before him." Speaker Mike Johnson's office did not respond to a request for comment. The intrigue: President Trump helped drive Massie out of Congress by backing a primary challenger, but the Kentucky Republican is using his final weeks in office to challenge the administration on some of its most politically sensitive topics. This latest effort could force Republicans to revisit a scandal that dogged the Trump administration for more than a year, even after Congress overwhelmingly voted to require the release of Epstein's files. This time, Massie wants to give Epstein survivors, state prosecutors and lawmakers the power to sue the Justice Department over records they believe it has unlawfully withheld. Catch up quick: Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) led the original push to force the release of the Epstein files. Their first bill passed the House 427-1 in November 2025 after they secured enough signatures to bypass Speaker Mike Johnson. Trump ultimately signed it into law. The law required DOJ to release its Epstein-related investigative records by Dec. 19, 2025, with limited exceptions to protect victims, ongoing investigations and other sensitive information. The department missed that deadline but announced in January that it had released nearly 3.5 million pages. The controversy: Epstein survivors and lawmakers have accused DOJ of withholding too much information while simultaneously exposing victims through inadequate redactions. A report released Tuesday by the Republican-led House Oversight Committee faulted the Trump administration's handling of the disclosures, including failures to protect victims and excessive redactions concealing alleged co-conspirators. The committee also said its investigation found no evidence implicating Trump in Epstein's crimes. What's next: Massie's petition is expected to become eligible for a floor vote by early December, with more than enough legislative days remaining under the House's current schedule. But passage is not guaranteed, and Senate Republican leaders could still decline to consider the measure before the new Congress takes office in January. Editor's note: This story has been updated to add the White House's comment.

events.title: Russian cloud Yandex says drone attacks on its datacenters caused data loss
events.summary: Russian cloud operator Yandex has admitted to data loss after a drone attack on one of its datacenters. The attack, which Ukrainian press said was ordered by Kyiv, happened in early October and caused a fire and subsequent outage at Yandex’s ru-central1-b availability zone. Subsequent strikes targeted more Yandex datacenters and disrupted more of the company’s cloud and payment services. On Tuesday, Yandex posted an update on its recovery efforts, which it spun as something of a triumph because it restored over 97 percent of customer data. Of course that also means the company lost 2.84 percent of customer data, which it blamed on “critical hardware damage and a lack of backups on the platform.” It’s unclear if Yandex’s use of the phrase “on the platform” indicates it doesn’t keep backups of its own cloud, if whatever resilience techniques it employs don’t create multiple copies of customer data, or if clients didn’t protect their data. Whatever happened, Yandex has decided to enable backups by default for all VMs customers create in its cloud. That decision will mean customers will consume and pay for more Yandex resources, unless they opt out of the automated backups. Given that drones damaged three Yandex locations, and the war with Ukraine continues, users have good reasons to consider alternatives to its services. Indeed, Yandex’s announcement of its recovery efforts links to a page extolling the virtues of a hybrid cloud when devising data protection strategies. That page also mentions Yandex’s own Stackland product, which brings its stack on-prem, as an example of a hybrid approach. On Wednesday the company also launched a new availability zone named ru-central1-f. Yandex didn’t say where it’s located, other than to say it’s in “a new location.” Interestingly, Yandex has imposed quotas that limit the amount of resources users can access in the new availability zone and says it can’t yet handle traffic to private endpoints at the new facility. Many nations have imposed sanctions that restrict sales of technology products to Russia. It’s therefore unsurprising that Yandex might struggle to provision enough infrastructure to allow untrammeled access to a new availability zone. ®

events.title: Scott Colom ousts Cindy Hyde-Smith in historic Mississippi Senate flip
events.summary: Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a stunning Mississippi upset , becoming the first Democrat elected to the state's Senate delegation since 1982, AP projects. Why it matters: Colom's victory marks another extraordinary breakthrough for Democrats in the Deep South, extending the historic blue wave that handed the party control of both chambers of Congress. Colom also becomes Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction. Hiram Rhodes Revels became the nation's first Black senator in 1870. Mississippi's last Black senator, Blanche K. Bruce, served until 1881. Catch up quick: Colom's victory expands Democrats' 55–44 advantage over Republicans in the Senate. Worries of a recount — which requires a court order, as Mississippi has no recount law — seemed moot as Hyde-Smith posted a video message to X shortly after AP called the race, appearing to concede to Colom. "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state," she said. Hyde-Smith also addressed another worry from Mississippi voters following a significant purge of the state's voter rolls, saying that her campaign "has worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election." "I am proud of what we have accomplished together, but I want to make one thing very clear: an election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will," she said. The big picture: Colom's victory followed a late surge of Democratic spending and organizing in a state Trump carried by 23 points in 2024. Hyde-Smith faced warning signs in the campaign's closing months, when Colom raised twice as much as the GOP senator despite her overall cash advantage. She was also outspent on TV advertising , with a flood of ads from left-leaning PACs and super PACs pushing support for Colom and attacking the senator for her vote not to release files related to the convicted human trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. Hyde-Smith's campaign also faced criticism over an interview she gave to WLOX-TV in Biloxi, Mississippi, where she fumbled an answer about the price of beef, saying that Mississippians had "so many other proteins to choose from." Colom's campaign capitalized on her blunder, creating a viral campaign ad urging voters to "choose another senator." The GOP made a late push to help Hyde-Smith, including President Trump speaking at a rally for her in Alcorn County, where he won by 68% in 2024. But it wasn't enough. Hyde-Smith's term will end after eight years. She was appointed to the Senate in 2018 by then-Mississippi Gov. Phil Bryant, and ran for a full term in 2020, where she bested her Democratic challenger Mike Espy by 10 points. Zoom in: Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney from Columbus, campaigned on lowering the cost of living, raising wages and protecting rural hospitals. His campaign also drew in heavy Democratic hitters to stump for him, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock. The bottom line: Colom's win adds Mississippi to a growing list of Republican strongholds where Democrats broke through in the midterms, including Texas and South Carolina. It also reinforces the role of Black voters in the Democratic comeback, after the party rebuilt support among a crucial voting bloc that showed signs of shifting toward Trump in 2024. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated. This story has been corrected to show that Hyde-Smith's interview was conducted in Biloxi (not Jackson, Mississippi).

events.summary: China’s marriage rate fell to its lowest level in almost two decades , adding to worries about the country’s demographic crisis. Data this week showed 4.65 million couples tied the knot from January through September, while 2.08 million couples got divorced. Beijing has in recent years rolled out a series of measures aimed at increasing marriage rates and childbearing. events.title: What it takes to bring an AI research assistant to thousands of medical experts
events.summary: From custom infrastructure to hosted agents What we learned rebuilding Novo’s clinical trials data agent on Microsoft Foundry: a simpler operating model, a stronger session isolation, and a direct path from tracing to evaluation and optimization. Clinical research rarely ends with the questions defined in a trial protocol. Medical experts also explore the data from new angles: testing a hypothesis, comparing patient populations, visualizing a trend, or identifying a promising direction for further research. As part of a forward-deployed engineering engagement, a joint Microsoft and Novo Nordisk development team built an agent that helps medical experts perform this kind of secondary analysis of clinical trial data. We described the original project in a Microsoft customer story . More recently, we reimplemented the solution as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry . The move gave us a simpler operating model, stronger session isolation, and a direct path into Foundry’s tracing, evaluation, experimentation, optimization, and governance capabilities. It also taught us practical lessons about infrastructure planning, observability, and preserving the learning loop that already made the agent better over time. Here’s what changed, what we measured, and what we would recommend to teams making a similar move. An agent for questions that don’t have a fixed workflow Secondary analysis of clinical data is a great task for an agent because the execution path depends heavily on the question. The agent interprets the request, inspects the available data, writes and executes analysis code, examines the result, and often revises its approach before returning a summary and visualization. This isn’t just attaching a chat interface to a single API. The agent needs a reasoning loop, access to domain-specific skills, and tools for working with data. In our implementation, code execution is the central tool. The agent can generate analysis code and visualizations inside a controlled environment while the surrounding application manages the conversation and presents the result to the user. Our first production architecture ran the agent in Azure Container Apps . We used PostgreSQL for conversation storage and Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions for sandboxed code execution. That architecture gave us explicit control over every component, and it proved the value of the use case. It also meant that our team owned much of the platform around the agent: container scaling, session lifecycle, conversation persistence, execution isolation, networking, telemetry, and the integration among them. Foundry hosted agents offered a simpler division of responsibility. Moving the runtime boundary into Foundry A hosted agent is our code, packaged as a container, running on infrastructure managed by Foundry Agent Service . We retain control of the orchestration logic, models, tools, and runtime behavior. Foundry manages the endpoint, agent identity, session compute, state persistence, scaling, and lifecycle around it. At runtime, each session gets its own VM-isolated sandbox. Foundry provisions compute on demand, keeps it active while the session is in use, and de-provisions it after the configured idle period. Session files can persist and be restored when the session resumes. Scaling follows active sessions rather than a replica count that we have to predict and configure. For Novo’s workload, that model aligned well with the unit of work we were building for: one expert conducting one analysis session. It also changed the architecture in four important ways: Scaling became session-native. We no longer needed to connect application-level session creation to a separately scaled pool of execution environments. The platform owns that lifecycle. Isolation became the default unit of execution. Each session runs in a VM-isolated sandbox rather than sharing a process or general-purpose application container with other sessions. That matters when the workload includes model-generated code operating on sensitive clinical data. Network isolation became part of the service architecture. Foundry Agent Service supports private networking, including virtual network integration and private access to dependent Azure resources. This lets us design controls for both ingress and egress around the agent environment. Those controls are especially important for data that must remain inside an approved network boundary. The agent joined a broader development lifecycle. Traces, evaluations, experiments, monitoring, and optimization can now be connected through the same platform. Microsoft Agent 365 integration also provides a path to enterprise inventory, identity, access control, and lifecycle governance. Using Foundry hosted agents didn’tt remove our responsibility for security or quality. We still had to define access controls, minimize and protect telemetry, test the agent for our use case, and review every system it can call. What changed is that several controls we previously assembled ourselves are now platform capabilities we can configure and operate consistently. Here are the top lessons we learned during this project—and some practical advice for your own hosted agents projects in Foundry: Lesson 1: Treat infrastructure choices as product decisions Private networking should be an early architecture decision, not a production hardening task left until the end. Hosted agents consume network capacity according to sessions. The Foundry account, its projects, hosted agents, concurrent sessions, and agent revisions all contribute to IP usage. Because the assigned subnet is an immutable reference at the account level, an undersized range can turn a capacity adjustment into a broader infrastructure migration. Our advice is to estimate peak concurrent sessions across the account, include headroom for deployments and growth, and involve the network team before creating the Foundry resource. The current networking guidance recommends a /24 subnet for production hosted agent deployments and documents /27 as the supported minimum for smaller deployments. We used Azure Verified Modules as the foundation for repeatable environments. That gave us a strong starting point, but infrastructure as code doesn’t remove the need to inspect generated dependencies. Throughput for resources like Azure Cosmos DB should reflect expected concurrency and data access patterns. Where a setting requires an operational adjustment, capture it in the deployment process or operator runbook rather than leaving it as unwritten production knowledge. Subnet sizing, database throughput, private endpoints, DNS, and concurrency aren’t separate infrastructure details. Together, they shape the scale ceiling and reliability of the product. Lesson 2: Make traces easy to navigate Foundry tracing uses OpenTelemetry and stores telemetry in Azure Monitor Application Insights.

events.title: Local media startup City Cast reshuffles leadership
events.summary: The locally-focused media startup City Cast has named Andi McDaniel, the company’s chief creative officer, its new CEO, replacing David Plotz. City Cast launched in 2021 as a local podcast and newsletter venture aimed at serving cities where local news was shifting from old newspapers and radio to screens. The company has since expanded to 13 cities, including Austin, Las Vegas, and Philadelphia, among others. “This next chapter for us is about expanding audiences. It’s about adapting to AI, and it’s about making the business successful,” McDaniel, a veteran public radio executive and co-founder of City Cast , told Semafor. City Cast has gained greater visibility in recent months, primarily for its expansion in its hometown. As Semafor first noted last year, in response to what the company saw as an opportunity created by the turbulence at The Washington Post, City Cast scaled up its newsroom and business in Washington. City Cast is backed by Graham Holdings, which owned the Post before selling to Jeff Bezos. City Cast DC now has 20 people on staff, and said it has found some success attracting a younger audience to its content, tripling the size of people it reaches regularly from roughly 100,000 at the beginning of the year to around 300,000. Not every bet has paid off. The company shuttered two arms, in Boise and Houston. In a telephone interview, Plotz said Houston was too large and sprawling an area to cover with the company’s resources — most cities operate with a staff of just 5 or 6 employees — while he said the company didn’t understand Boise enough when City Cast launched there. The company learned that their podcasts were not a replacement for radio, and that the City Cast model seemed to resonate best within mid-sized cities with concentrated downtowns that orient residents’ perspectives. Plotz said that revenue was up 40% this year, but the company was still not profitable. In the six years since the company’s launch, the company’s founder told Semafor he’d grown to better understand habits in the local media landscape. He noted that many people under the age of 60 largely got their information from social media, neighborhood listservs, local newsletters, and Reddit. “People do not want local news,” Plotz said. “They want to know about things to do in their city. They want to know what’s going on in their city. But if you ask them about local news, they do not express an interest. “Local news as a concept does not really have a lot of valence. It’s more like learning about my city.” He also noted that national media narratives and big political fights were not as animating to local audiences, who seek out information to be connected to their local communities. “The need that people are finding met in local media has almost nothing to do with the highly partisan, cortisol-driven conversations that drive national media and national news media,” he said.

events.title: Scoop: Lutnick stalled curbing Nvidia chip sales to China — again — after Oval Office showdown
events.summary: President Trump on Thursday authorized a crack down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — even consulting Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead. One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Why it matters: This standoff illustrates a breakdown in efforts to keep American technology out of China's hands as the world wonders why the Trump administration has not taken action against the company at the center of suspected chip smuggling — and an espionage scandal. This report was assembled from interviews with six high-level sources who were briefed on or, in some cases, heard the discussions. Inside the room: On Thursday, as the spy scandal rocked the administration, Lutnick met in the Situation Room with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. During the meeting, Bessent confronted Lutnick about why his department has resisted implementing the export controls, particularly on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the spy scandal. The group sided with Bessent. Lutnick appeared to agree, but then muttered under his breath, "I need to check with the president." Friction point: Lutnick's seemingly innocuous comment raised concerns, the sources said, because officials have repeatedly believed the Commerce Department would impose the export controls, only to have nothing happen. "He's stalling it out," said one official, describing how Lutnick had previously met privately with the president to change his mind about the export limit. "This is an ongoing concern with Howard and this issue," said another. This time, one person in the room called his bluff by saying: "Great. Why don't we do it today?" Around 5pm, the group headed to the Oval Office. Trump called tech advisor Elon Musk and agreed to move forward. Musk supported Rubio, Bessent, Greer and Hegseth's case to impose the controls while Lutnick warned it "will start a trade war with China." "Everyone argued back that China is already doing to us what Lutnick warned would happen," a source said. Behind the scenes: With Lutnick the lone holdout, Trump made his decision: "Let's get it done." But once everyone was outside of the Oval Office, Lutnick proposed a new delay tactic. "I'll develop some options and come back," he said. "Everyone was like: 'No, no, the decision's been made. Go fucking execute,'" one source said. "Well, it still hasn't happened." The other side: Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer denied that Bessent confronted Lutnick and would not immediately comment on the other allegations. Flashback: On at least three separate occasions — in May, August, and Nov. 5 — Trump approved taking action against suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China. But Lutnick and Commerce Undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler resisted pressure from Bessent and others to move forward. In May, a highly classified memo warning about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed employee suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese agent, was shared with the president and other officials. In a subsequent meeting, Bessent, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Hegseth and White House officials pressed Lutnick and Kessler to act, the source said, "and they were refusing." Catch up quick: The Trump administration last year announced it would loosen export controls on Nvidia H200 chip sales to China — something Nvidia has lobbied hard for. Trump has taken a more lax approach to export controls on China, agreeing to allow sales of Nvidia's H200 chips, which are older but still powerful, in exchange for a 25% tariff. Long before the affair with Alice Huang, Jensen Huang has pushed for tapping into the Chinese market. The CEO at the center of an AI boom Trump is dead set on winning has largely been successful at convincing Trump and Lutnick that selling less powerful chips to China is good for national security because it prevents China from developing its own alternatives and keeps the adversary dependent on the U.S. The bottom line: While Lutnick oversees the department squarely at the center of export control policy, Trump is the ultimate decider.

events.title: Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
events.summary: The U.S. has asked Russia to submit a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe that includes Russian steps to ease tension with the continent, two sources with knowledge of the matter said. Why it matters: For years, Russia has sought a European security deal that limits NATO expansion and scales back its military presence in Eastern Europe. The U.S. has rejected those demands in the past, but now appears open to them in some form as part of a broader agreement to end the war in Ukraine. But many European governments are deeply suspicious of the administration's approach. State of play: President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday to reiterate the request. They also want Putin to allow European representatives to join the next round of Russia-Ukraine peace talks, a U.S. official said. From Moscow, Kushner and Witkoff are expected to travel to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday night. Catch up quick: The talks on Tuesday and Wednesday were the first time Ukrainian and Russian officials met with U.S. mediators present since February, when they were suspended due to the war in Iran. In recent weeks, Witkoff and Kushner met with both Putin and Zelensky, creating a bit of momentum. Putin agreed to resume peace talks and release U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was detained by Russia in 2022 . Together with first lady Melania Trump and her team, Witkoff and Kushner also brokered a humanitarian ceasefire in the city of Oleshky. Driving the news: The talks in Abu Dhabi started on Tuesday with Witkoff, Kushner and commander of the U.S. European Command Gen. Alexus Grynkewich mediating between the Russians and the Ukrainians. The parties agreed to a prisoner exchange deal that Kushner and Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said could be the biggest since the war began. U.S. and Ukrainian officials said the exact number of prisoners to be released will be decided during meetings with Putin and Zelensky on Thursday. Before and after the talks, the U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams briefed a delegation of senior diplomats from Germany, the U.K., France, Italy, the EU and NATO. Behind the scenes: The meetings between the Russians and the Ukrainians on Tuesday were tense and at times emotional, with both sides airing grievances after nine months of not talking directly, according to a source in the room. Kushner and Witkoff tried to lower the temperature, telling Russian and Ukrainian negotiators that the goal is to end this round of talks with options for the leaders on both sides. Eventually, after each party made its case, the discussion became more constructive, the source said. "We had pretty tough discussions," Kushner said at a press conference after the talks concluded on Wednesday. "The Russians came with strict directives. It was very hard to soften it, but it ended productively," Arakhamia said. Zoom in: The U.S. proposal to secure a deal on a new Europe-Russia security architecture as part of an agreement to end the war in Ukraine was a key focus of the Abu Dhabi talks. Russian negotiators said Putin launched the invasion of Ukraine because then-President Biden did not reply to his 2021 letter laying out his security concerns, two sources with knowledge of the talks said. According to one of the sources, Kushner and Witkoff told the Russians that the world has changed a lot since 2021. They proposed that Russia draft a new proposal that includes its security concerns and demands, but also lays out what "symmetrical steps" it's willing to take to de-escalate and reassure Europe that it will not attack in the future. Kushner and Witkoff also told the Russians that in order to seriously discuss security issues in Europe, they need to agree to allow European representatives to participate in future peace talks. "We told the Russians, they have their desires and fears, but they have to provide different de-escalation and different proposals as well, if they want Europe to be able to receive those proposals in a good way," Kushner said at the press conference. The other side: So far, Russia has been unwilling to allow Europeans to be part of peace talks with Ukraine. "As for the leadership of a number of European countries, they are essentially engaged in a collective deception of the Ukrainian people and contributing to the mass deaths of civilians," Putin adviser Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation, said at a press conference after the talks. "Therefore, I don't understand what can be discussed with them." Still, Medinsky said that Russia wants to reach a broader security deal with Europe as part of an agreement to end the war. "In Ukraine, an abscess has simply burst. The entire body needs to be treated — a Band-Aid won't do the trick," he said. What to watch: The Trump administration wants to negotiate a new Europe-Russia security architecture and a Russia-Ukraine peace deal simultaneously. But the implementation of a security arrangement would only happen after a deal to end the war is reached, according to a source familiar with the White House's thinking. The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said before the talks in Abu Dhabi that Europe will discuss a new security architecture only after the war in Ukraine ends. But two sources with knowledge said European officials who were in Abu Dhabi this week agreed to engage on both tracks simultaneously, while stressing that final decisions on European security architecture would be made only after the war in Ukraine ends. The U.S. hopes giving European representatives a seat at the peace talks will make their governments more willing to discuss and agree on a broader security agreement before the war ends. "Zelensky won't agree to a deal until he knows what happens next regarding security guarantees and Putin wants to know this, too. This is why the security issue is so important," the source said. The source added that the U.S. made it clear to European countries that it would not agree to a security deal with Russia unless Europe and Ukraine are on board. The U.S. also wouldn't give Russia a veto over Europe's security considerations, the source said. The bottom line: Security will be a key issue at a summit of European leaders in Dublin later this week. European diplomats said the idea of a Russia-Europe security arrangement still faces a lot of resistance and unanswered questions.

events.title: Trump administration to pursue public land sales and a decrease in federal ownership
events.summary: President Donald Trump’s administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate.” BILLINGS, Mont. -- President Donald Trump's administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate," according to a new five-year plan presented by the Interior Department. Agency officials said the sale of federal property would allow the government to focus resources on “nationally significant" lands. They offered no details on what lands could be sold, nor the scope or location of potential sales. The proposal drew quick objections from some lawmakers, including Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke of Montana, who was Interior Secretary in Trump's first term. The plan also calls for strategic land transfers and exchanges to support greater energy production, a centerpiece of the administration's pro-fossil fuel policies. It reflects the Trump administration’s view of most public lands as assets to be used, rather than to be set aside for preservation . The Interior Department oversees more than 750,000 square miles (1.9 million square kilometers) of land — an area greater than Texas and California combined — along with vast underground mineral reserves. That puts the agency at the center of a contentious, decades-long debate over whether the government controls too much land. The Associated Press sent emails to Interior officials Wednesday requesting comment and further details. Most public lands are in Western states. In some, the government controls the vast majority of land, protecting it from potential exploitation but also hindering growth. Nevada, for example, is almost 80% under federal control. Interior officials said that under the plan a portion of any land sale proceeds would go back to the buyer for conservation purposes elsewhere. Yet it’s uncertain if Interior Secretary Doug Burgum can achieve the administration’s goals without cooperation from Congress. Zinke’s office said in a statement that he “remains firmly opposed to the sale or transfer of public lands." He will vote against any legislation on the issue if it happens before the lawmaker leaves Congress at the end of this term, the statement said. The ranking member of the Senate Natural Resources Committee also pledged to fight any federal land sales or privatization efforts. Public lands belong in public hands,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich, a New Mexico Democrat. Some Western lawmakers last year sought to sell vast tracts of land in Utah and Nevada, saying that could generate revenue and ease growth pressures in booming cities. Among the proposals, Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee suggested selling more than 2 million acres (8,000 square kilometers) to states or other entities. Those efforts failed amid bipartisan opposition. The plan sets out a road map for the Interior Department's priorities and actions between 2026 and 2030. Future administrations would not be bound by it. events.title: I Saw the Future of Robotics in a Virtual Duck That Chases My Cat
events.summary: Allow me to introduce you to the robot cat butler I’m developing with help from AI. Using OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol , I taught a virtual version of Microduck —a cute robot from Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face—to walk around a room and identify any bengal cats in its vicinity. (The clip above shows the robot waddling toward a target feline; its eye view is shown top right.) I’m still waiting patiently for a physical Microduck— please hurry up and ship it, guys —but simulated behavior is relatively simple, so it should transfer over to the real thing. I plan to have the robot automatically dispense a treat for my pet bengal, Leona, perhaps by bowing its head to release one from a 3D-printed, head-mounted storage chamber. I was able to code and train the virtual robot in just a few hours, which is, quite frankly, incredible. Previously, this kind of thing might have taken me weeks to figure out. It was possible because OpenAI’s latest models are remarkably good at understanding and manipulating 3D representations of the physical world and then translating that into useful code, agentic actions, and robot training. Real roboticists are using the latest models to do some amazing stuff. When OpenAI released Astra this past September, University of California, Berkeley professor Ken Goldberg and his students saw demos that showcased its ability to render 3D images. They wondered if it could help with the simulations required to train different kinds of robots. These simulations need to be incredibly detailed and extremely accurate to ensure that sophisticated behavior—a humanoid that can dance or a robot hand that can grasp—will transfer faithfully to the real world. One member of Goldberg’s lab gave Astra access to an Nvidia tool called Newton , showed it a video clip of a real robot in action, and asked if it could create a simulation of the scene. “What blew us all away was that within an hour it had produced a full 3D simulation with all the parameters set—the position of the camera, the lighting, the background, all the materials,” Goldberg tells me. Astra is also able to automate much of the drudgery involved with training a robot in simulation, Goldberg says, by running experiments and examining the results. This is precisely what I found while training the virtual Microduck. Along with GPT-6 Sol, I used an agentic harness from Nous Research called Hermes and a Nvidia DGX Spark, a personal computer that contains a powerful AI chip. I’ve previously written about using agents and coding models to configure, program, and debug physical robots. Normally, this kind of work requires significant expertise; modern coding models make it a cinch. But OpenAI’s newest model went far beyond just writing code. It used a piece of Nvidia software called Isaac Sim to feed instructions to a model that controlled the virtual robot, watch videos of it in action to assess how well things were working, and suggest tweaks to its training regime. This process allowed me to train the Microduck to walk around without toppling over. I initially tried getting GPT-6 Sol to teach the robot to moonwalk—I fed it a GIF of Michael Jackson sliding across the stage, which it tried to copy—but after hours of effort, it only resulted in a very jaunty backward jog. (The robots don’t have us totally beat quite yet.) Jim Fan, a researcher at Nvidia who has collaborated with Goldberg, says the way AI can now control robots mirrors how software agents function. LLMS can use models trained to control physical actions—visual language action (VLA) models—just as they access different software on a computer. This week, Fan, Goldberg, and others open sourced an agentic framework for robots called Aspire , which allows a robot to discover and use new skills. One example: GPT-6 Astra figured out how to use a pair of robot arms to solve a Rubik’s cube. “It picks it up, tries to twist it, but has the wrong angle,” Fan says. “Then it reasons for a very, very long time, but it eventually is able to solve it because it learns the skills over time.” At the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), held in Austin, Texas, this week, Fan gave a keynote speech in which he talked about the incredible realization that AI models can automate a lot of the work needed to have a robot do sophisticated things. Fan showed off a demo in which Astra was put in control of a robot arm and told to paint a picture of the Golden Gate Bridge. Using some paint and brushes nearby, it duly completed the task . Of course, getting robots to work reliably and efficiently is still extremely difficult, requiring significant engineering expertise. The vision system on my robot duck does not work well enough to be deployed in a real product. Still, the ease and speed of training robots with AI could soon have an enormous impact on manufacturing and e-commerce, and Goldberg says a number of industrial robotics and automation firms have shown an interest in the approach.

events.title: Airwallex’s CEO isn't worried about AI
events.summary: Jack Zhang isn’t worried about AI taking over global finance, but he is concerned about cybersecurity. Zhang co-founded Australian fintech unicorn Airwallex, which allows businesses to make cross-border payments and manage finances in dozens of countries, and is now morphing into an agentic finance company. Zhang joined Future Proof to discuss how his company is using AI to build systems to help companies handle their finances — essentially building an AI-managed CFO office. The company currently relies mainly on ChatGPT and Claude, but Zhang also said it’s looking at developing proprietary models using open-weight solutions. Zhang doesn’t think AI will get so good that it can entirely replace humans, at least not in his field. “The laws still require you to have somebody sign off as auditor, and how the auditor does that sign-off can be assisted by agents,” he said. “I don’t think we can completely get rid of the human in the loop.” What Zhang is “very, very, very, very worried” about is cybersecurity. With news about cyber breaches emerging almost daily, the company is tackling the issue by using behavioral monitoring and hiring experts from the Australian Department of Defence and Palantir, among other strategies. “We’re moving hundreds of billions of dollars today ... We’re constantly paranoid about how good our defense [is] against this type of threat,” he said. — Reed Albergotti

events.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
events.summary: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia. Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June). The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com. Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub . The head of Qilin goes by the handle “ Haise ,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise. The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP , a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44 . Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog]. The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com. Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations. The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk , which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals. IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure. Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket , Verified , and Zloy . Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru . The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru , the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation. Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia. Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521 , recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems. A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number + 79602347275 . Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru . IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites. That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014. More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane. Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful. Further reading: GangExposed , an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helpi

events.title: Scoop: Inside Bessent's Situation Room confrontation with Lutnick over China chip security
events.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over a failure to place Nvidia customer Megaspeed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, sources familiar told Axios. Why it matters: The Commerce Department oversees the export of sensitive U.S. technologies and Lutnick's actions — or lack thereof — are increasingly under scrutiny following revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huan g had an affair with Megaspeed employee and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. Driving the news: At a White House Situation Room meeting on Thursday after the midterm elections, Bessent pressed Lutnick on why Megaspeed had not been added to the Commerce Department's entity list, to which Lutnick responded he would "look into it." Commerce Undersecretary Jeff Kessler also was repeatedly warned about Megaspeed in deputy meetings. But Kessler deferred to Lutnick, saying "That's a decision for the secretary." Sources told Axios that Lutnick has spent the last year "undoing" efforts by other administration officials to hold Megaspeed — a company accused of illegally diverting U.S. chips to China — accountable because of concerns it would escalate the trade war with China. Spokespeople for Treasury couldn't be immediately reached for comment. The other side: The Commerce Department denied the Situation Room confrontation occurred. "This is false. Secretary Bessent and Secretary Lutnick had no such conversation," spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said. Catch up quick: The Commerce Department is increasingly at the center of scrutiny over the broader Trump administration's handling of an intelligence memo overseen by State Department head Marco Rubio. Lutnick was among the officials who received the report in May, ahead of a trip to China, Axios first reported. On Tuesday, the New York Times reported Commerce Undersecretary Kessler abruptly stopped an investigation into Megaspeed after Nvidia intervened. The Financial Times reported the department was delaying efforts to blacklist Megaspeed despite several U.S. government agencies pushing it to do so. Inside the room: White House and intelligence officials have pressed Lutnick and his top advisers to take action against Megaspeed since the fall of 2025, sources tell Axios. But they refused, so Bessent spoke up Thursday. "How come Megaspeed isn't on the entities list?" Bessent asked Lutnick, according to a source briefed on the meeting. Lutnick initially stammered, sources said, and then replied: ""I don't know. I'll look into it." One source, who has extensive experience concerning the chip controversy, said the reply was "bullshit" because Lutnick had resisted action ever since he was personally handed a memo, drafted by National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, that outlined the problems with Megaspeed. The big picture: Nvidia's AI chips provide the computing power needed to develop cutting-edge artificial intelligence, including systems that could transform warfare and cyberattacks. Between the lines: The rivalry between Bessent and Lutnick dates to Trump's transition, when both sought the Treasury secretary job. After Trump chose Bessent, the two clashed over trade policy. Bessent's confrontation comes amid a broader slowdown in Commerce's enforcement of U.S. export restrictions, with national security officials increasingly frustrated by decisions to avoid antagonizing China . Blacklisting a company is an interagency decision, with Commerce leading a committee that includes State, Defense and Energy, and consults Treasury when appropriate. Commerce has not added a single company to its Entity List in more than a year, according to a review of the Federal Register , despite mounting pressure from national security officials. events.title: Nvidia is more than a chip company
events.summary: Reed’s view Nvidia has been battered over the past couple of days, but it could get worse. That is, if founder and CEO Jensen Huang is forced or chooses to step down, or if investigations pin him down for doing something illegal. In most sectors of the economy, CEOs are expected to run businesses well, but they are generally interchangeable parts — albeit expensive ones. Google and Apple show that founder CEOs, which are harder to replicate, can be replaced. But even among founder CEOs, Huang stands apart for bold bets that helped him endure short-term suffering in return for long-term gain. Most people know Nvidia for the climbing stock in their portfolios, or the GPUs on every tech company’s Christmas list. But his creation of the CUDA platform in 2006 is perhaps the best example of how he’s been able to step ahead of the industry for decades. Nvidia’s computing platform and programming model, the software that essentially underpins the modern AI industry, created one of the most valuable moats in business history. A half dozen years later, seeing the progress in neural networks, he pivoted to AI. Huang realized AI would require massive data centers with interconnected chips, and concluded that networking would become the bottleneck. He bet billions on the development of NVLink, a nervous system that allows discrete GPUs to act as one massive supercomputer, and the $6.9 billion acquisition of Mellanox Technologies, the Israeli networking company, in 2019. He funded neoclouds so he wouldn’t be reliant on a few customers and acquired Hugging Face to stay ahead of the game on open source. Huang is 63, and while he has said he could run the company for decades to come, the current investigations raise questions about the future of one of the world’s most consequential companies. Even if he does ride out the turmoil, will he still have the same bold personality that got him here? Nvidia may still mint money, as demand for the company’s products shows no signs of slowing down. But it’s difficult to imagine anyone stepping into the role with the strategic vision and gravitas to match Huang’s. The next handful of years are going to be even trickier. China is ascendant. Once it gains independence on semiconductors, it will be able to scale faster than the US. There won’t be any data-center red tape and China will have abundant energy compared to the US. Because Moore’s law is dead, AI chipmakers are no longer making exponentially better chips every year. Now, they must design entire systems with compute and cooling crammed into server racks like the world’s highest-stakes game of . They involve immensely complex supply chains colored by geopolitics, big personalities, and vast sums of money. Nvidia will be a crucial player in the effort to stay ahead of China. Without Huang, it will be fundamentally weakened. It may be already. Notable Semafor analyzed how Huang’s rhetoric on China has evolved in the past few years.

events.title: Kurdish minister rebuts 'nonsense' claims over Khor Mor gasfield attack
events.summary: A Kurdish minister has dismissed claims that a Kurdish group could have attacked the gasfield at Khor Mor, and warned against speculation while an investigation is under way. Ahmed Mufti, Deputy Minister for Natural Resources of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq , said he had confidence in the investigation launched by Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi in the aftermath of Sunday's attack. “We are open to giving all the related data to the related party for the investigation,” he said, speaking at the foreign affairs think tank Chatham House. Earlier on Wednesday, Basim Al Badri, the head of Iraq’s National Security Department, said the Iraqi government had not ruled out the possibility of an internal attack by feuding Kurdish groups on the facility. “Perhaps a Kurdish party made use of these attacks. We cannot definitely attribute it to a specific faction - it could even be a foreign entity. Therefore the Iraqi government must exercise great precision in handling this important matter,” Mr Al Badri said. Mr Mufti told The National the claims were “nonsense”. “I’m surprised that within 24 hours [of the investigation’s launch] a bold statement like this can be made. I believe this is emotional. Let’s wait for a conclusion,” he told a Chatham House panel. “My advice to all and everyone is to refrain from making any statements right now until the final investigation is out,” he said. Around 10 million people in Iraq were left without electricity and cooking fuel as a result of the attack, according to estimates by Crescent Petroleum, which had operations at the gasfield. The price of electricity more than doubled. Mr Al Badri’s comments come as Iraq's government is struggling to disarm Iran-backed Shiite militias in the country, which have attacked energy facilities in the Gulf in response to the US war in Iran. Oil and gas insiders in Iraqi Kurdistan told The National that Khor Mor oil and gas operators would be able to know which direction the drone came from, with one describing Mr Al Badri’s comments as “really insulting, it’s like saying the sky is green”. Majid Jafar, Crescent Petroleum’s chief executive, said that although it was the 12th attack on the facility, it had been among the worst. “This last one really was a shock, especially at a time when the wider war seems to be de-escalating. We saw significant damage to the production facilities. We’re still assessing the scale. There will be lots of repairs,” Mr Jafar said. But he praised the Iraqi government’s response. “The attack was an attack on the people of Iraq and on Iraq’s sovereignty. We welcome Prime Minister Al Zaidi taking quick action, sending an investigation committee,” he said. Mr Al Zaidi had met oil and gas companies in June, promising to protect the companies and ensure their compensation in case of attack, he said. This was followed up with an official letter from the Iraqi government reiterating those assurances. “This time we hope to see, unlike previous attacks, concrete steps for protection and for identifying and holding accountable the perpetrators,” Mr Jafar said. events.title: US bit barn boom sees energy needs grow 10x as fast as grid capacity
events.summary: Datacenter power consumption in the US is growing roughly ten times faster than grid capacity, meaning facilities may soon need to find a large chunk of their own electricity from other sources. Surging demand for AI infrastructure is driving a wave of new server farms across America, but it is exposing long-term underinvestment in the grid networks required to deliver power where it's needed. Insurance broker Howden calculates that datacenters would need to source up to 58 percent of their power off the grid by 2030 just to keep their share of grid capacity from growing. Gartner warned in June that the energy consumed by AI datacenters is on track to grow 26 percent this year, and grid supply may be unable to keep pace with demand by the end of this decade. Howden's analysis of data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and S&P Global found that since the year 2000, power being fed to data campuses has risen 19 percent a year on average, while the electricity grid expanded capacity by just 2 percent per annum over the same period. Datacenters' share of US grid capacity was circa five percent in 2025, up from 0.1 percent in 2000 – a 50-fold increase. Management consultancy Bain & Company issued a report two years ago warning that energy companies must switch gear and invest in building out grid capacity faster , as energy draw by server farms is expected to more than double by 2030. This doesn't mean that datacenters are in danger of eating all of America's electricity, at least not in the immediate future. The graph makes it appear that the two lines are about to cross, but the chart uses different scales: 1,400 gigawatts on the left axis for grid capacity, versus just 80 on the right for datacenters. Keeping datacenters at five percent of grid capacity requires 110 gigawatts of behind-the-meter capacity by 2030, Howden estimates – an expansion it considers unlikely. Instead, it expects a combination of greater reliance on the grid, slower development at power-constrained sites, and alternative supplies. For the largest, most power-constrained projects, Howden warns that grid delays of two to six years could mean $800 million to $2.4 billion in forgone revenue. "Power availability is becoming one of the defining challenges of the datacenter boom," says Howden head of Natural Resources Stuart Adam. "As demand for AI infrastructure accelerates, developers are increasingly looking beyond traditional grid connections to secure the electricity they need." Howden's business is insurance, and so Adam also notes that on-site generation introduces new operational and financial exposures, as operators take greater responsibility for their power infrastructure. ®
